#1. Gregg Helmich, Building Trades Instructor

Gregg Helmich has spent years building connections with tradespeople and companies around the world, using them to strengthen the building trades program he teaches at North Iowa Area Community College (NIACC).

During high school, Gregg took every shop class that he could. He loved the work, and his teachers made lasting impressions.

“The impact they had on me was exponential, planting seeds of knowledge and taking time to get to know me,” he explains. Gregg knew early on that he wanted to pass that same knowledge and support along.

After traveling with a music ministry for two years after high school, Gregg attended Murray State University for a four-year degree in industrial arts/technology education. He started his career in Kentucky, where he launched a tech ed program for a high school. Eventually, he made the jump to NIACC, where he is now in his 20th year as the building trades instructor.

The curriculum and tools have evolved over the years, but Gregg credits his first Building Science Symposium, about three years ago, with significantly advancing his approach to teaching. Before attending, he figured he could cover only the basics of hands-on carpentry in a one-year course, but the event inspired him to add building science to the curriculum. And that isn’t the only effect it had.

“The Symposium completely changed my approach to networking,” Gregg shares. Although he had been partnering with companies for 25 years to support his teaching programs, the Symposium introduced new contacts and showed him the power of social media.

Those connections have led to new guest instructors, sponsorships, and unexpected opportunities. Huepar, a laser manufacturer in China, discovered Gregg online, invited him to tour their plant, and donated 20 lasers to the school. They also asked him to write them a theme song, which he recorded during his visit.

For Gregg, it’s another example of how sharing what you know can help you build something bigger than yourself.

— Jennifer Morris, editorial assistant. Photo by Brittany Mueller.

#2. Autumn Arrangements Inspired by Nature

Hi GPODers! We’re back in New Jersey today with more fall container design inspiration from garden designers Ellen Goldfarb and Tracy Buttrick.

Yesterday, we saw how Tracy used colorful plants to make the most of limited planting space. Today, we’re looking at three arrangements that take a different approach, using dried flowers and other seasonal materials to bring autumn interest to front entrances and other outdoor spaces. Let’s check it out!

This pot (and a matching one on the other side of the front door) was made for a fall engagement party a few years ago in Ridgewood, New Jersey. Since space was limited because of traffic through the front door, we needed to keep the arrangements on the slender side. We used pampas grass plumes (Cortaderia selloana, Zones 7–11), bittersweet vines, pumpkins-on-a-stick (Solanum aethiopicum, annual), balloon plant seedpods (Gomphocarpus physocarpus, Zones 8–10), a small garden mum (Chrysanthemum × morifolium, Zones 5–9), ornamental cabbage and kale (Brassica oleracea cvs., annual), and ornamental peppers (Capsicum annuum cvs., annual). Because of its airy appearance, it has always been one of my favorites.

This bowl, one of a pair, was designed to sit on top of a column where it could be seen from a large sitting room window. It contains bottle gourds (Lagenaria siceraria, annual), wild rose hips (Rosa multiflora, Zones 3–9), balloon plant seedpods, panicle hydrangea flowers (Hydrangea paniculata, Zones 3–8), and broom corn (Sorghum bicolor, annual).

This pot, one of a pair flanking a grand entrance in Saddle River, New Jersey, was designed for a client who traveled frequently and couldn’t water. For stability, we used a wooden dowel in the middle of the arrangement and wired the stems to it. We began with broom corn, northern sea oats (Chasmanthium latifolium, Zones 3–8), dried eucalyptus (Eucalyptus cvs., Zones 8–11), drumstick flowers (Craspedia globosa, annual), foxtail millet (Setaria italica, annual), red brunia (Brunia albiflora, Zones 9–11), panicle hydrangea flowers, and seeded eucalyptus stems.

Thank you again to Ellen and Tracy for sharing these autumn beauties with us! This is my favorite set so far, and I absolutely love the second image. It’s amazing how much character a gourd can add to a container. Looking forward to seeing more of these!

#4. We Tested Ryobi’s $129 Pressure Washer — Here’s What It Can (and Can’t) Do

Can this portable power washer possibly compare to the real thing? We put it to the test.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Nothing sets you up for a better spring than taking some time for some seasonal cleaning in the fall, and one of the best tools for autumn home cleanup is a classic pressure washer. If you’ve got a surface or a screen you need sprayed, a pressure washer can deliver enough pressure for all kinds of scrubbing.

But even the most avid pressure washer advocates would tell you they’re also pretty cumbersome tools that require a lot of setup and garage storage space. That’s exactly why I wanted to try out this portable pressurized washer from Ryobi. The concept is intriguing, promising users a fraction of the size, cost and power of a standard pressure washer. I was very curious whether this tool would actually provide more cleaning power than a standard garden hose nozzle.

The first thing I noticed when unboxing the Ryobi One Plus Electric Power Cleaner was how substantial the tool felt. I was expecting it to feel a little flimsy, but the tool felt well-built in my hands. It all assembled easily in just a few clicks, taking only a small fraction of the time it would’ve taken to set up a full-size pressure washer. And if you’re worried about water ruining your battery, don’t be. The entire battery chamber is enclosed by a tightly sealed plastic housing.

For this test, I decided to replicate a classic fall cleanup task: hosing down screens. I wanted a big surface to clean, so I pulled the screen door off the back door and set it up in the backyard. Then, I applied a light coating of flour to the middle of the screen and a light mist of water to lock the flour in place.

From there, I just had to finish setting up the Ryobi pressure washer. It comes with three different nozzles: two flat angled nozzles and one “turbo nozzle” that sprays the water in a speedy spiral. All I had to do was attach the pressure washer to a garden hose, and the tool was ready to go. Then I just set myself up in front of the screen with the pressure washer the recommended distance (1-2 feet) from the screen. ‘

All that was left to do was let it rip. The first thing that stands out when you use this portable pressure washer is that it feels a little underwhelming when you pull the trigger- especially if you’ve ever used a full-sized pressure washer. There’s not much kick, and the water leaves the nozzle at a steady but uninspiring speed. For a few seconds, I was worried the 700psi of pressure wouldn’t be enough to clean up the floury mess I’d created.

But my worries lessened the longer I used the tool. It was gentler than the pressure washers I’d used before, but it provided a consistent stream that quickly started knocking the flour loose from the screen. Things started going even better once I switched to the turbo nozzle. The spin action really helped compensate for the lack of PSI pressure. Within another minute, I had knocked off a ton of the sticky flour from the screen.

A post shared by Family Handyman (@familyhandyman)

So enough waffling… what’s the verdict? It’s pretty clear, as soon as you start using this tool, that the Ryobi tool isn’t going to fully replace a full-sized pressure washer… especially if you need to really blast something. But there are many use cases for a pressure washer where consistency is more important than power. And if you’ve ever accidentally damaged something with a pressure washer, the reduced power of this tool might even be something you consider a pro.

It took a while, but eventually the screen was sparkling clean- so clean, in fact, it was nearly invisible in the doorway. I should also point out that real-world conditions are rarely as messy as the sticky flour mess I created. If you just need to get dust off a screen or mud off a sidewalk, this tool is a significant upgrade over a simple stream from a garden hose. Ultimately, you’re trading power for portability, and whether that works for you will depend on the job you have to tackle. If it’s only needed for routine seasonal cleaning, this pressure washer could be perfect for you.

Just don’t expect it to peel paint off a pole.

#5. 11 Ways to Keep Your Garage Workshop Warm in Winter

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Updated Oct 20, 2026 1:37 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Most garages aren’t designed to stay warm inside when outdoor temperatures are frigid. Garages usually lack insulation, and their concrete floors remain chilly all year around. Even with a small space heater running, the temperature inside the garage probably won’t rise more than a few degrees.

When the air inside your garage is bitterly cold, it’s not just the DIYer who doesn’t function well: Tools are icy, paints and glues won’t bond properly, and automotive repairs and woodworking tasks can be difficult to complete. To be able to tinker in your garage in all seasons, not just the warm ones, combine some of these tips for heating the garage to a comfortable temperature. You’ll have a productive work space, whatever the weather.

Visit your local home improvement store in late fall, and you’ll find aisles of portable energy-efficient space heaters, both large and small. Most of these options, however, aren’t powerful enough to heat an entire garage. If you’re looking for a serious heat source, consider installing a ceiling-mounted forced-air heating unit such as the hardwired Dr. Infrared 7,500-Watt Garage Heater, or Comfort Zone Garage Heater, confirming, of course, that the heater model you choose is adequately sized for the square footage of your garage. This type of heater is best situated in a corner of the garage, pointed downward at a 45-degree angle to provide the best distribution of warmth. Most of today’s ceiling-mounted garage heaters come with a remote control and a thermostat so you can set the temperature you prefer and rely on the shop heater to do the rest. For other terrific heater options, refer to our tested guide to the best garage heaters.

The only real downside to a ceiling-mounted heater is that the inches nearest the floor may remain cold. If your feet are still chilly, try supplementing with a baseboard heater placed where you’re most apt to be working—one likely spot is the area beneath your workbench. Hydronic baseboard heaters like the Slant/Fin Fine/Line 30 Series Hot Water Baseboard Heater are hooked up to a home’s boiler. As hot water runs through the pipes in the heater, warm air radiates out into the space, keeping things toasty at floor level and beyond.

No matter how much power your garage heater packs, you’ll find it difficult to maintain comfortable warmth in your garage if the walls aren’t finished. Many garage walls consist of just the studs, covered on the outside with sheathing and siding. Without garage insulation, cold air outside will quickly transfer to the inside of the garage and detract from your heating efforts.

Insulating a garage is a project that’s easy enough for most homeowners to take on themselves. To create an insulated barrier, install fiberglass batt insulation (such as Johns Manville R-19 fiberglass batt insulation) in each stud space and then finish the interior walls by installing drywall panels, plywood sheets, or oriented strand board (OSB). Insulated and finished walls will help retain heat in the garage, and you’ll save money on heating bills.

Often manufactured from thin metal, garage doors are notoriously cold in winter. In fact, if you live in a northern climate, it’s not unusual to find frost clinging to the inside of a metal garage door. Insulating the garage door will help keep the cold outside air from transferring indoors and cooling the workshop. An insulated garage door can make the space an average of 10 to 12 degrees warmer in winter, even before you crank up any heaters. And the process isn’t so intimidating for DIYers, who can buy garage door insulation kits that contain all the necessary supplies. Be sure to measure the doors carefully before purchasing a kit—garages with oversize doors (or two or more doors) will require additional kits.

Reach Barrier’s kit has a laminated bubble layer between layers of aluminum to create a boundary between the garage and the outdoors. Read the review.

Investing in insulation and heaters will help you keep your garage comfortable in the winter, but you should also seal any gaps that let cold drafts blow through. To get started, take a walk around your garage, focusing on these three most likely sources of drafts.

If you enjoy working on your car in your garage, you probably dread having to lie on a frigid concrete floor while changing oil or making repairs. One effective way to remedy this problem is to install a radiant floor heating system. Unfortunately, this is a viable solution only for those who are building a new garage or are planning to tear out and replace an existing garage floor. Radiant floor heating is installed before the concrete floor is poured. The installation process is roughly as follows:

If you spend a lot of time in your garage and are thinking of renovating it, this solution may be right for you. It’s not a DIY project. You’ll need to hire a plumber who specializes in installing radiant floor heating systems. The cost to install radiant floor heating is usually about $5 to $9 per square foot for installation, plus the cost of the boiler. The resulting system is ideal for heating a garage workshop: It warms the space without blowing wood chips and dust around as forced-air heating would, keeping your workspace clear of particles that might interfere with detail work.

Many houses are connected to natural gas lines, but garages often aren’t, and that leaves homeowners with fewer options for heating their garages.

Electric heating is almost always a possibility, but in many regions electricity is pricey. Electric garage heaters also pull a lot of juice, which can cause circuits to overload and breakers to trip, particularly if you’re running a few tools at the same time. Also, relying on electric heat may require additional electrical circuits. For all of these reasons, using a propane heater for the garage may be a reasonably priced alternative. (For our recommended manufacturers and models, read our tested guide to the best propane heaters.)

A standard, 20-pound propane tank can power a small propane heater. If that’s not enough heat, you can opt for a larger 500-gallon tank and have a plumber run a gas line to the garage to fuel a larger propane gas garage heater. Where venting isn’t possible, look for a vent-free propane heater that’s designed to burn cleanly and safely.

For those who plan on spending a lot of time in a garage workshop during the colder months, it’s tough to beat the soothing warmth of a wood-burning stove. Not only will a wood burning stove provide heat, but it also adds a cozy ambience to the space. If you have a ready source of wood, this can be among the best options for cheap heat. (Our researched guide to the best wood stoves highlights high-quality stoves at a variety of price points.)

Safety considerations should be top of mind if you decide to install a wood-burning stove in a garage. The stove must be positioned on a nonflammable surface—a concrete garage floor is ideal—and located a safe distance from walls, cabinets, and any flammable or combustible items. Models vary, however, and some of the newer wood-burning stoves feature insulated exterior shells that don’t get dangerously hot.

It’s important to note that a wood stove must be appropriately vented to keep smoke from backing up in the garage. Local building codes come into play here and usually require that a triple-wall stovepipe be installed vertically through the ceiling. Check with your local building authority for additional restrictions.

Electric space heaters are great for supplemental heating during cold weather, but if a space heater will be the only source of heat in a garage, it should be a powerful one. A kerosene-powered heater fits the bill.

This type of space heater, often called a “torpedo” or “salamander,” generates a lot of heat and concentrates it in a specific direction, so a craftsperson or mechanic at work in the garage can stay nice and warm. Because these heaters often have fans that run on electricity, you’ll still need an electric outlet to run it, but the heat itself is generated by kerosene.

Kerosene space heaters, such as the Dyna-Glo 50,000 BTU Forced Air Heater, a top performer in our tested guide to the top non-electric heaters, can generate up to 215,000 BTUs. That’s a heck of a lot of heat! When selecting a kerosene heater for a garage, buy one that’s designed for indoor use to ensure that it won’t emit toxic fumes. Kerosene torpedo heaters designed for outdoor use may not burn as cleanly, and they are not intended for use in closed spaces. Make sure the model you choose is properly sized for the space in which it’ll be used.

Some types of heaters blow out hot air that warms up a space, but radiant heat works a bit differently, and it’s among the best options for heating a garage on a chilly day.

Radiant heaters use infrared energy that’s generated in a number of ways, via a heating element, an infrared lamp, or even actual flames. The way they work, however, is fundamentally different from forced-air heat. Imagine standing outdoors on a cold day. When the sun comes out, you immediately feel its warmth—that’s radiant heat—even though the air temperature may not have risen perceptibly.

In a garage or workshop, radiant heaters can be installed overhead or on walls. Comfort Zone’s ceiling-mounted hardwired garage space heater uses forced air to radiate heat outward, where it will make you, and everything around you, warm.

For homeowners who already have a ductless mini-split air conditioning system for heating and cooling, it should be fairly easy to add an indoor air-handling unit to your system if the compressor you have is large enough to handle heating and cooling an additional “room.” If you don’t already have a mini-split system, purchasing a mini-split compressor and indoor unit for your garage is still a terrific option, but doing so will cost you more than a few space heaters will.

While heaters and insulation will certainly help keep the air in your garage warmer during the winter, there’s one zone that will still feel frigid: the garage floor. Concrete floors can be bitterly cold, particularly so for anyone who has to scoot under a car or kneel on the floor to work on a project.

Covering the floor is the simplest solution to cold concrete: Consider putting down an indoor/outdoor rug that can be vacuumed or blown clean with a leaf blower. To make a hard concrete floor more comfortable, you might instead install interlocking rubber mats—the kind that’s used for the best gym flooring. These mats both insulate the floor and pad it, making it easier to be on your feet for long periods of time.

#6. I Thought I Wanted a Single-Family Home. Turns Out, I Missed the Rental Income

We thought we wanted a single-family home, but adding an ADU made it the perfect place for us.

I’ve always had benchmarks for knowing when I’ve “made it” in life: a car with power windows and locks, a refrigerator with a water dispenser and owning a single-family home. The last one stems from the fact that my wife and I always owned two-family homes. We lived in one unit and rented out the other for over a decade before we finally had the means to move into a single-family home.

But the funny thing was, when we finally got there, something was missing. Our single-family home didn’t feel as rewarding as I thought it would. Ahead, I share why this long-sought-after dream house didn’t quite feel like one and how a new Massachusetts law allowed us to add the missing piece to our family’s forever home.

After 10 years of renting, my wife and I wanted to buy a home. We decided on a two-family property because we were nervous about taking on too much financially. A single-family home seemed like a luxury that was out of reach, but the rental income from a two-family home made homeownership seem feasible and financially safe. Collecting that first rent check was an amazing feeling, and it cut our mortgage payment in half. We were hooked. Being landlords wasn’t always stress-free, but regular rental income gave us so much financial freedom.

Seven years later, we moved into another two-family home that better suited our growing family and kept the first one, too. We continued to work and save for another five years. As we approached 40, buying a single-family home felt like the next logical step. It was the ultimate end goal, right? So we bought a single-family fixer-upper in a nice neighborhood and started making repairs. Our kids settled into a new school district, and we made friends with the neighbors.

At first, it all felt great, but living in a single-family home wasn’t everything we’d hoped it would be. Mostly, we found we really missed the rental income we were used to in our two-family homes. It felt foolish to have a house that only took money out of our bank account without putting any back in. We didn’t want to move, and soaring home prices made buying another property out of the question. To find ways to generate income from our property, I tried renting out our in-ground pool, second garage, and backyard to dog owners. None of those ideas panned out, leaving us without a way to recreate the two-family experience we missed.

Then, in August 2024, Massachusetts enacted a new law to encourage homeowners to build accessory dwelling units (ADUs), or in-law apartments, to ease the state’s housing shortage. These secondary, self-contained living spaces, complete with kitchens and bathrooms, can house extended family members or paying tenants.

My wife and I immediately knew this could be the solution we’d been looking for. Instead of moving to a two-family home, we could add a small apartment to our existing home. We considered our options and decided that converting a portion of our house into a one-bedroom apartment was the most cost-effective.

We researched town and state ordinances and building codes, then applied for a building permit and submitted plans for the proposed project. Because we weren’t changing the footprint of our home, the process went very smoothly. We started the work in August and had everything completed and inspected by December 2024. We received a certificate of occupancy from the town, and our first tenant moved in on January 1, 2025.

Nearly two years later, we have absolutely no regrets about our ADU conversion project. The rental income has been a fantastic addition to our monthly budget, and we’ve had amazing tenants from the start. It has been the missing piece of our dream home and is making a more secure financial future possible for our family.

If you’re considering adding an ADU to your home or property, here are a few things to keep in mind:

While we had been happy in a two-family home, we mistakenly thought we could do better. But after moving into what was supposed to be our perfect, single-family home, we realized we had made a mistake. Our “dream” house began to feel like a financial burden that only sucked up money and never gave anything back. Staying put and adding a small apartment has given us so much more breathing room and transformed our forever home from a burden into a boon.

#7. Strategies for New Developers

After years of building beautiful second homes for affluent out-of-state clients, my friend Zeb wanted to build for himself—to be the developer, creating homes his own neighbors could actually afford.

Zeb is one of the most competent builders I know. He runs clean jobs, completes projects on budget, and has spent over a decade earning a strong reputation in his community. But when he set off to develop his first project, a modest duplex on a lot just down the road, he didn’t fully understand all the work that is required before a shovel hits the ground.

Zeb assumed that the permitting process would take six weeks. It took eight months. During that time, he was still running his carpentry business and paying his crew, and the duplex project was an additional cost. The carrying costs on the lot, the insurance, the loan interest—they all added up. By the time he was ready to break ground, he was already behind the financial projections he’d based the project on.

He got through it. The duplex is finished and rented to two local families. Zeb is proud of it. But he’d tell you himself that if he’d known then what he knows now, the project would have been a lot less stressful and more profitable.

“I knew how to build it,” he told me recently. “I just didn’t know how to develop it.”

While a builder is responsible for the construction of a home or building, and ensures that it is constructed according to plans and codes, a developer has the responsibility for the overall planning for the project. This includes acquiring land, securing financing, and overseeing the entire project from concept through completion. It may also include choosing a builder or doing the actual construction oneself.

If you’ve spent years managing construction and delivering projects on time and on budget, development can feel like a natural next step. Done well, development can ­create real wealth while helping address local housing shortages. Done poorly, it can sink even experienced builders.

In my role as an owner’s project manager at HELM Construction Solutions, I draw on my background in architecture, building, and land-use planning to guide development projects. When a new developer is starting out, a few principles matter more than anything else: understanding capacity, managing risk, finding the right funding, and doing preconstruction planning.

Builders are used to ­managing multiple projects, juggling subcontractors, and solving problems on the fly. But development requires a different kind of commitment—financial, professional, and personal. The first question to ask yourself is not “Can this project work?” It’s “Can I carry this project?”

Capacity has several dimensions. Financial capacity may be the most obvious, as development requires upfront capital alongside the income lost while spending time on the project. You will need to fund pre­development costs, carry property taxes and insurance, and cover all the building expenses up front. Construction loans reimburse your expenses after work is completed and verified, which means you may need to float weeks of material and labor costs before each draw is processed.

Before you sign anything, ask yourself: Can I purchase materials before loan draws are processed? Can I pay subcontractors on time without waiting for loan disbursements? Do I have reserves to cover delays in reimbursement? If not, the project may require more capital than you have.

Builders often overlook the income they’ll give up while working on their own development projects. When you build for clients, you are paid for your time, overhead, and expertise as you go. When you build your own project, that revenue may disappear while you focus on development.

That forgone income should be treated as a real cost. Some builders choose to pay themselves a project management or general contracting fee from the development budget. Others accept reduced income during the project but expect to recover it through profits or long-term equity when they sell or rent the finished project. Either approach can work—but the numbers must be realistic and ensure that you can still pay your bills while the project is underway.

Time capacity is just as important as financial capacity. Development can’t be treated as a casual side project if the goal is to complete it efficiently and profitably. Many builders assume they can develop their personal project during nights and weekends while continuing to work full-time for paying clients. Projects run this way often take longer than expected—construction costs escalate, ­subcontractors move on to other jobs, financing timelines tighten, ­permits and approvals need ­updating, and emotional burnout becomes a real danger.

And the hard truth is that in development, time is money in a way that’s more literal than in almost any other business. Every month a project runs long is a month of loan interest, insurance, taxes, and lost rental income. The only situation where a loose timeline might make sense is if you can comfortably carry the property and all its costs for an extended period without incurring any debt and you can absorb inevitable cost increases.

There is also a personal capacity consideration that is rarely discussed but critical. Development is stressful. You are responsible for all the decisions and the financial outcome of the project. Have honest conversations with your family and your business partners. If the project’s failing will threaten your personal finances or family stability, it isn’t worth the risk.

Once you understand your capacity and have a sense of how a development project might be financed, the next step is building a detailed pro forma. The pro forma is the financial model that determines whether a development project is viable. It balances total project costs, financing requirements, and expected revenue so you can see whether the revenue will cover the project costs.

It is an iterative process; you should expect to tweak and revise your pro forma repeatedly as you gain information and need to adjust other costs. You can find basic pro forma templates online, or you can ask your local community loan fund or other housing lender if they have a template to share.

You already understand hard construction costs well. While building your pro forma, you’ll also need to capture the many soft costs and site costs that can add up outside the basic construction estimate. A realistic pro forma should include:

Site and infrastructure costs vary dramatically by location. In rural areas, you may be drilling a well or extending electrical service; in urban areas, expect water and sewer connection fees or stormwater requirements. These utility and site costs are frequently underestimated.

Another item that is often overlooked is carrying costs. Every month you own a property during design, permitting, and construction, you’re paying property taxes, insurance, and possibly loan interest. If a project takes longer than expected, these costs can add up.

The safest way to build a pro forma is to assume things will take longer and cost more than you hope. Building a pro forma that only works in a best-case scenario does not protect you when there are surprises. If the project remains financially feasible when you use conservative assumptions, then it is probably viable.

Builders are used to managing production risk, but developers manage every type of risk. A project that looks profitable on paper can quickly fall apart if one of those variables shifts.

Take the example of my contractor friend Amaya, who purchased a historic fourplex in rough shape, mostly vacant, in a town that desperately needed two- and three-bedroom rentals for working families. She had a full rehab in mind, and planned to rent the units through a local affordable housing agency.

But Amaya inherited a handful of tenants with the building, and one refused to leave. The eviction process, which she expected to resolve in a matter of weeks, dragged on for nearly nine months. During that time, rent went unpaid, legal fees mounted, and the carrying costs on the building kept accumulating. It was an expensive lesson in tenant risk, which isn’t part of most construction budgets.

When she finally broke ground on the rehab, Amaya made a decision that seemed reasonable at the time. To save money, she would act as her own general contractor and hire individual workers rather than an established crew. On paper, the labor costs looked lower. In practice, the decision cost her far more than she saved.

The workers she hired were unreliable—some ­disappeared mid-job, ­others were unable to sequence trades or estimate remaining work—and every decision had to be made on the fly, often without Amaya present to make it. The rehab that was supposed to take several months took nearly two years and came in hundreds of thousands of dollars over budget.

Amaya’s project is finished now, and those apartments are housing the exact families she hoped they would. But she’s the first to say that the savings she thought she was capturing by hiring cheap labor were an illusion. A professional crew would have cost more per hour. They also would have finished the job in a fraction of the time, with work that didn’t need to be redone. When you account for the extra months of carrying costs, the cost of correcting poor work, and the income she lost while the units sat unfinished, the “savings” evaporated entirely.

The most valuable habit a new developer can learn is practiced skepticism. When reviewing a project, assume that some assumptions will be wrong. Ask questions: What approvals are required and how long will they take? Are utilities already available, or will they need to be installed? Are there environmental or zoning constraints? Is there demand for this type of housing in the area? What is my own experience with this building type? If a project only works under ideal conditions, it doesn’t work.

Construction experience helps when discussing projects with lenders, but financing development requires understanding where you’re getting your capital. Most projects rely on two main sources: debt and equity.

Debt typically comes from banks or construction lenders and must be repaid with interest. A construction loan usually funds the building phase and is later repaid through a sale or permanent financing like a mortgage. Lenders will evaluate your project management experience, your financial stability, and the strength of the deal itself. Builders have an advantage on the experience side, but lenders still expect conservative budgets and realistic timelines.

Equity comes from the developer or outside investors, and if the project loses money, they’re the first ones to feel it. Because equity carries more risk, investors expect higher returns than a commercial lender. Many emerging developers start by partnering with investors who provide equity while the builder contributes project management and construction expertise. Others begin with smaller projects financed with personal savings and a construction loan.

For builders stepping into development, it’s worth investigating state and local housing incentives that may help fill funding gaps. Many communities offer programs designed to encourage the creation of affordable or workforce housing. These can include grants, tax abatements, low-interest loans, or forgivable loans tied to affordability requirements.

One of my clients, a first-time developer named Catherine, spent months trying to make a small rental project work financially. She had found a neglected former commercial building she wanted to convert into a three-unit rental, but the rehab costs were too high relative to the rents in her local market. Then she learned about Vermont’s Housing Improvement Program. The forgivable loan VHIP offered—tied to renting the units at affordable rates—was exactly the gap she needed to close. Now she is already looking for her next project, with plans to use VHIP funding again.

Once you know your financing options, developing a detailed financial model will give you a sense of whether you’ll be able to carry the project (see “Get Clear on Your Costs,” p. 79).

Here’s the rule of thumb I give every builder who’s new to development: Plan for your preconstruction phase to take just as long as construction itself, if not longer. Many beginning developers are surprised by all the work that needs to happen before construction begins.

A detailed preconstruction schedule is one of the most valuable tools for a developer. It should outline the entire process, including realistic timelines for feasibility and financial modeling, survey and site analysis, design development, construction drawings, permitting, final construction pricing, loan approval, and closing.

If you’re both the builder and the developer, your construction experience is extremely valuable here. For example, one of the most common mistakes new developers make is starting construction based on rough-cost-per-square-foot assumptions. Builders know better than anyone that those numbers can be misleading.

Before committing to a project, put together a real construction estimate based on actual subcontractor pricing and current material costs. That might mean completing enough design work to send drawings out for bids or at least confirming numbers with your regular subcontractors. If the estimate comes back higher than expected, you still have time to adjust the design, rethink the scope, or decide the project doesn’t make sense. Those are far easier decisions to make before construction begins.

Across the country, communities are struggling with housing shortages. Small projects such as duplexes, accessory dwelling units, infill homes, and thoughtful rehabs can make a meaningful difference. Builders are often in the best position to make those projects happen. They already understand how buildings go together, how to manage trade partners, and how to solve problems when surprises occur.

The leap from being a builder to becoming a developer is real, but it isn’t as wide as it might look—provided you do the planning, run the numbers honestly, and understand the risks. I think of my client Leah, a contractor who spent 20 years building other people’s visions before she developed a modest four-unit building on an infill lot in her hometown.

It took her longer than she expected and challenged her in ways she hadn’t anticipated. But those four apartments are full, the rents are affordable, and Leah owns an asset that will generate income for decades. She told me recently that it was the hardest project of her career, but also the most meaningful.

— Hannah Bryant is an owner’s project manager at Helm Construction Solutions.

Empty food cans usually head straight for the recycling bin. But with a quick wash and a few nail holes, they can have a second life in the garden.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Canned beans, tomatoes, and soup move through plenty of kitchens at a steady clip, and the empties usually get a quick rinse before they go out with the recycling. At that point, old tin cans still have plenty of life left. They’re stiff, hold soil and water without leaking, and cost nothing after being discarded.

Cans make for one of the easiest garden recycling projects, and the basic projects need nothing fancier than a hammer, a nail, and a can opener. One can might hold a pepper seedling in March, then lose its bottom at transplant time and slip right back over that same plant as a cutworm collar. That’s a lot of mileage out of something headed for the curb.

I start my stash in fall. Soup and chili season brings in a steady supply, and a box of clean cans in the shed will be ready when seed starting rolls around in late winter. Some can go to work right away, too – as lanterns on chilly evenings or as a winter home for hollow stems cut back during fall cleanup.

Clean cans first. Hot, soapy water and a bottle brush get the food out, and a soak loosens the label and glue. The edges are the real hazard. If you’ve got a smooth-edge can opener, like this Oxo Good Grips one on Amazon, use it, since it cuts through the side seam and leaves a dull lip. Regular openers leave a sharp ring. Pinch any jagged bits flat with pliers or take a file to them, and wear gloves for this part.

Won’t they rust? They will, eventually. On most cans, the “tin” is only a thin coating over steel, and rain and wet soil wear through it over time. That takes a while, and a can with a few orange spots still holds soil and water just fine for seasonal jobs. I paint the outside of any can that’ll sit out for a long stretch, and punch drainage holes so water doesn’t sit in the bottom. A can too far gone can usually still go in with the metal recycling.

Without further ado, in this latest installment of our Dirt Cheap Gardening series, here are my eight favorite ways to upcycle tin cans.

Thin plastic cell packs can split or tip over, but a tin can is heavier and less likely to get knocked around. You can use cans to start seeds or root cuttings. Turn one upside down on a scrap board and tap a nail through the bottom in several spots to make drainage holes – a basic 16-ounce claw hammer, like this Irwin one from Amazon, is plenty for the job.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Fill your tin can pots with a light, sterile seed-starting mix, such as Espoma Organic Seed Starter from Walmart, instead of garden soil. Metal doesn’t breathe like terracotta, so feel the mix before you water. When it’s time to transplant, cut the bottom out with the can opener and push the root ball up and out.

A tin can can help protect seedlings from a few garden pests, although it won’t keep them all away. Burying a can around a young plant may make it harder for slugs to reach, but they may still climb over it, so don’t rely on it as a dependable barrier.

Where a can collar is more useful is against cutworms. These caterpillars hide in the soil by day and chew through young stems at ground level after dark. Cut a can open at both ends, slip it over the seedling, and press it 1–2 inches (2.5–5 cm) into the soil, leaving a couple of inches above ground. Put it in place when you plant, while the seedling is most vulnerable.

You can also hang cans near vulnerable plants as a makeshift bird scare. Moving, clattering cans may startle birds, but the effect can wear off as they get used to them, so treat it as a short-term deterrent. Perhaps try alternating tin cans with a predator decoy, like the Dalen Lifelike Great Horned Owl Decoy Bird Repellent on Amazon.

My potting benches end up buried under twine, plant labels, and hand tools. A few cans fix that for free. Drop a ball of garden twine (like this PerkHomy green jute twine from Amazon) into one can, and it won’t roll off the bench anymore. Put labels and pencils in the next can, and pruners and a trowel in the one after that. Mark each one with a weatherproof Garden Marker pen (on Amazon) so you don’t have to guess later. Nail them to the shed wall through the back.

Bare hands make a mess of granular fertilizer, bone meal, and compost, and a clean can scoops them out without bending or cracking the way a plastic cup might. Make it do double duty. Pour a measured cup of water in, scratch a line at the waterline with a nail, and you’ve got a rough measuring cup for any rates listed in cups. Keep a second can just for compost.

Fertilizer residue can speed up rust, so knock the scoop clean after each use, store it dry, and never bring it back into the kitchen.

Thyme, chives, and oregano stay compact enough to grow in a can on a sunny windowsill or balcony rail. Get the drainage holes in first, then paint the outside. Home Depot stocks Rust-Oleum Stops Rust spray paint in gloss white, and white is the better pick for a patio since dark cans heat up fast in full sun.

Skip painting the inside, and let the paint cure before you plant. This time of year, aim for a south- or west-facing window. In summer, a can on a hot patio can dry out quickly.

Punched-tin lanterns throw speckled light across a patio table, and they’re a nice touch now that it gets dark earlier. Freeze a can full of water first. The ice keeps the walls from denting while you tap a nail through them in dots, swirls or stars. Once it thaws, dry it and paint it if you like, then drop in a battery-operated LED tea light, which you can get from Walmart in a pack of 12. An LED carries far less fire risk than a candle if wind tips a lantern into dry leaves. Thread wire through two holes near the rim to hang it.

Many native bees are solitary and nest alone in narrow tunnels rather than hives. A tall can filled with hollow stems gives them just that. Fall cleanup supplies the material. Bamboo, reeds, and the hollow or pithy stems of sunflowers, sumac, or raspberries all work in mixed widths. Cut them a little shorter than the can so the rim shelters the openings, keep a closed node at the back when possible, and pack them in tight. Keep the bundle dry over winter.

Around the last spring frost, mount the can on its side about 5 feet (1.5 m) up, facing southeast. Replace the stems every one to three years to keep mites and fungal disease from building up.

The other ideas on this list use the cans, but this one makes use of the lids by turning them into plant labels. Flatten each lid carefully, then write the plant name on it with a permanent marker. You can attach it to a wooden stick or tie it to a plant support with garden twine. The metal stands up to rain better than paper labels, and you’re giving a useful second life to something that might otherwise go in the recycling. Be careful handling the edges, which can be sharp.

Clean cans don’t take up much room on a shed shelf, and they keep a lot of little purchases off the shopping list. Start a stack this fall, and by seed-starting season there’ll be one ready for nearly every job!

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#9. Fall Container Designs That Make an Entrance

Happy Monday, GPOD! Today we’re heading to New Jersey for some fall container inspiration from garden designers Ellen Goldfarb and Tracy Buttrick. The two have shared a collection of seasonal arrangements they’ve created for homes throughout the area, and there’s so much to enjoy!

We’re starting with four designs by Tracy, who shows just how much color and texture you can fit into a pot, even when planting space is limited. These arrangements are full of ideas worth borrowing for our own front entrances. Let’s take a look!

Tracy designed this pot, one of a pair flanking the front door on a large porch. Because the house is white, she wanted the pots to have lots of color to stand out. At the top is purple fountain grass (Pennisetum setaceum ‘Rubrum’, Zones 8–11), along with balloon plant seedpods (Gomphocarpus physocarpus, Zones 8–10), broom corn (Sorghum bicolor, annual), great millet (Sorghum bicolor, annual), ‘Intenz’ celosia (Celosia argentea ‘Intenz’, annual), pumpkins-on-a-stick (Solanum aethiopicum, annual), ornamental peppers (Capsicum annuum cvs., annual), garden mums (Chrysanthemum × morifolium cvs., Zones 5–9), and ornamental cabbage (Brassica oleracea cvs., annual).

Tracy designed this pot with broom corn, ‘Jade Princess’ ornamental millet (Pennisetum glaucum ‘Jade Princess’, annual), crested celosia (Celosia argentea var. cristata, annual), ‘Durango Red’ French marigolds (Tagetes patula ‘Durango Red’, annual), pumpkins-on-a-stick, mums, ornamental peppers, ‘Concertina Pink’ celosia (Celosia argentea ‘Concertina Pink’, annual), and Snow Princess sweet alyssum (Lobularia ‘Inlbusnopr’, annual).

Although this pot looks big and round, it has a very small planting area, so it is always a challenge. Tracy used purple fountain grass, pumpkins-on-a-stick, ‘Dragon’s Breath’ celosia (Celosia argentea ‘Dragon’s Breath’, annual), ornamental kale (Brassica oleracea cvs., annual), ‘Twisted Dark Orange’ celosia (Celosia argentea ‘Twisted Dark Orange’, annual), heather (Calluna vulgaris, Zones 4–8), and Snow Princess sweet alyssum.

This matching smaller round pot at the base of the porch steps presented similar challenges. With only an 8-inch opening, branches helped give height and body to the design. Tracy used yellow winterberry (Ilex verticillata, Zones 3–9), pumpkins-on-a-stick, ‘Intenz’ celosia, ornamental kale, ornamental peppers, ‘Concertina Red’ celosia (Celosia argentea ‘Concertina Red’, annual), heather, and ‘Violet Knight’ sweet alyssum (Lobularia maritima ‘Violet Knight’, annual).

Thank you to Ellen and Tracy for sharing these beautiful fall containers with us! We’ll be featuring more of their designs throughout the week, so stay tuned!

Looking for a more understated way to decorate for Christmas? Michelle Obama's minimalist twig-tree look is all the inspiration you need – and you can recreate it at home using branches from your own garden.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Decorating for the holidays doesn't always have to mean a towering evergreen, baubles in every colour and tinsel from floor to ceiling. Sometimes, the simplest ideas make the biggest impact, and Michelle Obama's understated twig tree look is well and truly proof of this!

There is something magical about using natural shapes and soft lighting to create an elegant display, isn't there? And, while a Christmas tree is very much an 'only for December' kind of vibe, the Obamas' approach of using illuminated branches offers a more pared-back alternative, with a gentle glow that can work well beyond the festive season.

It's a look that feels particularly suited to anyone who prefers a more minimalist Christmas, or who wants to introduce a little seasonal magic without buying another large decoration that will spend most of the year in storage. Check it out if you don't believe me:

A post shared by Michelle Obama (@michelleobama)

Love it? The good news is that you don't necessarily need to buy a ready-made twig tree to achieve a similar effect. In fact, with a few suitable branches from your garden, a sturdy vase and a string of delicate LED fairy lights, you can create your own version of Michelle Obama's holiday display for a fraction of the cost.

It's a lovely way to make use of branches left over from routine pruning, giving them a second life as part of your Christmas decorating. And, brilliantly, it's one of the simplest DIY projects going! All you have to do is choose branches with interesting shapes, arrange them so they form a loose, tree-like silhouette, and add lights sparingly enough that the natural structure remains the star of the show.

You don't need specialist crafting skills to recreate Michelle Obama's holiday look. The most important things are choosing branches with an appealing shape and making sure your finished arrangement is stable.

Whether you leave the finished display unadorned or add a handful of small ornaments, this easy DIY is a beautiful way to bring the outdoors in for the holidays.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

With that in mind, then, let's get our Michelle Obama on...

Start by looking for branches with plenty of natural character. A mixture of upright stems and smaller offshoots will give your display a fuller (aka more tree-like) shape, while branches with interesting curves can add a sculptural quality.

You can use fallen branches or suitable cuttings from routine garden pruning. If cutting from a living shrub or tree, make sure you're pruning at an appropriate time and in a way that won't damage the plant. Avoid brittle, rotten or diseased wood, and check branches for insects before bringing them indoors.

Choose a vase or planter with a wide and heavy base to help prevent your tree from tipping over. Position the tallest branches towards the centre and arrange the shorter ones around them, allowing the natural shapes to spread out.

Add small stones or pebbles around the base of the branches to help hold them in place. And take care to step back occasionally to check the overall silhouette, adjusting the stems until the arrangement feels balanced without looking too uniform.

This is where the magic happens. Wrap your LED fairy lights loosely around the branches, starting near the base and working towards the outer stems. Try to distribute the lights evenly, rather than clustering them in one area.

Warm white lights will give the arrangement a soft, inviting glow, while a more delicate micro-LED string can create a subtle, almost starry effect. Battery-operated lights can also be useful if you want to position your display somewhere without a nearby socket.

Shop Fairy Lights For Your DIY Twig Tree:

The trick to nailing that MIchelle Obama look is to make sure you pick some with a flexible wire that is easy to wind around smaller branches. Take care, too, to check that the length is sufficient for the size of your arrangement.

A timer function is a useful extra if you'd like your tree to illuminate automatically in the evenings.

One of the best things about Michelle Obama's holiday display is that it doesn't need much embellishment; you can leave the branches bare apart from the lights for a minimalist finish, or add a few small ornaments if you prefer something more traditionally festive.

A restrained palette of white, silver or muted gold will complement the natural wood without making the display feel too busy. Alternatively, a simple velvet ribbon tied around the vase can introduce a little texture without distracting from the branches.

Once your arrangement is finished, place it somewhere it can be appreciated after dark, and take care to position it on a level surface, away from candles, fireplaces and other sources of heat.

The beauty of this Michelle Obama-inspired DIY is that it doesn't have to disappear as soon as Christmas is over. If you keep the decorations minimal, your illuminated branches can continue to bring a soft glow to your home throughout the winter – and beyond.

#12. Bonfire Season Is Here — Here Are the Dos and Don’ts for Staying Safe

How to not to expose yourself to toxic fumes, burn down the neighborhood and injure the kiddos, plus other tips for enjoying a stress-free bonfire.

Cool fall evenings naturally put our minds on the merits of bones-warming bonfires. And while many create cherished family memories and set the backdrop for festive community events, some end up in tragedy, with emergency room visits and property damage.

“Every season there are always the same preventable mistakes made that lead to injuries,” says attorney Kevin Henrichson. “Falling into the fire, using gasoline, adding fuel when you shouldn’t, failing to supervise children and consuming alcohol all raise the stakes of something bad happening.”

Ahead, experts walk through exactly what to do and not to do to stay safe while enjoying a bonfire.

Notify your local fire department of your plans and ask them for guidance concerning:

“One phone call to the fire marshal’s office takes two minutes,” says fire and home safety expert Eugene Klimaszewski. “Otherwise, the consequence of burning without a permit on a restricted day is a fine, and if it gets away from you, it’s your liability.”

Look for a flat, open spot away from fences, barns, houses, trees and ground vegetation. The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) recommends keeping bonfires at least 25 feet from the house and other structures.

“That number isn’t arbitrary,” says Klimaszewski. “Radiant heat and drifting embers are what ignite a deck railing, a vinyl fence or the mulch bed against the house. Every ember that lands on a roof or in a gutter full of dry leaves is a coin flip. Most go out. The one that doesn’t becomes a structure fire.”

Build the fire downwind of your home and close all windows and doors on the fire side, to prevent smoke from getting in.

“Even a small amount of smoke reaching an indoor smoke detector is enough to set it off,” says Klimaszewski. If you have a monitoring system, that could trigger a call to the fire department. “At best that’s an embarrassing conversation with the engine company. In towns that charge for repeat false alarms, that’s a bill on top of the embarrassment,” he says.

Pro-tip: If you have an older home, which isn’t airtight, put your alarm system on test mode or notify your monitoring company about your bonfire plans.

Wind can carry embers up to a mile, which means a bonfire on a windy day can easily end with a wildfire or house fire. If your planned bonfire day turns out to be windy, reschedule it. And even if there isn’t a breeze, plan for one by clearing all debris from around the fire pit and building rocks or bricks up higher on the windy side, which protects the fire from the wind plus radiates heat toward you for extra warmth.

Kiln-dried wood is the best. Seasoned hardwoods like oak, cedar and hickory are particularly good because they burn cleaner, longer and hotter than soft woods like pine and aspen (though a little soft wood kindling makes starting a fire a lot easier).

Steer clear of gasoline or other accelerants, as they too often lead to burn injuries, out-of-control fires and noxious fumes. (One year, my neighbor used so much gasoline to start a bonfire that the resulting shock wave from the explosion knocked pictures off of people’s walls three blocks away).

“A lot of people think they can use gas or lighter fluid to get the fire started or revive it, but please never do that because the vapors can flash back and get everyone nearby,” says Henrichson. “Gasoline is particularly dangerous and should never be used to start or revive a fire.”

Pro-tip: If you struggling to start a fire, build up a good kindling base and use a campfire starter or small bit of tightly twisted newspaper. Ample kindling will help you get a hot coal-bed established, which will burn larger logs more effectively plus lessen smoke.

Avoid newspaper, cardboard and other paper products, which tend to break down into large flying embers. Also, never burn anything with adhesives, plastics and other chemicals. The health risks of this are obvious, but plastics and chemicals are hiding in many items you might not realize, including: dryer lint, food packaging with shiny ink, glossy magazines, pressed woods including butcher block, varnished furniture and clothing made with synthetic fibers.

Before lighting the fire, set up a water source in case embers become a problem. That will also make it easier to put it out completely when you’re done. NFPA actually requires a hose, bucket or extinguisher be on hand for all recreational fires, and for fires to be attended at all times.

“A fire that’s left alone for ten minutes while everyone goes inside for more drinks is the one that ends up on the local news,” says Klimaszewski. “And an unattended fire that spreads is the homeowner’s liability, full stop.”

Assign someone to supervise the flames at all times to prevent the fire from getting out of control, and to keep kids and pets from standing too close. Equip the supervisor with proper protective clothing, including a fire-resistant glove, long-handled poker tool, shovel, closed-toe shoes and eye protection.

“The most common injuries I’ve seen are from people falling into the fire, and young children are vulnerable to this because they may want to play in the area where everyone is hanging out by the fire,” says Henrichson. “There should be a no-enter zone that is explained to children every single time, and the person tending the fire should not have any alcohol.”

Watch for loose sleeves, blankets, boots and other combustibles that are too close to the fire. “Those fun marshmallow-roasting memories are great to make, but shaking a burning marshmallow can cause trouble, and if you use metal skewers, they can burn you too,” says Henrichson.

Also, know what to do beforehand if something ends up catching fire. “The old advice that we were told years ago is still true: stop, drop, and roll if your clothes catch fire,” says Henrichson. “Repeat this as necessary every time kids approach, because they don’t always know to stay back.”

Embers can easily reignite hours or even days later, so the best practice for putting out a bonfire is to drown it, stir the ashes, and then drown it again until everything is cold to the touch. Don’t cover embers with dirt, as that actually insulates them, leaving open the possibility for them to reignite if they’re uncovered by a stiff wind.

Pro-tip: Put ashes in a metal container with a lid, on a non-combustible surface, away from the house, garage and deck for several days before they go in the trash, says Klimaszewski. Never put them in a plastic bin or next to the house.

#13. Guide to Old-House Maintenance

Old houses have a reputation for being maintenance nightmares, and there’s enough truth in that stereotype that I’m not going to pretend otherwise. Owning one can, and usually will, require a lot of work. But in my experience, people don’t choose old houses because they’re looking for the easiest possible form of homeownership.

They choose an old house because there’s a nonfinancial payoff to living in a building that has already been around for generations: the worn stair treads, old glass, handmade doors, oversized moldings, crooked floors, and all the other things that give an old house a sense of history and character that’s difficult to reproduce in a new one. If you love those things, then maintenance is just part of the bargain.

But charm and romance aside, living in an old house can sometimes feel like having an endless to-do list. There’s always paint that could use attention, a gutter that needs cleaning, a window with loose putty, a mortar joint that’s opened up, or something else you’d rather put off until next year. And because most maintenance issues aren’t emergencies, putting it off until next year is often an easy choice.

The trouble is, if you wait too long, a deferred maintenance job becomes a repair, and a deferred repair becomes restoration or replacement. If you’ve ever watched what happens to an abandoned house, you know it doesn’t take long before vegetation becomes overgrown, water starts finding its way in, and a building that stood solid for a century starts deteriorating like Mother Nature has her finger stuck on the fast-forward button.

The point isn’t to follow a rigid schedule like you’re a maintenance crew. It’s to know what to look for, understand what can wait and what can’t, and recognize the small failures that have the potential to become big ones.

Binoculars: This inexpensive and widely available piece of equipment is surprisingly useful for zooming in on roofing, chimney details, high sidewalls, gutters, and trim tucked beneath a cornice.

Borescope: The closest an old-house owner will ever come to having X-ray vision, a borescope is a small illuminated camera that allows you to see inside cavities or tight spaces—often with the ability to take photos—without cutting large inspection holes.

Drone: A small camera drone can provide a surprisingly good look at roofs, chimneys, flashing, gutters, and up-high trim that might otherwise require a ladder or staging. Save the photos and they become a useful record for comparison over time. A drone doesn’t replace a hands-on inspection when one is needed, but it can help identify where a closer look is warranted.

Most building materials don’t just suddenly fail. Paint, roofing, mortar, glazing putty, flashing, and sealants all deteriorate gradually, and all require some level of periodic inspection or maintenance. In other words, they have a maintenance cycle.

The cycles aren’t set in stone, and may change based on climate, exposure, deferred maintenance or neglect, or quality of materials or craftsmanship. Some things, like gutters, may need attention multiple times a year. Other things, like a masonry chimney, may only need some love every handful of years; and some things may go decades before you need to touch them.

Of course, an old house may have a dozen things competing for your attention, and in my experience, the part of the house that looks worst usually isn’t the one that should come first. So how do you prioritize? The question to keep in mind is this: “What happens if I leave this alone?” Some problems can sit essentially unchanged for years, while others will actively worsen every time it rains.

A door that functions well but has ugly peeling paint is a far lower priority than the smallest of roof leaks, which can be slowly damaging the structure of the house. In other words, always prioritize by consequence, not appearance. Above all else, deal with the problems that are likely to spread, accelerate, or make the eventual repair more difficult and expensive. Cosmetic problems, which are always the more tempting place to put your time and money, can usually get in line behind those.

A good example of a problem that is likely to worsen quickly is when porch posts are installed directly on top of the porch flooring. Once water gets underneath the post, the floorboards begin to rot and the post settles slightly. This creates a low spot that holds more water, which causes more rot and more settling. We have seen many examples of this; in one case, the floorboards had actually curled upward around the post enough that they were effectively funneling water underneath it. Often by the time we are called to look at the issue, the posts have dropped enough that the roof has actually begun to sag.

When deciding what to tackle first, I tend to favor anything allowing water into the building, anything affecting structure or safety, and anything where waiting is likely to turn a small repair into a much larger one.

Not every part of an old house has to be inspected and maintained every year, but there are some general guidelines on maintenance cycles that are worth knowing about. This table, summarized based on information in National Park Service Preservation Brief 47, is a helpful cheat sheet for old-house maintenance.

A good inspection isn’t just a hunt for things that look broken. You’re looking for clues. If one windowsill is rotten while the other 15 are fine, ask what’s different about that window. Does it get more exposure to sun or rain? Is a gutter overflowing above it? Is there an open joint in the trimwork or a flashing problem directing water toward it? Finding the damage is half the job, but the more useful question is why it’s happening.

Paint failure is another place to look for patterns during an informal inspection. If paint is peeling uniformly across an entire sunny elevation of your house, the coating may be simply reaching the end of its life. If the failure is just in one patch, say under a window, then you need to start looking for a moisture source before thinking about repainting, otherwise you have treated the symptoms and not the problem itself.

By now you’ve likely noticed the trend: Maintenance problems tend to have a strong correlation with water. This is why one of the best times to inspect a house is during a hard rain. Gutters that look fine on a sunny afternoon may be overflowing, leaking at joints, or dumping water behind them once they’re carrying a real load.

Follow each downspout all the way to where it discharges and make sure the water continues moving away from the foundation rather than pooling alongside it. Then go back inside the attic and basement to look for leaks, staining, or damp areas. Water problems are much easier to understand while the water is actually moving.

Don’t be afraid to touch things, either. If wood looks suspicious, gently probe it with an awl or a small screwdriver. Sound wood will offer resistance, but deteriorated wood may feel soft or allow the tool to penetrate easily. A moisture meter is another useful tool, allowing you to compare a suspicious area with similar wood nearby that you know is dry. Readings that climb as you approach a window corner, column base, or roof intersection can tell you much more than any single number.

Certain parts of a building deserve extra attention simply because of their geometry. Horizontal surfaces like flat roofs and wide railings tend to show problems faster than surfaces that are pitched for drainage. Exposed endgrain will soak up more water than edge grain, so check deck frames and boards, porch flooring, and notched wooden stringers, all of which are prone to damage.

Transitions and choke points where debris can collect are also important: roof valleys, where a porch roof meets the house, where a chimney passes through a roof, and where wood trim meets masonry. Anywhere two different materials or assemblies come together is high on the list of areas to inspect.

Remember, not every issue demands immediate repair. Sometimes the first step is just taking photos and maybe moisture readings, and keeping track over time to figure out whether anything is changing. The point of a good maintenance plan isn’t to give yourself more things to fix, but to understand your house well enough to know which problems need your attention today and which ones you can comfortably keep an eye on for another year.

— Justin Fink owns Fink and Son Historic Restoration in Plainville, Conn. Photos by Justin Fink.

#14. Rhonda’s Fall Garden in West Grove, Pennsylvania

Hi GPODers! Today we’re visiting Rhonda in West Grove, Pennsylvania (Zone 7a), where the garden is beginning to wind down for the season. But there’s still plenty to enjoy!

Here are some photos of my waning garden. Begonias, hardy begonias (Begonia grandis, Zones 6–9) my favorite, colchicums (Colchicum cvs., Zones 4–8), tradescantias (Tradescantia cvs., Zones 4–9), toad lilies (Tricyrtis cvs., Zones 4–9), anemones (Anemone hybrids, Zones 4–8), and hostas are on their last legs!

I’ve been trying to make my gardens more manageable by allowing some plants to take over. The beds with the anemones and hardy begonias don’t have any weeds because there isn’t any room!

A winding stone path leads through more Japanese anemones, ferns, and other shade-loving plants.

These bright magenta double begonias (Begonia cvs., annual) are still putting on quite a show! The weathered urn is a beautiful container for them, and even the scattered petals add a little color to the brick patio.

Colchicums are a welcome surprise in the fall garden. Their flowers appear long after their spring foliage has disappeared.

And here’s a closer look at Rhonda’s favorite hardy begonias! Their delicate pink flowers mingle with hostas (Hosta cvs., Zones 3–9) and other shade-loving plants.

Thank you for sharing your garden with us, Rhonda! When I think of fall gardens, pink isn’t usually the first color that comes to mind. This was such a refreshing change from the oranges, yellows, and reds we typically associate with the season!

#16. Why Do Construction Barricades Come in Different Colors? The Colors Decoded

Red, yellow, and orange barricades don't always mean the same thing. Learn what common safety colors signal and when to stay clear.

Yellow caution tape is a pretty familiar sight, whether it’s blocking off a wet floor or keeping people out of a construction area. Orange barriers along the highway and red warning signs at job sites are just as common. But barricade colors aren’t random, and they don’t all mean the same thing.

In the U.S., OSHA has rules for certain workplace safety colors, while ANSI provides guidelines for signs and warning tape. Road construction follows a different set of standards. Depending on the location, the same color might serve a different purpose.

Learn what the most common barricade colors mean, where people are likely to see them, and what to watch out for.

There’s a reason red is a common choice for warning signs. OSHA uses it to identify danger, emergency stops, and fire protection equipment. At a construction site, a red “Danger” sign might warn of exposed electrical equipment or another hazard that could cause serious injury. OSHA’s general-industry rules also call for red warning lights at barricades and temporary obstructions.

Of all the safety colors, yellow might be the one people see most often. It shows up on caution tape, warning signs, and around areas where crews are working. OSHA uses yellow to warn of physical hazards, including falls and falling objects. A damaged walkway or an area undergoing maintenance might have yellow tape around it.

There’s no shortage of orange around construction sites. On workplace warning signs, the color often identifies hazards that could cause serious injury, particularly around machinery or equipment undergoing repairs. Orange also makes road construction easier to spot. Crews use orange barriers and signs to warn drivers about upcoming work, lane changes, or other temporary traffic conditions.

Instead of warning people away from something, it usually helps them find safety equipment. A green sign might point toward a first aid station, identify emergency equipment, or provide instructions for workers. It’s especially useful in workplaces where people need to find these resources quickly.

Blue signs typically provide information about workplace equipment or procedures that don’t directly involve a hazard. For example, a blue notice might explain that a machine is temporarily out of service. Unlike red or yellow warnings, blue notices generally provide information rather than warn of immediate danger.

Purple isn’t a color people encounter very often on construction barricades, but it does have a specific safety use. OSHA requires certain radiation warning signs to feature the familiar radiation symbol in purple or magenta against a yellow background. These signs warn people about radiation hazards, including areas where access may be restricted.

Those orange-and-white striped barricades lining roads and highways aren’t quite the same as the warning signs used inside workplaces. The Federal Highway Administration has separate rules for these barriers, which crews use to close lanes, block roads, and direct traffic around construction.

There’s also a purpose behind the diagonal stripes. When a barricade directs drivers around an obstruction, the stripes slope down toward the side where traffic should pass.

OSHA, “29 CFR 1910.144, Safety Color Code for Marking Physical Hazards” OSHA, “29 CFR 1926.200, Accident Prevention Signs and Tags” ANSI, “Z535.1-2022: Standard for Safety Colors” ANSI, “Z535.5-2022: Safety Tags and Barricade Tapes” OSHA, “29 CFR 1910.1096, Ionizing Radiation” FHWA, “Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, 11th Edition with Revision 1”
