Plant these winter-flowering shrubs in October and their beautifully perfumed blooms will bring cheer to short dark days.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Winter’s short, dark days don’t give us much time to enjoy our gardens, but planting a sweetly scented winter-flowering shrub in your front yard will deliver a plant-based mood boost every time you return home. Fall is the perfect time to add one to your garden as plants will have time to settle their roots into the ground before it’s time to bloom. And then – ahhh! On crisp winter days, the air will be full of fragrance, and you’ll want to stop for a moment to breathe it in.

All these scented shrubs are great picks for a front yard because, as well as brightening dismal winter days with glorious fragrance, they'll boost your home's curb appeal. They’re all very easy to grow, don’t need much in the way of care, and look good year-round. Just enrich the ground with a few spade-fulls of compost such as Back to the Roots Organic Compost, available from The Home Depot, when you plant them, add a further 2-inch layer of compost on top of the soil to act as a mulch to keep roots cozy through their first winter, and water during dry fall spells, and they’ll thrive.

Whether you favor the scent of comforting vanilla or sweet honey, gloriously floral perfumes or fresh and spicy aromas, there’s a winter-flowering shrub to suit. So, if you're wondering what to plant in October, start right here because growing a garden then smells good is just as important as one that looks good! Which of these scented front-yard shrubs will you plant this fall to cheery you through chilly winter days?

The name of this fabulous shrub announces its best asset: an incredible scent that’s intensely floral yet has citrus undertones with a hint of spice that stops it from becoming cloying. Daphne shrubs had a reputation for being finicky plants to grow, until ‘Perfume Princess’ came along and put these shrubs on the must-have list, even for beginner gardeners. It’s hassle-free, boasts flowers that are four times as big as traditional varieties, and blooms earlier and for longer, all the way from January to May.

Unlike most Daphne that only flower on branch tips, it also produces its blush-pink and white flowers all the way down its stems once established. And yes, that means lots more of that lovely fragrance.

Princess Perfume daphne, available from trees.com, grows well in full sun or partial shade in zones 7-11. It’s a winner for a front yard because it naturally grows into a dense, rounded shape around three feet high and wide without the need for frequent pruning, and is evergreen for year-round good looks.

Sarcococca are hardy evergreen shrubs that lift the darkest of winter days with a sweet, honey-like fragrance, often with a comforting vanilla layer – the kind of smell that makes you take a deep breath and relax. These easy-to-grow plants perfume the air all around them with flowers in late winter and spring followed by highly ornamental berries, adding year-round curb appeal. They thrive in partial to full shade, making them a useful option for a tricky dark corner in zones 6-9.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

There’s a sweetbox variety to suit every front yard. Fragrant Valley sweetbox, available from trees.com and flowering from late December is a great fit for most front yards because you can grow it as a low-maintenance groundcover, as it only reaches 2 feet high and 3 feet wide. Extend the aromatic experience with the newly introduced Sweet & Lo sweetbox, also available from trees.com and making great groundcover, as this flowers slightly later from February to March with bright pink tips to its white blooms.

If your front yard is short on space then Monrovia sweetbox, available from Lowe’s, can be grown flat up against a wall or fence, forming an attractive cloak of glossy evergreen leaves up to five feet high and wide but easily kept smaller. It flowers from December through March and though the blooms are tiny, their warm perfume carries up to 20 feet.

If you’ve got room to play with in your front yard, then witch hazel is a highly fragrant choice. The varieties with yellow flowers are far more fragrant than those with orange or red blooms, and Hamamelis x intermedia 'Arnold Promise’ is my standout choice for a scented front-yard showstopper. Highly aromatic with a sweet floral fragrance that carries well through crisp cold air, this pretty vase-shaped shrub (you can grow it as a small tree, too) flowers from late December to March, peaking in February – and we all need cheering up in February!

Hardy in zones 5-8, its ribbon-like blooms last for weeks, curling up during severe freezes then unfurling again as temperatures rise. Blooming on bare branches, it’s quite a sight on snowy days. Deciduous Arnold Promise witch hazel, available from Plant Addicts, has pretty fall foliage, too, and grows to 6-8 feet high though is easy to keep smaller by pruning right after the flowers fade. As long as it has its basic needs met in a spot with at least 5 hours of sun a day and neutral-to-acidic soil (it struggles in chalky soils with a pH above 7), witch hazel is a low-maintenance choice and drought-tolerant once established.

Also known as Japanese pieris, Japanese andromeda aren’t all fragrant but there’s one variety that will light up dark winter days with a wonderful perfume: Pieris japonica ‘Dorothy Wycoff’. Its fragrance is rich yet clean, reminiscent of lily of the valley and a promise that spring is on its way.

Though it doesn’t flower till March, its reddish-purple buds form in summer and sit on the stems all through autumn and winter among the evergreen leaves. So it’s a joy as winter turns to spring to watch the buds expanding then bursting into cascades of bell-shaped blooms. Plant one of these beauties in your front yard and I wager you’ll be checking on bud progress every day you arrive home!

Dorothy Wycoff andromeda, available from Plant Addicts, flourishes in zones 5-8 and though it’s capable of growing to 5-7 feet high and wide, is easily kept smaller and can even be grown in a container.

There are over 150 species of Viburnum, and among them sit some that bring intense fragrance to cold winter days. An excellent choice for a front yard is Viburnum farreri ‘Nanum’, commonly known as dwarf fragrant viburnum. Extremely low-maintenance, this dwarf viburnum is compact and naturally rounded, and although it can reach 2-4 feet high and wide, it grows incredibly slowly so there’s no need for heavy pruning. Hardy in zones 5-8, dwarf fragrant viburnum thrives in full sun to partial shade.

The strength of its perfume belies its small frame, however. And what a scent! The base is warm with almond and vanilla, like walking into a bakery, cut with a spicy dash of clove. The aroma can hang in the air on still winter days, and snipping a single flowering stem to bring inside will fragrance a whole room.

Dwarf fragrant viburnum, available from Nature Hills, takes a little time to settle into a new home, so for the first year you can expect it to bloom lightly in late winter and early spring. But once this shrub matures and has grown its roots deep into the ground, it can flower intermittently from October all the way through to March. It doesn’t open all its buds at once but bursts into bloom during mild spells then pauses when temperatures plummet, producing another cluster when the weather improves. Because this little shrub is deciduous, the flower show is all the more beautiful because it happens on bare branches.

Adding a fragrant winter-flowering shrub to your front yard in fall is such a smart move to cheer you through to spring. And it's not just you who will be pleased – their intoxicating scent makes all these shrubs easy for early-flying pollinators to find.

#18. See It Seated

Push-to-connect plumbing fittings are reliable and easy to install, but they’re not foolproof. One of the most common causes of failure occurs when a pipe isn’t fully seated into the fitting. This can happen if the pipe isn’t cut square, is contaminated with dirt or debris, or simply isn’t pushed in far enough to engage the fitting’s internal stop.

To reduce the chance of an incomplete connection, manufacturers typically recommend measuring and marking the required insertion depth on every pipe before assembly, adding an extra step to an otherwise simple installation.

To reduce the chance of errors, Legend Valve has introduced ClearLOC, a line of transparent push-to-connect fittings. The clear body eliminates the need for insertion-depth marks and allows installers to visually confirm that a pipe is fully seated. ClearLOC fittings are compatible with PE-RT, PEX, copper, and CPVC pipe and are certified to ASSE 1061 standards for behind-the-wall installations.

The fittings are manufactured from PPSU, the same durable material used in many plastic PEX fittings, and are removable and reusable. ClearLOC fittings cost less than traditional brass push-to-lock fittings and are available at plumbing supply retailers.”

— Mark Petersen, tech editor. Photo by the manufacturer.

#19. From the GPOD Archives: Gardening in Antarctica

We’re going to Antarctica today! After our recent trips through the first 10 Garden Photos of the Day and the next 10, Michelle Gervais, who started GPOD, stopped by the comments and suggested I dig up an old submission from Antarctica. Of course, I had to see what she was talking about! I think you’ll enjoy this one! Here’s a look back at Darryl’s remarkable garden.

A few weeks ago, just for fun, I started wondering what extremes people will go to to garden. You hear of soldiers in Iraq having little garden plots, and I’ve seen my share of photos of fire escape gardens in Manhattan, but for some reason, I wanted to go a little more extreme. So I did a little digging, sent out a few emails, and hit a jackpot. Behold, the garden at Australia’s Davis Station in ANTARCTICA. That’s right, Antarctica. Those are the lengths I go to for you people. Because I love you.

Hi, I’m Darryl Seidel, one of the plumbers and manager of the hydroponics this year (2012) at the Australian Antarctic Division’s Davis Station, Antarctica. The role of the hydroponics manager is just one of many community jobs on station. I had never done any hydroponics until I got a job in Antarctica, my experience with gardening really only consists of small vegetable and flower patches at home in Adelaide, Australia. The challenge it poses is one of the main reasons I wanted to take it on.

Our hydroponics set up consists of two lined shipping containers joined together to form 3 rooms. Our goal with hydroponics is primarily hobby and morale based, as we don’t grow enough produce to feed the entire station. The station population over summer can be over 100, and in winter anywhere from 16 to 25 people. This season we have 21 staying over winter (April – November), 14 of these are in our hydroponics crew. Hydroponics at Davis has a real nice community feel about it, if there is a problem, there is always more than enough people on hand to help fix it!

The winter temperatures at Davis vary greatly over winter depending on the weather outside. Clear days can bring temps of -30 degrees Celsius (-22F) and winds up to 100 knots (185 kmh or 115 mph), with an average temperature around -20 deg C (-4F). This certainly eliminates trying to grow anything outdoors!

We are only allowed to grow edible produce due to quarantine and space restrictions, which this season includes iceberg and cos lettuce, varieties of tomatoes, Lebanese cucumbers, capsicums (bell peppers) and a range of herbs. We try to spend as much time in ‘the garden’ as we can because it is usually 27 degrees (80F) and 60% humidity!

We roster two people on per week to monitor the plants twice daily and also have two crew members who look after seeding and propagation. Every season our crops are removed and incinerated, including the media in which the crops are grown, to help prevent the spread of disease and so we don’t introduce any non-native species into the Antarctic environment.

Keeping the water and building from freezing is our main challenge, being hydroponic and in Antarctica there aren’t many (if any) diseases to affect the plants. Around mid June we had a ‘door malfunction’, which let the heat out and the cold in for 12 hours. Most of our crop was lost due to extreme cases of frost, amazingly the majority of the herbs and lettuce survived! But we’ve started again and have bounced back stronger than before! In the 8 months that we have been running hydroponics we have harvested over 60 kg (132 pounds) of fresh produce.

Davis Station in Winter Photo/Illustration: Photograph © Darryl Seidel /Australian Antarctic Division

What an incredible place to have a garden! I can only imagine how welcome all that greenery and fresh produce must have been during the long Antarctic winter. It’s amazing what a little ingenuity and dedication can accomplish, even in one of the harshest environments on Earth.

A big thank-you to Michelle for pointing us back to this memorable submission, and to Darryl and the Davis Station crew for sharing their garden with GPOD readers all those years ago!

#20. This 30-Minute Weekly Car Reset Will Prevent Deep Cleaning Later

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Published Oct 20, 2026 11:19 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Cars are a necessity for many people, and a clean and organized vehicle is especially important for those who spend hours in their car during daily work commutes or driving their kids around to football, dance, school, and other activities. But it’s not always reasonable to find the time in your busy life to open up the car, pull all the mats out, vacuum the entire interior, wipe down every surface, clean the windows, wash the exterior, and the list goes on.

So, if you don’t have the time to devote to deep-cleaning the car every other week, what can you do to keep the car looking good until the next time you get a free afternoon to devote to a full clean? We spoke to a car detailing pro to discover these quick car-cleaning tips that can give your car a 30-minute weekly reset so you aren’t stuck with hazy mirrors and a grimy steering wheel.

The DeWalt 6-Gallon Poly DC Wet/Dry Vacuum delivers powerful cleaning performance in a compact design that goes wherever the mess is—like behind the dryer in a laundry room or under the passenger seat of a vehicle in the garage. With its 20-volt battery operation, wet/dry versatility, and semi-automatic filter cleaning, this portable tool helps DIY homeowners work efficiently without being tethered to an outlet.

Instead of vacuuming every surface in the car, you can stick to the high-traffic areas for this car hack. Parham Koukia, lead car detailer and operations manager at Panda Hub in Toronto, Canada, says you should “vacuum carpet and mats using a soft brush attachment and use compressed air to dislodge debris stuck in vent openings and seat tracks.”

Simply remove the mats from the vehicle, vacuum the driver side floor and passenger side floor. You can skip the rear floor if you haven’t had anyone in the backseat recently. Make sure to vacuum or use compressed air to clean out the seat tracks, then vacuum your floor mats before returning them to the car to give your car floor a quick refresh.

Cleaning the car windows and mirrors does more than give your car a well-maintained appearance. The task also makes it safer to drive, since you won’t be struggling with hazy glass or smudges when you are trying to see your surroundings. Grab a microfiber cloth and use a store-bought cleaner or make a vinegar and water solution, depending on personal preference and convenience.

“Wipe down all glass, inside and out, to remove haze, beginning with vertical strokes and ending with horizontal strokes to remove any remaining streaks,” explains Koukia. It’s also worth it to spend a few minutes cleaning off your headlights and tail lights to ensure that they are clean and clear enough to help you see and to help others see your car when driving at night.

Since you won’t be breaking out the pressure washer for this quick clean, focus instead on which parts of your car get dirty the fastest due to daily use. In most cases, that’s the interior driver side of the car. Target high-touch areas, like the dashboard, steering wheel, shifter, door handles, and cup holder to remove oil and grime that might have built up over the week.

“Use a damp microfiber cloth to gently wipe the dashboard and other surfaces with an interior cleaner. Never spray any cleaning solution directly onto the interior surfaces, since that will oversaturate and potentially damage the materials,” Koukia says. You can also use a compressed air canister to blast dust out of the air vents, followed by a quick swipe over the dash and steering wheel to remove any dust particles.

Organization is just as important as cleaning, but one area car owners often overlook is keeping the various compartments inside the car tidy. You might have a tendency similar to your approach to closets: simply stuff things inside the glove box, console, or door pockets, then forget about them entirely.

To keep your car clean and organized, Koukia says to “empty and clear all compartments, including consoles, glove boxes, and door pockets. Wipe each compartment with a damp microfiber cloth. Put back only the items you need for daily operation of the vehicle, like the registration, owner’s manual, and insurance cards.” If you do have other items you need, like gloves for winter driving, make sure the compartments are organized enough so that these items are easily accessible.

Cleaning out the trash inside your car on a weekly basis is quick, easy, and necessary. Take time to clear out the coffee cup that’s been sitting in the cup holder, packaging from a snack your kids were eating in the back seat, or even a receipt that found its way to the floor of the car.

For items that you use regularly, Koukia notes that you should “give each item a spot in the vehicle to make it easier to stay organized. Once organized and cleared of clutter, keep up with routine maintenance: remove trash at each stop for gas, and do a quick search of the vehicle every week for new or misplaced items.”

#22. ‘The Garden Brought Me Back to Life’: A Revitalized Yard for a Sag Harbor Couple

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

When Bette Lou Fletcher and her husband Bruce moved to Sag Harbor, New York, during their retirement, Bette Lou was determined to build the garden she’d always dreamed of. She connected with local landscape designer Daria Szalinska, who had just established her own design practice, Landelier Landscape Atelier.

Bette Lou told Szalinska she longed for a garden room, an abundance of flowers that would feed and attract wildlife, and a deer-free zone to grow vegetables and cut flowers. One thing she didn’t need? A lawn. “I was beyond excited when Bette Lou told me she did not want a lawn,” says Szalinska. “I had been following Meadow Lab for some time, waiting for their wildflower sod to become available and for the right project where I could use it.” Bette Lou was game to try it out. In Szalinska’s redesign of the Fletcher’s yard, turf grass is used only for pathways and parking, with meadow sod replacing much of the former front lawn.

Bette Lou was also keen to keep the brick walkway, picket fence, and trellis that Bruce had built, a request that at first felt like a design challenge to Szalinska. As is so often the case, the constraints brought about especially lovely solutions. After debating the idea of weaving brick into a larger patio, Daria decided to use organic bluestone pavers, pushed right up against the existing brick, creating a moment of contrast. And surrounded by meadow and perennial plantings, the fence “took on a much softer, almost nostalgic character,” says Szalinska. To create the “rooms” that Bette Lou desired, Szalinska leaned on rigid geometry for the patio and paths; she also designed a fire pit surrounded by a ring of crepe myrtles and a fenced area in back to grow fruits, vegetables, and Bette Lou’s beloved dahlias.

One of the biggest changes Szalinska made is not visible in the photos because it was an act of concealment. She shifted the driveway closer to the edge of the property line, carving out more space for the garden. The landscape contractor Coastal Arborcare raised the grade of the garden, which helped hide the driveway. The final touch was to plant a hedge of native northern bayberry, which screens the driveway from the garden in a naturalistic way. “Bruce got a practical working area and Bette Lou a beautiful garden—making both of them happy,” says Szalinska.

Already, in its first year, the garden is lush, filled with blossoms and wildlife. Bette Lou finally has the garden she’d always imagined, but more significantly, she says, “The garden brought me back to life.” Not only is she surrounded by beauty, she’s been inspired to pick up her camera after years away from photography. “I can’t express the joy that it’s brought me,” she says.

Let’s take a tour of this Sag Harbor garden. (And be sure to scroll to the end for the “before” shot.)

Photography by Laura Castrillón, courtesy of Landelier Landscape Atelier.

#23. Why You Should Pay Attention to Diamond-Shaped Signs on Trucks

Those metal diamonds on the back of trucks serve a purpose. Learn how hazmat placard holders work and what an empty one actually means.

Drivers have a lot to pay attention to on the road. They watch their speed, check their mirrors, and keep an eye out for sudden stops. But one detail most drivers probably haven’t given much thought to is the diamond-shaped designs on the back of trucks, even after seeing them countless times.

No, they aren’t decorations. It’s a small detail that serves an important safety purpose, especially if there’s an accident involving dangerous cargo. Learn how the holders work, what the warning signs mean, and why some appear empty.

They’re called hazmat placard holders. These metal frames hold warning signs that identify certain hazardous materials a truck might be carrying. The bare diamond in the photo is simply a holder. Its lines and clips don’t send any special message to other drivers.

Truck operators leave the holders attached and change the signs depending on their cargo. Some hold removable placards, while others have several signs that drivers can flip between. Labelmaster, a company that makes flip-placard systems, explains that drivers can change the warning without replacing the holder.

The placards use colors, words, and symbols to identify different hazards. Red often indicates flammable materials, while a black-and-white sign marked “CORROSIVE” warns about chemicals that can cause damage. Other signs identify dangerous gases, explosives, or toxic substances.

“Placards serve as an easily identifiable, visual source of information used by millions of workers in the transportation, public safety, and hazmat industries,” according to the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA).

These warnings help emergency responders recognize potential hazards during an accident or spill. Some placards also display numbers that identify specific hazardous materials.

An empty holder may mean the truck doesn’t need to display a warning for its current shipment. Trucking companies leave the frames attached because their vehicles might carry different types of cargo from one trip to the next. An empty holder doesn’t necessarily mean the truck isn’t carrying hazardous materials, though. Federal regulations don’t require placards for every hazardous material or quantity.

When trucks do need placards, PHMSA requires them on both sides and both ends of the vehicle. Carriers must also keep the signs secure, readable, and visible. Federal regulations also prohibit misleading signs that resemble official hazmat placards. The rules specifically mention “Any sign, advertisement, slogan (such as ‘Drive Safely’), or device” that could be confused with an official warning placard.

A bare metal diamond, however, isn’t a hazard warning by itself. It’s simply a holder for the appropriate sign when the truck needs one.

U.S. Department of Transportation, Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, “Identifying Hazardous Materials in Your Community” PHMSA, “DOT Chart 17: Markings, Labeling, and Placarding Guide” Labelmaster:, “Flip Placards” 49 CFR § 172.516, “Visibility and Display of Placards” 49 CFR § 172.502, “Prohibited and Permissive Placarding“

This October trick will set up your garlic crop for the biggest bulbs ever and it's so easy to get right!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Garlic is such a satisfying home crop to grow, and switching up one simple element will bring you bigger bulbs. It's such a no-brainer, yet it takes most gardeners a few years of growing garlic to realise this easy trick at planting time makes a huge difference to the size of harvested bulbs.

Traditional advice tells us to plant cloves knuckle-deep when we grow garlic, which equates to 1-2 inches. However, this rule-of-thumb hails from times when we all gardened in the ground, often in soil that sat wet through winter, so rotting cloves were a real risk. Today, in the loose, well-draining soil of a raised bed or in ground much-improved with compost, you can afford to plant cloves a little deeper, and that results in plumper bulbs.

Why? With a couple more inches of soil above them, the cloves are better insulated from the weather above, allowing roots to carry on growing for far longer before they’re halted by freezing temperatures. This big root system will power strong growth in spring, resulting in fatter bulbs. A deeply-planted clove will resist frost heaving which can pop a shallow-planted clove right out of the ground, too. Ready to grow garlic with bigger bulbs? Here’s exactly what to do.

If you want to know how to grow garlic with bigger cloves, it's important to realise that you can only plant garlic cloves deeply in soil that's loose and well-drained. Try this trick in heavy, wet soil and if the cloves don’t rot over winter, the plants will waste energy pushing shoots through the dense ground that they could have ploughed into bulb expansion. So, only plant garlic this way if you have a raised bed which naturally gives good drainage, or you’re lucky enough to have loamy, free-draining soil.

Either way, improve the soil’s structure and drainage some more by digging in compost. If you make your own garden compost, great. If not, use a manure-free plant-derived compost like Back to the Roots Organic Compost, available from Walmart.

If you have already-fertile soil, the compost will also supply all the nutrients the garlic needs to grow plump bulbs. In poorer soil, or if you’re growing in a veg bed that’s been full of crops all summer, replenish nutrients before you plant with a slow-release fertilizer that’s high in phosphorous to boost root growth: Down to Earth Fish Bone Meal from Amazon is ideal.

To get the biggest bulbs, you want to get your cloves planted early enough to allow them plenty of time to grow a strong root system before winter, but not so soon that they move onto sending lots of shoots above ground that may be hit by freezing weather. The sweet spot to plant garlic cloves for big bulbs is around three weeks after your first frost, depending on your USDA zone.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

So, tailor the time you plant garlic in fall to the conditions in your garden. In zones 1-6, you’ll want to plant garlic in October; in zones 7-8 you may need to wait till the end of October; and in zones 9-10, you’re perhaps looking at November.

Most garlic varieties need an 8-10 week period below 45°C to trigger cloves to split and form bulbs, a process known as vernalization. So, in zones 10+, you’ll need to pop your garlic into the fridge, in a paper bag or a lidded jar, for a couple of months to mimic this cold period before planting.

When you split open your garlic bulbs, discard any smaller cloves as research shows bigger cloves grow bigger bulbs. Now your soil is loose and fast-draining, you can safely plant the cloves around 4 inches deep, using a dibber such as this Hand Hole Digger from Amazon to create planting holes.

Space holes 6 inches apart, because good airflow around the leaves will help prevent fungal diseases such as rust that can slow bulb growth. Then drop a single clove into each hole, pointy end up, and push that lovely loose soil over the top.

And that’s all you need to do to double the size of your homegrown garlic bulbs! You see, the expert secret to growing big garlic bulbs is to grow big root systems. Kept cosy beneath that extra couple of inches of soil, with all the nutrients they need, the cloves you planted will quickly get busy growing deep roots through fall. While root growth will pause in frozen soil, as soon as temperatures creep back above 41°F it will resume, off and on, all through winter.

When spring arrives, that strong root network gives plants access to plenty of moisture and nutrients to grow lots of foliage. And because you’ve planted your garlic in a sunny spot, all those leaves act as solar panels to generate energy to fuel plumper bulbs. The loose soil you created will also allow bulbs to easily expand to their full potential.

Make sure you water the soil through any dry spells in spring and early summer when bulbs are swelling, then slow once the bulbs are fully formed – you’ll know when to stop because the foliage will start to yellow – and you’ll be harvesting garlic that's grown into showstopper bulbs.

In zones 1-8, opt for hardneck garlic varieties as they're much hardier and won't mind sub-zero temperatures a jot. Hardneck garlic bulbs have fewer but bigger cloves, strong flavor and store for 4-6 months.

With a pleasing flavor and pretty pink tones, this variety grows 4-7 jumbo easy-peel cloves even in colder climates.

This variety is less pungent than most hardnecks and has a high concentration of immune-boosting allicin.

Adapted to flourish in colder zones, this variety produces plump cloves with a buttery flavor enjoyed raw or cooked.

Choose softneck garlic in zones 6 and above, because it copes far better in warmer temperatures. Softneck garlic tastes milder, typically has lots of smaller cloves, and stores well for up to a year.

Producing bigger cloves than most softnecks, this sweet-tasting variety crops before mid-summer heat arrives.

With creamy-white cloves and a crowd-pleasing flavor, this productive variety is particularly easy to grow.

Producing unusually big cloves, this variety regularly wins taste tests with its rich, layered flavors.

#25. Stick With the Good Stuff

I recently tried to fix a cracked storage box with some cheap duct tape. As I pulled the tape from the roll, it split along its length so that only one section of the tape came off the roll, forcing me to backtrack to gather up the rest of the strip. It was hard to tear to length, and when it did tear it left long dangling strings.

Once removed from the roll, it was so thin that it kept fo lding in and adhering to itself, rendering it useless. This frustrating failure prompted me to search for a better solution. On my next run to the home center, I bought a roll of USA-made T-Rex duct tape.

This tape came off the roll in one clean strip, tore cleanly, and was thick enough that it didn’t constantly stick to itself. One 1.88-in. by 30-yd. roll of T-Rex costs about $9 online and at home centers. Sure, that’s almost twice as much as the cheapest roll, but the extra $5 would have probably ended up in my swear jar if I had gone the cheap route again.

— Mark Petersen, tech editor. Photo by the manufacturer.

The abundance of summer might be waning, but there are still many things to do in the garden—fall bulbs, I’m thinking of you—before the ground freezes and you can kick back and dream big with your stack of seed catalogs. Here is some handy gear that will help you tackle your tasks with ease.

This carbon-steel hori hori knife is indispensable. It has to be the most-used tool in my garden kit. The sharp point pierces the ground easily, and the serrated edge cuts through pesky roots. I use it to transplant seedlings, weed, and I especially love it for planting bulbs.

Now is an ideal time to plant a tree. (Pro tip: If you become a member (starting at $10) of the Arbor Day Foundation, they will send you 10 free trees.) Fall planting gives saplings a head start in getting established before the heat of summer hits, which can stress out new plants. To get digging, grab this sharp border spade from Sneeboer, the gold-standard of tool brands. It is versatile for a myriad of tasks like tree planting, transplanting perennials, and edging borders. And thanks to its manageable size, it’s not too heavy.

I always make sure my head is protected when I’m gardening to keep the sun away and deter insects from buzzing or biting my face. This chic hat has an extra wide brim and a chin strap to keep it snug on my head during wind gusts. Plus, it’s waterproof and packable. Available in multiple colors including this vibrant blue, red, and mossy green.

Winter’s freeze-and-thaw cycle can be murder on clay and ceramic pots, causing them to crack and chip. Before freezing temperatures set in, I bring them inside and scrub each one with this brush to remove any soil and debris before storing them for the winter.

These sheepskin gloves are form-fitting (even for small hands) and will mold to your fingers, so you can tackle detailed work with ease. They also feature strategic pads on your fingers and palm for comfort and to prevent calluses. When you’re done, just toss them in the wash and air dry.

“Leave the leaves” is the new fall mantra, especially when it comes to planting beds where they will provide habitats for insects over the winter. But in areas where you do want to remove them, such as paths and driveways, don’t bag them up and send them to the landfill. Instead place them in a compost bin, like this one, to create leaf mold, a rich mulch made from decomposing leaves. When the leaves have broken down to a dark, crumbly consistency—anywhere from a year to three—spread this invaluable mulch on beds or mix it into your soil.

This lightweight, steel rake can extend from 3 feet to 5 feet with a quick twist of the handle. The tines also open to 22 inches and close to 7 inches to maneuver tight spots.

Every fall, after my major outdoor jobs are done, I thoroughly clean and dry each of my tools and then rub a thin layer of camellia oil on them to prevent rust.

#28. Campbell House: A Restoration-First Renovation by Nuud Studio

From house tours and expert advice to favorite finds and DIYs.

Design-forward shops, hotels, and restaurants for your itinerary.

Renovating? Start here for expert advice, deep dives, and helpful tips.

Two years ago, we shared the sensitively renewed “bush modernist” home of architect Brad Mitchell and interior designer Kerli Valk—a thoughtful renovation that won a 2023 Australian Interior Design Awards Commendation and a 2023 Houses Award for Sustainability. Now the couple, founders of Melbourne-based Nüüd Studio, have produced another award-winning design by following the same successful formula: maximize natural light, create functional flow, focus on exquisite joinery. And, above all else, where possible, make the most of what’s already there.

“One of the most effective ways to manage a budget is to work with the existing character and materials of a building rather than trying to contradict them,” says Kerli. Here, she expounds on the idea.

“When we first saw the property, much of the interior was a combination of pine lining boards, bagged brick, and whitewashed timber ceilings. At the time it felt quite dark and dated, and understandably it was difficult for the clients to imagine how those elements could form part of a new, more contemporary interior.

“Rather than removing them, we looked at how color, texture, and light could change the way they were perceived. The existing ceilings were left largely untouched, the brick walls were celebrated rather than concealed, and the pine-clad walls were painted.

“Retaining these elements was probably one of the largest savings in the project, but it also gave the finished interior much more character. We are often more interested in transforming what is already there than replacing it. Sometimes a relatively light intervention—a change in color, texture or the way light reaches a surface—can completely alter how an existing material is experienced.”

Photography by Sean Fennessey, courtesy of Nüüd Studio.

#29. How to Clean a Dryer Vent

If you’ve recently noticed that your clothes dryer is taking longer to dry clothes than it used to, it’s time to clean the dryer vent. A dryer vent that’s clogged with lint and other debris can make for a longer drying cycle, but it also can trigger a much more serious problem—a dryer fire. Clogged dryer vents are one of the top causes of dryer fires, so it’s critical to know how to clean a dryer vent.

Although it’s a much less dramatic concern, an inefficient dryer can cost you both time and money, tacking on as much as $20 a month to your utility bill. Sure, you could hire a professional to clear out the vent for you, but this is a job that many DIYers can do. Read on to learn how to clean a dryer vent, and how to keep it well maintained.

The DeWalt 6-Gallon Poly DC Wet/Dry Vacuum delivers powerful cleaning performance in a compact design that goes wherever the mess is—like behind the dryer in a laundry room or under the passenger seat of a vehicle in the garage. With its 20-volt battery operation, wet/dry versatility, and semi-automatic filter cleaning, this portable tool helps DIY homeowners work efficiently without being tethered to an outlet.

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

With a few tools on hand and safety precautions in mind, cleaning a dryer vent is an easy project you can do yourself.

The first and most important step is to cut power to the clothes dryer. To maintain safety, don’t do any work on the vent while the appliance is drawing electricity. The simplest and safest way to cut power is to unplug the unit. Keep in mind that this may require pulling the dryer out from its current position. Don’t strain yourself. If the machine is too heavy to move on your own, enlist help from another person. If you have a gas dryer, close the valve on the gas line as well.

Dryer vents are typically easy to find. Look for a thick silver or white hose coming from the back of the dryer. It should be about 4 inches in diameter and can be made with flexible white vinyl, thin aluminum foil, semi-rigid aluminum, or completely rigid aluminum piping. Once you have located the vent hose at the back of the dryer, just follow it along to the place where it exits the home. It should be held in place at both ends by a circular bracket that fits over the top of the 4-inch hose and tightens around the transition vent piping.

Pull the dryer out from the wall as far as your vent hose will allow (typically, about 1 to 2 feet). Place a drop cloth on the floor to catch debris. (This is especially important for a vent that has never been cleaned, because there is likely to be a large amount of accumulated hair, lint, dust, and dirt.)

Use a screwdriver to loosen the clamp that keeps the vent hose attached to the dryer. Depending on your dryer vent set up, you may only need to detach the hose at the back of the dryer. If your circumstance requires it, detach the hose from the wall as well and place the hose on the floor.

With the vent hose detached, you have a few choices for how to quickly remove the bulk of the debris in the vent:

No matter which dryer vent cleaning method you choose, be sure to clean up the debris inside or outside of your home. The method illustrated in the photos above (inserting a dryer vent brush from outside of the home and pushing debris downward into the basement laundry room) requires sucking up the lint and other gunk collected on the drop cloth with a shop vac.

Once the debris is removed, reattach the hose and tighten the clamps. Then slide the dryer back into position against the wall.

Use your hands or a vacuum attachment to clear out any accumulated lint in or around the exterior dryer vent cover. Wipe away remaining dust and debris with a microfiber cloth to ensure that the ventilation system is completely clean.

When the vent looks clear, go back inside the house, plug the dryer back in, reopen the gas line if you have a gas dryer, and run the empty machine on the air-dry setting for about 20 minutes. Check outside to make sure that both air and any remaining lint are blowing out of the vent before checking this important to-do off of your list.

There are several dryer vent cleaning safety precautions that make the job easier and safer.

It’s important to clean your dryer vent at least once a year. If the buildup is so great that you can’t break through the lint, hire a professional.

A thorough yearly cleaning isn’t quite enough, however. It takes regular dryer maintenance to ensure that the appliance operates safely and efficiently.

While there are some electric dryers that are designed to vent indoors for locations like apartments and condos, this isn’t the case with most household dryers. If you have access to an exterior wall, it’s better to vent outdoors. Gas-powered dryers always need to vent outdoors to prevent the buildup of hazardous gases.

There are some apartment-sized electric dryers that may vent indoors, but venting inside can lead to serious mold, mildew, and other moisture-related issues. Venting indoors with a gas dryer, however, is absolutely not safe. The fumes produced by burning natural gas can build up indoors and cause serious harm or even death.

Venting an electric dryer into the garage may seem like a good idea, but unless the garage is always open to the outdoors, you will run the same risk of creating moisture-related problems, like mold and mildew. Likewise, venting a gas dryer into the garage can cause toxic fumes to increase within the enclosed space, causing a significant hazard to anyone within the garage.

To reconnect a dryer vent hose, simply loosen the existing brackets to allow the vent hose to slide over the transition pipe. Then tighten the brackets, making sure that they are tight enough to prevent the vent hose from sliding off or shifting. If the problem persists, you may need to replace the brackets or the vent hose.

‘Tis the season for a refresh. Start here with our checklists, tutorials, and cleaning product recommendations to get your home and property in shape for Spring.

#30. Your Home Flooded? Here’s Exactly What to Do Next To Minimize Damage

Parts of the U.S. are facing an increased risk of flooding. Here’s your no-panic playbook for if it ever happens to you.

As the warm air from a super el Niño makes its way across the North American continent, parts of the U.S. are facing increased risk of flooding in 2026 and 2027, according to Newsweek. The potential for disastrous wind and rain events during the winter is so great that the governor of California had already declared a statewide state of emergency as early as September. Southern states, from California to Florida, face the possibility of heavy rain, making flood response preparations even more important for people in these areas than in previous years.

Of course, you don’t have to wait for torrential rains to be at risk of flooding. A plumbing problem, like a toilet overflow, a burst pipe or a backed-up floor drain, can be just as serious. Whether your house flooded because of a natural disaster or a plumbing problem, timely response is of the essence to avoid mold and structural damage to your house and belongings as well as denials on your insurance claims.  The following checklist — informed by insurance and home restoration experts — will help you get ready.

“Water and electricity are the biggest immediate safety risk after a flood,” says damage remediation expert Sam Hickerson. Water flooding your basement or ground floor may come into contact with wall receptacles or other electrical equipment. If the power is still on, the water may be electrified.

Shut off the power yourself if you have a dry pathway to the main panel. If you have to wade through water to get to the panel, call the power company to have them do it remotely. Stay dry until you know the power is off.

Even after you’ve shut off the power, it’s important to stay out of the water, because it could be contaminated with sewage, animal waste and agricultural runoff. The bacteria, viruses and toxic chemicals these contaminants carry are obvious health hazards.

If the water is deep, there could be all sorts of debris in it that you can’t see, including broken glass and sharp metal. One false step, and you could suffer a cut that would be instantly infected if there are pathogens in the water.

“Many policies have specific windows for reporting flood damage, and delays can complicate a claim,” warns Hickerson. To avoid delays, call the insurance company as soon as it’s practical to do so and file a claim.

You don’t need to provide any details at this point; you’re just getting the claims process started. It will be the adjuster’s job to assess those details at some point in the (hopefully) near future.

Houston Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images

You’ll need photos to document the damage, and foundation repair specialist Shane McClintic recommends taking them before you start the cleanup. “Go around your house and film everything that suffered damage,” advises Gulf Coast flood insurance specialist Brad Spurgeon. “Once you have cleaned up your damage your pictures won’t be as useful to the insurance company.”

In particular, advises restoration expert Vinnie Guaderrama, take a picture of the highest point of water on the wall. “Always photograph the data plates with the model and serial numbers before you remove water heaters, furnaces, washers and dryers. Many people forget to do this, and it can be difficult to find these numbers at a later date.”

Try to have a restoration professional on site quickly. Restoration pros are in short supply during widespread disasters, however, so you might be working by yourself. If so, “work fast,” says McClintic.

According to the EPA, mold probably won’t grow on water-damaged materials if they dry within a 24-48 hour period. Once mold gets a foothold, it’s much harder to eradicate, so time is of the essence.

Because you need to work quickly to prevent mold from getting a foothold, water extraction should begin as soon as you can do it safely. “A wet/dry shop vac works for smaller amounts,” says Hickerson,  “but a sump pump is worth renting for anything beyond a few inches of standing water.”

When you can’t reach a hose into corners and under cabinets, don’t be afraid use a bucket and sponge to get the water out. Any standing water you leave will raise the room humidity and promote mold growth.

When you uncover previously submerged carpet, McClintic recommends either taking it outside or, if you can’t, pulling it back to air it out. “Prop up furniture on wood blocks to stop wicking,” advises Hickerson, “and pull baseboards, not just carpet, in flooded rooms.”

Drywall is a porous material that wicks water upward, and once waterlogged, you need to replace it. To avoid having to replace entire walls, McClintic advises cutting the drywall about a foot above the water line.

If you have valuable documents or photos,  Guaderrama suggests putting them in the freezer (if it’s working) until the house dries out. Strangely enough, the freezer is a low-humidity environment.

Run fans and dehumidifiers and, if it isn’t raining, open doors and windows to get air circulating and dry the space as fast as possible. Hickerson warns that things may look dry when they really aren’t, so he recommends keeping the fans running for at least 48 hours, and perhaps as long as 72 hours.

Once the area is dry, Florida restoration pro Darren Impson advises cleaning and sanitizing with an anti-microbial cleaner. He says you should call a restoration company for this, but it might be hard to schedule one immediately after a disaster.

If you do it yourself, the CDC recommends using dish detergent and water or one cup of bleach per gallon of water. Use bleach only on hard, non-porous surfaces. It doesn’t penetrate porous materials like wood and won’t reach mold embedded in them, so scrub porous surfaces with detergent until the mold is gone.

People often forget to look in HVAC vents, says Hickerson, and if they’re wet enough to support mold, the blower could contaminate the rest of the house as soon as the HVAC system turns on, despite your sanitation efforts.

Uncover any vents that were submerged, ventilate the ducts to dry them out, then sanitize the metal with a bleach solution (metal is non-porous, so bleach is effective). It’s best to wait until you’ve done this before you operate the HVAC system.

Orchids slow down in fall, but a few key October changes to light, water, and feeding will keep the roots healthy and set up the next round of flowers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Plenty of people care for a moth orchid the same way in fall as they do in summer. But by October, days are shorter, the sun sits lower, and the furnace dries out the air. Growth slows down, and that slowdown is when the plant starts setting up its next flower spike.

Fall orchid care isn't hard. You'll move the plant, water it less and feed it less, and you'll want to look it over more closely than you did in summer. Most of that takes only a few minutes.

These six tasks apply to moth orchids (Phalaenopsis) and other common types of orchids sold in grocery stores as houseplants. Yellow leaves, wrinkled leaves, and stray roots show up a lot this time of year, too.

Light fades fast this month, and that bright spot from July might not cut it by November. East windows are the safest bet most of the year for meeting orchid light requirements. Once winter settles in and the sun hangs low and weak, though, a south window usually works, too.

With orchids, the leaves will tell you if you've got it wrong. A deep, dark green is the giveaway for not enough light. Too much shows up as a reddish edge, although that's less of a worry this time of year. For an interior room or a dim corner, try a grow light like the Sansi full-spectrum LED plant lamp, available on Amazon, which clips onto the side of the pot.

Whatever you do, just don't let the leaves rest against cold glass, as this can cause chilling damage, leaving unsightly dark patches on the foliage.

Slower growth means the potting mix stays wet longer. That makes overwatering the bigger danger until spring. Wait until the mix is nearly dry, then water thoroughly and let it drain. Never leave the pot sitting in a saucer of water.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Root color is often the best guide for watering orchids – they're silvery white when dry and green right after watering. Traditional moisture meters like the popular Yamron 4-in-1 don't work very well with orchids, as chunky bark mixes throw off probe readings; however, the Sustee Aquameter, available in a pack of 5 on Amazon, uses a moisture-absorbing wick rather than electrical conductivity, making it better suited, as long as it's in contact with plenty of potting mix. The indicator changes color from blue to white as the growing medium dries out.

Hold off on repotting orchids in the fall unless the bark has started to break down and become compacted, which can restrict airflow around the roots and increase the risk of rot.

It's tempting to keep the summer feeding schedule year-round. But an orchid's fertilizer needs follow its growth, and growth slows as the days shorten. You can still feed moth orchids that are putting out new leaves, just less often. Every third or fourth watering is enough. Use a water-soluble fertilizer like Better-Gro Orchid Plus, which you can pick up at Walmart.

Plants with no new leaves, roots, or spikes can go without until growth starts again. Extra fertilizer on a resting plant mostly means soft, leafy growth and fewer flowers. It also leaves salts in the bark, so flush the pot with plain water now and then.

So what does the furnace do to an orchid? Indoor humidity can drop below 30 percent once the heat runs regularly. Most tropical orchids prefer humidity around 60 to 75 percent. A spray bottle won't close that gap. The mist is gone within minutes.

To increase humidity for your orchids, try a pebble tray. Simply fill a shallow tray with gravel, add water about halfway up the stones, and set the pot on top. This Brussel's Bonsai tray from Amazon is a ready-to-go solution. Don't let the roots touch the water.

If you have a lot of houseplants grouped in one space, humidity will naturally increase. But if orchids are still struggling, try a small humidifier – this Pure Enrichment MistAire Ultrasonic Cool Mist Humidifier from Walmart runs up to 25 hours per fill.

Healthy-looking orchids can still have pests. Many hide where you'd never notice unless you go looking, and a warm, dry house helps some of them along. Grab a flashlight and magnifying glass (this Large Magnifying Glass with 37 LED Lights from Amazon covers both) and check under the leaves, down in the joint where each leaf meets the stem, and along the flower stems.

Isolate any orchid with pests. Then dab the mealybugs with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol (you can buy it cheaply at Walmart), and keep the alcohol off the leaves.

Cool fall weather triggers a new spike in many moth orchids (Phalaenopsis). Four or five weeks of days around 77°F (25°C) and nights near 68°F (20°C), or a little cooler, reliably bring one on. Days above 82°F (28°C) can hold it back.

New spikes look a lot like new roots at first. Check the tip. Spikes have a flattened, mitten-shaped tip and usually come up between the lower leaves, and root tips are round.

Stake the spike while it's still flexible – you can pick up a pack of bendable orchid stakes from Stroller on Amazon – and don't turn the pot once buds form.

Prune old brown spikes off at the base. Viruses can spread on tools, so dip the blades in a 10 percent bleach solution between plants.

Three problems come up again and again once orchids move indoors:

An orchid doesn't need much from you this month. More light, less water, lighter feeding, and a quick pest check cover most of it. Keep those habits going through winter, and there's a good chance a fresh spike shows up before spring, followed by a gorgeous run of flowers.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#32. Thermostat and Then Some

At the most recent International Builders’ Show, I stopped by the Resideo booth and learned about the range of smart home offerings from its Honeywell Home and First Alert brands. After speaking with a product rep about replacing my unreliable thermostat, I decided to give a few products a try: the Honeywell Home X8S Thermostat, a remote sensor, and the First Alert VX1 HD Doorbell.

The thermostat performs all the tricks you would expect from a smart home product, like scheduling and remote access, and the doorbell images show up on both my phone and the thermostat screen.

I’ve had more fun than I probably should using the intercom feature.

Of the new products, the remote sensor is my favorite. It functions as a remote thermostat, so by placing it in the bedroom, my wife and I keep our sleeping space comfortable all night instead of relying on the hallway temperature. And like the main thermostat, the sensor also monitors air quality.

The thermostat, sensor, and doorbell work on the First Alert app, as do the products I soon plan to buy: the First Alert smoke detector and the water leak/freeze detector, both of which push notifications via the app when triggered. I will also be upgrading my security cameras, which are woefully outdated.

There is also an interface module that would allow control of my ERV via the app, but it requires the ElitePro thermostat. Be sure to check compatibility with all your equipment before taking the plunge.

In addition to the app, all these products are compatible with the leading smart home ecosystems like Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and more. They are available at many major retailers or via resideo.com.

#33. 9 Drought-Tolerant Plants for Challenging Sites

Every plant at Skyline Meadow Farm in Oakland, California was chosen to thrive in conditions that would challenge many others: wind, compacted clay, searing sun, and recurring drought. The selections below combine California natives with Mediterranean and drought-adapted ornamentals to deliver year-round interest while supporting the region’s pollinators and conserving the water table.

See More from this Garden: Transforming a Large Property with Functional Landscape Design

‘Santa Barbara’ sage is a fragrant subshrub prized for its soft silvery foliage, whorls of lavender flowers, and relaxed, coastal beauty that evokes the wild hillsides of the California Coast.

Vibrant flowers in hues of red, orange, and yellow make this annual (sometimes short-lived perennial) an eye-catching addition to almost any garden.

This is an odd little shrub with cascading, fine-textured blue-green foliage that forms an unmistakable mop-like mound, providing softness and playful textural contrast along borders, slopes, and retaining walls.

A deciduous small tree prized for its extravagant, orchid-like blooms in shades of pink, lavender, and white that repeat from late spring through fall, this woody attracts hummingbirds throughout the season.

You’ll love this standout native for its magenta flowers that erupt along bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge, followed by heart-shaped foliage and rich fall color. It tolerates clay soil.

This upright, densely branched evergreen shrub forms effective privacy screens and windbreaks quickly, with deep green and white foliage that holds on even through drought.

With its large, wine red leaves and billowing clouds of smoky pink plumes in summer, ‘Grace’ delivers dramatic foliage color and textural contrast on a grand scale.

A spreading, fast-growing ground cover smothered in deep powder blue flowers each spring, it suppresses weeds, stabilizes slopes, and supports native pollinators with minimal irrigation.

An evergreen hybrid tree with spectacular cinnamon-red peeling bark, clusters of urn-shaped pink flowers, and strawberry-like red fruit, ‘Marina’ provides year-round multiseason interest as a specimen or large screen.

#36. Pamela Anderson’s Best Garden & Landscaping Tips, Straight From Her Backyard

The actress and activist shows how a thoughtfully designed landscape can create a memorable first impression.

In Pamela’s Garden of Eden, Pamela Anderson transforms her grandparents’ former property into a peaceful, sustainable retreat. In the second episode, Anderson and her team reimagine the landscape surrounding the “roadhouse,” a tree-shaded home with plenty of character but an undefined entrance and overgrown gardens.

By rethinking how visitors move through the space—from the first step onto the property to the front door—they create a lush landscape that’s both welcoming and romantic. Here are a few ideas worth borrowing for your own yard.

A latticed wooden arch sets a clear threshold, making the transition into the garden feel inviting and purposeful rather than purely decorative.

Flagstone pavers set in an irregular pattern create a path that feels naturally worn rather than newly laid.

A landscape refresh doesn’t have to mean starting over. Anderson and her team transplanted existing plants with their roots intact, preserving established growth while reshaping the layout.

What could have been an all-white patio setup is elevated with subtle patterns and soft colors, adding personality without overpowering the space.

Swapping gray trim for white and introducing black window frames adds contrast and gives the exterior an updated look without structural changes or a major investment.

Butterfly bush may attract butterflies, but this native shrub is just as easy on the eye and offers even more for wildlife.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When I think of a butterfly garden, butterfly bush (Buddleja davidii) is one of the first plants that comes to mind.

The clue's in the name: with its colorful flower clusters and nectar-rich blooms, it's easy to see why this shrub is such a favorite among gardeners looking to attract butterflies. However, butterfly bush has a complicated reputation, as it can become invasive in parts of the United States.

Sterile cultivars like this stunning Psychedelic Sky™ Butterfly Bush from Nature Hills offer a promising solution, producing little to no viable seed and reducing the risk of unwanted spread. That being said, if I was looking to create a garden that's as beneficial to local wildlife as it is beautiful, I'd also consider adding another native flowering shrub to the mix.

Shop Non-Invasive Butterfly Bush Options:

Native to much of the United States, buttonbush (Cephalanthus occidentalis) has its own distinctive charm, with spherical white blooms that attract pollinators and fruits that provide food for birds.

It's a wildlife-friendly butterfly bush alternative worth considering, particularly if you have moist soil or a rain garden, and a way to add another valuable native plant to the landscape.

Rather than producing tapered flower clusters like a butterfly bush, this uniwue alternative develops distinctive round, white flower heads that look a little like pincushions. Each globe is made up of many tiny tubular flowers, which typically appear during summer and fill the air with their sweet honey-like fragrance.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Its flowers provide nectar and pollen for bees, butterflies, and other pollinators, including hummingbirds. In fact, it's also one of the plants to add if you want fireflies in your garden, too. Win!

As if that weren't enough to make it a must-grow, the shrub also develops rounded clusters of fruits after flowering, which provide food for birds, including some waterfowl and songbirds (and likely your birth month bird, too!). Basically, for gardeners who want a shrub that looks interesting as well as serving a purpose, buttonbush is an appealing choice.

There's one important thing I'd consider before bringing buttonbush home: its preferred growing conditions. This butterfly bush alternative naturally grows in wet habitats, which means it thrives in moist to wet soil and can tolerate poorly drained areas where many ornamental shrubs struggle. All of which means that, if I had a spot that regularly stayed damp after rainfall, buttonbush would be high on my list of shrubs to consider.

It grows in full sun to partial shade, although flowering is generally better with adequate sunlight. Once established in the right location (aka not a dry garden or a hot border with fast-draining soil), though, it can become a standout and long-lived feature of the landscape.

So, sure, butterfly bush may still catch the eye, but buttonbush offers a compelling alternative for the right garden. If your soil stays moist and you have room for a larger shrub, this native beauty deserves a closer look... and, in return, it'll soon reward you by becoming a buzzing neighborhood hot spot for birds, butterflies, and more!
