#38. The Best Wood-Burning Tools of 2026, According to Our Tests

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

By Mark Wolfe, Additional research provided by Tom Scalisi

Published Oct 20, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

If you’re looking to express yourself creatively in a new way, whether adding an extra touch to DIY projects or starting a small craft business, pyrography is a great place to start—and all it takes is the right wood-burning tool. With one of these heated metal pens, you can burn intricate designs onto wood, leather, and other materials.

To help you find the best model for your needs, we spoke to a skilled wood-burning artist for professional insight, then put seven popular options through hands-on tests. The TruArt Stage 1 Pyrography Pen Wood-Burning Tool Set earned our top pick thanks to its comfortable ergonomic grip, precise temperature control for both soft and hard materials, and a wide assortment of tips neatly organized in a carrying case. Whether you need a simple standalone pen or a complete setup for advanced projects, this guide breaks down what to look for and reviews the best wood-burning tools.

Bottom line: Discover the best wood-burning tools of 2026, tested for comfort, precision, and versatility to suit all skill levels and budgets.

With so many wood-burning products available, choosing the right tool or kit can feel overwhelming. The following list of products, considered among some of the top picks in each respective category, will help you pick the best wood-burning tool for your projects, skill level, and budget.

If you’re fired up to start wood burning, the TruArt Stage 1 pyrography tool set can get you going. This kit features a dual-temp 15-watt (W) and 30W craft-style solid-tip wood-burning pen, a steel letter and number stencil, a tool stand, and a plastic carrying case for safekeeping. It also comes with 21 interchangeable tips, including calligraphy, groove, dot, hot knife, and universal.

The TruArt Stage 1 wood-burning tool has two temperature settings, allowing you to choose between 15W for soft materials and 30W for heavier woods. It’s lightweight and has a comfortable, grippy rubber handle, so beginners can practice their craft for long periods without tiring.

The TruArt Stage 1 pyrography pen was a pleasure to work with, included all the accessories we needed for a variety of craft projects, and didn’t break the bank. The curved handle shape and rubber grip infused a high degree of comfort and control, while the twin heat diffusers reduced heat transfer to the handle, keeping it cooler than the cheaper models we tested.

We especially liked having the three-position power switch built into the handle. Cheaper models have only one power setting and either no power switch or one located midway along the power cord, which gets in the way. Having it built into the tool handle improves range of motion. Also, the option to use either 15W or 30W makes this tool a better pick for a wider range of materials and artistic effects.

Read our full review: TruArt Stage 1 Pyrography Pen Wood-Burning Tool Set

Get the TruArt Stage 1 wood-burning tool at Amazon or TruArt.

The Walnut Hollow Creative Woodburner offers convenience and capability in one package. This tool’s power converter has a built-in stand and an adjustable temperature range between 600 and 1,000 degrees Fahrenheit, despite a relatively low 16W power. It comes with a drawing point, universal shading point, ball point, and a rounded shading point to cover most beginner tasks.

The standout feature of the Walnut Hollow Creative Woodburner is its quick-change wire nibs. Using the included tweezers, you can pull hot points out of the tool and push new ones back in without loosening and tightening any fittings.

We found the Walnut Hollow Creative Woodburner to be a simple and relatively inexpensive entry point into woodburning with wire nib tips. The kit was uncomplicated, and the adjustable power converter let us create lighter or darker patterns in the wood as needed. It was fairly easy to get good results, even with zero prior experience. The tips did not get as hot or heat as quickly as the pro-quality kits we tested, but this kit cost significantly less and took up less space on the work table and in storage.

We had mixed feelings about how the tips on this set connect to the pen body. The large plug-style base is sturdy enough to last a long time, but they fit so tightly into the socket that they require a good bit of force to install and remove. We also wish the kit came with a storage case for the nibs. Still, this pyrography tool is a good value for an occasional-use hobbyist.

Get the Walnut Hollow Creative Woodburner wood-burning tool at Hobby Lobby.

This Plaid wood-burning tool takes much of the guesswork out of getting started in pyrography at a price that might encourage you to start a new hobby. This kit comes with a simple craft-style 25W wood-burning pen with a basic on/off switch and can reach temperatures up to 750 degrees Fahrenheit. It allows beginners to start working without worrying about temperature settings.

This tool has a rubber handle to promote a positive, comfortable grip and a metal stand for storing your pen while taking a break. It comes with two tips for cutting stencils and four tips for pyrography, as well as a plastic case for storing them.

The Plaid wood-burning tool was a budget-friendly pick that worked well for wood burning but produced a bit too much heat for soft materials like leather. Although the kit didn’t come with many extra features, the basic set was adequate for line drawing and silhouettes. With no temperature-adjustment feature, we relied on tip changes, pattern varieties, long and short burn times, and other techniques for shading. The effects were pretty good, but they were more rustic with this kit than with adjustable-temperature models.

For the price, this is a really good buy. The overall quality was comparable to the entry-level Walnut Hollow wood burner, but the price was lower. It would have been nice to have a storage case to keep everything organized when not in use, though.

Get the Plaid wood-burning tool at Amazon, Walmart, or Plaid.

The Professional Dual-Pen wood-burning kit from TruArt is a complete wire-nib kit that comes with 46 wire nibs, a digital 60W power supply, a dual pen stand, and a wire brush and set of files to keep the nibs clean. It also includes a set of needle-nose pliers and tweezers to safely change hot tips.

The digital power supply allows you to dial in the perfect temperature, making small temperature adjustments as you work. It also powers two separate pens, so you can keep two different tips ready without switching tips.

When we opened the TruArt dual-pen wood-burning kit, we were impressed by the sheer variety of tips and provisions for keeping them clean for efficient and precise work. This high level of precision and adaptability came at a premium price that some users may deem excessive.

In operation, the first thing that we noted was that the two pens do not operate simultaneously. A power switch on the side of the control box serves as the “main,” and you can select Pen 1 or Pen 2 with a toggle switch. The pen heats almost instantaneously (in less than 30 seconds), which was much faster than any other wood burners we tested. On the high temperature setting, the tips become glowing red hot.

We also noted that the relatively short posts on the wire nibs reduce the distance between your hand and the workpiece. This makes the tool feel very natural—more like a writing pen and less like a clunky soldering iron. The high control and precision levels set this kit apart from all the others we tested. Those who don’t mind paying a premium for a pro-quality tool will get their money’s worth.

Get the TruArt professional wood-burning tool at TruArt.

Our best pick for beginners is a sturdy yet inexpensive tool with broad functionality and a selection of the most commonly needed tips. The Walnut Hollow Creative wood-burning tool is a basic kit that comes with a wire tool rest and four craft-style twist-on tips: a cone point, a shading point, a universal point, and a flow point.

This 25-watt tool attains tip temperatures up to 950 degrees Fahrenheit, allowing you to effectively work with most woods. With no temperature control, you learn how to control effects by pen position and timing. The tool features an on/off switch wired into the power cord and a heat shield between the element and the handle.

Although it was a rather spartan kit with none of the bells and whistles found on pricier models, the Walnut Hollow tool tested very well in terms of basic functionality. The tip heated in less than 2 minutes. The included tips were adequate for making wide and narrow lines, dots, curves, circles, and shading. Between this model and our budget pick, this one heated faster, reached higher heat, and seemed to maintain its heat more consistently. For just a few dollars more, we would choose this pick.

Get the Walnut Hollow Value wood-burning tool at Hobby Lobby.

Woodworking projects sometimes require higher tool temperatures to effectively burnish dense hardwoods. With a maximum output of 1,050 degrees Fahrenheit, the 30W Wall Lenk wood-burning tool is more capable than most other single-temperature hot tools. The kit includes a tool rest; 10 craft-style tips for woodburning, soldering, leatherwork, stenciling, and foam cutting; and a molded plastic storage case.

This professional-grade hot tool features a shortened element shaft that enables a high level of control and dual heat shields to maintain a comfortable handle temperature. The assortment of twist-on tips includes universal, calligraphy, shading, flow, texture, cone, script, knife, soldering, and dot points.

In light-colored woods like balsa, birch, and pine, it was tough for us to see the effects of the temperature difference between this 30W 1,050-degree-Fahrenheit Wall Lenk wood burner and the Walnut Hollow burners that are rated 25W and 950 degrees Fahrenheit. To test this tool, we did a side-by-side comparison on harder, darker oak.

This tool produced darker burns after simply tapping the surface with the hot tip and holding it in place for 1 to 3 seconds. It also produced smoke about 2 seconds faster than the competitor, so consider the potential for this tool to overheat more sensitive materials. For outstanding temperature control, pair it with the Wall Lenk Temperature Regulator.

Get the Wall Lenk wood-burning tool at Amazon, Woodcraft, or Rockler.

Our favorite wood-burning kit includes a variety of pyrography, crafting, and soldering tips to serve the widest range of hobby and home-repair needs. Equipped with a built-in variable-temperature controller, the 25W Walnut Hollow Versa-Tool heats up to 950 degrees Fahrenheit. It also boasts a cushioned rubber grip for outstanding comfort and control.

The tool comes with a folding stand, storage case, 11 interchangeable twist-on tips, and a spool of lead-free solder. The list of tips includes universal, flow, shading, calligraphy, tapered, soldering, hot-knife, mini-flow, mini-universal, cone, and hot-stamp points.

The Walnut Hollow Versa-Tool tested similarly to our Best Overall pick but missed out on the top spot because of its chunkier build and the clunky controller location on the power cord. Those two issues made it a little less comfortable to work with, even though the temperature range and accessories were excellent. We really liked this tool’s versatility, and although comfort was somewhat less than ideal, it was still easy and relatively comfortable to work with. The rubber overmolded handle was definitely a plus.

Get the Walnut Hollow Versa-Tool wood-burning tool at Hobby Lobby.

Before getting our hands on the products, we reached out to Aney Carver, owner of Pyrocrafters, who has over 10 years of experience creating gorgeous art with wood-burning tools. Her advice? “Make sure you are investing in a quality machine from a good company. It’s tempting to buy something low-cost online, but I’ve had so many people reach out to me when the low-cost unit they bought breaks.” We took this advice into consideration and looked at reputable brands across a range of price points.

With this in mind, our testing prioritized user comfort and convenience, fast heating, and steady heat maintenance. We included picks for both craft-style and wire-tip tools. In addition, all of our craft-style tool recommendations include multiple tips to suit a wide range of design uses.

Carver added that temperature control is a worthy consideration. “Most wood burning is done at a low to medium heat, but you want a tool that offers a variety in case your types of projects vary.” We know that shoppers will be working with different types of wood, leather, and other materials, requiring a change in temperatures for optimal results, so we included several of our favorite products that boast an excellent temperature-control range.

Following the manufacturers’ instructions, we tested each wood-burning tool on basswood, pine, and oak. We timed the heating process, tested multiple tips, evaluated the burn patterns, measured power cords, and noted any special high and low points. We recorded our observations on a scoring rubric to determine the overall winner and the best picks.

There’s more to choosing the best wood-burning tool for you than deciding between craft style and wire nib. Consider the projects and materials, as well as how much flexibility and convenience will suit you. Keep the following points in mind while shopping for your new wood-burning pen.

Pyrography is an ancient art form that’s becoming a hot trend! For beginners, it’s important to understand a few things about wood-burning tools before purchasing a kit. There are two main types of tools, and they offer different levels of ease of use and level of detail, so it’s worth choosing one to fit your project needs and abilities.

Craft-style (also known as solid-tip) pens are essentially soldering irons with a solid brass tip. They take a while to heat up, but they hold their temperature well, making them a bit more user-friendly and less fussy than some finer tools. This is why they’re an excellent choice for beginners to learn some pyrography basics.

Craft-style pens have their limitations, however. As mentioned, they take a while to heat up and cool off, which can slow you down a bit. Also, they don’t allow you to create very fine details, regardless of what kind of tip you use.

For more professional results, look for a wood-burning tool with a wire nib. These wire elements operate like the heavy brass tip of a craft-style pen but with some additional benefits. Since there is less mass, they heat up much faster, allowing you to jump into your work almost instantly. They also allow a greater level of detail with intricate patterns and drawings.

Though wire nibs heat up quickly, they also cool swiftly. They take some getting used to, but once you have the knack for regulating the temperature, your crafting should become easier.

The species and type of wood you burn on has a significant impact on the end product. While some species may be more readily available than others, you should select wood with the right texture and grain. For pyrography, wood with small, tight pores and a smooth surface yields superior results. Use a relatively soft wood that burns easily. Birch, alder, beechwood, balsa wood, pine, and mahogany all work well and vary in affordability. Conversely, oak, walnut, and hickory can be too hard and grainy for quality work. That said, if you opt to burn challenging woods, use a wire-nib wood-burning tool so you can manipulate the temperature more easily.

Both styles of wood-burning tools allow you to swap out tips to get a variety of results. Each type of tip excels at a specific job, so you may wish to own an assortment for your pyrography creations.

Universal tips are general-purpose workhorses that do a decent job of outlining, shading, some detailing, and some lettering. For smooth curves and outlines, you might find a rounded flow tip works, as it coasts across the surface easily. Calligraphy tips work very well when creating advanced cursive text. There are many other types of tips that you can collect as your work becomes more advanced.

When shopping for a wood-burning tool, there will be a wattage rating in most product descriptions. The wattage refers to the amount of power the pen can produce, which relates to the temperature the pen can reach. The most capable wood-burning tools will have power ratings around 60W, but beginners will likely find a 30W wood-burning tool will serve them well enough.

The wattage rating relates to the temperature the tool can produce at the tip. The higher the wattage, the higher the temperature. Higher-wattage tools can reach temperatures higher than 900 degrees Fahrenheit, but not all materials need 900 degrees Fahrenheit at the tip to produce a quality burn.

Look for a wood-burning tool with an adjustable temperature range to dial in the perfect temperature for your project. Harder, denser woods may require the highest temperature setting, while softer materials (including leather) can do quite well with a lower setting.

In general, these temperatures can range from 500 degrees Fahrenheit on the low end to 900-plus on the high end. Not all quality burners allow you to choose an exact temperature value; instead, select a wattage rating like 15W, 30W, or 60W, with the higher rating producing the most heat.

Craft-style tools are generally slower to warm up. Their brass tips have more thermal mass, which can take between 5 and 8 minutes to reach the appropriate temperature. Wire-nib tools, on the other hand, can be ready to go in under a minute. Their wire points are simply heat elements, and an electrical charge can pass through very quickly. For speed and convenience, wire nibs are by far the better option.

What feels comfortable while practicing pyrography may change as your skill level increases. Newbies may find that a large, thick tool with rubber padding feels comfortable and ensures a good grip. These tools can prevent cramping, allowing you to put in plenty of hours honing your craft.

In time, as your grip becomes more natural and less likely to cause cramping, you may prefer a thinner tool. This will offer a bit more flexibility and dexterity, allowing you to tackle fine details with more elegance and flow.

As a new wood burner, you might be interested in purchasing a kit with all the accessories to get started. These kits include things like a tool stand with a sponge for cleaning the tip, pliers for changing hot tips, stencils, and other pieces to help your creative journey.

Some kits even come with accessories for soldering, allowing your wood-burning tool to pull double duty as an electrical repair tool. In fact, a soldering-iron stand can be very helpful while cutting your teeth in pyrography, as it provides a safe place to hold your hot tool when your hand needs a break.

If you decide to purchase a stand-alone tool, you can still buy an accessory kit separately. You can also buy sheets of carbon paper to make pattern transfers an easier process.

Now that you have a bit of background on some of the best wood-burning tools, you may still want more info. Check out the answers to some commonly asked questions and answers about wood-burning tools. If you still have questions, reach out to the tool’s manufacturer to chat with customer service.

Using a wood-burning tool takes some practice, but the actual process is straightforward. Plug the tool into an electrical outlet, turn it on, and adjust the temperature, letting it heat up (this can take up to 8 minutes). Then, holding the tool by the rubber grip, slowly drag the tip across the surface of the wood or other material, allowing the tip to burn in your design.

You can’t keep your tips from getting dirty, but you can clean the carbon buildup. Some kits come with sponges that you moisten and use to wipe the tip clean. You can also pass the tip over a piece of fine sandpaper to remove carbon buildup.

Yes. Wood-burning tools work great on leather. If you work on a piece of fresh vegetable-tanned leather, lower the converter to a low setting for ideal results.

#39. Two Tools, One Clear Picture

Thermal imaging is one of my go-to diagnostic practices for investigating comfort complaints, air leaks, missing insulation, and moisture problems. In recent years the cameras themselves have become smaller, more affordable, and easier to use, but the biggest advancement isn’t better image quality—it’s better image interpretation.

The Testo 860i takes a different approach than a traditional thermal camera. Instead of building everything into the camera body, it uses your smartphone for the display, processor, image storage, and reporting platform. The wireless camera communicates through the free Testo app, which keeps the tool compact while taking advantage of a phone’s high-resolution screen and computing power.

What caught my attention, though, isn’t the camera itself; it’s the way the camera works with the Testo 605i thermometer/hygrometer. Connected wirelessly through the app, the two tools combine surface temperatures with ambient temperature and relative humidity to automatically identify areas at or approaching condensation conditions.

Instead of manually comparing surface temperatures to the dew point, the app performs the calculations and highlights potential problem areas using a simple green-yellow-red color scale.

Cold corners, thermal bridges, window perimeters, and attic bypasses can all be evaluated more quickly because the software helps interpret what the camera is seeing. That combination reduces one of the biggest challenges of thermal imaging—knowing whether a temperature difference is a problem or not.

By combining thermal imaging with humidity measurements and automated dew-point calculations, the two tools help reduce interpretation errors and let an investigator spend more time diagnosing the building instead of crunching numbers. The Testo 860i is available for $413 and the 605i is available for $145.

— Randy Williams, editor, Green Building Advisor. Photos by the manufacturer.

#40. A Little Bit of Everything in Christine’s Deck Garden

Hi GPODers! Today we’re visiting Christine (@the_blooming_deck) in Bethesda, Maryland (Zone 7b), where she’s transformed her two-level deck into a thriving container garden filled with vegetables and flowers. As I’ve always said, you don’t need a ton of space to have a garden. Just a vision and the determination to make it happen.

My garden is a little oasis of beauty, food, and tranquility, created primarily in containers on my two-level deck in Bethesda, Maryland. What began as a love of growing my own food has evolved into a welcoming outdoor retreat filled with vegetables, herbs, fruit trees, colorful flowers, and visiting wildlife.

I grow everything from tomatoes, peppers, and leafy greens to lemons, olives, and seasonal flowers, making the most of the different sunlight conditions throughout my space. One of my favorite features is the seating area surrounded by lush plants, where I can enjoy my morning coffee, listen to the birds, and appreciate the changing seasons.

Even the shadier corners of my deck have become beautiful little gardens of their own. My garden is a reminder that you don’t need a large yard or elaborate landscape to create something special. With creativity, patience, and a collection of containers, even a modest outdoor space can become a place that nourishes both body and soul.

My Meyer lemon (Citrus × meyeri, Zones 9–11) tree

#43. If You See a Traffic Light With a Yellow Border, Here’s What It Means

Some traffic lights have yellow borders while others don't. Here's why reflective frames matter and why they aren't on every signal.

Traffic lights are something drivers encounter almost every day. And even though they’ve been looked at countless times, most drivers barely even notice some of the subtle details about them.

One detail that stands out at some intersections is a bright yellow border around the traffic lights. It’s a small change to a familiar piece of road equipment, and it can make a difference at busy intersections. Learn what the borders do and why they’re not on every traffic light.

The yellow borders around traffic lights are strips of reflective material attached to a black panel called a backplate. Much like reflective road signs, they catch vehicle headlights and help drivers spot traffic signals at night. The black background also makes the colored lights easier to see against bright skies and nearby buildings.

“This treatment is recognized as a human factors enhancement of traffic signal visibility, conspicuity, and orientation for both older and color vision deficient drivers,” according to the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA).

The borders also help drivers recognize intersections during power outages.

“This countermeasure is also advantageous during periods of power outages when the signals would otherwise be dark, providing a visible cue for motorists to stop at the intersection ahead,” according to the FHWA.

Research suggests the borders can improve road safety. A 2005 study found that adding yellow reflective borders reduced crashes at the intersections researchers examined. The FHWA now recognizes them as a proven safety measure. However, the borders don’t change how traffic lights operate or how long each light stays on. Drivers still need to follow normal traffic rules, including when a signal stops working.

Federal traffic safety standards allow yellow reflective borders, but don’t require them at every intersection. State and local transportation agencies generally decide where to install them. Some intersections may need better visibility because of glare, nearby buildings, or poor lighting. Transportation agencies may also add reflective borders when installing new signals or upgrading existing equipment.

Cost can influence those decisions, too. Adding reflective strips to an existing backplate is relatively simple, but installing a new backplate may require additional support. That’s why two intersections along the same road might have different traffic lights. The lack of a yellow border doesn’t necessarily mean a signal is unsafe.

#44. 19 Fall Gardening Practices That Will Protect and Enrich Your Soil in Winter

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Updated Oct 19, 2026 4:13 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Throughout the growing season, garden plants work together with microbes to break down and use organic matter within the soil, depleting the soil’s nutritional content. During the offseason, unprotected garden beds are at risk of erosion, a process that strips away the topsoil, contributing to additional loss of nutrients as well as soil compaction, which reduces water infiltration and drainage, damaging the soil structure.

The seasonal cycle can leave a garden infertile and unproductive. “They say nature abhors a vacuum,” says Peggy Riccio, horticulturist and garden communicator at Pegplant.com. But when the growing season comes to an end, the soil-building season begins. With help from Riccio, research, and experience, this list of tips can help gardeners focus on rebuilding soil.

Harvest all you can before the first frost. Then, remove spent plants and compost them. Keeping the dead vegetable plants in place increases the chance that disease-causing pathogens make their way into soil and survive the winter, so it is best to remove the plants before winter arrives. Riccio removes her vegetable garden plant material to prevent pathogens from thriving, “though adding fallen leaves or other organic matter can help prevent winter weeds and can break down to feed helpful organisms in the soil,” she says.

Place healthy removed plant material into your composting bin or pile instead. Composting generates heat that kills insects, disease spores, and weed seeds, and breaks down matter into a soil amendment that retains a bulky structure and nutrient value plants love.

While tilling a garden often is touted as a solution for opening the soil structure to improve drainage and stimulate soil microbial activity, it is best used only when preparing a new garden bed or vegetable plot—particularly if the area has endured foot traffic—that will be planted in the coming spring.

It is better to skip yearly tilling for established beds. “Rototilling brings up dormant weed seeds, causing them to germinate,” says Riccio. Sand- or clay-based garden soils that are low in organic matter are degraded by tilling.

When you use a rototiller on an area for a new bed, aim for about 8 to 10 inches of soil depth to account for future root growth. Add some compost and let the soil do its work over winter before full spring preparation and planting.

Turning just the top few inches of soil ahead of seeding fall cover crops can work in organic compost or soil amendments such as bone meal and shredded fall leaves, and give the growing medium a boost. After removing summer garden debris, add a layer of compost to the soil surface, and use a broadfork or shovel to gently pierce the surface and open it up to enable air and organic matter to permeate the soil. Follow up with a cover crop, cool-weather garden crop, or organic mulch.

“Another way to prevent erosion is by planting a cool-season vegetable like lettuce or spinach,” says Riccio. This extends the growing season by offering fresh vegetables well into fall or even winter in climates where temperatures seldom dip below freezing. “You also can cover cool-season vegetables with a row cover,” adds Riccio, to protect them from chill. According to North Carolina State Cooperative Extension, a 2-ounce row cover lets in 30 to 50 percent of light but protects down to temperatures of 24 to 28 degrees Fahrenheit.

In addition to providing tasty produce, these winter vegetable plants are good for the soil. Actively growing plants eliminate soil compaction and erosion, improve drainage, and add beneficial organic matter to the soil.

Winter garden cover crops, like winter rye, hairy vetch, and winter peas and other legumes are grown solely for their soil-building capabilities. They eliminate erosion and compaction of the soil, and help retain fertility by scavenging nutrients. Planting cover crops (also called green manure) is one of the best things you can do for your garden soil. “Check with your local extension agent to find the recommended cover crops for your state,” Riccio suggests.

The garden is a perfect place to dispose of fallen leaves. Use a lawn mower to mulch and bag the leaves before spreading them in a 3-inch layer on the garden bed. Mix them into the garden soil for a boost of trace minerals and a source of earthworm food.

You can leave a thin layer (an inch or less) of mulched leaves on grass under trees to rejuvenate the soil underneath. Or, pile them up to 2 feet deep or more, shredded or not, and cover them with permeable fabric to hold them in place. The decomposed leaves will be incorporated deeply into the soil by assorted soil dwellers, transforming the bed by spring.

Ego’s 21″ Select Cut has cutting capability and power, plus an upgraded self-propel system and a specialized multi-blade deck. Read the review.

It takes time for bacteria and fungi that live in the soil to turn compost, soil conditioner, and organic fertilizers into a part of the soil. These materials feed soil-dwelling microbes, which release nutrients that plants can use. In warm weather this happens quickly, but the processes slow down in the cold.

Organic soil amendments like kelp meal, blood meal, and bone meal are loaded with beneficial nutrients that gardeners can add in fall to promote healthy soil during cold months and into spring. When applied in the right amounts, they break down slowly over several months. If overused, blood meal can burn plants because of its high ammonia content, so add it in fall to prevent chance of ammonia toxicity.

Adding fresh manure from your chickens or your neighbors’ horses in spring also can do way more harm than good. Fresh manure needs at least 6 months to age and let high levels of ammonia leach out. Applying manure in late fall ensures it will age and that the nutrients will be available for an early spring planting. Wait to add bagged (or aged) manure until the soil temperature has dropped to 50 degrees Fahrenheit and work it into the soil immediately.

Fall is also the time to care for the soil around perennial crops like asparagus, rhubarb, horseradish, and sunchokes. When the plant tops have died back for the season, remove and compost them. Then pull any weeds and apply a fresh layer of organic compost that will slowly replenish the soil all winter long. Finally, mulch around the plants and in the pathways between.

Likewise, some perennial shrubs and flowers can benefit from a layer of mulch around the root zone to help warm them through summer. Apply mulch to plants that are more cold-tender. If possible, wait until right after the first hard frost to mulch around tender shrubs with an organic type of mulch, such as wood chips. This helps stabilize the temperature of soil right around freezing, and with luck avoid freezing and thawing cycles, which are detrimental to plants.

Fall is a good time to use up old compost and free up space in the compost bin for the new material being removed from the garden. Whether you mix it in or spread it on the surface, a fall compost application replenishes the organic matter that was used up during the growing season. It increases the living space for beneficial soil microbes, and cool weather veggies and winter cover crops grow better with the added nutrients.

It might sound counterintuitive, but keep weeds growing in your garden through in fall and winter. Cool-weather weeds like chickweed and henbit provide a valuable service, similar to cover cropping, by holding the soil in place and scavenging nutrients. Even among the crops you’ve planted they are unlikely to cause real damage. So let them grow until late winter, then hoe the tops off and add them to the compost pile.

Although you are quite familiar with the garden layout by fall, you might not remember come spring the location of plants and how each fared. Taking a few notes before winter hits can help you prepare for the coming year. For example, did afternoon sun do a number on one of your perennial plants or vegetables? If so, think about how to introduce afternoon shade for next summer.

Rotating crops is essential to balancing nutrients in the soil you’ve worked so hard to prepare. Vegetable families vary in how much of a particular nutrient they take up and in the types of diseases or insects they attract. Make a quick sketch or notes about the locations of your tomatoes and green beans before pulling them all up so you can switch them next year. While you’re at it, note problems you had so you can do a little research and avoid repeating mistakes.

If you’re unsure about your soil type or if you noted problems like slow plant growth or soil that drained too quickly (or not at all), use the garden’s downtime to test the soil. Get some clues from neighbors and gardening associations in the area, since soil types can be similar across regions. For an even better idea of your soil’s health, test it for pH and nutrient levels.

Send out for comprehensive testing if you’re serious about improving soil health over winter, or try a home test kit, like the MySoil Test Kit, the top pick in our tested guide to the best soil kits. Then, use the results to start amending the soil’s nutrient or pH imbalances.

Raised beds solve some soil issues and with hugelkultur, a traditional permaculture practice, you can build healthy soil with rotten wood and plant debris. Layer organic materials, including logs of old trees, from largest (or least decomposed) to smallest (think grass clippings) as you mound up to create a mini ecosystem. If mounded correctly, a hugelkultur bed can stand on its own. Or you can bury it about 10 inches deep in a trench.

For a more contained and attractive approach, use hugelkultur to fill most of a large raised bed. As with the mound, place the largest logs or branches on the bottom and add smaller ones as you go up. Let it sit all winter to begin decomposing and settling. Fill the top of the bed with your preferred mix for raised beds. Having built the base with found materials saves some money on the amount of soil you’d otherwise have to purchase. And at the same time, you’re practicing a sustainable gardening method that reuses organic materials.

Cover empty garden beds to keep topsoil and soil amendments in place, and help protect soil structure and composition over the cold months. First, heap on some compost or an organic mulch; there is no need to work it into the soil. Then, find an old blanket, cloth, or permeable landscape fabric and cover the bed. The blanket or fabric will let in some moisture, but not full snowfall or rainfall at once, reducing compaction of the soil.

In spring, remove the cover and let the organic compost take in some air for a week or so before mixing it into the soil.

If soil tests reveal an imbalance in pH levels, start amending in the fall. Most plants require neutral pH (6 to 7). If soil is too acidic to grow vegetables, start adding lime. If it is too alkaline, begin adding sulfur. According to Riccio, the level to work toward depends on soil test results and the plants you want to grow in a particular bed. “If you want to grow blueberries, you know it has to be acidic,” she says. That requires adding sulfur to get the pH level to the desired 4.5 to 5.2 range. “But it takes time, so you have to add the sulfur in the fall and plant the blueberries the following year,” says Riccio.

Likewise, Riccio says that when trying to change hydrangea color with acidity, many instructions suggest applying it in spring and waiting 60 days before reapplying if needed. “By then, you’re already in and it could take months to work,” she says. It is better to start acidifying the soil around the shrubs with aluminum sulfate in the fall, and then apply again in spring.

When cleaning up in fall, enthusiastic gardeners often dig down and remove all the roots of annual vegetables and ornamental plants. Consider, however, some of those remaining roots as living elements that can keep feeding the soil over winter. The tiny microbes that are already in the soil will digest the root matter and help turn soil into healthy humus. It’s the same concept as planting cover crops or applying organic matter in fall; those small roots should work into the soil and not be messy or in the way come spring.

One caveat: Only leave the roots of healthy plants. You’ll want to thoroughly remove the entire root system of any diseased plant.

Fruit trees might settle down for a winter’s rest, but more goes on in those cold months than you might think. For example, fruit set depends on a certain number of chill hours, depending on the fruit type. Keep fruit trees healthy through their rest period by applying any of a number of dormant sprays in late fall or early winter. Horticultural oil mixes with water to smother insects or their eggs that are using fruit trees for their own winter rest. Sulfur controls fungal growth in cool damp winter conditions; dormant oil can control scale in apples and pears; and copper spray can control some bacterial or fungal diseases like peach leaf curl.

The specific timing and fruit tree sprays to add can get complicated, so research instructions by fruit type and product information, or call a tree service professional to perform this fall task.

The lasagna gardening method, also known as sheet mulching, is about building healthy garden beds. Riccio has a small space and says that the lasagna method is easy to use in her backyard in fall to create a new bed. This involves putting down several overlapping layers of cardboard and alternating green and brown organic matter such as leaves, straw, and kitchen scraps on top. “Cardboard comes into this house; you’ve got to get rid of it,” she says.

When making your lasagna bed, wet the bottom layer of cardboard to secure it in place and jumpstart decomposition. Then add layers of the same kind of organic ingredients you might put in a compost pile. It can take several months to break down, so fall is the best time to start. “This gets rid of cardboard, and adds organic matter to the soil,” says Riccio. The decaying cardboard feeds soil microbes and earthworms.

All You Need to Care for Your Lawn & Garden

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.

You don't need a sprawling backyard or a celebrity budget to enjoy the calming effects of water. Four experts explain how to get started.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Jennifer Aniston, also known as Rachel from my favorite show, Friends, has one of the most famous homes/gardens on the internet right now. Rachel Green never had a garden, and Aniston is clearly making up for it. Really, this Bel Air property is having a moment; from the Japanese-inspired planting to the roses, people are trying to copy it in even the tiniest of spaces. But it’s her koi pond (pictured below) that is really doing some heavy lifting, especially when it comes to the Japanese aesthetic.

It’s the kind of feature that looks like it required some serious money and expertise, but it actually starts with one pretty straightforward question. As Kendahl Kreps, Director of Marketing at Oase North America, puts it: “Do you want fish?” Everything else follows from there.

A post shared by Stephen Shadley (@stephenshadley)

Before even thinking about logistical questions like what size, depth, and budget you’re working with, it’s helpful to get clear about what exactly you want from a water feature. Kreps says to ask yourself, “What do I want from this? Sound? Aesthetics? Nature habitat? All of these things can help you decide what kind of water feature you should go with.”

Joe Zawistowski, founder of Black Koi Water Features and a certified Aquascape contractor with 25 years and over 300 ponds behind him, agrees: “A pond that fits your lifestyle is one you will enjoy for decades.”

If the answer is fish, you’ll want to head toward a proper koi pond. If it’s sound and movement without the maintenance commitment, a pondless waterfall delivers almost the same experience. “A pondless waterfall gives you the sight, sound, and planting of a full water feature without an open body of water,” says Zawistowski. “Most of the water sits invisibly in a buried reservoir under a floor of rocks, and the pump recirculates it continuously. No fish, almost no maintenance, and the footprint can be as small as ten by ten feet.”

Two things you absolutely can’t compromise on when it comes to a koi pond are depth and filtration. Koi need a minimum of 18 inches (45 cm), but Zawistowski pushes for three feet (90cm): “Three feet eliminates successful heron hunting because herons wade to strike and can’t reach fish at that depth.”

Aiza, a sustainability writer at GreenerPulse, adds that depth also matters for temperature stability: “Shallow ponds heat up and cool down too fast, and the fish get stressed."

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

When it comes to filtration, every expert is on the same page. “Prioritize filtration,” says Jacob Romkee, landscape expert at Thumbtack. “A poor filtration system can undermine the whole project.” Aiza is equally direct: “The filter is the worst place to save money.”

Almost every first-time pond owner will encounter an algae problem. Kreps recommends a combined UV and mechanical filter system, like this TotalPond system on Amazon. She says, “UV bulbs and filter foams polish the water to make the fish look as if they are floating.”

If you don't have fish in your pond, a floating solar-powered fountain, like this Mademax design, is a simple, affordable way to add movement to the water. It can also help improve circulation and aeration, keeping the pond fresher and reducing stagnation.

While you may think you need to have a full koi pond to get the same look as Jennifer Aniston, it’s actually not the only option. If you have a small space in an urban garden or patio, a container pond or raised feature can give you most of the same benefits. Romkee has seen genuinely creative approaches: “I’ve seen people turn bathtubs, hot tubs, tiered fountains, and even disguised kiddie pools into water features.”

Aiza and Zawistowski are quick to point out one big caveat, both claiming that a smaller water volume is much less forgiving. They tell me that temperature swings happen much faster and water quality can shift very quickly, so a container pond actually requires more attention and maintenance, not less, as you might assume.

Plants around the pond are essential to making it look embedded in the garden rather than simply dropped into it. Zawistowski uses marginal plants like iris and pickerelweed to soften the edges, water lilies to shade the surface and suppress algae, and, for the surrounding landscape, weeping and upright Japanese maples, catmint, ornamental Carex grass, and coneflowers.

Romkee adds ferns, Japanese iris, and creeping ground cover as strong options, with one firm disclaimer: “I’m much more cautious about bamboo because it’s so hard to get rid of once planted.”

Jennifer Aniston’s koi pond works so well because of the restraint she and her designer, Stephen Shadley, used. Kreps says, “An asymmetrical pond shape, a few carefully selected stones, controlled planting, and one strong focal element such as a bridge or sculptural rock.”

Aiza puts it even more simply: “Resist the urge to add three fountains.” Still water, well-placed stone, and a limited plant palette make a complete formula. The engineering, as Zawistowski says, should disappear entirely, “so the feature looks like natural erosion rather than something that arrived on a truck.”

#47. Previous Homeowners May Still Have Access to Your Smart Home — Here’s How To Check

Smart cameras, locks, and thermostats may still be linked to former owners. Experts explain how to check access and secure each device.

Moving into a new property can be a scary and intimidating process. There are so many new things to learn, and the last thing a new homeowner wants to worry about is home security. And while you should absolutely change the locks after moving in, proper safety measures don’t end there.

It’s possible for previous homeowners to still have access to smart home tech they left behind. Security cameras, thermostats, and other smart devices can remain linked to the previous owner’s account without the new homeowner realizing it.

Learn which devices need resetting, and what new homeowners should do to keep their homes secure.

Unfortunately, there’s no easy way to tell just by looking at a device.

“It is much safer to just assume the old owner can still access them,” says Kurtis Baron, an offensive security specialist at the cybersecurity company Echo Secure.

Nathan Connell, founder and editor of Future Technology, recommends trying to register each device through its manufacturer’s app. If the app says someone else already owns it, the previous account may still be linked. For example, Ring has an ownership transfer process for previously registered cameras and doorbells. Connell also recommends checking the app’s shared users list for unfamiliar accounts.

“The previous owner, or anyone they shared access with, can still unlock doors, open the garage or watch camera feeds remotely,” Connell says.

Baron recommends resetting all inherited smart devices, including cameras, alarms, locks, thermostats, and connected appliances. Some might be harder to identify than others. According to the Federal Trade Commission, “light bulbs or security systems may be difficult to detect as ‘smart’ devices.”

Homeowners should follow the manufacturer’s instructions to remove the previous account, factory reset each device, and register it under their own account. Google’s moving guide explains how to transfer Nest devices, some of which require the previous owner to remove them first.

“Old PIN codes on keypad locks and alarm panels often stay active too,” Connell says.

“The key to privacy in the Internet-of-Things (IoT) world is your router,” according to the FTC, since connected devices typically access the internet through it.

Baron recommends getting a new router rather than reusing the previous owner’s equipment. Homeowners should also set up their own Wi-Fi password and check for unfamiliar connected devices.

Some older smart devices may need replacing, especially if the manufacturer no longer provides security updates. Baron recommends replacing anything that can’t be fully factory reset or has become outdated.

A device linked to a previous owner’s account doesn’t always need replacing, though. Some manufacturers offer ownership transfers or can help new homeowners regain control. Until then, homeowners shouldn’t rely on an inherited smart lock or security camera for protection.

Connell recommends asking sellers for a list of every connected device included in the sale, along with manuals, hub information, and account transfer instructions.

The FTC also recommends leaving behind manuals that explain smart features, particularly those that might be difficult for new homeowners to identify. Sellers should confirm they’ve removed their accounts and revoked access for anyone previously authorized to use the devices.

Baron suggests including a requirement in the closing paperwork confirming that the seller has removed access to all smart devices included in the sale. That gives new homeowners a chance to set up their own accounts and passwords without leaving access in someone else’s hands.

Kurtis Baron, offensive security specialist at Echo Secure, a UK cybersecurity and penetration testing company Nathan Connell, founder and editor of Future Technology

Federal Trade Commission, “Buying or Selling a “Smart” Home? Read This” Federal Trade Commission, “Securing Your Internet-Connected Devices at Home” Ring, “Transfer Ownership of a Ring Device” Google Home and Nest Help, “Moving Guide for Google Home and Nest Devices”

#48. Alliums: Just As Good As Tulips—But Better

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

Though tulips are highly prized for a spring bloom, they do have their drawbacks, among them the need for a team of gardeners planting thousands every autumn to achieve the ideal look. Also, they die disgracefully. Alliums, on the other hand, are the most versatile of bulbs, taking on multiple personalities, channeling elegance with the best of them. They last forever, multiplying among themselves, and are a fraction of the price of the needy tulip.

Photography by Kendra Wilson, unless otherwise noted.

Allium is a sociable bulb, making friends wherever it goes. It thrives in the company of silver or gold, feathery or spiky, in a gravel garden or formal border. The bulbs are not fussy and the seed heads are so attractive that they stay in place, multiplying the population at the same time. Tulips? What are they?

Allium christophii is the horticulturalist’s favorite, its starry, metallic flowers complementing all of its neighbors. A pack of 15 Allium christophii bulbs is €8.85 at J.Parker’s. In the US, they are $19 for 12 at White Flower Farm.

There is one caveat which needs to be dealt with sooner than later. The leaves look lovely in the bare earth of early spring but they shrivel later—allium needs to be have an understory.

For a crowd of alliums, ‘Purple Sensation’ is the one, flowering over a long period from May. ‘Purple Sensation’ bulbs are widely available. In the UK, Crocus has them starting from £6.79 for 10 bulbs (£9.99 for 5 organic bulbs). In the US, the bulbs are $20 for 12 at White Flower Farm.

Tulips are the glamor flower of late spring. Well, Allium siculum–also known as Allium bulgaricum–has wonderfully wafting green/cream/plum blooms that rival the elegance of tulips. Overlapping with tulips in May, the pendulous flowers are doing interesting things in July, like reaching straight upwards, as they turn into seed heads.

Different heights and colors of allium mix well together. Allium varieties planted in this English seaside garden in Kent  include A. nigrum, ‘Mount Everest’, and A. atropurpureum.

Allium has an uncanny way of adjusting color as the season progresses. The shorter, later-blooming Allium sphaerocepholon (above), reaching about two feet, begins its bud life as a green drumstick before slowly turning claret red.

Months after tulips have acted out their protracted slide into dormancy–or death–the allium is entering its next phase.

N.B.: This post was first published October 2013; it has been updated with new images, links, and prices.

#49. Loch Capsule Countertop Dishwasher Review: Tested Against a Bosch

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Published Oct 19, 2026 11:52 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

I’ve used plenty of full-size dishwashers, but the Loch Capsule was the first countertop model I’d tested, and I had my doubts. Could something only 10.3 inches wide really clean dinner plates and glassware as well as a built-in dishwasher?

The Capsule is sleek and modern, but at 18.3 inches tall, it won’t fit beneath every set of upper cabinets. I set mine on a stainless-steel rack over my sink, which worked well. It doesn’t require permanent plumbing; a separate clean-water tank feeds the dishwasher, while a hose drains the dirty water. At 26 pounds and with a built-in carrying handle, it’s portable enough to move between locations.

That was my biggest question, and the side-by-side comparison to my built-in Bosch answered it. The Capsule holds about two place settings; I generally had room for dinner dishes from two people along with a couple small bowls or pans. Removing the flatware holder creates additional space when needed.

Loch offers cycles ranging from a 15-minute Quick Wash to Heavy Duty and Intensive Clean, plus settings for glassware and everyday loads. The Capsule reaches temperatures as high as 167 degrees Fahrenheit, and its stainless-steel tub helps retain heat. It’s relatively quiet while operating, too.

As a comparison test, I served a big Italian dinner, complete with spaghetti, then let the dirty dishes sit for a couple of hours. After a quick rinse, I divided them between the Capsule and my Bosch dishwasher and ran both. The dishes and glassware that came out of the little Capsule were every bit as clean as those from the Bosch. That got my attention.

The feature I didn’t expect to appreciate so much was UV-C sanitizing. The Capsule has dedicated short and long UV cycles that can be run without water, plus a fruit-and-vegetable program that incorporates UV light. I put newly purchased produce through the fruit-and-vegetable cycle and then I felt better about serving it to my family. Loch also suggests the UV function for items such as baby bottles and other small household objects.

Water conservation is another strong point. The 15-minute cycle uses just 2.69 liters, or about 0.7 gallon, making the Capsule appealing anywhere water use matters.

At $459.99, the Capsule isn’t inexpensive, and I wouldn’t buy one for my own kitchen because I already have a full-size dishwasher and don’t mind washing a handful of dishes by hand. But I’m not really who this dishwasher is for.

I can see it being exceptionally useful in an RV, houseboat, tiny home, cabin, dorm room, or other small living space without a dishwasher hookup. A college student who uses a few dishes throughout the day or an RV couple who wants to load the day’s dishes and wash them all at once could get far more value from it. Its biggest limitation is capacity, but buyers who understand they’re purchasing a personal dishwasher rather than a miniature replacement for a full-size family dishwasher may be surprised by just how well the Capsule performs.

#51. Fall Container Designs Full of Color and Texture

Happy Friday, GPOD! Another week in the books, and there’s no more pretending it’s summer. Fall temperatures have officially arrived here in the Midwest, and the changing leaves are putting on quite a show before winter returns.

While the growing season is winding down for many of us in colder climates, there’s still plenty of opportunity to enjoy color in the garden with seasonal containers. And few people do it quite like Howard, a Chicago-based container designer who has been creating seasonal displays for nearly four decades!

Howard has previously shared his spring container creations and creative Halloween displays with us. Today, he’s sharing a new collection of fall containers from a project in Glencoe, Illinois (Zone 6a). Enjoy!

Ornamental cabbage and kale (Brassica oleracea cvs., annual) make up the bulk of this stunning fall arrangement. But for me, those clusters of deep burgundy berries are the real stars of the show! The twisting woody stems add a touch of whimsy that ties the whole thing together.

I love how the earthy tones of these pots complement the stonework beneath them. The boxwoods (Buxus sempervirens, Zones 5–8) really make the ruffled foliage of the ornamental cabbage and kale stand out. It’s a great example of how containers can complement the surrounding landscape and elevate a small corner of the garden.

At first glance, I thought these weathered containers were one long planter box! Grouping them together rather than spreading them throughout the space makes such an impact. Ornamental cabbage and kale remain the stars of the arrangements we’ve seen so far, while accents of purple and burgundy appear again and again, whether through foliage, flowers, or berries like those in the first photo. It’s a great example of how repeating colors and plants can tie a design together without making every arrangement look identical.

Another gorgeous combination! The pots and plant tags scattered on the ground are all too relatable. The work can be messy, but the results are beautiful.

One more from Howard, this time at a different house on the same rainy day. Everything about this arrangement is a 100/10! The sculptural effect of those twisting woody vines with golden berries hanging throughout is just stunning. WOW! The colorful croton foliage complements the berries beautifully. There’s so much to love about this design, and I’m definitely saving it for future inspiration. What a way to say “Welcome home!” Thanks for sharing these with us, Howard! Looking forward to the next.

#52. Expert Advice: The Retrouvius Guide to Using Reclaimed Stone in Remodeling Projects

From house tours and expert advice to favorite finds and DIYs.

Design-forward shops, hotels, and restaurants for your itinerary.

Renovating? Start here for expert advice, deep dives, and helpful tips.

Our catalog of more than 10,000 products featured on Remodelista.

Remodelista’s members-only directory of architects, designers, and landscape professionals.

Stone is a natural resource that’s been used in interiors since before the wheel was invented. Though durable and costly—not to mention inimitably patterned and textured—it’s almost never thought of as reusable. But it should be say the eco-minded team behind Retrouvius, a combination salvage company and design studio in London’s Kensal Green that lead by example.

Founded by Maria Speake and Adam Hills, who met in architecture school, these master recyclers approach just about all building materials as worth reclaiming—and all design projects as opportunities for creative reuse. They recognize that reclaimed stone is challenging—supplies are limited, unpredictable, weighty, and often require specialist contractors. But its many appeals and workarounds lead them to salvage all sorts: stone concourse floors, office foyers, fireplaces, dead stock from masons’ yards, and fishmongers’ slabs, among other things. Inspired by Retrouvius, we enlisted them to show us their work and fill us in on ways to consider applying saved stone in our own quarters.

Photography courtesy of Retrouvius (@retrouvius), unless noted.

Finding the right materials can take some digging. Search everywhere from architectural findings dealers and salvage yards to Facebook Marketplace, Craig’s List, and Buy Nothing. Stone yards also offer remnants and other discards at a notable discount. And Los Angeles salvage business Unbuilt showcases “luxury leftovers,” unused residential construction goods, including stone slabs and tiles, priced to sell. Adam, who runs Retrouvius’s salvage business, notes that shifting fashions impact stone prices: “Some marbles are relatively affordable and some are pricey depending on current desirability: Rosa Aurora, for example, is not expensive; sought-after onyx, meanwhile, is costly, so we reuse small and broken pieces in resourceful ways.”

In addition to being incredibly heavy, much salvaged stone requires a stonemason with the right expertise and tools to cut it. That can get complicated and expensive, which is why the Retrouvius team’s top tip is to “work with the salvaged stone in its existing format and dimensions when possible.” A simple approach is to use a slab as found to create a tabletop, shelf, or backsplash (scroll to the end for a prime laundry sink example). When building or remodeling an interior, carved ornamental stone panels can be incorporated into the wall design. And if you sort reclaimed stone into common widths, you can create flooring and wall paneling in patterns that minimize the need for cutting. Examples of all of these approaches below.

Retrouvius spokesperson Nicolas Hughes also mentions that the reverse side of a lot of reclaimed stone is marked by “dots and dabs” or “little metal pegs,” used as positioning marks.”These are easy to scrape off and not a problem. Likewise, for future reuse, it’s responsible to choose an adhesive that is weaker than the stone itself, so the stone doesn’t shatter on removal.”

A cautionary note: some polished stone can get slippery: test it before use as flooring, and, if needed, hone it or add a runner.

One detail they’d do differently: the walls are cast concrete, a material Retrouvius no longer uses because of its high environmental cost.

The whole project is a puzzle work of saved materials: the cabinet fronts are faced with 18th-century Viennese marquetry floorboards and the newly restored and raised flooring is a mix of original and reclaimed pine. For a full tour, go to A Country Home in the City By London’s Masters of Salvage. Photograph by Tom Fallon for Retrouvius.

Nicolas, notes that wood and stone pair well, and “since timber is much cheaper and easier to cut, it can be used as a spacer to reduce stone wastage.”

Many of Retrouvius’s featured projects also appear in their recent book, Retrouvius, Designing Houses from a Philosophy of Reuse.

Think of it as composting on the go. The right kitchen scraps can break down directly in garden beds, enriching the soil for future planting.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’m a big believer that you don’t have to spend much money to have a beautiful garden. I often repurpose containers and other household items outside, but one of my favorite ways to recycle is to return food waste to the earth. Each fall, I bury kitchen scraps in my empty raised beds using a mix of ingredients I’ve found that makes an ideal free soil improver. The scraps break down in place over winter, adding organic matter to the soil before spring planting.

This on-the-go trench composting method doesn't require a compost bin, but I keep a countertop caddy, similar to this best-selling Oxo Good Grips Bin on Amazon, in my kitchen and add suitable scraps as I go. Every few days, I empty it into a shallow trench in one of my beds, then move on to another spot. I keep going until the ground freezes.

You don’t need every ingredient in my mix; simply leave out anything you don’t have. I can’t recommend adding other ingredients in their place, though. Think of it as an easy, personal way to put kitchen scraps to work in the garden, rather than a precise recipe.

Fruit and vegetable scraps are the main ingredient and make up the bulk volume of the mix. I save things like banana, citrus, and cucumber peels, apple cores, carrot tops, and other uncooked trimmings. As they break down, they return organic matter and some of their nutrients to the soil.

I chop larger or tougher scraps into pieces about 1 inch (2.5 cm) long. Smaller pieces are easier to mix into the soil and should break down more readily. I avoid scraps covered in oil, sauce, or dressing, and I never add any meat, fish, bones, or dairy to the mix.

I add about 1 cup of used coffee grounds to a batch of scraps. Grounds contain small amounts of nutrients and organic compounds, but despite what you may have seen in viral gardening videos, they need time to break down before the bed is ready for planting.

I let the grounds cool first, then stir them through the scraps so they don’t clump together. I keep the amount modest: coffee grounds are best used in moderation.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Eggshells are one of the most widely used food scraps in gardening. For my mix, I save the shells from a couple of eggs, rinse off any residue, let them dry, and crush them as finely as I can – with a blender or pestle and mortar, like this Gorilla Grip design on Amazon.

Eggshells contain calcium, although they break down slowly, so I don’t expect them to act like a quick calcium feed. I add them because they’re easy to save and can eventually become part of the soil.

Many gardeners also sprinkle eggshells around plants in the hope of deterring soft-bodied pests such as slugs. I don’t rely on them for pest control, though, so I crush mine and add them to the mix instead of scattering them around plants.

While not technically a scrap, I add a small handful of plain rolled oats – about ¼ cup – to my recipe. Oatmeal is grain-based, so it’ll break down into organic matter in the soil, adding lots of nutrients. Oats are also believed to help stimulate root growth, as they contain phosphorus and feed beneficial mycorrhizal fungi in the soil.

I add a little cinnamon to my mix for its much-touted properties as a natural fungicide, rooting hormone, and pest deterrent. These uses are popular with gardeners, although I wouldn’t rely on a small amount buried in the soil to solve an existing problem. You don’t need much – around ½ teaspoon is plenty for my mix.

If I have some flat beer left over, I add a small splash – about ½ cup – to my caddy. Beer contains yeast and other organic compounds, which is why some gardeners use it in compost or homemade plant feeds. I don't know whether it makes a measurable difference to my soil, so I wouldn't open a bottle specifically, but it’s a way to use up a little leftover beer rather than pour it down the drain.

Once my caddy is at least half full, I take it out to an empty bed. I dig a trench about 12–18 inches (30–45 cm) deep, add the scraps, and mix them with some of the soil, then I fill the trench back in. I make sure the food waste is fully covered, with at least 6–8 inches (15–20 cm) of soil above it, so that it doesn't attract animal pests.

One key point is that I don’t try to fill the whole bed with one enormous batch. As a rough guide, I use about 1 gallon (4 L) of mixed scraps for each 4-by-4-foot (1.2-by-1.2-m) bed, spread along a short trench. If I have any leftovers, I bury the rest in another empty spot or save it for another trench. Alternatively, buy a cheap compost bin, like the Vevor small compost tumbler from Home Depot, and start building that up as you go.

The exact amount isn’t a strict recipe. I keep the layer of scraps fairly modest, chop everything small, and cover it well. I avoid digging close to established plants, whose roots could be disturbed, and don’t bury food waste in beds where I plan to plant immediately.

Kitchen scraps are moist and break down more easily when mixed with some dry material. If I have them, I add a couple of handfuls of shredded leaves to my trench batch. They contribute carbon and help keep the scraps from clumping together.

I sometimes add a small handful of fresh grass clippings, too. They’re nitrogen-rich, but I use them sparingly and mix them through the scraps and leaves so they don’t form a dense, soggy layer. Both additions are optional home composting extras: I just use what’s available in the garden.

By spring, the scraps will have had several months to break down. When I’m ready to plant, I check the area first. If I can still see recognizable pieces, I leave that part of the bed alone for a little longer and plant elsewhere. If the soil looks settled and the scraps have mostly disappeared, I loosen the surface and get the bed ready for planting.

I don’t expect this one mix to replace compost or a soil test, and I don’t use it as a precise fertilizer. For me, it’s a simple way to make use of kitchen leftovers and add them back to an empty garden bed while there’s time for them to break down before spring.

#54. The 2027 Colors of the Year Are Here — Here’s What Your Favorite Paint Brands Picked

Paint brands have revealed their 2027 Colors of the Year, from soft greens to deep browns. See which shades could work in your home.

Top paint brands around the world have announced their featured paints for 2027, giving homeowners new options to consider for their next project. This year’s selections cover quite a range, including soft greens and blues, darker earth tones, and even a wood stain.

Each brand has its own approach to what homeowners might want in the coming year.

Sherwin-Williams and HGTV Home by Sherwin-Williams chose Celery (SW 6421), a light green with yellow undertones.

“With subtle yellow undertones, this soft, muted green strikes a perfect balance between an airy pastel and a grounded, herbal hue,” according to Sherwin-Williams.

The color pairs with cream trim and natural wood and works well on walls, cabinets, and ceilings.

Behr selected Grounded (T27-01), a dark olive green with brown undertones inspired by nature.

“The shade’s organic warmth creates a sense of calm and renewal, making every room feel inviting and effortlessly livable,” said Kayla Kratz, Head of Color at Behr Paint Company, in a company release.

Behr recommends Grounded for interior and exterior projects, including living rooms and kitchens.

Valspar chose Cottage Door (8004-38E), a muted blue-gray with warm undertones.

“A cultural shift toward intentional living and self-reflection calls for authentic and heartfelt hues,” according to Valspar.

The color pairs with light neutrals and natural wood, making it suitable for bedrooms and living rooms. It also works on exterior siding and front doors.

Glidden selected Artifact (PPG10-16), a smoky blue-gray with hints of aqua.

“A calm, fresh aqua that feels like a reset for your whole space,” according to Glidden.

The shade works in bedrooms, bathrooms, and living rooms. Glidden also pairs Artifact with lighter blues and earthy greens.

Dunn-Edwards chose French Press Coffee (DEBN07), a dark brown with subtle purple undertones that resemble dark roasted coffee.

“The overall effect is one of layered, lived-in luxury,” according to Dunn-Edwards, describing its 2027 color trends.

The brand recommends French Press Coffee for powder rooms, home offices, and entryways, where its darker color can stand out against lighter finishes.

Dutch Boy selected Deep Rooted (311-7DB), a warm orange that resembles terracotta.

“As paint trends show people seeking more grounding, authenticity, and connection, Deep Rooted brings stability and a sense of calm to the home,” according to Dutch Boy.

The brand suggests pairing the color with soft whites, blues, or greens on walls and furniture.

Clark+Kensington, available at Ace Hardware, selected Vantage Point (38B-4), a rich blue with muted undertones.

“Vantage Point brings a sense of warmth and character to interiors,” said Kim Lefko, Chief Marketing Officer at Ace Hardware, in a company statement.

The brand pairs it with warm neutrals and lighter colors through its Drift and Mellow palettes.

Graham & Brown chose Rose Earth, a soft pink with earthy undertones.

“Rose Earth takes its cue from the natural mineral pigments traditionally sourced from clay deposits in Italy,” according to Graham & Brown.

The brand designed it to complement its Roselle Grove floral wallpaper, though the color also works with greens and warm neutrals.

C2 Paint selected Pueblo (C2-510), a warm shade between dusty pink and terracotta.

“For 2027, we’re looking outward again, toward the things that make us feel alive,” according to C2 Paint.

Pueblo changes with the light, appearing pinker during the day and darker in the evening. C2 Paint suggests pairing it with deep browns, muted greens, and natural materials.

Minwax chose Pickled Oak, a light wood stain with warm undertones, as its 2027 Color of the Year.

“As homeowners gravitate toward more organic interiors, Pickled Oak answers the call for clarity and connection,” according to Minwax.

Unlike paint, the stain lets the wood grain show through. Homeowners can use it to lighten the appearance of old furniture, shelving, and other wood projects.

#55. Garden Visit: Niwaki Founder Jake Hobson’s Japanese-Inspired Mini-Forest

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

Jake Hobson is a master pruner. He’s written two books on pruning: Niwaki: Pruning, Training, and Shaping Trees the Japanese Way and The Art of Creative Pruning: Inventive Ideas for Shaping Trees and Shrubs. And he’s the founder of Niwaki, a Japanese-inspired garden tool company headquartered in England. So, it should come as no surprise that his home landscape in Dorset is full of artfully shaped, precisely pruned shrubs and trees. But it isn’t your usual English garden with clipped hedges—nor is it a replica of Japanese gardens.

“Everything I do is inspired by Japan, but I’m deliberately not making it all Japanese,” explains Hobson. “There’s no koi pond or red bridges.” Not only does Hobson eschew any decorative Japanese elements, he avoids ornaments altogether. “For me, a Japanese garden is creating a sense of a landscape—an idealized landscape—within the plot. If you bring in ornaments, you ruin the magic of scale. Whereas, if all you’ve got is plants, you can create a sense (if you squint and after a couple of drinks) that maybe you’re looking out into a deep forest.”

Hobson has successfully created this illusion of landscape within his small space. Looking out the windows of the home he shares with his wife, Keiko, and their son, or gazing at photographs of Hobson’s green, layered garden, it’s hard to believe that it’s not much bigger than a tennis court.

When Hobson and his wife bought the house, the backyard had four sheds, a mismatched bunch of overgrown conifers, and a ton of concrete paths. They ripped it all out, leaving just the evergreen hedge that blocks the view from a neighboring building. Hobson commissioned a local carpenter to build a single new shed inspired by a Japanese “summer house” at the back of the plot. Then he planted dozens of evergreen and coniferous shrubs and trees that he has been training and pruning for the last fourteen years. The result is a garden that feels like its own miniature world, full of living sculptures.

Let’s take a tour of Hobson’s garden, which he photographed himself. (You can follow him on Instagram @niwakijake.)

N.B.: This post was first published November 2025.

#56. Kitchen of the Week: A London Architect’s Sky-Lit Compact Kitchen

From house tours and expert advice to favorite finds and DIYs.

Design-forward shops, hotels, and restaurants for your itinerary.

Renovating? Start here for expert advice, deep dives, and helpful tips.

Our catalog of more than 10,000 products featured on Remodelista.

Remodelista’s members-only directory of architects, designers, and landscape professionals.

We love every inch of this compact 14-by-10-foot kitchen in the Peckham neighborhood of London. Designed by architect Jonathan Nicholls and his partner, Alex Randall, a lighting designer, it occupies the rear extension of their Victorian home. While many architects find the experience of designing their own home an existential nightmare, Nicholls found it be quite the opposite:

“As an architect, working on your own house is great fun. Because of time constraints, I didn’t get a chance to do full, proper drawings, so a lot of the time I’d scribble some plans on the wall at night for the builders to interpret a few hours later,” he told The Modern House. “Because it was our own house, I could experiment a lot more with things I wouldn’t risk at work.”

Nowhere is that playful spirit more on display than in their artful kitchen.

Let’s take a tour. (To see the rest of their house, see the listing at The Modern House.)
