#57. Rules for Mechanical Rooms

The International Residential Code (IRC) and other model codes typically base their requirements on the likely use of a space. “Habitable room” and “sleeping room” are two examples where the code’s terminology makes the intended use of the room clear. In this Know the Code, I’m going to talk about a space that doesn’t have a consistent name in the IRC, or even among building professionals.

As far as the code is concerned, “mechanical rooms,” “furnace rooms,” “utility rooms,” and “boiler rooms” are essentially the same thing. What matters is the permanently installed plumbing or mechanical appliances in the room, how the space is designed, and how the room containing that equipment interacts with the rest of the dwelling.

For example, just because a wall furnace is installed in a bedroom doesn’t make the bedroom a “furnace room,” which is a code term indicating a space primarily used to house a furnace. Similarly, an unfinished basement that includes a water heater isn’t necessarily a mechanical room. There are several things that help a building inspector decide what code rules apply to the space where HVAC and water-heating equipment is located.

Does the space contain an “appliance”—what the code defines as a device using electricity, gas, or fuel oil to produce light, heat, power, refrigeration, or air conditioning? Is combustion taking place in the room? Will the appliance’s operation mean extra humidity or heat in the room? Will outside air be brought in for combustion? Is condensation produced by the appliance? What are the needs of repair personnel when they’re inside the space?

Writing and interpreting codes for mechanical spaces is difficult, so let’s start with the easy requirements and then we’ll move to the more complicated ones. For the sake of this article, I’ll refer to rooms with the primary purpose of containing plumbing and mechanical appliances as mechanical spaces, without quotes. When mechanical appliances are in a basement that’s not exclusively used for heating, air-conditioning, or plumbing appliances, I’ll use the term basement without quotes. Generally, a word or phrase in quotes indicates a term used in the IRC or other model code document.

The electrical code used by the IRC comes from the National Electrical Code (NEC). IRC Chapter 39, “Power and Lighting Distribution,” covers the lighting and receptacle outlet requirements for dwelling spaces of all types. There are NEC provisions that cover both “basements” and “utility rooms” (both terms used by the code), so there are rules that apply to both dedicated mechanical spaces and a water heater or furnace in a multi-use basement.

IRC section E3903.4 (NEC 210.70(C)) requires at least one “lighting outlet” in these mechanical spaces if the space is arranged so there’s room for storage or if the “appliance” inside the space requires servicing. (A “lighting outlet” is an outlet intended for the direct connection of a light fixture.)The code language mentions the need for “servicing” the equipment. “Equipment” is a broad term that includes “appliances,” and it should be expected that building and electrical inspectors will assume all “appliances” require servicing. So, count on installing a light fixture in any mechanical space.

Section E3903.4 also requires a wall switch or control device for this lighting outlet near every entrance to the space. When lighting is required because of equipment servicing (which we can assume will be true in all cases), the light must be located near the equipment or appliance to be serviced. And on the subject of lighting, Chapter 11 (“Energy Conservation”) section N1104.2.2 requires all permanently installed lights in “utility rooms” and “unfinished basements” (i.e., mechanical spaces that aren’t also living spaces) to be controlled automatically so the lights turn off within 20 minutes after occupants have left the space. Motion sensors are the easiest way to accomplish this.

Chapter 39 of the IRC also provides requirements for “receptacle outlets,” but here it gets a little tricky. IRC section E3901.9 (NEC 210.52(G)(3)) requires each unfinished portion of a basement to have a receptacle, so if the mechanical space in the basement is unfinished, a receptacle is required in the room. This provision is tough to wrap your head around as it relates to mechanical spaces, because its focus is on unfinished portions of basements whether they house appliances or not. If that same unfinished room exists on the main floor, you don’t need a receptacle inside the room.

These requirements overlap with those of section E3901.12 (NEC 210.63), which is specific to mechanical spaces that house heating, air-conditioning. and refrigeration equipment and appliances, whether in a basement or not. This section requires a receptacle on the same floor and within 25 ft. of the appliance. The receptacle does not have to be inside the mechanical space. The intent of the receptacle is so anyone servicing the mechanical or plumbing equipment can plug in tools and lights to do their work.

IRC section M1305.1.1 provides general requirements for mechanical systems and specifies that the opening into a room with “appliances” must be at least 24 in. wide, and wide enough to remove the largest appliance in the space. If the appliance is accessed through a hinged door, section M2408.5 (which covers fuel-gas-burning appliances) requires that all clearances to appliances, venting, and the like be maintained throughout the door’s swing. Door stops cannot be used to prevent the door from impeding on the required clearances.

The IRC doesn’t address the required height of the opening to the mechanical space, but that’s consistent with section R313.1, which doesn’t include a minimum ceiling height for any kind of mechanical room. (There are minimum heights for attics and crawlspaces that house appliances, but those requirements are outside the scope of this article.)

HVAC equipment and water heaters are often located in laundry rooms, and those rooms do have a minimum 6-ft. 8-in. ceiling height—but for rooms whose primary purpose is housing HVAC or water-heating appliances, there is no minimum, with one notable exception. Section R313.1.1 requires all nonhabitable spaces—those areas of the house not intended for living, sleeping, eating, or cooking—to have a minimum 6-ft. 8-in. ceiling height, but only when located in a basement.

So, according to the IRC, a mechanical room in the basement must be at least 6 ft. 8 in. tall, but if you move it to the main floor or above, there is no minimum ceiling height. During hearings for the 2027 edition, this was identified as an oversight in the wording of the IRC. The intent was never to require a specific ceiling height for mechanical spaces in basements.

Designing code-compliant mechanical spaces means balancing access, safety, and electrical requirements. Recent code changes now allow return-air registers to help manage temperature and humidity, provided combustion appliances have sealed burners and there’s sufficient airflow to prevent depressurization. Additionally, mechanical spaces must include a light controlled by a timer or sensor and a dedicated receptacle, and have adequate clearances for appliances.

Drawing by Francisco Javier González y García. Click here to enlarge.

The next two topics related to mechanical spaces are relatively new and stem from modern energy-conservation codes. Sometimes mechanical spaces need combustion air from outside for safety and the proper operation of the equipment. But a direct opening to the outside can also allow conditioned air to escape, making the house harder to heat or cool, so the code tries to address that.

IRC section N1102.1.6 requires that any room in climate zones 3 to 8 containing a fuel-burning appliance with an open combustion chamber that gets combustion air through ducts or openings to the outside have its walls and ceiling insulated to the minimum R-value required for basement walls in the applicable climate zone.

Presumably, the energy code doesn’t require insulating the floor because it’s assuming this room would be in a basement. If the room is above grade, you could go above code and include insulation in the floor. In addition, all doors accessing the room must be gasketed, and any HVAC ducts in or passing through the space must be insulated to a minimum of R-8.

Historically, forced-air heating systems could not have return-duct vents in mechanical spaces due to concerns of combustion by-products entering the duct­work and spreading through the house. Return-air vents can also cause depressurization of mechanical spaces, which can cause atmospherically vented combustion appliances to backdraft. Backdrafting, or spillage of exhaust gases, is dangerous and can lead to severe illness and death from carbon-­monoxide poisoning.

However, mechanical spaces, because they don’t have return air vents, are often uncomfortably hot or cold and sometimes have high humidity. The need to ventilate these rooms has led to changes in the 2024 IRC. Ventilation isn’t required, but return-air openings for forced-air distributions systems can now be included in mechanical spaces in an effort to manage elevated heat and moisture.

Section M1602.2 allows these opening under strict details. First, only sealed combustion appliances are permitted in the room. This means outside combustion air is piped directly into the appliance and the combustion by-products (flue gases) are sent outdoors through a sealed and pressurized vent. Sealed combustion means concerns about room depressurization, managing unconditioned combustion air, and dangerous flue gases are greatly reduced.

Second, to install one of these returns on the HVAC ductwork, the room with the mechanical appliances must also have a transfer opening for makeup air, so air that’s drawn into the return can be replaced with air from outside the mechanical space. The transfer opening can be an undercut or louvered door, a transfer grille, or any means acceptable to the code official. It must be large enough that the pressure differential across the door is no greater than 2.5 pascals when the system is running. Allowing a return-air grille in a mechanical room is a big change from previous codes, thus the very specific requirements.

That’s a pretty comprehensive explanation of the IRC’s general requirements for mechanical spaces, but I want to mention one feature that is often thought to be a requirement for mechanical rooms, but isn’t—a floor drain. There is no direct or universal requirement for a floor drain anywhere in a house.

Air conditioners, high-efficiency furnaces, and other appliances that produce condensation are only required to have an “approved place of disposal.” This is the same requirement for temperature and pressure (T&P) relief valves on water heaters. Although a floor drain is an excellent way to dispose of condensate or water from a T&P relief valve, there is no code requirement.

— Glenn Mathewson is a consultant and educator with BuildingCodeCollege.com.

Fancy turning your backyard into the ultimate cardinal hangout? These three trees and shrubs are a great place to start...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Is there anything more magical than spotting a bright red cardinal among the branches of your backyard?

Honestly, I'm not so sure that there is; there's a reason we all love these beautifully vibrant birds so much, and it's not just because they've become synonymous with the holidays (a study back in 2022 determined that 34% of the birds featured on Christmas cards are cardinals, if you don't believe me!). They are laden with symbolism, and many believe that if they're the first bird you spot on January 1st, you're owed 12 months of love, hope, optimism, and good luck for the year ahead.

Now, these beautiful songbirds are year-round residents across much of the eastern and central United States, and with the right planting choices, you can make your garden a more inviting place for them to visit. So, how best to go about it?

The secret to charming these birds into your yard? Think beyond bird feeders and give cardinals more of what they naturally need: food, shelter, and places to nest.

Now, cardinals eat a varied diet of seeds, fruit, and insects, and they particularly favor gardens with plenty of dense vegetation where they can hide from predators and forage safely. All of which means that, if you're hoping to welcome more of these ruby-red visitors to your yard this season, these three trees are a great place to start.

If you want to make your garden more appealing to cardinals, hawthorn is a great tree to consider. Depending on the species, these trees produce small fruits often called haws, which can provide food for birds into the cooler months. Their dense, sometimes thorny branches also offer useful shelter for wildlife.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Hawthorns can be particularly valuable in a wildlife-friendly garden because they provide more than one benefit. Their flowers attract insects, their fruits feed birds, and their branching structure offers places to perch and hide.

When choosing a hawthorn, look for a species suited to your local growing conditions and available space. Native varieties are especially worth considering because they can support a wider range of local wildlife, although the La Vida Más® Indian Hawthorn from Nature Hills is an undeniably spectacular option if you are in the mood for endless clusters of pink flowers (and how could you not be?).

Crabapple trees are another excellent option for a cardinal-friendly garden. Their spring blossoms bring seasonal color, while the small fruits that follow can become an important food source for birds in fall and winter.

The fruits of some crabapple varieties persist on the tree after the leaves have dropped, creating a welcome food source when other options become scarcer. The branches also offer perching spots and can contribute to the layered structure that makes a backyard more attractive to birds.

For the best wildlife value, choose something like the Louisa Weeping Crabapple Tree from Nature Hills. It has the added benefit of being stunning, too!

Dogwood is a particularly good choice if you're looking for a plant that combines ornamental appeal with wildlife benefits. Many dogwoods produce berries that cardinals and other fruit-eating birds enjoy, and Cornell's Lab of Ornithology specifically lists dogwood among the fruits eaten by cardinals, too!

Depending on the species, dogwoods can grow as small trees or shrubs, making them useful for gardens of different sizes. Their seasonal flowers, foliage, and fruits can provide interest throughout the year, while their branching growth helps create cover for all visiting birds (very likely including your own birth month bird in the mix).

For a particularly wildlife-friendly planting, look into native dogwood species that are well suited to your region. Personally, I love the White Flowering Dogwood from Nature Hills.

Planting these trees can help, but the best cardinal-friendly gardens offer more than fruit alone. Cardinals are especially fond of dense shrubs and tangled vegetation, which provide shelter from predators and suitable nesting locations, and they also need a reliable source of water.

Finally, try to choose plants native to your region and avoid pesticides wherever possible. A diverse garden with food available across different seasons is more likely to support birds and other wildlife over the long term, after all! Still, with hawthorn, crabapple, and dogwood in the mix, you can create a backyard that looks beautiful through the seasons while offering cardinals more reasons to stop by.

If that's not an excuse to get growing, I don't know what is!

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

#59. A Front Garden Designed for Fall Color

Hi GPOD! Today we’re visiting John’s Zone 7a garden in Readington, New Jersey. His front garden is full of late-season color, so much so that I imagine anyone walking by would immediately think, “Fall is here!” It’s one of those gardens that grounds you in the season and makes you appreciate what’s happening right now. With flowers and ornamental grasses layered throughout the long border, there’s plenty to take in. Here’s John to tell us more!

Although the beds in front of my house in Readington, New Jersey, have different perennials blooming throughout spring and summer, the current flowers in bloom include garden mums (Chrysanthemum × morifolium, Zones 5–9), asters (Symphyotrichum cvs., Zones 3–8), English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia, Zones 5–9), bee balm (Monarda cvs., Zones 3–9), salvia (Salvia cvs., Zones 4–9), and speedwell (Veronica cvs., Zones 3–9), along with ornamental grasses and shrubs.

I especially enjoy creating a layered look by combining different heights and textures and repeating colors along the border. These photos, taken in late September and early October, include wider views showing the garden’s layout as well as closer looks at individual plant combinations.

Thanks for sharing your garden with us, John! A home wrapped in color is a fantastic example of front-entry appeal and how repetition, color, and texture can bring a landscape together. #60. 10 Home Heating Mistakes That Spike Your Utility Bills

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Updated Oct 19, 2026 11:23 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Despite our best efforts to economize and lead more eco-friendly lives, few of us are are paying less for our utilities than we were a few years ago. According to an October 2026 report by the U.S. Energy Information Administration, households that use electricity will pay about 4 percent more than they did last year; households with oil will pay about 21 percent more this winter. Most of us are willing to try new cost-saving measures to get our utility spending out of the stratosphere, but these ill-advised actions will only cost you more in the long run.

If you’re away from home for most of the day, or if you travel on the weekends, don’t leave the house on the same temperature settings you would if you were home all day. Purchasing a programmable thermostat can save you money on energy bills. Set the temperature to go down while you’re away, and warm up the house right before you return.

Of course you keep your windows closed in the winter, but do you remember to lock them? If your windows are not sealed tightly, cold air can seep into your home, and the warm air your furnace is producing could leak out. Be sure to lock all your windows during the winter months.

Don’t make the mistake of trying to heat your home faster by cranking up the thermostat higher than it should go. Turning your thermostat too high has no effect on how quickly your home will warm up. Your furnace will just end up running longer, which just means a higher electric bill for you.

The Google Nest Gen 4 excels as an energy-efficient thermostat, quietly optimizing performance without constant input. Read the review.

When the air filter is dirty, your furnace has to work—and will use more energy doing so. Make sure you change the furnace air filter on a regular schedule. Your system will work more efficiently, and more economically. If you’re in the market for replacement filters, be sure to check out our tested guide to the the best furnace filters.

Don’t underestimate how much heat your home could be losing as a result of air that leaks from doors, and drafty windows. Check all the doors, windows, and exterior walls for drafts. Seal and caulk any areas where cold air is coming in and warm air could leak out. Pay special attention to the basement and attic—they are generally the draftiest spots.

You might think it would make sense to close the vents in unoccupied rooms to save money on your utility bill. After all, why heat a room that’s empty? The fact is, the ductwork for your heating system is sized to provide even heating throughout the house, and the system won’t work efficiently if you disrupt that balance by closing vents.

Just like your car, your furnace needs regular maintenance to keep it in good working order. Don’t put off this task: A well-maintained HVAC system will run more efficiently, and keep your energy bills down. Also, regular checkups will ensure that a minor furnace maintenance issue doesn’t balloon into a costly maintenance problem.

While you don’t want to heat your house when you’re not home, don’t make the mistake of turning the thermostat down too low while you’re out. Doing this will just force your furnace to work harder when it’s time to bring the thermostat to the right temperature again, and you’ll end up spending more money in the long run.

It might seem like a good idea to turn your thermostat down and use a fireplace to heat your living area, but you’d be doing more harm than good. Most of the warm air will go straight through the chimney and out of your house. That very same chimney will also let in the chilly air from outside, making your house colder and forcing your furnace to work harder.

As soon as you’ve finished using a kitchen or bathroom fan that vents exhaust outside, turn it off. Exhaust fans are necessary to purge moist or odiferous air from your home, but you definitely don’t want to be sending warm air out of your house longer than is necessary.

#61. 50 Haunted Buildings That Show Every State Has a Ghost Story

From old hotels and historic homes to former prisons, every state has a building with a past and a few lingering ghost stories.

Spooky season is right around the corner, and what better way is there to celebrate than to learn a little history and some fun facts about some of the most haunted places across the country?

Each state is home to unexplainable stories, whether that’s at historic hotels, residences, prisons, and more. Many of the buildings still welcome visitors today, giving anyone interested in old architecture and local lore a chance to see them firsthand.

Learn about famously haunted buildings from every state.

Built in 1837, Selma’s St. James Hotel has spent much of its life welcoming travelers, some of whom say the historic hotel has a few guests who never checked out.

The Red Onion Saloon opened in Skagway in 1898 during the Gold Rush, and stories about former occupants still follow the historic building today.

Built in 1895, the Victorian-era Rosson House is one of Phoenix’s best-preserved historic residences and has inspired local stories about strange sounds and unexplained happenings.

The Crescent Hotel has overlooked Eureka Springs since 1886, and its unusual history has helped make it one of the state’s most famous spots for ghost stories.

Built in San Diego in 1857, the Whaley House served as both a family home and courthouse before becoming known for reports of strange sights and sounds.

The Stanley Hotel opened in Estes Park in 1909, and its grand halls have since become nearly as famous for ghost tales as for overnight stays.

Samuel Clemens and his family moved into Hartford’s Mark Twain House in 1874, and visitors today occasionally report footsteps and other odd happenings inside.

Built in the 1850s on Pea Patch Island, the former Civil War fort has a long history as a military prison and is now a popular setting for stories of unexplained activity.

The famous pink hotel opened in 1928 and is associated with stories about its founder, Thomas Rowe, whose ghost is reportedly seen around the property.

Since opening in Americus in 1892, the Windsor Hotel has hosted generations of guests and gathered its share of ghost tales along the way.

Built in 1882, ʻIolani Palace was the residence of Hawaii’s last ruling monarchs. There are stories about apparitions of Queen Liliʻuokalani and unexplained sounds, including reports of a piano playing.

The Old Idaho Penitentiary opened in Boise in 1870, and its years as a prison left behind plenty of stories about strange noises and shadowy figures.

Opened in 1858, the former prison has a dramatic history and is now open for tours.

This 19th-century inn is associated with the “Blue Lady,” reportedly seen in rooms and hallways and sometimes accompanied by the smell of cherry tobacco.

Built in 1868, the Villisca Axe Murder House became infamous after the 1912 killings there and later gained a reputation for unsettling experiences inside.

The current Eldridge Hotel building opened in Lawrence in 1925, continuing a hotel tradition on the site that stretches back much further and includes several ghost tales.

Louisville’s Waverly Hills Sanatorium opened in 1926, and the former hospital has since become closely associated with stories of strange figures and unexplained sounds.

Built in St. Francisville in 1796, The Myrtles now welcomes overnight guests, many of whom arrive already familiar with the home’s long haunted reputation.

The Kennebunk Inn began as a private home in 1799, and stories about former residents and workers have followed the property through its later life as an inn.

Baltimore’s Lord Baltimore Hotel opened in 1928, and guests over the years have shared stories about unexpected elevator rides, unexplained noises, and unusual sightings.

The Lizzie Borden House, built in Fall River in 1845, became famous after the 1892 murders and now attracts visitors interested in both the case and the home’s ghost stories.

The iconic 1887 hotel has long been associated with reports of apparitions and unexplained activity.

These former sandstone caves date to the 19th century and have accumulated stories of ghostly activity.

King’s Tavern dates to the 1700s and began serving travelers in Natchez in 1789, with ghost tales becoming another chapter in the building’s long history.

The former prison operated for 168 years and is now open for history and paranormal tours. Its enormous cellblocks and long institutional history add to its spookiness.

Fort Benton’s Grand Union Hotel opened in 1882, and its long life on the frontier has produced more than a few stories about strange sounds and sightings.

The Argo Hotel was built in Crofton in 1912 to serve railroad passengers, though today its history also includes stories of unusual encounters reported by guests.

Opened in Tonopah in 1907, the Mizpah Hotel is best known in ghost lore for a mysterious figure commonly called the Lady in Red.

The Mount Washington Hotel opened in Bretton Woods in 1902, and one of its best-known stories involves the supposed appearance of a former owner’s wife.

The 1923 hotel is associated with the “Lady in White,” reportedly seen wandering the hallways and accompanied by stories of singing, laughter and unexplained activity.

The current La Fonda on the Plaza opened in Santa Fe in 1922, continuing a long history of lodging on the site and adding a few ghost stories over the decades.

The Morris-Jumel Mansion, built around 1765, served as George Washington’s headquarters during the Revolutionary War and later became known for reports of ghostly figures.

Asheville’s Grove Park Inn opened in 1913, and its best-known ghost story centers on a mysterious guest remembered simply as the Pink Lady.

The 1880s mansion built by the Marquis de Mores is one of North Dakota’s most distinctive historic buildings. It has also been included in the state’s modern haunted-location lore.

The Ohio State Reformatory opened in Mansfield in 1896, and visitors to the former prison often hear stories about strange sounds and figures inside its cellblocks.

Oklahoma City’s Skirvin Hotel opened in 1911, and a century of guests has produced a steady collection of stories about unusual noises and sightings.

Completed in Portland in 1914, Pittock Mansion now operates as a historic house museum, where visitors have occasionally reported unexplained sounds and movement.

Philadelphia’s Eastern State Penitentiary opened in 1829, and the abandoned prison blocks have inspired ghost stories for decades.

Newport’s Belcourt was completed in 1894, and the Gilded Age mansion has become associated with stories about strange sounds and unexpected figures inside.

Charleston’s Francis Marion Hotel opened in 1924 and has since gathered stories of unexplained footsteps, flickering lights and a mysterious figure said to linger inside.

The Bullock Hotel opened in Deadwood in the 1890s, and local stories claim former owner Seth Bullock still makes the occasional appearance.

Nashville’s Ryman Auditorium opened in 1892, and more than a century of performances has also produced stories about mysterious figures and sounds after the crowds leave.

The Menger Hotel opened beside the Alamo in 1859, and generations of guests have contributed stories about former visitors who supposedly still wander its halls.

Built in Salt Lake City in 1901, the McCune Mansion has served several purposes over the years and has also become known for reports of ghostly figures inside.

The Green Mountain Inn has welcomed guests in Stowe since 1833, though some visitors say footsteps and tapping sounds continue after everyone has settled in for the night.

The 1927 hotel has a long history of celebrity guests and Prohibition-era stories, along with reports of apparitions and unexplained activity.

Built in Port Townsend in 1892, Manresa Castle began as a private home before becoming a hotel with stories about unexplained sounds and sightings.

The Trans-Allegheny Lunatic Asylum began receiving patients in Weston in 1864, and today its tours cover both the former hospital’s history and the ghost stories that followed.

Milwaukee’s Pfister Hotel opened in 1893, and guests over the years have reported unusual sounds and sightings in the historic hotel.

The current Occidental Hotel in Buffalo dates to the early 1900s, and one of its best-known stories involves the ghost of a young girl seen around the property.

#63. The Year of Shaker: A Design Movement Goes Mainstream (Plus 10 Sightings)

From house tours and expert advice to favorite finds and DIYs.

It’s been over a decade since a relatively fringe 1700s religious sect—the Shakers—found unlikely ubiquity in the modern world. It started with Shaker peg rails (this story, originally published in 2013, took us by surprise when it went wild). Then “Shaker-style kitchen cabinets” became a household term. A New York City restaurant, a French bakery, and a Mexico City hotel all took design cues from Shaker villages. And on it went.

In all the years since, enthusiasm for the simple, utilitarian design has barely dipped. If anything, it’s grown. But recently a new slew of Shaker-adjacent news leads us to believe the Shaker fervor is reaching a fever pitch.

First, Fan alerted us to this exhibit, at the American Folk Art Museum, on Shaker art (utterly “exuberant” compared to their pared-back furnishings). Then this pop-up, co-curated by the actress Frances McDormand, caught our eye; featuring Shaker cradles, it invited visitors to “take your time. Rock yourself. Mend if you’d like.” Now an exhibit called  “The Shakers: A World in the Making”, backed by the Vitra Design Museum in Germany and previously at the ICA in Philadelphia (where it was covered by the New York Times), is on view at the Milwaukee Art Museum through the end of January.

If you’ve ever wanted to adorn your envelopes with Shaker designs in miniature, now you can, thanks to a collection of Shaker Forever stamps. And with the debut of the Amanda Seyfried film The Testament of Ann Lee last year, filmed in part at Hancock Shaker Village in Massachusetts, it’s safe to say that Shaker design has officially entered the mainstream.

The 250th anniversary, in 2024, of the first Shakers’ arrival in America is perhaps a reason for this latest resurgence—though we can’t help but wonder whether Shaker cradles and handmade wares answer a yearning, now, for simpler times.

Here are 10 Shaker-inspired offerings we’ve bookmarked lately.

Above: From woodworker Brian Persico, the Manago Side Table is inspired by the shape of Shaker candle stands and painted vibrant apple green.

The journey to your best lilies ever starts this month with some simple wins. Here's what to tick off before winter kicks in to be sure of towering stems and majestic lily blooms

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

True lilies are some of the most striking, fragrant, and elegant flowers in the garden. As fall continues, those magnificent blooms may fade, but underground, their leaves and bulbs are working overtime to prepare for winter. October is a critical time when lily bulbs are drawing in late-season nutrients, developing healthy roots, and storing vital energy to push up towering stems next year.

Before diving into autumn chores, make sure you clarify which type of lily you need to care for, and distinguish true lilies (Lilium) from daylilies (Hemerocallis). Daylilies grow from dense, fibrous roots and die back quickly, while true lilies grow from fleshy bulbs. These fall tasks focus on early-blooming Asiatic hybrids, fragrant Oriental lilies (like 'Stargazer'), majestic Trumpet lilies, and robust Orienpet (OT) hybrids.

These simple October tasks outlined here ensure maximum winter survival, smart disease resistance, and better flower development next time. Because most true lilies are cold-hardy, they can remain safely in the ground (just a few tender types, or lilies in very cold climates, benefit from winter storage). By giving your lily beds a little expert attention now, you set the stage for an explosive, colorful display next year.

Before getting stuck into lily care, give some thought to your USDA hardiness zone and climate, as well as specific varieties. Because specific lily classes mature at different rates through late summer, individual plants in borders may sit at varying stages of dormancy in October. Early Asiatic varieties may have dropped their leaves weeks ago, while tall Oriental and Orienpet hybrids might hold green foliage into fall.

In addition to managing existing lily beds, October is a great time to introduce new lily bulbs. Soil temperatures remain warm enough for fresh roots to establish before deep winter freezes arrive. At the same time, growers in severe northern climates (zones 2–3) or those growing tender, exotic species like Formosa lilies can lift and store bulbs for protection.

It’s a good idea to invest in a soil probe that can give you a reliable idea of light and moisture levels in the ground at this time. A diagnostic tool like the Raintrip 4-in-1 Soil Meter, available from Amazon, can give you a heads-up about conditions around your lilies before you start. Checking can help you clarify root moisture, soil pH, and temperature levels before you mulch or plant new bulbs.

Whether you are tending established clumps, adding new varieties, or lifting tender bulbs for winter, these simple October tasks will ensure your lilies transition smoothly into dormancy. Following these quick checks this month gives you the best preparation for healthier plants and bigger blooms next summer.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Removing spent plant material is important for maintaining a tidy bed but also for plant health and preventing infections. Fallen leaves and spent lily foliage can harbor destructive fungal spores, most notably lily blight, as well as other pathogens. Collect and dispose of yellowing or dropped leaves as they loosen from the main stems. Any foliage showing dark spots, water-soaked streaks, or powdery mildew should be bagged and placed in the trash (not the compost pile) to prevent spreading disease.

Additionally, snip off any seed heads that form after flowering finishes. Unless you are intentionally saving seed for propagation, developing seed pods drain massive amounts of energy away from the bulb. Removing seed capsules redirects resources back down into the bulb, strengthening reserves for winter. Always use clean, sharp snips when removing seed heads, and wipe down the blades before and after use. Bonide Captain Jack’s Ready-to-Use Neem Oil Spray, available from Walmart, is great for sanitizing tool blades as well as treating beds against fungal spores.

This is an excellent opportunity to check remaining stems and leaf joints for signs of damage or insect activity, like spots or holes. Aphids, red lily leaf beetles, and scale insects frequently deposit overwintering eggs close to the soil line. Removing old stem tissue and clearing away leaf clutter can eliminate cozy pest harbors. To help you get a closer look, grab a magnifying glass or a loupe like the Carson LumiLoupe 10x Stand Magnifier from Amazon. This can help assess leaves or bulb scales for hidden mites, thrips, or early fungal rot.

If you are dividing or lifting tender varieties for indoor storage, inspect bulbs closely. Healthy lily bulbs should feel firm, plump, and heavy, with crisp white, yellow, or pinkish scales. Discard any that feel soft, squishy, or show signs of blue mold or basal rot. If you notice rot in multiple bulbs, it might be a sign of poor soil drainage. Correct this in October by working some coarse grit or perlite into the planting area.

While it is tempting to clear away all stems early to keep beds tidy, patience is essential – and timing is crucial. As long as a lily stem holds green leaves, it is actively performing photosynthesis, converting sunlight into carbohydrates and pumping energy down into the bulb. So while parts of the plant are working, it’s best to leave lilies as long as they are healthy. Cutting back green stems prematurely starves the bulb, resulting in stunted growth and fewer flowers the following season.

Wait until the foliage has turned yellow, brown or papery before cutting back. Once the stem is fully dead, use bypass pruners to cut the stalk down to about 2-3 inches (5-8cm) above the ground. Leaving a short stem stub helps mark the bulb's location. Dispose of dead stalks promptly, as hollow, decaying stems left standing over winter make ideal overwintering sites for pests and spores. After cutting back, add a gentle organic phosphorus booster to the soil. A little Down to Earth Organic Fish Bone Meal from Lowe’s around trimmed bases can encourage root development.

This is a chore many gardeners can skip, as most lilies are hardy in most areas of North America. Asiatic, Oriental, and Trumpet lilies are hardy in zones 4-9, but if you are in zones 2-3 or growing tender exotic species, it’s smart to lift bulbs in October. Once foliage dies back, carefully lift using a garden fork, taking care not to nick the bulbs. Brush off loose soil and allow the bulbs to air-dry in a cool room for 24 hours. Store them in cardboard boxes layered with slightly damp peat moss, wood shavings or vermiculite. Keep in a cool, dark location, around 40-45°F (4-7°C).

October is also a great time to plant new hardy lilies. Autumn soil retains summer warmth, allowing fresh bulbs to build strong root systems. Plant bulbs pointy side up at a depth 2-3 times the height of the bulb, 6-8 inches (15-20cm) deep. Choose a sunny site with well-draining soil, mixing a little organic compost or bone meal into the bottom of the hole. Add a gentle root tonic rather than a heavy dedicated feed. Go for a light soil drench with a seaweed or kelp tonic like GS Plant Foods Organic Liquid Kelp from Walmart. This is rich in trace minerals to help develop roots.

Bulbs that stay in the ground over winter benefit from a little protection, even if they are hardy in your growing zone. Mulching insulates the soil, moderates temperature changes, and reduces the risk of frost-related damage. Once beds are cleared and trimmed, apply a layer of mulch. If you’re looking for a great mulch for lilies, I recommend Back to the Roots Organic Premium Wood Mulch from Amazon. This dye-free organic bark mulch insulates bulbs, while suppressing early weeds. You can also use shredded bark, evergreen boughs or clean straw.

As well as insulating the soil against temperature swings, mulching prevents damage by freeze-thaw cycles. These can cause frost heaving, which is where shifting soil pops bulbs up to the surface. Wait until the ground cools down (or after the first hard freeze) before applying a 2-4-inch (5-10cm) blanket of your mulch. Don’t pack it too tightly or thickly, though, as this can trap moisture over the bulbs.

Finally, be sure to mark the exact locations of your buried lily bulbs. True lilies emerge relatively late in spring, and it is dangerously easy to forget exactly where they are and to slice through dormant bulbs in spring. Drive durable wooden or plastic garden stakes into the ground besides your trimmed stem stubs or fresh plantings. Taking a quick photo on your smartphone can also help to create a visual map that prevents accidental digging when spring arrives.

These well-timed tasks will help your lily bulbs survive the winter and thrive next spring with vigorous growth and abundant, majestic blooms. The most important priorities are to leave green foliage intact until it dies back naturally, clear away dead plant debris, and protect underground bulbs while ensuring excellent soil drainage for any additions. Take a little time to tend your lily beds well this fall, and you can enjoy an unforgettable display of lovely lilies next summer.

#67. Colorful Summer Plant Combinations in Dot’s Pennsylvania Garden

Hi GPOD! We’re heading back to Broomall, Pennsylvania, today to see what’s blooming in Dot’s Zone 7b garden. Longtime GPOD readers might remember Dot from her earlier garden updates, and it’s always fun to see how her garden continues to evolve. I really love all of the beautiful plant combinations she has put together. Here’s Dot with a brief introduction:

Although summer is slipping away, I am still planting perennials and bulbs. I’ve included some garden highlights that I hope you enjoy.

‘Abraham Darby’ rose (Rosa ‘Abraham Darby’, Zones 5–9) climbs the arbor, while veronica (Veronica cvs., Zones 3–9) fills in around its base. The purple-blue flower spikes contrast beautifully with the rose’s blush-pink blooms.

Daylily (Hemerocallis cvs., Zones 3–10) and Shasta daisies (Leucanthemum × superbum cvs., Zones 5–9) mingle together behind this seating area in Dot’s garden.

Cathedral Bells rose (Rosa ‘DELamo’, Zones 5–9) climbs alongside ‘Jackmanii’ clematis (Clematis ‘Jackmanii’, Zones 4–8). This pairing really helps both the rose blooms and the deep purple clematis flowers stand out when planted together.

Helenium (Helenium cvs., Zones 3–8) is a new addition to Dot’s garden this year. Its warm orange flowers bring another burst of late-season color to the garden, and the rabbit looks perfectly happy tucked among the blooms.

Lythrum (Lythrum cvs., Zones 3–9), white garden phlox (Phlox paniculata cvs., Zones 4–8), bush clematis (Clematis cvs., Zones 3–9), agastache (Agastache cvs., Zones 4–9), and Russian sage (Salvia yangii, Zones 4–9) are planted together in this area of the garden. The white phlox breaks through the layers of purple and blue flowers and keeps the eye moving through the space.

Bright orange nasturtiums (Tropaeolum majus, annual) weave through purple coneflowers (Echinacea purpurea cvs., Zones 3–9). I really like how the saturated orange mixes with the deeper pink coneflowers. Nasturtiums also make a great seasonal ground cover for filling in bare spots between plants and spilling over the edges of raised beds.

Shasta daisies, purple coneflowers, and yarrow (Achillea millefolium cvs., Zones 3–9) fill this raised bed. I really like the use of white and pink here.

Thanks for sharing another update with us, Dot! I really enjoyed seeing all of the plant combinations you’ve put together in your raised beds. There are so many great color pairings here, but I think the orange nasturtiums mixed with the deeper pink coneflowers might be my favorite!

#68. What Is “House Blindness”? I Think I Have It

House blindness makes clutter, half-finished projects and little repairs fade into the background. Here’s how to spot it in your own home.

Hear no mess. See no mess. Speak no mess.

If only that actually made the mess go away. Sometimes in the life of a DIYer, you get a little too comfortable with living in a half-finished house.

For me, I often see straight through the small mountain of tools and materials stacked in the corner of the room where we’re currently (…have been for a while…) renovating. And the spackle on the wall that needs to be sanded down and painted? Invisible to my eyes.

The missing trim in the kitchen, sticky door to the basement, loose handle on the trash can are all obvious to anyone stepping foot in my home, but not so much to me and my family.

House blindness is simply when you get so used to the mess, clutter or unfinished jobs around your home that you stop noticing them. Think of it like going nose blind, but with imperfections in your home. It can also be referred to as “clutter blindness,” “mess blind,” “clutter creep”, or something similar.

A post shared by Emma Shoemaker | DIY & Home (@shoemakesnew)

Once I heard the term, it immediately made sense. I’m not purposely ignoring the pile of tools in the corner or that missing piece of trim. I’ve just walked past them so many times that they’ve basically become part of the room.

The concept of house blindness isn’t overly complex. However, it might be confronting or hard to realize that it’s something you’re doing too.

For me, the biggest giveaway is when I suddenly notice something that’s been sitting there for weeks or months. If guests are coming over, I take a photo of the room or I simply look at it from a different angle. All of a sudden, that pile I’ve walked past 100 times is impossible to miss. If that sounds familiar, you might be doing it too.

Now, for solutions. Here are some things I’ve discovered that help.

Because our house is usually a revolving door of major renovations, there’s almost always at least one major project going on. To help with construction mess spilling into other rooms, I keep a designated tool and materials box that everything goes into once the work is done for the day.

I’ve also prioritized 95% days, which are days I set aside specifically to finish all those little jobs I’ve been putting off instead of starting something new. Think missing trim, nail holes, outlet covers and all the other annoying final steps that keep a project at 95% instead of actually done.

Another one that might seem silly but does work is to look at your home from angles you don’t normally see from. If you’re tall, try kneeling or sitting on the ground and looking around. Or if you’re short, get a step ladder for a new perspective.

One trick I recently learned but haven’t tried is to take photos around your home and look at them on your phone later. Viewing them through this new lens helps strip away the usual filters your brain uses to block that clutter noise and can help you see more clearly.

Try one, or multiple, of these approaches and see what works best. Thankfully, clutter is usually a pretty easy issue to fix and if it’s something you’ve gone house blind to, it doesn’t take much to start noticing it again.

Spent tomato vines may look like a cleanup chore, but they can still provide seeds for next year, valuable compost material, and a head start on spring.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

By mid-October, many tomato plants look pretty rough, with yellowing leaves, a few stubborn green fruits, and stems flopping over their cages. The easy move is to yank the whole mess out and drag it to the trash or the compost pile. Before you do, though, there’s some useful work hiding in those tired plants.

Good end-of-season tomato plant care starts with a close look at what you’re pulling. Some vines can feed next year’s garden as compost, and the best fruit can give you free seed. Others may carry diseases you don’t want to spread around the yard or carry over into next summer.

That’s the main thing to keep in mind as you work. Healthy tomato plants can usually go in the compost, while diseased ones should be bagged and disposed of according to your local guidance. Nearly every other job, from saving seeds to cleaning cages, depends on knowing which kind of plants you have.

Walk the row slowly and look at leaves, stems, and fruit before a single plant comes out. A few problems should never go into a typical home compost pile. Late blight (Phytophthora infestans) is one, and the bacterial tomato diseases are others, including bacterial spot (Xanthomonas spp.) and bacterial canker (Clavibacter michiganensis), which can survive in plant debris. Mosaic viruses are worse still – tobacco and tomato mosaic viruses can hang on in dried plant debris for years. Most backyard piles never get hot enough, evenly enough, to kill these organisms. Bag those plants and get rid of them according to your local rules, and do the same with any plant that’s heavily infested with pests.

Seed saving only works with open-pollinated or heirloom varieties – hybrids won’t come true to type, so an F1 tomato’s seeds can give you something quite different next year. Pick fully ripe fruit from your healthiest, best-tasting plants and scoop the seeds and gel into a glass jar with a little water. Stir it twice a day for up to about five days, until it ferments and the good seeds sink. Pour off the floaters, rinse what’s left in something like the Farberware fine mesh strainers from Walmart, and dry the seeds on a coffee filter or paper plate.

Once a fingernail can’t dent them, they’re ready for labeled paper envelopes; the Lotmer seed-saving envelopes from Amazon are printed with seed name, variety, date collected, and growing notes. Kept cool, dry, and dark, tomato seed usually stays good for about four years.

This one’s optional, but if there’s a variety you loved this year, you can carry it through the winter indoors. Pick a few healthy side shoots about 3–4 inches (8–10 cm) long and snip them off with clean pruners – Fiskars' bypass pruning shears, available on Amazon, are a great budget-friendly pick if you need a new pair.

Cuttings will usually root in a plain jar of water, as long as the cut ends sit 1–2 inches (2.5–5 cm) under the surface and the jar stays somewhere cool and bright. Once roots show up, pot them and give them all the light you can. Don’t put this off until after a hard frost has already hit the garden.

Leave out any plant that had disease problems, and viruses in particular, since a cutting can carry them along from the parent.

Healthy vines are worth composting, but toss them on the pile whole, and they’ll take ages to rot. Chop them into short lengths first – 8–12 inches (20–30cm) or so – because smaller pieces break down faster. It also pays to strip off any leftover tomatoes. Seeds can make it through a backyard pile in one piece, and you may find volunteers popping up next summer.

Layer the chopped vines with dry leaves or other brown material. A compost bin like the Redmon 65-gallon compost bin from Walmart keeps it all corralled.

If you’re on the fence about whether a plant was healthy, use that compost away from where tomatoes will grow. Healthy potting mix from containers can go on the pile, too, so dump those pots before you stack them for winter.

For plants that stayed healthy all season, there’s a good case for leaving the roots in the ground. Just cut the stems off at the soil line, and the roots will break down in place, adding organic matter without much soil disturbance. A plant that wilted, stunted, or yellowed for no clear reason is another story. Loosen the root ball with a spading fork, like Home Depot’s Ames 4-tine forged spading fork. You’re looking for knotty swellings on the roots, a sign of root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.).

Remove infested roots soon after harvest and leave them out of the garden. The same goes for plants with Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici), which can persist in soil for many years. In containers, tip the root ball out and check it the same way.

Some disease organisms ride along on tomato supports. Bacterial canker can persist on stakes, and mosaic viruses can last weeks to months on stakes and trellises. Knock off the dirt first, then scrub or hose them down, since soil blocks disinfectants. Then soak them fully in a 10% bleach solution (1 part bleach to 9 parts water) for at least 20 minutes.

Rather skip the bleach? ZeroTol 2.0, an OMRI-listed hydrogen peroxide product sold on Amazon, is labeled for hard, nonporous surfaces like metal cages and tools. Wooden stakes are trickier – bacteria can hide in the wood – so toss any that held canker-infected plants. Plastic pots can get the same bleach soak, followed by a good rinse.

Bare soil over winter is a missed opportunity. Winter rye is very cold-tolerant and grows in cool weather. In mid-October, it’s still an option in many areas, as long as you sow it at least four weeks before steady cold sets in. You’ll find Mountain Valley Seed winter rye on Amazon in a 5-pound bag on Amazon. Mow it in spring before it sets seed, then turn it under two to four weeks before planting.

If it’s too late for a cover crop, spread compost such as Back to the Roots organic compost, available from Home Depot, or a blanket of shredded leaves, instead. Next year’s tomatoes should go somewhere else, too – keep tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, and potatoes out of that spot for three to four years. For containers, reuse potting mix only if the plants stayed healthy, and replace the top 6 inches (15 cm) in big pots with fresh mix.

Once the last tomatoes are picked, here’s the whole job in short form. Pin it somewhere you’ll see it, because October tends to get busy.

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#72. Fix Your Fridge: All Your Questions About Refrigerators Answered

Frustrated by refrigerator issues? Use these tips to handle common problems and routine maintenance.

Not usually. In older refrigerators, water is often stored in a reservoir near the crisper drawers. But in many modern models, water flows through tubing that runs up the back of the refrigerator to the water filter, then down to coiled tubing that serves as a storage tank, and back up to the door dispenser. Along the way, it’s exposed to warmer parts of the refrigerator. Because the water is constantly flowing through the tubes instead of chilling in a reservoir, it may not be as cold as you’d like. Here are a few ways to enjoy colder water:

If the ice from your refrigerator has an unpleasant smell or taste, it’s probably time to clean the ice maker. Do this once or twice a year, depending on how often you use it:

We all learned in school that water freezes at 32 degrees. While that temperature is fine for making ice cubes, it’s too warm for safely storing frozen food because mold and bacteria can continue to grow on food surfaces. According to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, the ideal freezer temperature is zero degrees. This is also the recommended factory setting for most major refrigerator brands, helping keep food safely frozen while conserving energy and extending the life of the appliance.

Dirty condenser coils are a common culprit. When they’re clogged with dust, the refrigerator can overheat, causing the compressor’s overload protector to shut it down. The refrigerator may restart automatically once the compressor cools, but by then your food may already be warming up. Vacuum the coils regularly to clear debris and prevent overheating.

Also check the condenser fan. If it’s blocked by debris or not spinning freely, the fridge can’t release heat efficiently. Remove any obstructions and clean the fan thoroughly.

Finally, check the interior light. A stuck or misaligned door switch can leave the light on even when the door is closed, raising the temperature inside the refrigerator. To test it, close the door and use a butter knife to pull the door gasket slightly away from the frame. If light shines out, the switch may be faulty or out of alignment.

Dish soap is a trusty staple. Put a drop on a microfiber cloth with warm water and wipe with the grain of the metal. Wipe again with a clean damp cloth, then towel-dry to prevent water spots and soap residue.

For tough grease or fingerprints, use a stainless steel cleaner. These products are formulated to cut residue without leaving streaks, making them a good step up when soap and water aren’t enough.

For a quick polish after cleaning, a little olive oil can help restore shine. Apply it with a microfiber cloth and buff with the grain until smudges disappear. Follow with a dry microfiber cloth to remove excess oil and prevent a greasy finish; this leaves behind a thin protective layer that resists fingerprints.

Dust and debris can easily accumulate on refrigerator coils, forcing the appliance to work harder and use more energy. Fortunately, cleaning the coils is simple. First, unplug the refrigerator and access the coils (they’re usually behind the front kickplate or on the back of the unit). Use a shop vacuum to remove dust and debris. For hard-to-reach places, use an air compressor with a blower nozzle to loosen the dust, then vacuum it up. Remove any stubborn dirt with a soft-bristled brush or duster, then vacuum again. Finally, clean the floor around your work area, reattach any panels and plug the fridge back in.

First, listen. Do you hear anything? There should be a rumbling from the auger inside the ice bin. If there’s a rumble and no ice, ice is likely stuck in the door chute and needs to be cleared out. If you hear a hum but no rumble, the auger is probably stuck and can’t spin; emptying the bin and reloading the ice may fix it. If you don’t hear any sound at all, the dispenser switch may be broken and will likely need to be replaced by a pro. If you hear the auger turning and nothing’s clogging the chute, move on to these steps:

A great place to start is with the handles, which tend to yellow and collect grime over time. Instead of replacing them, clean and repaint for a quick, budget-friendly refresh. You’ll need spray paint formulated for plastic, plus a degreaser and a scrubbing pad.

Pry off the caps that cover the side screws, then open the door and remove the remaining screws. Take off the handles and wash them with degreaser and hot water, scrubbing any textured areas to remove buildup. Wipe them with a dry cloth and let them air-dry completely. Mask off any emblems or chrome trim, then spray-paint, coating the sides first, followed by the flat surfaces. Once the paint has dried, reinstall the handles.

Baking soda is a highly effective odor neutralizer. As bacteria break down food, they release smelly molecules that can be either acidic or alkaline (basic). Baking soda, aka sodium bicarbonate, reacts with these compounds to help reduce odors. Stash an open box in the refrigerator and replace it about every three months. Tip: Date the box so you know when to replace it.

If your refrigerator isn’t cooling properly, start with these quick checks. You may be able to solve the problem yourself before calling a pro.

From scarlet elf cup to shiitake, your birth month mushroom might reveal more about your personality than you think...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's that time of year that sees them pop up all over the place, but did you know you have a birth month mushroom?

Yes, mushrooms might not be the first thing that springs to mind when you think about personality (indeed, many of us tend to think about them in terms of how best to remove these fungi from our garden), but these fascinating plants have plenty of character.

From patterned caps peeking through woodland leaves to clusters of mushrooms growing on fallen logs, they come in an extraordinary range of shapes, sizes and colors. Some are easy to grow at home, while others are the sort of unexpected find that can make an ordinary walk feel a little more magical. And some are, of course, killers in disguise.

If you've already explored your birth month bird, birth month animal, and birth month bug, you might think you've covered all the ways to find a nature-inspired match for your birthday. Mushrooms, though, are here to prove that wrong.

We've picked 12 mushrooms, one for every month, taking inspiration from fungi you might encounter in the wild across the US and UK, alongside varieties you can grow at home. From springtime morels to fall's woodland favorites and a wonderfully pink number, each has something special to recommend it.

So, which mushroom matches your birth month? Read on to discover your fungi counterpart, learn a little about where it grows and find out whether your match is a familiar woodland sight or a colorful variety you could try cultivating yourself (hey, there's a reason the Back to the Roots Organic Oyster Mushroom Grow Kit is so popular!). Just remember that wild mushrooms can be difficult to identify, and some poisonous species resemble edible ones, so enjoy them with your eyes unless you're certain of their identity.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

January personalities are known for their determination and ability to keep going when the going gets tough. The velvet shank (Flammulina velutipes) makes a fitting birth month mushroom, then: this golden-orange mushroom can fruit in cold weather, often appearing in clusters on dead wood when many other fungi are less conspicuous.

Its ability to flourish through winter makes it a little symbol of perseverance. Pretty sweet going for a little mushi!

February's imaginative side finds its match in turkey tail (Trametes versicolor). Its overlapping fans can display beautiful bands of cream, brown, grey and other colors, making every cluster look like a tiny natural artwork. It grows on dead wood and is a lovely reminder that creativity can be found in unexpected places. It's a fungi match with plenty of visual personality.

Quietly striking rather than showy, the scarlet elf cup (Sarcoscypha species) is a lovely match for March. Its vivid red cups often appear among moss and leaf litter on fallen twigs in woodland, bringing a flash of color to the early-year landscape.

Oh sure, you might have to look carefully to spot this birth month mushroom out and about in the wild, but that is part of its charm: a little beauty for those who take the time to notice!

With its unmistakable honeycomb-like cap, the morel (Morchella species) certainly knows how to make an entrance! These sought-after spring mushrooms have an unusual appearance that makes them stand out from the crowd, just like April's bold, energetic personalities.

Morels can be found in parts of the US and UK in spring, although their appearance depends on local conditions. They're fascinating to spot, but never eat a wild mushroom without reliable expert identification: false morels can be dangerous.

May's dependable personality pairs nicely with dryad's saddle (Cerioporus squamosus), a large fungus that grows on tree trunks and fallen wood. Its broad cap has distinctive dark scales, giving it a sturdy, earthy appearance.

Often seen in spring, it's the sort of birth month mushroom that rewards a closer look at the trees around you, making it a lovely match for someone who likes to keep their feet firmly on the ground.

Shiitake (Lentinula edodes) is obviously the birth month mushroom for sensitive and sociable June babies. Its rich brown caps and familiar place in kitchens around the world give it a comforting, approachable quality.

Unlike mushrooms that are mainly discovered in the wild, shiitake can be cultivated on suitable hardwood logs or growing blocks, making it an interesting choice for anyone curious about growing their own food. And a mushroom that brings people together over a good meal? Yeah, that feels just right for June.

The golden chanterelle (Cantharellus cibarius) is a cheerful match for July, as its warm yellow-orange color and gently wavy shape make it one of the most recognisable mushrooms for experienced nature-watchers.

It can be found in suitable woodland habitats during warmer months. Chanterelles grow in association with trees, making them part of a much bigger woodland relationship. That connection to the surrounding ecosystem makes this a fitting birth month mushroom for someone who values family, friendship and looking after their own.

Few birth month mushrooms are as weirdly wonderful as chicken of the woods (Laetiporus sulphureus). Its brilliant orange and yellow shelves can stand out dramatically against a tree trunk, making it a natural choice for August's confident and charismatic personalities.

This striking fungus is found in parts of the US and UK, often on trees or dead wood. It's an attention-grabbing sight, and a reminder that nature doesn't always need a delicate touch to be beautiful.

September's practical and detail-oriented personalities are well represented by porcini (Boletus edulis), also known as – and get ready for the cutest name ever – penny bun. Beneath its rounded brown cap is a thick, solid stem, giving this birth month mushroom a robust appearance.

Porcini are associated with trees and are prized by experienced foragers and cooks. Finding them requires patience and attention to habitat, which makes this an apt match for people who like to do their homework before getting started. (You can also buy Porcini Mushrooms Spores from Amazon if you're interested).

I might be biased, but I love that October gets the most colorful match of all: the pink oyster mushroom (Pleurotus djamor). Its vivid pink and overlapping caps look almost too bright to be real, making it a wonderfully unexpected addition to the list.

Pink oysters are commonly grown at home in gourmet mushroom kits, but they prefer warmth and are less suited to cold outdoor conditions than grey oyster varieties. Their unusual color makes them a natural conversation starter, just like October's charming and people-savvy personalities.

Alright, fine; I love the birth month mushroom for October, but this one is a true stunner! Still, with its rich violet coloring, the amethyst deceiver (Laccaria amethystina) is a natural fit for November's mysterious streak.

It can be found in woodland, where its small purple caps stand out against fallen leaves and dark soil. Its color may become less vivid as it ages, which only adds to its elusive reputation, and making it a perfect match for anyone who has a passionate side that not everyone gets to see straight away.

December's birth month mushroom is the shaggy inkcap (Coprinus comatus), a distinctive mushroom with a tall white cap covered in – unsurprisingly, given its name – shaggy scales.

It can appear in grass, parks and disturbed ground, making it a potential find on an everyday walk rather than only deep in the woods. As it matures, its cap darkens and dissolves into an inky liquid – a surprisingly dramatic transformation for such an unassuming-looking mushroom, and making it well suited to our adventurous and slightly quirky babies born at the end of the year.

Of course, there's no scientific link between your birthday and a particular fungus, but that doesn't mean we can't have a little fun(gi) finding meaning in our birth month mushrooms, right down to their distinctive appearances and growing habits.

Whether yours is the sort that thrives in challenging condition, or a colorful attention-grabbing variety, there's meaning to be found in the world, wherever you look for it. And hey, if it means we have a unique mushi to call our own? So be it!

#76. When Should You Actually Use Your Hazard Lights? You May Be Using Them Wrong

Hazard lights can warn other drivers when a vehicle is stopped or disabled. Here’s when to use them, and when to leave them off.

Drivers are notorious for forgetting common traffic rules, and that can be especially true during extreme weather. A perfect example is knowing when to use hazard lights while driving.

Hazard lights are one of the simplest controls in a car, but drivers don’t always agree on when they should be used. Seeing hazard lights while driving is especially common during heavy rain, fog, sudden traffic backups, and other situations where drivers want to make their vehicles more noticeable. But should they be used during extreme weather?

Learn when hazard lights make sense, when drivers should leave them off, and what to do when bad weather makes it difficult to see.

There isn’t one nationwide rule for using hazard lights while a vehicle is moving. Some states allow them in certain situations, while others limit or prohibit their use.

AAA notes that hazard-light laws vary by state, so drivers shouldn’t assume the same rules apply everywhere. Anyone unsure about using flashers while driving should check the current driver handbook or motor vehicle agency guidance for the state where they’re traveling.

Hazard lights, also called emergency flashers or four-way flashers, make a vehicle’s turn signals flash at the same time. Their main purpose is to warn others about a stopped or disabled vehicle.

After a breakdown, flat tire, or similar problem, the driver should move as far from traffic as safely possible and turn on the flashers. The same applies after a crash if the vehicle has to remain near traffic. If it can move safely, getting out of an active travel lane should come first.

Extremely poor visibility is one situation where hazard lights may also help while a driver gets off the road.

“In extremely dense fog where visibility is near zero, the best course of action is to first turn on your hazard lights, then simply pull into a safe location such as a parking lot of a local business and stop,” according to the National Weather Service’s resources for driving in fog.

Hazard lights shouldn’t serve as a substitute for headlights during bad weather. AAA specifically advises against switching them on simply because heavy rain makes it harder to see.

“Do not drive with your hazard lights on,” according to AAA. “Hazard lights are meant to signify that your vehicle is disabled. Using them while driving could confuse other motorists.”

The flashing lights can also make a moving vehicle harder for other drivers to read. During heavy rain, drivers should instead turn on their headlights, slow down, and leave more space between vehicles.

“Hazard lights can actually reduce visibility making other drivers think you are stopped or stalled,” according to AccuWeather. “They make it difficult to see if motorists ahead are tapping on the brakes and they don’t allow you to use your turn signals.”

Avoiding dangerous road conditions can be safer than trying to manage them after a trip has already started.

“Check your local weather and traffic reports before heading out,” according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s winter driving tips. “If your roads are not in good shape, consider postponing non-essential travel until the roads are cleared. If you do have to go out, make sure you are prepared in case you become delayed while traveling.”

Not all irises need the same fall care. Knowing what to cut back, what to leave alone, and how to protect their roots makes all the difference.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In most gardens, October is a pivotal transition period for perennials as they go from active growing and flowering to winter dormancy. As early-season bloomers, irises can look pretty tired by fall, but that doesn’t mean they don’t need care.

October iris care is all about preparing plants for dormancy and ensuring they’ll emerge healthy and flowering next spring. From preventing rot to managing pests and diseases, good care now ensures healthier growth next year.

Here, we’ll focus on October chores for bearded irises, the most commonly grown type, with notes on how care differs for Siberian and Japanese irises. Essential fall care includes trimming foliage, cleaning up around plants, dividing as needed, and managing mulch appropriately by iris type.

Depending on where you live and garden, some or all of your iris foliage will be giving up the game by now. Much of the foliage will be yellow or dying. Use clean, sharp shears to remove spent leaves. For precise trimming around healthy foliage, try the Fiskars Titanium Micro-Tip Pruning Shears, available at Home Depot. Their narrow blades make it easier to snip away dying leaves without damaging neighboring growth.

In general, trim established plants back to about six to eight inches (15 to 20 cm). Leaving leaves intact can cause winter damage that collapses onto the rhizomes, increasing the risk of rot.

Leave any healthy green leaves intact, as they are still photosynthesizing and gathering energy for the plant to use next year. In milder climates, you might still see a lot of green leaves, so you’ll need to delay trimming until the plant has more yellowing leaves.

It’s very important to remove debris from around and under your irises before winter. Remove all fallen and dead leaves, stems, weeds, and other plant material and compost it, or, if diseased, dispose of it in the garbage.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

This chore is crucial because leftover material can increase the risk of plants getting diseases or being infested with pests later. The iris borer lays eggs in dead foliage, which overwinter there and hatch in the spring. Removing debris also opens up airflow, reducing the risk of fungal infections.

If iris borers have been a problem in your garden, make a note to tackle them again in spring. A spinosad-based insecticide, such as Bonide Captain Jack's Deadbug Brew, available on Amazon, can help control newly hatched larvae before they burrow into the plants. Apply when new iris shoots reach around 4–6 inches tall (10–15 cm).

Bearded irises store energy in fleshy rhizomes near the soil surface. They may rot if moisture levels are too high. It’s a good idea to check for and manage any areas of rot on rhizomes now, so they don’t get worse over winter. Brush back the soil from the tops of the rhizomes and inspect them for spots that look soft, mushy, or dark, or that have a bad smell.

Use a sharp, clean garden knife to cut out rotten areas until you reach healthy, firm rhizome tissue. A tool such as the Fiskars Big Grip Garden Knife, available at Amazon, is also handy for carefully lifting affected rhizomes to inspect them more closely. Disinfect the blade between cuts to avoid spreading infection. If a rhizome is severely rotted, it’s usually best to remove and discard it.

If you find a lot of rot, check drainage around the plants and make sure water isn’t pooling. Japanese and Siberian irises also grow from rhizomes, but these are generally less exposed than those of bearded irises. You can still check around the crowns for signs of rot or damage caused by excessive moisture.

Fall is generally a good time to divide bearded irises. However, October might be too late in some areas. In milder climates (zones 7 to 9), you can divide irises now. In colder areas, October is likely too late to move irises and expect them to establish before winter.

If you are dividing an iris now, lift the clumps carefully. A sturdy digging tool, such as the Radius Garden Root Slayer Shovel, available at Home Depot, has a serrated blade that makes it easier to dig around dense, established clumps. Take care not to damage the rhizomes as you lift them. Separate the rhizomes, ensuring each one has a healthy fan of leaves. Plant the divisions in suitable areas right away, making sure they have good drainage and that the rhizomes remain near the surface. Siberian and Japanese irises are best divided in spring.

If it’s too late to make divisions now, you can still plan ahead by identifying large clumps that could benefit from a spring division. Target bearded iris clumps that are spreading into dense patches, have a bare center, or have not produced as many flowers as in previous years.

Label or photograph the clumps you plan to target in spring, so you don’t forget. It’s not always easy to identify the overgrown irises in spring. The best time to divide next year is after flowering.

A little fall care goes a long way toward establishing healthy, flowering irises in spring. It’s easy to forget these early bloomers come fall, but don’t make the mistake of ignoring them. Irises need fall care to ease their way into winter in good health.

Bearded irises are different from many perennials in that they generally should not be mulched over in winter. The rhizomes need to remain near the soil surface and slightly exposed to air and sunlight to stay dry and avoid rotting. Never cover them in heavy layers of mulch or compost.

If you have very cold winters, you can apply a thin layer of more breathable mulch to prevent frost heaving. Use pine needles or clean straw, like CleanStraw Longleaf Pine Straw Mulch from Walmart. Other types of irises can benefit from a more typical layer of mulch to retain moisture and as protection against cold.

Growth is slowing and stopping this time of year as irises prepare for winter dormancy. This means they no longer need fertilizer. Stop feeding irises now to avoid promoting fresh new growth that will only expend energy and freeze in winter.

You can also slow down your watering routine as temperatures drop, especially if your area is getting more rain. Rather than following a fixed schedule, check the soil every few days for moisture and water as needed. A Yamron 4-in-1 Soil Moisture Meter, available at Amazon, can help you monitor moisture levels and avoid overwatering. Newly transplanted divisions will need more consistent moisture as they establish roots, but take care not to leave the soil waterlogged.
