#79. I Tried To Renovate Everything at Once. Here’s What Went Wrong…

Taking on too many renovation projects at once can leave everything half-finished. Here’s how to know when it’s time to slow down.

Home improvement isn’t the classroom: there’s no extra credit for taking on more work, and you’re not going to make the honor roll for having the most unfinished projects.

It can be easy to fall into the familiar cycle of jumping from one major renovation to another and finding your to-do list growing day after day without actually whittling it down. I know because I’ve done it. One project turns into two, then something else suddenly feels more important, and before long, several rooms are half-finished at once.

At one point during my current fixer-upper I had so many projects going that the house felt less like a home and more like a construction site.

Before you hit a metaphorical wall (continue as planned if you’re doing demo), take a step back and see if this is starting to sound familiar:

You’ve got several rooms torn apart, tools and materials everywhere, and you keep starting new jobs before finishing old ones. Or maybe working on the house just isn’t fun anymore and every weekend feels like another shift.

It’s much easier to fix a bad plan early than it is after you’re already in way over your head. Spacing projects out gives you time to finish, clean up and actually enjoy the work you just did before starting all over again.

I consider myself a bit of an expert in this area because, well, I’ve been guilty of overcommitting to projects more times than I can count. While I still find myself occasionally doing too much at once, I’m in a better position to recognize those warning signs/red flags earlier.

Recently, I wrote a column for Family Handyman about how I’m adding a 95% day to my DIY routine. Basically, I set aside a day every few months to finish all those little things I’ve been putting off. Missing trim, nail holes, outlet covers and other jobs that keep a “finished” project from actually being finished all go on the list.

I’m also getting better at utilizing my project planner to see projects through and stay on schedule. Writing everything down makes it pretty obvious when I’m trying to cram too much into one week and helps me decide what actually needs to get done first.

Learning how to triage projects will also go a long way. What do I mean by that? Instead of doing a little bit of each project every day, focus on finishing one and then move on to the next one. You can either pick the one that takes the least amount of time to complete so you can check things off your to-do list quicker, or the project that has a more time-sensitive deadline.

For people who think in financial terms, this is like the snowball vs. avalanche debt payment strategy. Or for a sports metaphor, decide whether you need the easy points or should focus on the bigger play first. I’m out of metaphors, but I think you get the general idea.

Also, remember there’s no shame in hiring a professional to finish a job you’ve started. Life gets busy and contractors are often happy to take an easy paycheck on a job that’s already been started. They might even appreciate that some of the early legwork is already done for them. If bringing in someone to do one or a few jobs allows you to finish other things, it might be worth it.

An important DIY skill is learning when to walk away. If you’re currently in this situation, or find yourself overcommitted down the road and are thinking back to this column, just remember it’s totally normal and you’re certainly not alone. If anything, it means you’re working on making your home a little better, and that’s definitely something to celebrate.

But not for too long… there are still projects to finish, after all.

#80. A Scottish Fisherman’s Cottage Gets an Update, with Make-Do-and-Mend Spirit

From house tours and expert advice to favorite finds and DIYs.

On the rugged coast of Scotland’s Isle of Mull, a small stone cottage sits just feet from the chilly water. The old bothy was a fisherman’s refuge and a sheep pen before it was purchased by Peter Harford-Cross’s family, who used it as a camping-style accommodation for years. Recently, though, the architect and his partner Rachel turned the semi-derelict structure into a cozy seaside getaway—while maintaining its original charm.

The duo, also known as Harford-Cross Architects, were careful to preserve the existing windows and pitched roof that Peter’s uncle installed in the 1980s—then infused the interior with modest contemporary comforts. “Our approach was fairly minimal,” says Rachel. “We needed surfaces that were hard-wearing and robust because of the location. There’s an element of the stone that we’ve kept and painted, but we’ve lined out the walls in durable plywood where it was necessary to provide improved thermal quality. Hopefully it has longevity and visual warmth, too.”

When it came to furniture and fittings, the couple reused and recycled as much as possible, reflecting the make-do-and-mend spirit of the island and of Peter’s grandmother, who once lived there. Nearly everything was bought on eBay or from local vintage shops. “Even though it was all secondhand and relatively inexpensive, we sourced the pieces quite carefully,” Rachel says. “It was about having a little bit of respect for the property. We chose fine pieces with their own inherent character.”

Photography by Alexander Baxter, courtesy of Harford-Cross Architects.

Your Thanksgiving cactus deserves its moment in the spotlight this holiday season, so make sure you have ticked off these easy jobs to enjoy weeks of festive blooms

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Thanksgiving falls reliably on the fourth Thursday of November, year after year. However, if you want your home filled with vibrant blooms right as the turkey hits the dining table, the most important month to give your Thanksgiving cactus (Schlumbergera truncata) love and care is October.

Despite its name, the Thanksgiving cactus (Schlumbergera truncata) bears little resemblance to desert-dwelling cacti like the towering saguaros of the American southwest. It’s got no spines at all and wouldn’t survive a day in a hot, dry desert. These plants are tropical epiphytes, native to the coastal rainforests of southeastern Brazil. Its flattened, arching green stems feature pointed, claw-like serrations along the segment margins, giving rise to its popular nickname, the claw cactus.

But the true magic of this plant lies in its vibrant flowers, erupting in radiant shades of red, magenta, soft pink, coral-orange, pure white, and gold. Yes, the plant typically blooms from mid-November to early December. Still, you only get those pretty blooms next month if you devote a little time to their care this month. By making a few simple adjustments to light exposure, night temperatures, watering and feeding now, you guarantee a breathtaking holiday display that lasts for weeks.

October is a transitional bridge for indoor houseplants, as outdoor temperatures decline and home heating systems kick on across most northern regions. For your Thanksgiving cactus, this month represents a delicate shift, as active leafy vegetative growth halts and reproductive bud development takes over. While vivacious cultivars like White Christmas, Samba Brazil and Madame Butterfly offer distinct bloom colors and stem habits, they all share a few key care needs.

If your plant spent the summer vacationing on a shaded porch or patio, early October is the time to bring it indoors before night temperatures drop below 50°F (10°C). Depending on your USDA hardiness zone, the next few days are critical. While southern areas may have a little latitude, in chillier northern areas a couple of days of sharp temperature slides can have a massive impact.

A quick check of holiday houseplants now prevents environmental shock when transitioning them indoors. However, even if your cactus has spent the summer indoors, this is still a vital time to make adjustments. Before you get stuck into key container care such as light exposure and watering, it’s a good idea to invest in a soil probe that can give you a reliable idea of light and moisture levels. I’d recommend getting hold of a diagnostic tool like the Raintrip 4-in-1 Soil Meter from Amazon, which can give you a solid heads-up about where your plant is at before you start.

Controlling light exposure in October is the single most important factor for triggering heavy flower bud formation. Thanksgiving cactuses are short-day (long-night) plants. During the day, position your cactus in a location that receives bright, filtered indirect sunlight. An unobstructed east or north-facing window sill is ideal. Avoid harsh, direct afternoon sun through south or west-facing glass, which scorches the flat green stem pads and turns them a stressed, purplish-red color.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Daytime light is only half the equation. Long dark nights are what induce flowering. To initiate flower buds, these plants require 12-14 hours of uninterrupted darkness every night for roughly 6 weeks. Even tiny bursts of artificial ambient light from living room lamps or passing streetlights can reset the plant's internal clock and stop bud formation. If needs be, gently move your cactus into a dark closet or cover it with a breathable cardboard box every evening from 6pm to 8am. Once tiny buds lock in at the tips of the green segments, you can place it back in indirect sun and leave it there for days and nights. In fact, it’s best not to move the plant after budding.

Alongside long nights, cool ambient air temperatures also help to initiate those all-important flower buds. Maintaining cooler indoor conditions during October reassures the plant that its natural blooming cycle is underway. The ideal temperature range for setting Thanksgiving cactus buds is between 55-65°F (13-18°C) at night, warming slightly to 65-70°F (18-21°C) during the day. If your plant is kept in a heated living room that stays at a constant 72°F (22°C), bud formation will be sparse or severely delayed.

If outdoor night temperatures in your region remain between 50-60°F (10-15°C) without dropping toward freezing, leaving your pot in a sheltered outdoor spot can work wonders. Alternatively, move the plant to an unheated bedroom, enclosed sunroom, or bright basement window well where nighttime temperatures run cooler. It’s well worth investing in a digital thermometer to help keep track of fluctuations. The AcuRite Digital Indoor Thermometer & Hygrometer, available from Amazon, helps you monitor daily high/low room temperatures and ambient air humidity.

As fall days shorten, your Thanksgiving cactus's metabolic rate slows. Although native to rainforests, these plants grow attached to tree branches, so their roots are susceptible to root rot in soggy potting mix. In October, shift to a conservative watering routine. Allow the top 1-2 inches (2.5-5cm) of potting soil to dry out between waterings. When you do water plants, soak until moisture drains from the bottom, and empty the drainage saucer 15 minutes later so roots never sit in stagnant water.

You also need to pause feeding. High-nitrogen feeds force the plant to push out weak, soft foliage segments rather than flower buds. So stop all feeding in October and November. You can add a diluted liquid fertilizer in late winter after flowering finishes. Additionally, pay attention to indoor humidity as household heating switches on. Maintain an ambient relative humidity of 40-60% by placing the pot on a shallow tray filled with pebbles and water, ensuring the pot bottom sits above the water line.

Placing your cactus alongside other moisture-loving tropical houseplants like ferns or calatheas helps buffer indoor humidity drops caused by household furnaces. You can also boost humidity levels with a reliable plant mister. The Gradvis Plant Mister from IKEA offers excellent pump action at a reasonable price. By establishing a consistent routine, you give your plant the precise signals it needs to set buds on stem tips.

By late October, hopefully your efforts will reward you with tiny, jewel-like flower buds forming at the tips of the arching leaf segments. Once these buds appear, the plant enters its most sensitive phase. The primary threat to your upcoming holiday show is a frustrating phenomenon known as bud blast, where tight, healthy flower buds suddenly turn yellow, shrivel, and drop off the stems overnight.

Bud blast is usually caused by sudden environmental changes or physical disruption. Selecting a permanent, draft-free location for your cactus before buds form is vital. Keep the pot far away from forced-air heat vents, cold window drafts, exterior doors, and direct fireplace radiation. You can pick up under-door buffers like Under-Door Draft Stoppers from Lowe’s, which protect your sensitive indoor plants from drafts.

Most importantly, avoid rotating, moving, or repotting the plant once flower buds exceed a quarter-inch (60mm) in size. Even rotating the pot by 180 degrees alters the direction of light, causing the plant to release ethylene gas that severs the delicate stems attaching the buds to the leaf tips. Set your plant in its holiday display location, then step back and let your cactus get settled (and hopefully bloom merrily).

Pests love this plant’s fleshy stem segments. Catching infestations now ensures your holiday blooms aren’t ruined by unsightly damage. Inspect your plant once a week under good light, checking the upper and lower surfaces of the segments, stem joints, and soil line. If you do catch pests, it’s best to do so before you start to see those flowers emerging.

Mealybugs are among the most common pests, appearing as cottony masses tucked tightly into the joints between plant segments. Scale insects present as raised brown bumps along stem edges, which scrape off easily with a thumbnail. Spider mites leave dusty stippling across stem surfaces and webbing in leaf crotches, thriving in dry indoor air. Fungus gnats show up as tiny black flies fluttering around topsoil, indicating that the potting mix is too wet. Aphids chow down on tender new growth and flower buds, sucking sap and causing buds to drop prematurely.

Address any pests before full flower buds open. Gently wipe down infected leaf segments using a soft cotton swab dipped in 70% isopropyl rubbing alcohol. Alternatively, spray the foliage with a gentle, organic insecticidal soap or pure cold-pressed neem oil drench. I recommend Bonide Captain Jack’s Ready-to-Use Neem Oil Spray, available from Walmart, for an organic blast that is tough on soft-bodied pests but gentle on stem pads.

#83. Maitake: The Expensive Mushroom You Can Forage for Free

In the Northeast, October is a special month. As red maples begin to blaze, maitake, a prized edible mushroom, appears at the base of some old hardwood trees (which it is slowly killing). Favoring oak, the dense, heavy mushrooms may be nestled against the tree’s trunk, or a few feet away, fruiting from—and feeding on—old roots. The mushrooms reappear on the same trees year after year. And they are exceptionally good to eat. It is my twelfth season of hunting maitake in the wilds of New York City, and the sense of fun has not diminished.

Here’s where to find maitake, how to cook them, and some precautions to bear in mind.

The name maitake means “dancing mushroom” in Japanese. It is very hard to control the excited wiggle in your walk as you approach the first mushroom of the season, and your next dinner. Maitake grow in temperate forests in the Northern Hemisphere, favoring cold winters and old hardwoods, and they do not differentiate between rural and urban forests. In cities you might even spot them on street trees.

Maitake is also known as hen of the woods: picture a fluffed-out gray hen sitting on her brood.

Oak trees are maitake’s usual host, and I have also seen them at the base of beeches, cherry, and even a London plane. The mushroom is parasitic, feeding on the trees’ roots, and causing a white rot, which will weaken its benefactor and contribute eventually to so-called tip-over (when a tree topples from the base).

While immature mushrooms can fit in the palm of your hand, grown-up maitake can weigh upwards of 10 pounds and sometimes double that. It is hard not to feel pleased carrying home such a prize on your way past a gourmet store charging upwards of $20/lb for foraged maitake. They are cultivated, too, a process pioneered by Japanese growers. These tame mushrooms look very different from their feral cousins: small, delicate, and frilly, versus sturdy and heavy. Their flavor is milder, although quite good.

Maitake appearing in carpets of fallen leaves are cleaner than those surrounded by bare soil, which splashes up if there is rain and is incorporated in the mushroom as it grows, making it gritty to chew. Use a sharp knife to slice the maitake at the base, trimming off any debris stuck to the bottom. Avoid mushrooms growing at the base of trees used by raccoons as a latrine (there will be tell-tale signs of scat). And always cook your wild-collected mushrooms.

What part of wild maitake is best to eat? In a young, butter-tender mushroom, the whole mushroom is delicious, cooked. On larger maitake, the gray caps, or “feathers” remain tender.

At home, slice smaller maitake in half to see how clean they are. Trim away any debris, and wash. For  tender mushrooms, you can also tear the caps, keeping a strand of the soft white core attached to each. Then wash.

For large mushrooms, cut off the caps for dinner and save the woody core to roast for broth.

In terms of flavor and fragrance maitake is exceptional. While the mushroom cooks, especially if it is roasted, the scent is—at least to my nose—reminiscent of chestnut honey. When I first made maitake chips that first bite was a revelation: It tasted as though the mushroom had been marinated in soy sauce. Maitake contains l-glutamate, a natural flavor-enhancer, and the embodiment of umami.

Two layers of maitake complexity make this woodsy pilaf sing autumn. The woodier heart makes a flavorful broth, while the roasted ears  intensify that unique flavor. (I soak the farro for 72 hours; the resulting texture of the grain, which will have begun to sprout, is wonderful.) The recipe doubles easily.

Broth: In a saucepan over medium-high heat warm the oil and add the maitake heart. Cook for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally. Add the onion, garlic, and carrots, stir well and cook for another 5 minutes. Add the wine, water, salt, sugar, and pepper. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat to cook at a simmer for 40 minutes. Strain the broth through a fine mesh sieve. Measure out 1 cup for the pilaf (use the extra for soup, sauce, or just do broth shots!).

Roast mushrooms: Preheat the oven to 375 degrees F. In a bowl toss the maitake caps with the oil and salt. Transfer to a large skillet and into the oven. Roast for 40 to 45 minutes; they should be turning crisp and smelling good. Remove from the oven, take out the mushrooms and reserve, leaving the mushroom-infused in the skillet.

To finish: Place the skillet over medium heat and add the farro with the chives, stirring for a minute. The grains will make appealing, popping noises. Push the farro to one side and add the nuts. Leave them to toast for a minute then stir everything together (you will notice that the germ of the farro is showing up whitely at the tip of each grain, now). Toast together for another minute and then pour in all the broth. Bring to a gentle boil and cook, simmering, until it has all been absorbed, about 20 minutes. Taste. Add salt. Now stir in the roasted mushrooms, and give them a minute to heat through. Serve at once.

(Although it is completely unnecessary no one has ever turned down the offer of some microplaned parmesan over the top…)

#84. When Are You Too Old To Move Furniture? Experts Weigh In

Learn how to factor in age, strength and safety before your next furniture-moving attempt.

While it’s nice to be able to tackle projects around the house yourself, it’s also important to know your limits, especially as you get older. Jobs you could easily handle in the past, like climbing a ladder to change a lightbulb, can become riskier with age.

This is especially true when it comes to moving furniture. Lifting and maneuvering heavy pieces can quickly lead to injuries, accidents or worse. But it can be tough to know when you’re too old to move furniture, as it varies from person to person.

Ahead, learn about the risks of moving furniture as you age, how to do it safely if you choose to and when it’s time to call in the pros, with advice from strength coach Zac Armstrong and physical therapist Joshua Holskey.

Moving heavy furniture becomes more hazardous as you age, posing risks like back injuries, joint sprains, pulled muscles, fractures and heart attacks.

According to Armstrong, moving furniture poses the greatest risk of injury to the lower back and shoulders. Improper lifting techniques or attempting to move furniture that is too heavy to control can lead to slipped disks, pinched nerves, pulled muscles or injuries caused by twisting. “Most injuries happen mid-carry, when you twist to avoid dropping something and hurt your back or rotator cuff,” he says.

Lower bone density, loss of muscle mass and poor balance are an unfortunate and all too common part of aging that make moving furniture especially hazardous. A trip and fall can easily lead to broken bones under these circumstances and moving heavy furniture only amplifies these risks.

Moving furniture is strenuous work that increases your heart rate and blood pressure. For older adults with cardiovascular disease, this can lead to serious medical events, including a heart attack. Know the signs of a heart attack, and work slowly to avoid overexertion. When in doubt, call a professional mover.

Before attempting to move heavy furniture, follow these tips to do it safely.

While there is no specific age, you’re too old to move furniture when the risk of injury is greater than the likelihood of success. “Is there an age to stop? No,” Armstrong says. “But there is a strength-and-control test: If you cannot pick the item up smoothly and carry it under full control, it is too heavy for you today — at 45 or at 75.”

If you feel uncertain about your ability to move furniture, err on the side of caution and ask for help or call in a professional. Many moving companies offer in-home furniture moving services.

The first frost is closer than you think... and there are three things you should do now to protect your container plants before temperatures drop.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There is so much to love about a good container garden. Pots let you experiment with color, move plants around when a border needs a little extra something, and squeeze more greenery into even the smallest outdoor space.

The trouble is, when fall arrives and the first frost is on its way, all of those lovely pots? Well, they need a little extra attention if you want them to make it through the winter unscathed. (Something I learned the hard way during my early attempts at gardening; it was devastating).

Thankfully, my husband is a professional gardener, so I've learned to listen when he starts talking about protecting plants for winter. Because, while I'm tempted to leave everything where it is and hope for the best, he has put a lot of effort into teaching me that a little preparation now can make all the difference to how well plants survive the colder months.

Temperatures are a little erratic this year, thanks to the ongoing El Niño, and things are set to be just as wildly unpredictable this winter. Planning ahead, then, is more important than ever.

So, if you've been wondering what to do with your container garden before temperatures drop, these are the three jobs that my husband recommends prioritizing.

When it comes to overwintering your container garden, my husband's first piece of advice is simple enough: figure out which of your plants can handle the cold and which can't.

"If you've got tender plants in containers, don't wait until the first frost is forecast to start thinking about where they're going to spend winter," he says. "Move them somewhere protected while the weather is still mild enough for them to adjust."

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Plants in pots are more exposed to cold than plants growing in the ground, because their roots aren't insulated by the surrounding soil. Tropical plants, tender perennials, and many plants that have spent summer outside may need to be moved indoors or into a frost-free greenhouse, conservatory, or garage, depending on their light requirements.

Top tip: Before bringing plants inside, check their leaves, stems, and potting mix for pests. It's also worth moving them gradually into their new environment where possible, rather than taking them straight from a sunny patio into a dark corner indoors.

Shop Container Plant Winterizing Essentials:

If you've got containers that need to stay outside, my husband advises you group them together in a sheltered spot. (Well, what he actually said was to treat them like penguins and get them in a huddle, but close enough).

Why? "It means they're less exposed to cold winds, and you can give the pots a little extra protection," he says. "Just make sure you're grouping plants with similar needs, and don't block drainage holes or leave containers sitting in water."

Grouping pots against a sheltered wall can help reduce their exposure to wind and make them easier to protect. It won't make tender plants frost-proof, but it can be a useful measure for hardy plants that are staying outdoors.

Top tip: Try to choose a spot that offers protection without becoming waterlogged, and raise pots slightly on pot feet or bricks if necessary to help excess water drain away. Good drainage is particularly important during winter, when cold and wet compost can put roots under additional stress.

One thing people often forget is that it's not just the foliage you need to think about. "The roots are sitting in a container that's exposed to cold air on all sides, so I always recommend giving them a little extra protection before the first frost arrives," says my husband. "You can wrap the outside of the pot with bubble wrap or hessian, and add a layer of mulch over the surface of the compost to help insulate the roots from temperature fluctuations."

Terracotta pots can be particularly vulnerable to cracking when moisture freezes and expands, so insulating the container can be helpful in exposed conditions. Bubble wrap provides an extra layer of insulation around the pot, while hessian is another option for wrapping containers.

Mulching the surface of the compost adds another layer of protection, helping to reduce temperature fluctuations around the roots. Well-rotted garden compost, manure, bark chips, straw, or shredded leaves can all work well, depending on the plant. "Just be sure to keep the mulch away from stems and crowns, and make sure excess water can drain freely," my husband adds.

Top tip: the important thing to remember is that insulation can help protect roots, but it won't turn a tender plant into a frost-hardy one. If you're growing plants that can't tolerate freezing temperatures, you'll still need to move them somewhere sheltered or frost-free.

It's important to remember that insulation is not a substitute for moving a frost-sensitive plant somewhere safe; the right approach depends on the plant, the container, and how cold your local winters become.

So, before the first frost arrives, check which plants need to move indoors, group the hardier containers in a sheltered spot, and protect exposed pots from the worst of the cold. It doesn't need to be an enormous job, either; honestly, just little time spent preparing now could help protect your plants through winter and leave you with a healthier collection to enjoy when spring comes around.

#87. The Energy Efficiency Problem With Your Fireplace—and How to Shore It Up Before Winter

A wood-burning fire to keep warm throughout the colder months might have cozy vibes, but basically you’re opening up your home to the chilly outdoors during and well past when the fire is roaring. This can result in inefficiencies that can lead to higher heating costs, poor airflow, and unnecessary wear on your fireplace and chimney system. A wood-burning fireplace is a very inefficient way to heat your home since drafts can pull the warm air up the chimney, causing other rooms to feel cooler, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Also, your heater will have to work harder to maintain constant temperatures throughout the house. Here we’ll explore the common causes of inefficiency, upgrades to boost fireplace efficiency, and best practices for maintaining your wood-burning fireplace.

There are several reasons why a fireplace is inefficient. By understanding the problems in your home, you can better address them to keep your fireplace performing at its best.

Burning wet wood in your fireplace can create excessive smoke, which is an indication of lost heat. Firewood should be dry, with a moisture reading of 20 percent or less.

Our product testers said this tool proved accurate and easy to use for sensing moisture levels in a variety of wood species.

Using the wrong type of wood can lead to inefficient burning and excessive creosote buildup in your chimney. The best types of wood for burning are dry and hard, such as maple, oak, cedar, and cherry.

A common cause of reduced fireplace efficiency is when creosote and soot—byproducts of burning wood—accumulate inside the chimney, restricting airflow and making it harder for smoke and heat to vent properly. This buildup can also become a safety hazard.

A fireplace packed with a large pile of logs can reduce airflow, which affects combustion and increases the chance for creosote buildup.

If your chimney is not drafting properly, smoke may linger in your home and fires may not stay lit for long. Draft issues can result from blockages, chimney height problems, or poor ventilation.

Keeping up with proper fireplace and chimney maintenance helps ensure efficiency, as cracked flue liners, damaged dampers, or other issues can result in more heat escaping and reduced ventilation.

To increase the energy efficiency of your wood-burning fireplace, consider making the following changes:

Constructed of clear tempered glass and available in a variety of styles, glass doors help a fireplace burn more efficiently so more heat is produced.

Made of heavy metal like stainless steel or cast iron, this fireplace accessory attaches to the back of the fireplace to reflect the heat from the fireplace into your living space.

This basic stainless-steel plate helps direct heat into the room, improving the efficiency of your wood-burning fireplace.

A fireplace damper, a metal door fitted above the firebox at the throat of the chimney, can help control airflow in and out of the chimney and enhance overall heat output. Fully open the damper when starting a fire, and then slightly close the damper to prevent excess heat from escaping once the fire is crackling. If the room still isn’t warm enough, close the damper a little bit more.

Upgrading an open, traditional fireplace with a modern, sealed insert can boost heating efficiency by about 50 percent. Traditional fireplaces waste most of their heat up the chimney, but sealed inserts trap that warmth and spread it evenly throughout the room. By burning fuel much more cleanly and efficiently, inserts help lower heating bills, cut down on smoke and chimney buildup, and prevent cold drafts. Fireplace inserts come in styles ranging from rustic to modern, allowing you to customize the look with attractive trims and mantels.

Keep your fireplace running as efficiently as possible by following these best practices:

Have a certified professional inspect and clean your chimney at least once a year. This clears out flammable creosote, soot, and blockages, while checking for damaged bricks, flue liners, leaky dampers, and chimney caps.

Use dry, seasoned hardwoods like oak, maple, or birch that have dried for 6 to 12 months and contain less than 20 percent moisture. Avoid softwoods like pine, which create excess creosote buildup. Check how wet the wood is by using a moisture meter, and look for shiny, tar-like creosote buildup using a flashlight.

For proper ventilation, make sure the damper is fully open before starting a fire. Once burning, adjust air controls to maintain a steady burn and minimize excessive smoke.

Stick to two or three logs at a time, leaving gaps between them to improve airflow and ensure a safe, efficient burn.

Leave about 1 inch of ash in the firebox to help insulate the fire and maintain a steady burn. When cleaning out excess ash, use a lidded metal bucket and ensure ashes are completely cooled before disposal to prevent unexpected fires.

Seal and insulate home cracks, gaps, windows, and doors to reduce drafts and overall heating needs. Address leaking dampers, cracked liners, and masonry deterioration immediately through professional repair services.

After months of scouring the market and putting products through their paces, we’ve named the best of the best in new tools. There’s something for everyone, from veteran pros to average Joes.

#88. Why Wind Is More Dangerous When the Leaves Are Still on Trees

Trees with full canopies catch more wind, while wet soil can weaken their hold. Here’s why fall storms can cause serious tree damage.

Trees are vulnerable to powerful storms, even a single gust of wind. While tree damage can occur any time of the year, wind damage is more dangerous in certain seasons.

Fall can be a key season for wind-related tree damage because deciduous trees may still hold their leaves when storms bring strong winds and heavy rain. That’s why anyone who has dealt with mature trees knows how much more movement a leafy canopy creates during a storm.

The reasons leafy trees face more stress during windy weather, and the role wet soil plays, help explain why some fall storms cause serious tree damage.

Tree professionals sometimes describe a dense canopy as having a windsail effect. Leaves and branches give the wind more surface to push against, placing extra pressure on the tree.

A video from arborist education account @fruitstitute on Instagram compared a thick canopy to a sail catching wind. Research published in the International Society of Arboriculture’s journal on red maples found that the makeup of a tree’s crown affects how much wind load it experiences.

A post shared by Fruitstitute (@fruitstitute)

Trees can reduce some of that pressure naturally. Leaves turn and cluster in the wind, while branches bend and move with gusts.

That doesn’t mean a tree should be heavily thinned before a storm. Pruning needs vary by species and tree condition, so major pruning decisions are best left to a qualified arborist.

Foliage can also increase the amount of wind a canopy catches. For example, an eight-year study of street trees in Rochester, New York, showed that most branch failures happened while the trees were in leaf.

Wet ground can add another risk during a windstorm. After heavy or prolonged rain, saturated soil may hold tree roots less securely. The U.S. Forest Service notes that saturated soil and shallow roots can make trees more vulnerable to being uprooted by wind.

Penn State Extension also notes that trees may begin leaning or uproot when wet soil can’t hold the root system securely. Raised soil around the roots can be one sign of movement. A full canopy catching strong wind while the roots sit in soaked soil can create a difficult combination for a tree.

Fall storms can arrive before deciduous trees have dropped their leaves, leaving a full canopy exposed to strong winds. If rain has already soaked the ground, the tree may also have less support around its roots. The combination can increase the chance of broken branches, leaning, or uprooting.

A tree’s condition still matters. Decay, root damage, weak branches, and earlier storm damage can all affect how well it handles high winds. After a storm, homeowners should stay clear of trees with new leaning, lifted soil, cracked limbs, or hanging branches. Penn State Extension recommends professional assessment when a damaged tree could threaten people or property.

Some plants earn their place many times over. These hardworking favorites deliver lasting color, impressive growth, and years of enjoyment.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you want to get the most for your money at the garden center, it helps to know which plants give you the biggest return on your investment. Some plants grow quickly enough to create a privacy hedge in just a few years, while others provide landscape interest across multiple seasons. Many produce absolutely beautiful blooms, while others can be easily propagated to fill out your landscape for free, without spending another dime.

I'm Gardening Know How's Digital Community Manager and in-house plant shopping expert. I'm also a former garden center manager with over 20 years of experience, so I know which plants give gardeners the biggest bang for their buck at the cash register.

This is the latest installment in my Garden Center Secrets series, where I share Insider tips only garden center employees know to help you shop smarter at the nursery. Here are the plants worth spending your money on.

If you want a plant that definitely earns its keep in the garden, panicle hydrangeas (Hydrangea paniculata) are hard to beat. Unlike some other types of hydrangeas, these reliable bloomers produce flowers every year, regardless of when or how you prune. This takes away one of the biggest frustrations gardeners have with hydrangeas: wondering whether you’ll actually get flowers this year.

This species also puts on a spectacular show, producing large, cone-shaped blooms that often emerge in one color and gradually change to richer, more vibrant shades as the season progresses.

Depending on the cultivar, they can grow in full sun or part shade in USDA zones 3–9, and a small, inexpensive 1-gallon plant can become a substantial landscape plant in just a few years. Plant several together, and you can even create an attractive flowering privacy hedge.

And there’s another way these hydrangeas can give you more for your money: they’re surprisingly easy to propagate from cuttings. In fact, I have even propagated them accidentally after leaving some of my clippings on the ground over winter.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

When it comes to getting the most bang for your buck from a perennial, few plants can compete with hardy cranesbill geranium ‘Rozanne.’ The price of this plant may catch you off guard, as it can cost a little more than some other perennials (though Nature Hills stocks them for about $20), but this is one plant where the extra investment is well worth it.

This is one of the longest-blooming perennials you can add to your garden in zones 4–8. Its violet-blue, saucer-shaped flowers appear in abundance above deep green foliage that remains attractive even when the plant isn’t blooming, and the blooms just keep coming from late spring well into fall.

But here’s where ‘Rozanne’ really earns its keep: that little plant you bring home can grow into a 2-3 foot clump in just a season or two, without becoming invasive. It can handle everything from moist soil to well-drained conditions and even periods of drought. It grows happily in full sun or part shade, making it an easy fit for just about any spot in the landscape.

And once your plant gets established, it can easily be divided and replanted elsewhere in the garden. So that initial investment can eventually give you even more plants to fill your landscape.

Serviceberry (Amelanchier × grandiflora 'Autumn Brilliance') is one of those trees I think just about every landscape should have because it offers something for nearly every season. It’s an especially useful small landscape tree, spanning zones 3–9, and you’ll often find it offered in both tree and shrub forms. The tree forms are compact enough to plant safely near the corner of your house, making them an excellent choice for foundation plantings.

You can pick up a small starter serviceberry at Walmart for a reasonable price.

I picked serviceberry for this list because it provides something interesting in just about every season. In very early spring, small white flowers cover the branches, often blooming before many other plants have even started to wake up. That makes them an important early source of food for pollinators when there aren’t many other flowers available.

Those flowers are followed by sweet, edible, blueberry-like fruits that can be enjoyed by both people and wildlife. So you get a harvest for yourself while also adding an excellent food source for birds and other wildlife in your yard.

And serviceberry doesn’t quit when summer is over. Its foliage provides beautiful seasonal interest in fall, often turning vibrant shades before dropping. In winter, the attractive, multicolored bark adds welcome color and texture to an otherwise dreary landscape.

Ornamental grasses are some of the most overlooked plants in the garden, yet they can offer some of the best bang for your buck. A single small potted grass can grow into a dramatic specimen in just a few years, filling a large area of the landscape for a fraction of what you might spend on a similarly sized shrub. Some varieties can reach 6 feet tall or more, creating an impressive focal point while adding movement and texture to the garden. Of course, not every landscape needs a 6-foot-tall grass, and there are plenty of dwarf and compact varieties that can fit into almost any garden.

Beyond their size and versatility, ornamental grasses provide structure throughout the seasons. Depending on the variety, they can also add beautiful winter interest, with seedheads that stand well into the colder months. And when it comes to maintenance, many require little more than a simple cutback in early spring before new growth begins.

They can also become an investment that keeps giving. Once a grass has had a few years to establish into a substantial clump, you can divide it in early spring or fall using a shovel or sharp blade to separate a portion of the root ball from the main plant. Replant those divisions elsewhere in your landscape, and one plant can eventually become several.

Just be selective about the grasses you bring home. Look for native species or well-behaved cultivars suited to your area, and always check whether a particular variety has a history of becoming invasive.

Catmint (Nepeta x faassenii) is hard to beat when it comes to stretching your garden budget. Depending on the variety, these plants typically grow anywhere from 12 to 36 inches tall and wide, making them incredibly versatile. You can tuck them into just about any corner or section of the garden that needs a splash of color in zones 3–8.

Some older catmint varieties can be prone to sprawl or flop open, but the recently introduced Cat’s Meow variety, available from Proven Winners via Amazon, maintains a more attractive, rounded mound that is often mistaken for lavender.

One of the best things about catmint is how easy it is to grow. It thrives in dry soil and easily handles drought conditions, so it doesn’t ask much from you once it’s established. After that first flush of blooms in spring, give the plant a good cutback to encourage a more compact, tidy shape while also promoting another round of blooms for an even longer display.

Catmint is also a fantastic choice for low-maintenance landscapes. It’s deer- and rabbit-resistant, has a long blooming period, and naturally forms a dense, rounded shape that works beautifully along borders, in front-of-house plantings, or throughout a perennial garden. Its aromatic foliage is another bonus, and its flowers are highly attractive to pollinators.

And the value doesn’t stop with the original plant. Like many perennials, catmint can be divided in early spring or fall, allowing you to turn one established plant into several new plants for other areas of the landscape.

Black-eyed Susan (Rudbeckia) is one of those perennials you can almost forget about until summer arrives and suddenly they burst into bloom. And what a welcome sight they are, especially when some of the earlier-blooming perennials are starting to fade, and the landscape needs a fresh splash of color.

These tough, long-blooming perennials produce masses of golden, daisy-like flowers with unmistakable dark brown central cones that return year after year. Once established, they can gradually spread to create even more color in the landscape. They look especially impressive planted in masses, but they also make excellent cut flowers.

Another reason black-eyed Susan offers so much value is how easily it can be divided. In spring, established plants can be divided to create even more color throughout your landscape or to share with family and friends. And when fall arrives, resist the temptation to cut those flowerheads back. The dark seed cones provide wonderful winter interest and remain attractive well into the colder months. Even better, those seeds provide an important food source for small birds.

They’re also remarkably adaptable. Black-eyed Susans perform well in full sun or part shade in zones 3–9, grow happily in average garden soil, and can tolerate dry conditions once established. Many varieties are native to North America, making them an excellent choice for creating a beautiful, resilient, and wildlife-friendly landscape.

Be sure to look for Black-eyed Susans in the clearance section in fall after the blooms have faded. You might even find an established plant at an even better price!

Plant Addicts has a great selection of black-eyed Susan plants, including the newly launched Treasure Trove variety, which offers superior disease resistance and is less prone to flopping.

If you really want to stretch your garden budget, there are a few more tricks that can save you a surprising amount of money. Sometimes the best value isn't finding the cheapest plant; it's finding a way to turn one small investment into an entire garden.

#90. The Painted Lumber Ends You’ve Always Overlooked Have a Very Specific Purpose

Painted lumber ends can slow drying cracks or mark a mill's product. Here's what the colors mean and why shoppers should check the stamp.

There are a few things you should always check when looking through a lumber pile at a hardware store or lumber yard. Are you getting a straight board? Is it free of major knots or defects? Is it the right size and grade for your project?

But what about the paint color at the end of the wood?

Anyone who has spent time sorting through 2x4s has probably noticed that some pieces have paint on the ends of them. But why?

The confusing part is that there isn’t one meaning that applies to every painted board. Learn why lumber ends may be painted, what the colors can identify, and what shoppers should check before relying on the paint alone.

Paint or another coating on freshly cut lumber can help slow moisture loss through the ends of the wood. The exposed end grain can dry faster than the sides of a board, which can cause cracks or splits as the lumber dries.

“End coatings are typically used to help prevent end checks on sawn lumber during the drying process,” according to research done by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, and Forest Products Laboratory. “These drying defects can cause a loss of valuable lumber.”

Timber Custom Woods describes the same process for logs and slabs.

“The ends of the slabs are painted in an effort to keep the ends of the wood from drying out to quickly causing cracking and checking,” according to Timber Custom Woods. “By painting the ends of logs before milling, we can help prevent splitting and cracking by slowing down water loss and allowing the logs to dry more evenly.”

The coating doesn’t stop the wood from drying. It helps slow moisture loss at the ends so the wood can dry more evenly.

There isn’t a standard U.S. color code for painted lumber ends. Blue doesn’t always represent one length, and red or green don’t automatically indicate a certain grade or species.

That helps explain the different answers in a Reddit discussion about 2x4s with blue-painted ends. Commenters described the colors used for certain lengths or products across different mills and lumber yards, showing how the meaning can vary by supplier.

A painted end may help slow drying, identify a particular product, or serve as an internal code for a mill or lumber yard. The color alone usually doesn’t provide enough information to identify the board.

Painted ends can also serve as a simple identification system. Lumber producers and mills may use different colors to separate types of lumber or identify species, grades, products, or brands.

U-C Coatings, which makes paint for lumber, says its end paints can serve these identification purposes. Because mills can choose from many colors, the shades don’t follow one nationwide system.

Individual companies may also use a recognizable color for a specific product. Dunn Lumber, for example, sells its signature blue-end studs. In that case, the blue identifies that company’s line of framing lumber rather than all lumber of a certain size or grade.

U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Forest Products Laboratory, “Effects of End Coatings on Defects During Air-Drying of Lumber” U-C Coatings, “GEMPAINT PLUS Premium Lumber Latex Paint” Dunn Lumber, “High-Quality Lumber: The Story Behind Our Signature Blue-End Studs” Timber Custom Woods, “Facebook post” Reddit, “Why are the 10 feet 2x4s being painted blue on one end?”

#91. Designer Visit: A Style Obsessive’s Own Saltwater Farmhouse, Restored

From house tours and expert advice to favorite finds and DIYs.

Design-forward shops, hotels, and restaurants for your itinerary.

Renovating? Start here for expert advice, deep dives, and helpful tips.

Our catalog of more than 10,000 products featured on Remodelista.

Remodelista’s members-only directory of architects, designers, and landscape professionals.

I first was notified of designer Hanna Wiegers’ impeccable taste when I rented a workspace across from hers in Portland, Maine. I was a year out from my wedding, and she showed me photos of hers, which was a whos-who of makers, designers, and creatives I’d come to know and love over the years at Remodelista: smokebush arrangements by Fox Fodder Farm; rings by Kate Jones of Ursa Major; party by event designer Molly O’Rourke.

We didn’t get much work done the days we were both in the office, but we did exchange sources: for weddings and for interiors, too.

So when Hanna and her husband, Fred, bought a tumbledown saltwater farmhouse in Maine’s midcoast, I was eager for all the details. Hanna is a designer by trade (she recently launched her own outfit, Hanna Wiegers Design), but tackling your own place—particularly one that’s a “funny mix of periods,” Hanna says—is another thing entirely. And all while pregnant to boot. I wanted to know: What was surprisingly worth it? What would she happily never do again? And, importantly, where did she source everything?

I put all these questions to Hanna, who helpfully revealed the behind-the-scenes of the project, where she now lives with Fred; their baby boy, Bert; and Huey and Ozzie, their two cats. Read on.

HW: We were hunting and hunting and knew we loved the Pemaquid peninsula because we met at Camp Kieve about 30 minutes away when we were in college. It felt like we manifested it: We wanted a place with a giant old tree, a long gravel driveway, an old barn, and a big project. This ticked every box, plus it had the most incredible mix of pristine meadow and dense forest.

The property is what made us love the house, which is ironic because we first saw it on the most disgusting, sleeting day in early April; the power was out across the southern half of the entire state. But they had the generator cranking, so it was warm and cozy inside, and it felt like a little retreat from the world. Even in the sleet and slush, you could tell the property was magical, with heron roosts and osprey nests. A bluebird was building a nest in the giant maple tree in the driveway.

HW: The house itself was a funny mix of periods. The entire first floor had been renovated with multiple additions in about 2001. The owners definitely had vast plans and ran out of money, so things felt unfinished or poorly done.

The second floor can’t have been touched since World War II. The bathrooms had peeling linoleum tile, sagging plaster walls, and a very scratched and tired cast-iron sink and tub (which we ended up giving to our painters!). There were wide pine floors that we wanted to keep, but in every crack between the boards there was so much lead paint that we couldn’t safely keep them. The upstairs felt like a perfect historic renovation project that needed help but not a full structural overhaul—the dream project for an interior designer.

HW: 1. Undo all of the weird things that the previous owners did. We’ve begun to do this but haven’t fixed everything!

2. Incorporate all locally made or vintage furniture and materials. When local wasn’t available, the goal was handmade or made using artisanal methods. We largely achieved this, with the exception of our upholstery, which was made in California and North Carolina. The plaster came from Montana, but there aren’t any New England plaster companies to choose from. The antiques and vintage furniture were all sourced in New England (shoutout to Brimfield) or NYC, with the exception of the dining chairs which I imported from someone in Denmark. There’s no such thing as perfection, but I think this project is a good example of my ethos of trying to avoid major big box stores and work with those I can develop a relationship with.

3. Update the bathrooms and tired second floor without compromising the historic beauty of a coastal saltwater farmhouse.

HW: So many! I am a Remodelista/Pinterest/magazine/vintage book addict, so images abound in my brain. Rose Uniacke’s plaster and warm wood kitchen with the Axel Einer Hjorth Uno chairs was a touchpoint for the finishes of the upstairs. Ulla Johnson’s Brooklyn brownstone by Elizabeth Roberts. Every project that Reath Design and Nickey Kehoe touch felt important for textures and fabrics downstairs. And my grandma’s uncanny ability to create a home by mixing antiques and incredible art and new furniture.

HW: Downstairs, we painted throughout, refinished the maple floors, re-did the laundry room (with Tess Tile checkered yellow and white floors, Bench Dogs blue millwork with walnut countertops, Boråstapeter wallpaper, and Urban Electric Co lighting), and swapped out a bunch of light fixtures.

Upstairs was the bigger chunk of the project. We removed all of the lead paint-laden pine floors (which we saved to potentially strip and use in another project) and restored the plaster walls and ceilings, which were sagging and not doing great. We created a new massive wall of millwork in our bedroom where there was a tiny nonfunctional closet. We redid both upstairs bathrooms. There also were only pull-chain lights in the entire upstairs, and not a single plug. So the electrical work was a HUGE part of the renovation to get everything operational for a more modern life. Ditto the radiators: The heat was via very unsightly radiators from the 1980s ,and we replaced them with Runtal units, which I love.

HW: I wish I could take credit for the blue floors but they’re original! It’s actually linoleum.

HW: Living with plaster walls is the greatest gift one can give themselves! We only did plaster upstairs because downstairs was a mix of drywall and original plaster walls, but everything had been painted, so plastering on top of that would have largely defeated the purpose of using plaster (avoiding paint fumes, allowing the wall to remain breathable, controlling moisture in the air—none of that can happen if there’s a layer of paint behind it).

But happily, upstairs was the original plaster and lath, so we could use it and get to experience how lovely it is to have a space with no drywall. It smells like warm wood and minerals upstairs, which is the most delightful smell. We had a lovely friend of Michael’s named Errol Towers apply the plaster, and it was amazing to watch him work. He was able to completely restore the original sagging laths and problem cracking areas in the ceiling, and he did it perfectly. I did take a virtual plaster application class with Jersey Ice Cream Co. to see if I might be able to give it a shot but I was too afraid in the end. We used untinted plaster from New Age Artisans and painted the trim and doors in Sherwin Williams’ Snowbound.

HW: Yes! I did so much research on this. I wanted them to be completely matte but have a super soft feel underfoot. We went to a bunch of different mills in the midcoast to look at samples of local wood floorboard and settled on red birch from AE Sampson. We then had our flooring installer test a ton of different stains and finishes on top and landed on Bona Traffic HD Raw. The installer, who is definitely accustomed to shinier and waxier finishes, was like “this is wrong,” but it was EXACTLY what we wanted. It has the same color as the unfinished wood, which was what I wanted because it has a pink tone that reflects onto the plaster and makes everything feel warm and cozy.

HW: I was pregnant during the renovation, which was insane—we moved in the week after he was born (would not recommend!). Bert’s bathroom was definitely designed to be playful for a kid, but I have things I’d do again to protect the house and the kid from each other. Some of the fabrics aren’t performance, and I’d also have designed the stair railing to be more kid-safe. It’s not to code at all, but it was historic and so beautiful that we couldn’t bring ourselves to remove it. It gives us a heart attack every time he walks down the hallway, though.

HW: Biggest difference is probably the Runtal radiators. I love the quality of heat that radiators give off. It’s just so pleasing and cozy, and the faint radiator sound feels nostalgic but these are very efficient and also made in the US.

HW: To be honest now that I’ve lived with plaster, I don’t think I’ll ever paint anything ever again. Paint peels over time and smells bad after you do it (even when you use nontoxic paint), and repainting is such a slog with all of the sanding that’s required. Plaster requires almost no prep and it has zero smell. The texture on the walls makes everything glow. It feels simultaneously grounded yet ethereal. It’s a perfect material. Also, surprisingly, plastering was less expensive than painting!

HW: The kitchen! It’s from the people who did the 2001 renovation and they really botched it, which is why it’s not pictured. The floors are blue linoleum, which we’ve actually become fond of and are quite functional, but the cabinets have a peeling plywood veneer on them, the organizational layout is terrible, the sink is tiny, and the oven barely works (to cook at 350 we have to heat it to 450)! So that, plus a major overhaul of the lighting in there, is the game plan.

For more of Hanna’s work, head to Hanna Wiegers Design.

#94. Your Garden Beds Need a Living Blanket This Fall – These 5 Cover Crops Fight Weeds and Enrich Soil

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Every Garden Needs One Plant That Makes It Feel More Private – These 7 Beauties Give You Year-Round Cover

I Managed a Garden Center for Years – and I Know These 6 Plants Give You the Biggest Bang for Your Buck

8 Fling-and-Forget Seeds to Scatter in Fall for Flowers that Grow Themselves – it’s Practically Magic!

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Fall is the perfect time to invest in next year's growing season. These hardworking plants quietly do their job while your garden rests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Call me sentimental, but I feel sad seeing those vegetable beds that overflowed with produce all summer lie empty in October. Gone are the bright red tomatoes, the sprawling zucchini, and the leafy greens growing in lush rows. All that remains is a little debris and bare garden soil. Likewise, beds once filled with colorful annual flowers may now look rather sorry for themselves.

Seeing those sad, abandoned rows was what originally prompted me to try growing cover crops in the fall. But once I got into the habit, I discovered so many other benefits that I now recommend them to friends, family, neighbors – and you. In fact, cover crops offer many of the same benefits as mulch, suppressing weeds, improving soil structure, and protecting against erosion. They can also act as green manure, adding valuable organic matter and nutrients to the soil when you cut them down and incorporate them before spring planting.

Growing fall cover crops isn’t difficult, but it helps to get the information you need up front, including how to prepare the soil, which cover crops to plant, and when to plant them. That’s why I’ve pulled it all together for you in this article.

Even if you don’t feel sentimental about the deserted autumn beds, there are many reasons not to leave garden soil bare over winter. The practice can damage soil health, structure, and fertility.

Let’s think about erosion first. When plants grow in soil, their roots anchor it in place, preventing the precious top layer from blowing away. Winter’s worst can easily blow or wash away bare soil. That reduces the amount of topsoil that spring crops have to grow in.

Beyond washing away topsoil, winter rain can leach water-soluble nutrients from the soil. These vital nutrients are essential to growing a healthy spring crop. In addition, it can leave the soil crusted over, damage soil structure by removing air spaces, and generally leave it severely compacted.

Soil like this is not a good place to plant spring vegetables or flowers, but the weeds don’t object. In fact, aggressive winter weeds invade the bare ground, followed by nettles and bindweeds, as well as other early spring weeds.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Cover crops address almost all bare-soil-over-winter issues, and they do it in spades. When you plant fall cover crops, their roots dive deep and hold the soil firmly in place. Weed roots are tougher than winter wind and heavy rain. That means that they prevent erosion. That’s important, but it’s not the whole story.

Installing fall cover crops also keeps winter weeds away, or at least dramatically reduces their number. They also stop the soil from crusting, improve the soil structure, and add additional organic matter back into the soil to get it ready for spring planting.

Be sure to wait 2–3 weeks after terminating the cover crops in spring before planting.

So, which cover crops should you grow? The best choice depends on your climate, soil, and what you plan to plant in spring. Some are particularly good at suppressing weeds, while others improve soil fertility or help break up compacted ground.

The good news is they are not expensive – you can pick up a 5-variety collection from Survival Garden Seeds on Amazon for about $10. For larger areas, consider a 10lb cover crop mixture from Outsidepride.

Here are some of the best options for protecting and improving your garden beds over winter.

If you are just wading into the world of fall cover crops, winter rye (aka cereal rye) is one of the best places to start. This extremely cold-hardy, cool-season grass should be planted about four weeks before the first hard freeze. It is easy to grow and very reliable. You can pick up a 10lb bag of winter rye seeds from CZ Grains at Walmart.

Winter rye has deep, fibrous roots that stop erosion in its tracks. In fact, those roots can also loosen and break up heavy clay and choke out weeds. But it offers a second layer of weed protection: the plants release chemicals that block some weeds, like pigweed. In addition, those roots trap and hold residual nitrogen and minerals over winter, preventing leaching.

Chop out winter rye in early spring before it gets too woody.

Hairy vetch is another great fall cover crop. It is a hardy winter annual legume and an especially effective cover crop because it fixes large amounts of nitrogen in the soil, up to 200 pounds per acre. That means that, come spring, you don’t need to add fertilizer.

The roots of this legume prevent erosion over the winter. It is a dense vining crop, with spring growth up to 12 feet (4 m) tall. It completely shades out any early-spring weeds.

Plant this cover crop early enough for the roots to be well established before the first hard freeze. You’ll want to take out your hairy vetch cover crop in spring while the plant is in the early bud or early flower stage.

Buy hairy vetch seeds from Sow Right Seeds on Amazon.

This cover crop is attractive and effective. Crimson clover is just plain pretty for a legume, with bright crimson, cone-shaped flowers that attract bees and beneficial insects in spring. It’s a good choice for those living in regions with milder winters.

Sweet Yards sells crimson clover in various pack sizes on Amazon.

Crimson clover is a cool-season annual legume that grows rapidly. It fixes nitrogen in the soil, adding up to 200 pounds per acre, which is perfect for fertilizing your spring garden. What about weeds? Crimson clover forms a dense ground cover mat that totally blocks weeds.

Plant clover seeds up to eight weeks before the first frost. It grows best in well-draining soil. This is a cover crop that is easy to terminate in spring since it dies back or breaks down easily, unlike aggressive root crops. Mow it down before it goes fully to seed. Wait a few weeks before planting your next spring crop.

Austrian winter peas – or winter field peas – are cool-season annual legumes that are popular fall cover crops. Like other legumes, these peas fix nitrogen in the soil, producing up to 150 pounds of nitrogen per acre, to the benefit of your spring crops.

Outsidepride sells Austrian winter peas via Amazon in various pack sizes.

These plants are lush vines that carpet the soil. Just by growing, they choke out winter weeds. If you use rye or oats as companion plants for fall cover crops, they will provide upright physical support for winter pea stems.

Plant Austrian winter peas a month or two before the first hard frost in your area. It’s best to give these peas five or more weeks of growth to establish strong root systems and low, compact growth before freezing temperatures arrive. Come spring, these are easy plants to terminate. Their hollow stems can be chopped down in spring once they hit full bloom.

These are fast-growing cool-season annual grasses that make an exceptional cover crop. You can pick up a pack of winter oats seeds from Sow Right Seeds on Amazon. The plants’ dense, fibrous roots anchor the topsoil in place all winter long and also break up compacted earth.

Winter oats germinate quickly, helping them smother winter weeds. The plants also absorb soil nitrogen and release it back to microorganisms as they break down.

Winter oats often die back from winter frost. But this doesn’t stop their cover-crop value. The dead grass forms a natural, easy-to-manage mulch blanket.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours.
