#95. That Stamp on Lumber Tells You More Than the Price Tag

Stop picking your lumber based on how it looks.

A lumber grader with almost 30 years on the job once watched a buyer reject five good boards for wane (bark or missing wood along an edge), then hand-pick five replacements. All five were below grade. Most of us choose lumber by the price tag and by eye, and the eye picks wrong more often than you’d think. The stamp on lumber tells you what the eye can’t. It says whether a board is rated to carry a floor, what decides how far it can span, and roughly how much shrinking it has left to do after it’s nailed in place.

I framed and renovated houses for years with Wargo Construction, and I didn’t really know what that stamp said until I read the federal standard behind it. It’s a block of black ink a foot or two from one end of the 2x4s, 2x6s and other framing lumber in the aisle, and it names the mill, the grading agency, the grade, the species and how wet the wood was when it was surfaced (run through a planer to its final size). A 2×4’s grade turns on what its knots, splits and holes do to its strength, a different question from the one behind plywood grades.

Ahead, you’ll find what each field on the 2×4 stamp means, which values it can hold, and what each one changes about the board you take home.

The 2×4 stamp tells you which grade a qualified grader, or an agency-approved grading machine, assigned the board under an agency accredited by the American Lumber Standard Committee (ALSC). That grade, with the species beside it, keys to the board’s design values (the published strength ratings that building codes are built on). Those values feed the span tables (the code charts that give how far a joist or rafter of a given size, species, grade and spacing can reach between supports).

The 2024 International Residential Code requires sawn lumber used for load-supporting purposes, meaning floor, wall and roof framing, to carry that stamp or a certificate of inspection.

The grader in that story is Pete Austin, Director of Quality at the Western Wood Products Association (WWPA), who has graded lumber for almost 30 years, 23 of them in sawmill production, and runs the association’s design-value testing for Western species. Most buyers never read past the grade, he says. They look at a board, see No. 2 and assume it will work. “I don’t think that they fully understand what it is they’re buying,” he says.

Paul Conway is Executive Vice President of ALSC, the standing committee behind the federal lumber standard PS 20 and the body that accredits the agencies grading under it. He wrote that grading is not an exact science, because a tree is a natural product and no two are alike. Agencies check a mill’s grading by the unit (the banded bundle of boards a mill ships as one lot), and a unit is on grade when 95 percent or more of its pieces make the grade. That is why the stamp “does not guarantee, however, that every single piece of lumber a buyer purchases in the big box store retailer’s bin will be on grade,” Conway wrote.

By the USDA Forest Products Laboratory’s Wood Handbook, the published bending value starts from a strength near the bottom of the grade, one that only about 1 board in 20 falls below, and is then divided by 2.1 for safety and for loads that stay in place for years. “These design values are intentionally conservative to account for the weakest pieces that could be found in each grade,” Conway wrote.

Every accredited stamp carries the same five fields in the agency’s own layout, and some carry a surfacing note beside them. Start with who made and graded the board, then read the three fields that say how it should behave.

This is the number, name or brand of the mill that made the piece. Three boards photographed for this article read 134, 167 and 338, all Stimson Lumber mills on WWPA’s list. The number won’t change what you buy. Read it and move on, because it only matters if a bad batch ever has to be traced back to where it was made.

The logo beside the mill number belongs to the agency that supervised the grading, not to the mill. ALSC’s January 2026 list, on alsc.org, carries seven U.S. grading agencies and ten Canadian ones, with a picture of each agency’s stamp for checking an unfamiliar logo. The ones you’re most likely to meet:

The Canadian agencies, where Spruce-Pine-Fir framing comes from, grade to the National Lumber Grades Authority’s rules and print their own logos. The grader is usually a mill employee, and the independence sits in the supervision. ALSC requires an agency to inspect each mill at least 12 times a year, and PS 20 bars accrediting any agency controlled by a producer whose products it inspects. Every agency’s dimension lumber rules have to conform to one National Grading Rule, so a No. 2 means the same thing under any of these logos. If the logo is one you don’t recognize, check it against ALSC’s list before you trust the grade printed beside it, because a logo that isn’t on that list isn’t an accredited grade stamp, and the board counts as unstamped (see the FAQ below).

The grade sets what’s allowed to be wrong with the board. The National Grading Rule for dimension lumber lists eight grades in three groups, with each group serving a specific purpose.

Stamps abbreviate them (SEL STR, 1, 2, 3, CONST, STAND, UTIL, STUD), and a combined grade such as “2 & BTR” means No. 2 or better, carrying No. 2’s design values.

Knots decide most of the grade, and where a knot sits matters as much as how big it is. A knot is where a branch grew out through the trunk, and the grain swirls around it instead of running the length of the board, so the wood there is partly cross-grain and the load piles up around the knot instead of passing through. A board carrying weight bends, stretching one edge and compressing the other; the stress is highest along those two edges and lowest along the centerline. So an edge knot costs far more strength than the same knot in the middle of the face. And a narrower board gives the same knot a bigger share of its width, which is why the allowances shrink as the board does.

The rule book turns that into numbers. On a 2×4, No. 2 allows a 1-1/4-inch knot at the edge and a 2-inch knot on the centerline, Stud allows a 1-3/4-inch edge knot, and Utility allows 2-1/2 inches anywhere on the face. Austin has measured the difference by breaking boards in WWPA’s test lab. A knot on the centerline leaves clear wood along both edges to carry the load, he says, so it takes far more force to fail.

At the rack, match the grade on the 2×4 stamp to the job as the list above gives it, and between two No. 2s, take the one whose knots sit away from the edges.

This names one species, or a group that shares design values, printed as an abbreviation. The groups you’ll meet most:

The species group sets the design values, so the same grade and size span different distances in each group, and the span tables in the residential code list Douglas Fir-Larch, Hem-Fir, Southern Pine and Spruce-Pine-Fir as separate rows. Canadian-graded Douglas Fir-Larch and Hem-Fir carry an (N) after the name and have rows of their own.

If your plans or a span table name a species, buy that species. When the store stocks a different group, read the row for that group on the stamp instead, which may mean a larger size or tighter spacing, or ask whoever drew the plans. And if nothing names a species, read the group off the stamp, not the shelf tag, and look up that row with the grade before you pick a joist size and spacing. The tables are in the residential code’s floor-joist and rafter chapters, which the International Code Council posts online. A tag reading “Premium Whitewood Stud” is store signage. “Whitewood” covers a family of pale softwoods, and the board underneath says Hem-Fir.

The code says how wet the board was at the planer, not how wet it is now. What you’ll see:

You’ll often see HT beside the code. It isn’t a moisture code but a heat-treatment mark, which says the board’s core was held at 56 C (about 133 F) for at least 30 minutes to kill insects, which is what export packaging needs. Most mills with kilns stamp everything KD HT, Austin says, because one kiln run earns both, and WWPA inspectors read the kiln charts and meter the boards every month. S-DRY usually means the board reached 19 percent some other way. One WWPA mill near Fairbanks, Alaska, dries its lumber in the yard over months and stamps it S-DRY.

The code matters because wood keeps moving after it’s stamped. It shrinks as it dries and swells as it takes on moisture, almost all of it across the width and thickness of the board and very little along its length. Conway puts the change at about 1 percent across the width and thickness for every 4 points of moisture. On the way from 19 percent down to the moisture of a heated room, that comes to about 1/8 inch on a 2×4 or 2×6 and about 1/4 inch on a 2×10 or 2×12.

Framing that does that shrinking after it’s nailed in place loosens around its fasteners and moves the finishes attached to it. Nail pops in drywall, cracks in plaster, open joints and uneven floors are the common signs of a frame that shrank too much after it went up. A board stamped S-GRN starts wetter, so it has far more shrinking ahead of it, and what it hasn’t dried off by the time it’s nailed in place, it loses in the wall.

Match the moisture code to where the board is going. For anything inside a heated house, buy KD or S-DRY. Buy S-GRN only where movement can’t hurt anything (temporary bracing, for instance), because it will keep moving.

The big-box chains often order No. 2 with in-house limits on wane and skip (a patch the planer didn’t touch), Austin says. Mills flag those orders with words like “Premium” or “Top Choice,” which ALSC allows only if they sit at least 6 inches from the grade stamp, and such a mark can’t borrow a grade name from the rule book the board was graded under. One mill had to drop an “APP” mark, Austin says, because APP is the rule book’s own name for an appearance-limited grade.

None of those words changes the grade or says anything about strength, and the same word on a shelf tag is the store’s own, not the mill’s. What the word buys you is fewer patches of wane and skip, which matters for looks and for nailing. A stamp can also carry a surfacing note beside the five fields, like the “1/4 EE” on the boards photographed here; it isn’t one of the five and doesn’t change the grade. Read past all of it to the grade stamp, and never take “Premium” as a strength claim.

Not for load-supporting framing, unless a grading agency issues a certificate of inspection for the pieces. Any of the accredited agencies can inspect the pieces and issue one; arrange it before the lumber goes in, because it stands in for the stamp.

Yes, and it voids it. Ripping (cutting along the length to narrow a board), resawing (cutting through its thickness) or planing a graded board cancels the grade and its design values under PS 20, and the old stamp is supposed to come off. Cutting to length doesn’t.

So never rip down a joist, rafter or header to make it fit. Buy the size the span table allows instead, and if a ripped piece has to count as graded lumber, ask your local code official before it goes in the wall.

Often it’s the other way around. A board with clean edges and a large knot is weaker than a board with wane and no knots, because wane and skip are appearance problems that don’t cost strength, while knots, holes and splits do. When Austin breaks No. 2 pieces whose only defect is wane, they test stronger than pieces carrying a knot or a hole, “every time,” he says. “I’ll buy lumber with wane before I buy lumber with large knots all day long.” That fits where the wood comes from. Wane is usually the rounded outside of the log showing on the board, and the outer rings of a trunk are its mature wood, while the weaker juvenile wood grows in the rings nearest the center.

Sight down it, because nothing on the stamp predicts warp. The grade caps how much curve and twist a board can leave the mill with, more can develop afterward, and neither says anything about strength. Austin’s test lab takes in boards as wet as 30 percent moisture, stacks them with spacer strips between the layers and lets them dry to the lab’s 12 percent before breaking them. Some warp badly and others never move, he says. “There’s no way to put on a stamp what it can do.”

So sight down each edge and each face from one end and set aside any piece with a visible curve or twist. Then stack the rest flat where it will be used, with spacer strips between the layers, and give it time to take on the room’s moisture. Austin’s lab allows a couple of weeks for stock that comes in wet; kiln-dried framing has less distance to travel, but give it time all the same. Then sight it again before you cut, and set aside anything that moved.

7 Underused Shrubs and Perennials to Plant in October for Extraordinary Fall Color that Lasts into Winter

I Managed a Garden Center for Years – and I Know These 6 Plants Give You the Biggest Bang for Your Buck

7 Underrated Perennials to Plant in October – For The Gorgeous Fall Color You Never Knew You Were Missing

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

While fall brings out gorgeous colors, it can also signal leaf drop, so this time of year is vital for adding plants that offer privacy – and these look lovely doing it!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Spending time in the backyard is high on most people’s priority list. Whether gardening or clearing, playing games, or just relaxing, most of us crave a sanctuary from all the pressures of life – without the worry of prying eyes. To help give that privacy, it helps to add evergreen hedges, screens, or specimen plants that naturally create a lush, living buffer between your space and the outside world.

Year-round foliage not only makes the yard feel more secluded, but it also reduces street noise, blocks unsightly views, and provides vital shelter and food for birds. By installing a green screen, you can soften property edges with ornamental value, especially if you use flowering or scented privacy ideas. For maximum sound dampening and visual screening, you can add layers, planting taller specimens in the background and medium shrubs and spreading groundcovers in front.

These privacy ideas can also incorporate vertical vines where space is restricted. Climbing vines cover trellises, fences, or arbors quickly, usually in as little as one season. Choosing evergreen species ensures your boundary stays lush even when deciduous favorites lose their leaves. Just be sure to select well-behaved varieties and avoid invasive runners like English ivy. The list below will hopefully inspire you to add vital layers of privacy in beautiful new ways.

October is one of the best times for planting evergreen screens, shrubs, trees, and woody vines. While top growth slows down as air temperatures cool, the soil retains heat from summer. This combination encourages new plant roots to establish rapidly without the stress of hot late summer days. Roots settled now will continue growing until ground frost hits, giving your privacy plants a massive head start come spring.

When preparing your sites, focus on soil quality. Dig planting holes twice as wide as the nursery container to give roots room to expand. It’s also a good idea to mix organic compost or worm castings into the earth to improve moisture retention and soil structure. Try a handful of Earth Science Earthworm Castings from Amazon to enhance soil health in a gentle, organic way. For heavy clay or sandy soils, dehydrated organic amendments help to boost proper drainage, preventing root rot.

Give some thought to your USDA hardiness zone and local climate. Regional considerations are key with fall planting. In colder northern regions (zones 3-6), you need to finish planting by late October, so roots settle before deep ground freezes. However, southern gardeners (zones 7-10) can plant through November. Finish each fall planting with a 3-inch (8cm) layer of organic mulch to insulate roots against freeze-thaw cycles. Let’s meet our privacy screens, hedge plants, vines and shrubs.

When you need rapid vertical privacy in tight spaces, Skyrocket juniper is a brilliant needle evergreen. Hardy in zones 3-9, this pencil-thin cultivar grows 15-20 feet (4.5-6m) tall, while maintaining a narrow spread of 2-3 feet (60-90cm). Its dense, silvery blue-green foliage holds its crisp color year-round, creating a formal living screen along property lines, narrow side yards, or patio borders without encroaching on lawn space. You can buy Skyrocket Juniper Trees from Nature Hills for fast-growing vertical screening in narrow spaces.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Skyrocket (Juniperus scopulorum 'Skyrocket') thrives in full or partial sun, and adapts easily to lean, dry or sandy soils, if drainage is sharp. It’s very drought-tolerant once established, and requires virtually no pruning to maintain its spire-like shape. Plant it in a sunny spot, where it can receive at least 6hours of sunlight daily. Don't overwater or plant in poorly draining, soggy soil. Pair it with low-growing flowering shrubs or ornamental grasses for a stunning layered boundary.

If you’re after a fence or trellis screening that can fill the space with unforgettable fragrance, star jasmine (Trachelospermum jasminoides) is an evergreen vine like no other. Hardy in zones 8-10 (and grown in sheltered courtyard containers in colder zones), this twining climber has glossy, dark green leaves that remain lush all year long. As a pretty bonus, in late spring and early summer, it erupts with hundreds of starry, pure-white flowers that can fill the yard with intoxicating scent.

This evergreen climber grows rapidly, reaching 18-20 feet (5.5-6m) tall with sturdy support. It handles full sun to partial shade, though flowering is most profuse in sunny spots. It just needs a sturdy lattice, pergola, or wire trellis for its twining stems to cling to in the first place. Don't prune heavily in early spring, as it sets flower buds on old wood. In autumn, its glossy foliage can often take on attractive bronze or purplish tones in cooler weather. You can buy Expert Gardener Star Jasmine Live Plants from Walmart for quick-growing fragrance and year-round lush growth.

Fragrant tea olive is a dense broadleaf evergreen shrub prized for intense scent and heavy cover in southern landscapes. Hardy in zones 8-11, this glossy green screen shrub produces glossy, dark green foliage that forms a thick barrier 10-15 feet (3-4.5m) tall. While its small flower clusters look subtle, they deliver a rich, sweet perfume reminiscent of ripe apricots and peaches during fall and early spring. You can buy Orange Flowering Fragrant Tea Olive from Amazon for its sweet scent and bright blooms as well as its dense year-round privacy screening.

Tea olive (Osmanthus fragrans) performs best in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-draining soil. Popular cultivars include Apricot Gold, which features striking apricot-orange blooms, and Butter Yellow for cream-colored flowers. Plant it near outdoor seating, windows, or entries where its fall fragrance can be appreciated. Just don't prune heavily in late summer, as blooms form on previous season's growth. It makes a lovely formal hedge or background screen with lower flowering perennials.

If you want an evergreen privacy shrub that thrives in cold northern climates, while offering vibrant seasonal shifts, the PJM rhododendron is a gorgeous plant for privacy. Hardy in zones 4-8, this tough broadleaf evergreen grows into a dense, rounded shrub that is 5-6 feet (1.5-1.8m) tall. In spring, it fills with lavender-pink blooms. Then, in fall and winter, its leather-like leaves transform into a mahogany-bronze tone that adds rich color to snowy winter borders.

This rhodie handles winter wind and freezing conditions far better than traditional large-leaf rhododendrons. It thrives in partial shade and dappled sun, and only needs acidic, moist, well-drained soil. Top-dress with some pine needles or acidic leaf compost to help maintain optimal growing conditions into winter, and underplant with shade-loving spring bulbs or Japanese forest grass. You can buy Rhododendron PJM Elite Plants from Walmart for lush year-round interest at an impressive scale.

Carolina jessamine (Gelsemium sempervirens) is a native evergreen vine that brings cheery sunshine color in late winter, as well as dense vertical screening. Hardy in zones 7-10, its wiry, reddish stems climb over fences, trellises, and arbors, reaching 10-20 feet (3-6m). Its glossy green leaves provide year-round privacy, while late winter and early spring bring clusters of bright trumpet blooms that attract early pollinators.

This low-maintenance climber grows happily in full sun to partial shade, plus a wide variety of soil types, quickly producing thick fence cover. It is naturally deer-resistant and heat-tolerant, making it an excellent choice for sunny fence lines, porch railings, or mailbox trellises. Just don't allow livestock or pets to ingest the plant, as all parts contain toxic alkaloids. You can buy Carolina Jessamine from Trees at a real bargain, plus there’s a discount code if you hurry.

For fast, impenetrable privacy screens that form a feathery living wall, arborvitae Green Giant (Thuja standishii × plicata) is an impressive choice. Hardy in zones 5-9, this hybrid evergreen tree grows at an astonishing 3-5 feet (90cm-1.5m) per year, rapidly maturing to 30-40 feet (9-12m) with a broad base 6-12 feet (1.8-3.6m) wide. Its soft, fan-like foliage remains bright year-round without bronzing in winter cold. You can currently buy Thuja Green Giant from Trees for a very generous discount.

This quick-growing evergreen is very adaptable, handling full sun to partial shade and thriving in rich, moist, well-draining soils. Unlike delicate arborvitae varieties, it has exceptional resistance to heavy snow and is rarely bothered by deer. Just space each tree 5-6 feet (1.5-1.8m) apart for a tight, solid hedge, and don't allow young trees to dry out during their first season in the ground. These evergreens make an effective windbreak, noise barrier, or background screen along wide property edges.

Camellias are gorgeous winter bloomers, combining dense broadleaf evergreen privacy with jaw-dropping color, as many other plants are resting. Hardy in zones 7-10, Camellia sasanqua species grow into lush shrubs 6-10 feet (1.8-3m) tall. From October to December, when much else is dormant, they produce elegant ruffled flowers that pop against dark, glossy foliage. Buy Warm Hearted Ruby Camellia Plants from Plant Addicts for magenta blooms and a substantial upright habit.

Camellia sasanqua is more sun-tolerant and open-growing than its spring-blooming cousin (C. japonica), making it ideal for hedges. These vibrant beauties prefer partial shade, protected from harsh afternoon sun, and thrive in moist, acidic, well-drained soil. Use as formal hedges, specimen patio plants, or foundation plantings alongside hydrangeas and ferns.

Creating a private sanctuary doesn't require lots of extra tall wooden fences. By introducing a thoughtful mix of fast-growing evergreens, fragrant broadleaf shrubs, and lush climbing vines this October, you can quickly create a living, multi-layered green wall that shields your home year-round. Pick your favorite varieties, get planting this fall, and enjoy a secluded, beautiful garden for years to come…

#98. Common Parking Rules Drivers Often Get Wrong

Parking rules are as important as driving rules, and although some vary from city to city, most are the same everywhere.

Driving around the country is a favorite American pastime, and I’ve certainly done my share. When I arrive in a city in which I’ve never been before, I like to ditch the car for a while and walk around. But that can be risky if you don’t know the parking rules that apply there. And given the traffic flow modifications that many cities have recently adopted, the rules (some of them, anyway) seem to be changing faster than drivers can keep up.

Where can you park and where can’t you? If parking is legal, how long can you stay without getting towed, and how much will it cost if you get towed? But really, there’s no mystery, according to auto insurance specialist Melanie Musson.  “Knowing where you can and cannot park is pretty easy if you pay attention.”  All you have to do, she says, is follow the signs.

You can always park in a municipal parking lot or parking garage, as long as there’s room and you pay the fee. It’s usually also OK to park on the street, especially if other cars are there, but if the space you choose has a meter, it’s important to feed it. Fines in congested urban areas can be expensive. The cost of a meter violation rose by 40 percent in San Francisco since the pandemic and can set you back more than $100, according to the San Francisco Standard.

Signs usually identify the places you can’t park, as well as curb colors and symbols, such as the universal handicap symbol. Anyone who has taken a driver’s test should know them, because they’re the same all over North America. Engineer Paul Dorr of The Traffic Group refreshes your memory. You can’t park in front of:

Double parking, which means parking alongside a car that is legally parked, is also a violation that some big cities take seriously, even if you do it for only a few minutes. The base fine in New York City is $115, and it rises quickly if you do it repeatedly.

If you see a sign near an open parking space, be sure to read it. It’s probably advising you:

When you pull into a space with a meter, read the meter label before you feed it, because in most cities, parking in a metered space is free after a certain time of day, usually 6 or 8 PM. You might not have to pay.

The label also tells you the rate per hour and, if the meter takes payment cards, it usually provides basic instructions for using one.

In increasingly congested cities, cars compete for curb space with bike lanes, commercial loading zones, pedestrian walkways, outdoor dining, bus stops and EV charging stations. To manage all this, some cities prohibit street parking in certain areas altogether.

Two big changes across the country have an increasing impact on your ability to park. One is the sheer number of cars on the road, which has grown steadily over the years, jumping by 13 million in 2023 alone. The other is that some cities — San Francisco, San Jose, Austin and Hartford among them — have reduced available parking to make room for more buildings. This puts a premium on parking spaces, and meter rates may be significantly higher or vary according to time of day or demand in these cities.

The signs near an available parking space may be advising you of alternate street parking. That’s a parking rule that requires drivers to move their cars from one side of the street to the other on specific days and times so street sweepers can clean along the curb.

“Typically,” explains Dorr, “parking is restricted for one day during the week between certain hours so the street sweeper can clean that side of the street. The following week the parking restriction is on the other side allowing the other side of the street to be cleaned.” Needless to say, you can get a ticket if you ignore these signs, and your car could get towed or sideswiped by a street cleaner.

If your car gets towed, it’s important to retrieve it quickly, because storage fees accumulate every day the car is impounded. You can usually find out where it is by calling the local police non-emergency line. According to Dorr, you ‘ll have to pay some or all of the following fees:

“Look up the municipal government page (such as the local Department of Transportation or Parking Authority) for the city you plan to visit,” advises Dorr. “They often list street sweeping schedules, permit zones, and meter rates.” In addition he suggests consulting a parking app like Spot Angels or ParkMobile, or a GIS parking restriction map on your mobile device for the city you’re visiting.

You can park on any street as long as there are no painted curb colors or posted signs. To avoid a fine, you must stay the legal distance from fire hydrants and intersections, you can’t block a driveway, and your car must be within 18 inches of the curb. Some cities require you to turn your front wheels toward the curb when parking on a slope and fine you for non-compliance.

It’s pretty standard, but it can vary depending on the city. According to Dorr, the standard rule is 15 feet. Two outliers are Washington, D.C., where it’s 10 feet, and Salt Lake City, UT, where it’s only 5 feet.

This depends on local laws. It’s generally legal unless “no overnight parking” signs or signs advising of alternate side parking are posted. In some residential neighborhoods, you may see a sign advising that a permit is required to park there. “If there are “permit parking only” signs and you don’t know what a permit means,” says Musson, “that’s a good sign that you don’t have a permit and can’t park there.” She also advises paying attention to what other drivers do. “If no cars are parked on the street, that’s a good sign that it’s not allowed.”

“In recent years, we’ve seen retail drift into a sort of sameness,” write Nancy and Kimberly Wu. “Building Block Etc. is our way back to meaning—a space for connection, where relationships happen face-to-face, and where you might hold something in your hands before choosing to make it part of your life.” The sisters are both industrial designers who studied at the ArtCenter College of Design in Pasadena and had impressive corporate careers before teaming up. Kim was a car concept designer for Honda in Tokyo and Nancy worked on performance footwear for Nike in Portland. They’re first generation Taiwanese-Americans, raised in Southern California—their father is an engineer—and after moonlighting long distance on their own designs, they returned home to their parents’ house in Orange County to launch Building Block.

That was back in 2011—the sisters were 25 and 27—and the brand started as a collection of five geometric handbags that attracted a cult following. It led to a successful shop and workshop in LA’s Chinatown, where the line expanded to include housewares. In 2023, Kimberly and Nancy transitioned their business into a creative consultancy, Studio Building Block, offering industrial design solutions. And more recently, they opened Building Block Etc., a shop showcasing a tightly edited array of their own designs and work by fellow maker friends. Explains Nancy, “we’re drawn to pieces that have clarity in material and form, a sense of utility, and the ability to reveal more over time.”

Photography courtesy of Building Block Etc. (@buildingblock).

Building Block Etc. is at 3021 Rowena Ave. in Silver Lake; it’s open Wed.–Sun., 11-5.

#100. 13 Types of Holly Plants All DIY Landscapers Should Know

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Updated Oct 16, 2026 4:53 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Holly bushes—which can usually be identified by their stiff, spiny foliage and red, yellow, or black berries—require little care unless you want to keep them sheared into hedges. In most cases, you will need both male and female bushes should you want the females to produce berries.

Hollies can serve as foundation shrubs for the front of your house, or you can shape them into trees instead. The popular types of holly bushes below include the Japanese, Chinese, American, English, yaupon, blue, and winterberry categories, each of which have their own cultivars, recommended hardiness zones, and best uses within a home landscape.

Due to their small, spineless leaves and (usually) black berries, Japanese holly bushes don’t look like typical hollies and may be mistaken for boxwood shrubs. The ‘Drops of Gold’ cultivar grows up to 4 feet tall and wide with yellow variegated leaves; that variegation is brightest in full sun. Because it is a female clone, it will require a male holly nearby if you want berries. According to Dirr’s Encyclopedia of Trees and Shrubs by Michael Dirr, any male holly can pollinate any female holly if both flower at the same time.

USDA plant hardiness zones: 5 to 8Best for: Foundation planting, hedge, groupWhere to buy: Get a 1.6-gallon Drops of Gold Holly at Monrovia for $103

One of the greenest of holly evergreen shrubs and named for its elegantly slender profile, this cultivar grows up to 8 feet tall but only about 3 feet wide. It, too, is female and lacks the typical spines, so it is not “the sharpest pencil in the cup”—or pot. This can be a good thing when it is positioned in high-traffic areas, but it will need a nearby male to produce its dark-purple berries.

USDA plant hardiness zones: 5 to 8Best for: Large containers, living fence, vertical accentWhere to buy: Get a 1–2 ft. Sky Pencil Japanese Holly at Trees.com for $21.95

Chinese hollies are a bit pricklier than the Japanese type, but each leaf has only a single spine at the tip. They also don’t require pollination to produce their red fruits during fall and winter. One of the most popular holly tree types, Burford usually matures at 15 feet and often is sheared into high hedges. But it is capable of reaching 25 feet in height if allowed to grow as a tree rather than a shrub.

USDA plant hardiness zones: 7 to 9Best for: Hedge, small tree, specimen plantWhere to buy: Get 3-gallon Evergreen Dwarf Burford Holly Shrub (2-pack) at The Home Depot for $76.92

For those who prefer a small holly bush, ‘Carissa’ should measure up—or down! This slow-growing shrub generally doesn’t exceed a height of 4 feet, though it is capable of reaching 8 feet tall, and its dense growth makes it ideal for a low holly bush hedge. The University of Florida notes that ‘Carissa’ can revert back to a ‘Rotunda’ form and produce more spines than is typical and that its “berry display is mostly inferior to Ilex cornuta ‘Burfordii’.” Because holly flowers (which appear in spring) are small and white, the plants typically are grown for their foliage and berries rather than their blooms.

USDA plant hardiness zones: 7 to 9Best for: Border, foundation plant, hedgeWhere to buy: Get a 3-gallon Carissa Chinese Holly at Shadetreesandshrubs.com for $23

American hollies are among the largest and hardiest types of holly plants—growing upwards of 50 feet tall in the wild. They also have the spiniest foliage for a winter holiday vibe. However, they don’t always produce the typical red berries, which might be a good thing if you prefer a less Christmassy plant. The ‘Canary’ cultivar instead offers yellow fruits on plants that can grow up to 30 feet tall, but it will require a nearby male to produce those berries.

USDA plant hardiness zones: 5 to 9Best for: Foundation plant, bird garden, or woodland gardenWhere to buy: Get a 3-gallon Canary American Holly at Wilson Bros. Gardens for $94.97

Those who prefer showier foliage may want to opt for ‘Steward’s Silver Crown.’ Named for nurseryman T. Linwood Steward, who discovered it, this mutation is sometimes erroneously advertised as ‘Stewart’s Silver Crown’ instead. It is a female cultivar with silver-edged leaves, tinged with pink when young, and can grow to 25 feet tall. As with other types of American holly, it will require a male pollinator nearby to produce its red berries. (Keep in mind that “nearby” means no more than 100 feet away.)

USDA plant hardiness zones: 5 to 9Best for: Foundation plant, hedge, or specimen plantWhere to buy: Get a 1-quart ‘Steward’s Silver Crown’ Holly at Holly Ridge Nursery for $22

Similar to American hollies in that they, too, usually have spiny foliage and red berries, English types are less hardy. ‘Argentea Marginata,’ which can grow to 40 feet tall, offers frost-edged (white variegated) foliage that can be set off by contrasting red berries, provided the female plant is pollinated by a male. Keep in mind that this showy cultivar is not drought-tolerant and performs best in coastal climates, where it can even become invasive.

USDA plant hardiness zones: 7 to 9Best for: Accent plant, barrier, privacy screenWhere to buy: Get a 6.2-gallon Variegated English Holly at Lowe’s for $110.50

If you prefer a holly bush with yellow variegation, opt for ‘Gold Coast’ for leaves with gilded edges. A male type which grows to 6 feet tall, it doesn’t produce fruits itself but can pollinate female hollies. It is hardier than most English cultivars. Since it drops no berries, it’s also a good choice for areas where those hollies may otherwise be invasive through self-sowing. Gold Coast English holly should be provided with afternoon shade in hot climates.

USDA plant hardiness zones: 6 to 9Best for: Accent plant, foundation plant, hedgeWhere to buy: Get a 1.6-gallon Gold Coast English Holly at Monrovia for $103

Acclimated to the South, yaupon hollies produce kinder, gentler (spineless) foliage than most other hollies. They also have an easy-going nature and will tolerate more shade and/or drought than those others do, though they still require pollinators. A fast-growing holly, yaupons typically top out at about 20 feet, but ‘Bordeaux’ plants are dwarf holly bushes and seldom grow taller than 5 feet. The cultivar name refers to the new foliage and winter foliage, which has a burgundy tinge.

USDA plant hardiness zones: 7 to 9Best for: Bonsai, container plant, hedgeWhere to buy: Get the 3-gallon Bordeaux Yaupon Holly at The Home Depot for $37.81

One of the more unusual holly tree varieties, this one grows to 30 feet tall and lets its hair, er, branches down in a pendulous growth pattern resembling that of weeping willow. It makes a good stand-alone tree; if you want red berries too, however, you will need to provide the female tree with male company. Also, because the tree does sucker, it won’t be on its own for long unless you remove those suckers.

USDA plant hardiness zones: 7 to 9Best for: Accent plant, specimen plant, topiaryWhere to buy: Get a 5–6 ft. Folsom’s Weeping Yaupon Holly at Treeland Tree Farm and Nursery for $166

Introduced by Kathleen K. Meserve, the so-called blue hollies actually derived from crosses between English holly, Chinese holly, and the prostrate-growing Ilex rugosa. They are considered, by Oregon State University, to be “the hardiest of the hollies that have the stereotypic ‘holly look,’” and they sometimes can survive in USDA Hardiness Zone 4 as well as in the recommended Zones of 5 to 7. ‘China Girl’ derives from a cornuta cross, grows to 10 feet tall with kelly green foliage, and will produce red fruits when paired with ‘China Boy’ or another male holly.

USDA plant hardiness zones: 5 to 7Best for: Foundation plant, hedge, shrub borderWhere to buy: Get a 2.25-gallon Dwarf Burford Holly at The Home Depot for $44.38

One of the offspring of an English holly cross, ‘Blue Girl’ grows to 8 feet tall with blue-green foliage and red berries and will require a pollinator such as ‘Blue Boy.’ You sometimes can purchase a combo package with two plants—one of each sex—growing together in a container. Otherwise, when acquiring male plants, try to provide at least one for every three female plants for the best fruiting. Grow these in full to partial sun in well-drained acidic soil with a little organic fertilizer.

USDA Plant Hardiness Zones: 5 to 7Best for: Barrier plant, border, privacy screenWhere to buy: Get the 4–5 ft. Blue Girl Holly at Bay Gardens for $189.99

Not all hollies are evergreen. The winterberry type drops oval leaves in winter, so only colorful fruits remain to decorate bare branches. ‘Winter Gold’ makes sunny yellow berries on a winter shrub that tops out at 8 feet tall; consider it your holly berry plant. And, yes, you will need a male holly berry bush pollinator to get all those fruits. Keep in mind that holly berries are toxic and shouldn’t be eaten by people or pets. They often will last into early spring if not consumed by wild birds first.

USDA plant hardiness zones: 3 to 9Best for: Shrub border, bird garden, native gardenWhere to buy: Get a 3-gallon Sparkleberry Winterberry Holly at Woodies Garden Goods for $89.95

#102. You May Be Able to Get Your Lowe’s Order Delivered By Drone Soon

Lowe’s drone delivery can bring select tools and supplies to eligible homes in minutes. Here’s how the new pilot works.

Trips to the hardware store might soon look different. Or at least, less frequent. That is the expectation after Lowe’s launched a new drone delivery option. The retailer has started a pilot at one of its stores, allowing eligible customers to order small project supplies through DoorDash and receive them via Wing drone. The service is still limited, but it offers a look at how a quick hardware store run could change.

Learn where the option is available, how the service works, what shoppers can order, and more.

Lowe’s launched its drone delivery pilot in September 2026 at its Matthews, North Carolina, store. Customers place eligible orders through DoorDash, while Wing handles the flight.

Available products include hand tools, paint supplies, tape, batteries, cleaning products, and other lightweight essentials. Lowe’s says some orders can arrive in as little as 20 minutes.

“Home improvement projects rarely go exactly as planned,” according to a press release by Lowe’s. “Whether halfway through a paint project, tackling a weekend repair, or working on a jobsite, forgotten supplies can stall momentum by requiring a trip to the store.”

If an address qualifies, DoorDash shows a “Lowe’s by Drone” storefront with eligible products. Wing drones currently carry about 2.5 pounds per flight, so the service is limited to lightweight items.

After an order comes in, Wing automatically plans the flight. “When a customer places an order, our system automatically chooses a route to safely and efficiently deliver your package, avoiding other aircraft and obstacles,” according to Wing’s website.

At the destination, Wing says the drone checks the delivery area for obstacles before lowering the package to the ground on a tether.

Lowe’s announcement did not include plans or a timeline for a broader rollout. Living nearby does not guarantee access. DoorDash checks each delivery address and only shows drone delivery when the location qualifies.

The delivery site must also have enough open space for Wing to lower the package safely. Customers who do not qualify can still use Lowe’s other pickup and delivery options.

“Any technology we implement is designed to eliminate that friction so our customers can complete their projects quickly,” said Seemantini Godbole, chief information and AI officer at Lowe’s, in a press release by the company. “By piloting drone delivery, we’re addressing a real project pain point with an innovative solution that is integrated into the retail journey, giving our hometown customers next-generation fulfillment right when they need it.”

For homeowners and DIYers, the service is designed for small supplies that can hold up a project when they are forgotten. It gives eligible customers another option for getting those items without making another trip to the store.

#103. Kitchen of the Week: Minimalist Cabinetry Meets Medieval Stonework in Somerset, England

From house tours and expert advice to favorite finds and DIYs.

Design-forward shops, hotels, and restaurants for your itinerary.

Renovating? Start here for expert advice, deep dives, and helpful tips.

Our catalog of more than 10,000 products featured on Remodelista.

Remodelista’s members-only directory of architects, designers, and landscape professionals.

According to local lore, Isobel Rorison and Dominick French’s English countryside home once served as a rest stop for monks making the pilgrimage between Glastonbury and Sherborne Abbey. That’s why the couple lovingly refers to the stone abode (parts of which date back to the 1380s) as The Priests’ House—though it also functioned as a dairy, a farmhouse, and an ex-ambassador’s residence throughout the centuries. Most recently, Dominick’s mother had been the historic home’s steward and had made few updates in her 40 years there. So when he and Isobel took the reins after her passing, they promptly decided a kitchen renovation was in order.

“We opened up the bottom floor to what would’ve been the original layout when it was built, which actually fits perfectly with modern living,” says Isobel. “Since it’s Grade II* listed, we couldn’t move anything else. There are two walls of windows and one with a huge fireplace, so that only left one wall for cabinets.”

With the floor plan set, Isobel and Dominick considered the aesthetic direction for their old/new cookspace. Thinking that ornate, Victorian-style cupboards would clash with the medieval wood beams and stonework, the duo opted for minimalist custom cabinetry by Husk, with clean-lined flat Fenix fronts that highlight the rustic original features. As for the palette? The couple chose muted hues of rusty red, dusty blue, and gray-green because they would’ve existed in the 15th century, when this section of the house was constructed.

#104. Yeti LoadOut GoBox 15 and 30 Review: Rugged Gear Cases That Keep Contents Dry

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Published Oct 16, 2026 2:27 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

I’ve tested several Yeti coolers, but the company’s LoadOut GoBoxes are different animals. They’re hard-sided gear cases that are designed to keep supplies dry, clean, and organized whether they’re riding in a truck bed, boat, campsite, or garage.

I tested the LoadOut GoBox 15 and the larger LoadOut GoBox 30 gear cases, loading them with food and supplies, rolling them over, inspecting the latches and seals, and finally doing what any curious tester would do—I tied ropes to them and threw them into a lake.

Both came back with their contents dry. That was the test that sold me.

Very. I started with simple ordinary abuse—loading them, carrying them around, and deliberately rolling them onto their sides and tops. The latches stayed closed and the cases never felt flimsy or prone to popping open.

Then came the lake. I attached a rope so I could retrieve each GoBox, tossed it into the water, let it get thoroughly wet, and then pulled it back out. The contents inside stayed bone dry.

That matches what the cases are designed to do. Both meet IP65 and IP67 standards for protection against water and dust, making them useful for boating, fishing, camping, overlanding, or storing electronics and emergency supplies where moisture could ruin expensive gear.

The  GoBox 15 became my favorite for smaller loads because it’s easy to grab and carry. It makes sense for electronics, first-aid supplies, fishing gear, tools, cameras, or anything else you don’t want bouncing loose in a vehicle.

The GoBox 30 offers substantially more room and includes organizational features that make it useful as a camp pantry, tackle box, camera case, or general gear locker. The removable tray keeps smaller items from disappearing at the bottom, while the divider helps separate different types of equipment.

The boxes are also designed to stack together, which I can see being useful in an RV, boat, truck bed, workshop, or garage where storage space matters.

No—and that distinction is important. I carried food and supplies in mine, but Yeti specifically says the GoBoxes are not insulated and should not be filled with ice. If food needs to remain cold for an extended period, use a real cooler or place an insulated lunch box inside the GoBox.

What the cases do exceptionally well is protect whatever is inside from water, mud, dust, crushing, and general travel abuse. That can include packaged food, cooking supplies, dry ingredients, or camp kitchen gear, just not perishables that depend on the case itself for refrigeration.

The two sizes I tested make the most sense for people who routinely carry gear that’s either expensive or important enough that getting wet isn’t an option. Anglers, boaters, campers, photographers, hunters, DIYers, and contractors could all put them to work.

The GoBox 15, at about $125, is the better grab-and-go size for smaller essentials. The GoBox 30, at about $250, offers enough capacity to organize a much larger assortment of equipment and adds a divider along with its removable tray.

Yes, they’re expensive for storage boxes. But they don’t behave like ordinary totes, either. After deliberately knocking mine around and tossing them into the water, I came away thinking of them less as storage bins and more as protective cases for the things I really don’t want damaged.

I don't know about you, but I'm always looking for a little inspiration to get me out into the garden as the seasons change. And if there's one person making fall cleanup look positively magical right now, it's Pamela Anderson.

The actor and gardening enthusiast recently shared a video on Instagram captioned, "A beautiful fall morning from the garden… another clean up day," along with a few of her favorite October gardening jobs.

Honestly, it's the sort of thing that makes you want to put the kettle on, pull on your gardening gloves, and spend a few hours pottering among your plants, Pamela Anderson-style.

A post shared by Pamela Anderson (@pamelaanderson)

Moving through her garden in the soft fall light, Pamela has her pruners at the ready as she tends to her roses and gathers fresh produce, including carrots, tomatoes, and peppers. There's even a wonderfully whimsical soundtrack, accompanied by little murmured observations such as "the early bird gets the first worm."

Honestly, if all gardening chores came with that kind of fairytale atmosphere, I might be a lot more enthusiastic about getting them done. But beneath the dreamy aesthetic, Pamela Anderson's video is also a timely reminder that fall is an important season for garden maintenance (even if it's just to do this one expert-approved job).

That's right, folks; Pamela Anderson's video isn't just a mood, but a blueprint for a well-functioning garden in the autumn.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

With that in mind, then, here are a few jobs worth tackling now to help your plants make it through the colder months – and to make the most of any vegetables still growing in your beds.

One of the first things that caught my eye in Pamela Anderson's video was her tending to her roses, pruners in hand. Still, fall generally isn't the time for a dramatic cutback, as hard pruning can encourage vulnerable new growth or leave plants more exposed to winter weather.

Instead, focus on what your roses really need in October and stick to removing dead, damaged, or diseased stems, along with fallen leaves and other debris around the base of your plants. And, while you may also be tempted to deadhead every spent bloom, remember it's worth exercising a little restraint. Some roses develop attractive rose hips that provide winter interest and a food source for wildlife, so you don't necessarily want to remove every fading flower.

If you're unsure whether your roses need attention, a little tidying is often better than reaching for the pruners with too much enthusiasm. Save any substantial pruning for the appropriate time for your rose variety and local climate.

Pamela Anderson's garden isn't just about beautiful flowers. In the video, she also gathers carrots, tomatoes, and peppers, which is a timely reminder to check what's ready to come inside before colder weather sets in.

If you've been growing vegetables this year, fall is a good opportunity to make the most of your hard work. Carrots can often remain in the ground until you're ready to harvest them, provided the soil conditions are suitable and it isn't at risk of freezing. Tomatoes and peppers, meanwhile, should be picked as they ripen, with any remaining fruit monitored as temperatures fall.

Regular harvesting also gives you a chance to assess which plants have finished producing and which might continue for a little longer. Once your vegetable plants are spent, you can remove them and clear away any diseased material, helping prepare your beds for the next growing season.

Just remember that the best timing depends on your local climate and USDA zone, the varieties you're growing, and the forecast. If a frost is on the way, you may need to harvest tender crops sooner rather than later.

Still, there's something especially satisfying about bringing a basket of homegrown vegetables into the kitchen on a crisp fall morning. It's a lovely reward for all those hours spent watering, weeding, and tending your plants through the summer.

What I love about Pamela Anderson's video is that she makes gardening look less like a checklist of chores and more like an opportunity to slow down and enjoy the season. Between the soft light, the whimsical music, and her gentle reminders to pay attention to the world around her, it's a welcome change of pace from the usual rush to get everything ready for winter.

Of course, not every garden needs the same jobs at the same time. Your climate, the plants you're growing, and the weather ahead will all influence what needs doing. But checking on your roses, harvesting ready vegetables, and clearing away diseased plant material? Why, they're all very useful places to start.

So, if your fall garden to-do list has been sitting untouched for a little too long, perhaps Pamela's latest video is the nudge you need. Grab your gloves, find your pruners, and head outside for a little while. You might even find that, with a bit of sunshine and a slower pace, those garden chores feel rather magical after all.

#106. Why Trump’s Federal Fuel Standard Cuts Could Make You Pay More for Gas

Dropping fuel standards from 50 to 30mpg seems drastic. Here's what's going on with these rule changes.

It’s not exactly a secret that gas prices are pretty high right now. Anyone who took a road trip this summer, commutes regularly or works in trucking can tell you that the simple act of driving a vehicle is currently very costly. And when gas prices are this high, one thing tends to dominate the minds of drivers everywhere: fuel efficiency.

Owning a vehicle that gets high miles per gallon is one of the simplest ways to get more out of your gas. Unfortunately, a recently announced rule may make it easier for auto companies to lower their fuel-efficiency standards and start producing vehicles that use more gas on average.

Earlier this week, the Trump administration announced a new rule that dramatically reduces the fuel-efficiency requirement for new vehicles. Let’s take a look at the new rule and how it will shape the next half-decade of car manufacturing.

Under the Biden administration, strict fuel efficiency rules were set that required automakers to meet a fleet-average fuel economy of 50.4 mpg. Trump’s new rule, dubbed the “Freedom Means Affordable Cars” initiative, slashes that requirement from 50.4 mpg all the way down to 34.9 mpg.

For those of us who are new to this kind of lingo, a “fleet-average fuel economy” means the combined performance of all vehicles produced by an automaker. So this rule doesn’t mean that every car a manufacturer makes has to hit that new 34.9 mpg— it just means they have to hit that mark as an average across all of the cars you sell.

The Trump administration believes that the former standards set by the previous administration are too high and have forced automakers to produce vehicles that their customers do not want to buy.

“This rule restores integrity to the national fuel economy program, balancing vehicle affordability and energy conservation goals while improving safety on our roadways,” said NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison. “Newer cars are safer cars. By reducing vehicle prices, more American families will be able to afford newer vehicles, and sensible standards allow automakers more freedom to design and produce vehicles consumers actually want.”

Critics of the plan are skeptical that the changes are being made in good faith, as most of the savings gained from dropping fuel standards will go straight to the automakers. In theory, cars will be cheaper to produce, which is obviously good for the company that makes them.

But is it good for the consumer? Sure, these new standards might knock some money off your monthly car payments. But there’s a good chance you’ll have to put that savings directly into gas, with lower fuel efficiency naturally leading to more time and money spent at the gas pump.

Atid Kimelman with the Natural Resources Defense Council called the new rule a “get out of jail free” card for U.S. car companies.

“Fuel economy standards are supposed to improve fuel economy over time,” said Kimelman. “For Americans facing prolonged high prices at the pump, the administration has made the stunning move to basically force them to pay more.”

These fuel regulations are set for 2031, so it will be a while before consumers actually see any change in auto prices related to these new rules. It will likely have a noticeable impact on the number of electric vehicles that U.S. automakers develop and produce in the near future. Part of the new rules is eliminating the “CAFE credit trading program” which allowed automakers to sell or trade credits earned when their lineups exceeded fuel economy targets to other manufacturers that didn’t meet the CAFE requirements.

That trading program will now be gone by 2028. That means that electric vehicle companies like Tesla, which were able to sell credits to other automakers and use that revenue to develop their own vehicles. Removing that revenue stream will certainly impact the number of electric vehicles developed and produced in the United States— which is the ultimate goal of the current administration.

“Eliminating the credit trading program restores fairness, puts all automakers on an even playing field, and ensures that manufacturers are spreading fuel-saving technologies throughout their fleets,” reads the White House’s official statement.

For now, the average American is not going to feel the impact of this new rule. Just don’t be surprised if the next time you go to shop for a car, you find yourself looking at some low fuel efficiency numbers and a lack of electric options.

#108. Before & After: An Architect Couple Reimagines Their Austin Landscape with Help from a Friend

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

As soon as architects Annie-Laurie Grabiel and Arthur Furman, the couple behind the firm Side Angle Side, completed the renovation of their 1939 Austin bungalow, they turned their attention to the outside. “It was almost like the day we finished the renovation, we realized we needed to have outdoor dining,” says Grabiel. The couple loved the H-shaped footprint of their house, and how it created intimate indoor-outdoor connections, especially with the patio between the two back wings. Inspired by the home’s emphasis on outdoor living, they extended the roof of one wing to create a dining pavilion off of the kitchen.

The rest of the yard, however, was a bit of a puzzle. Located in the path of a drainage easement, the yard had a moat-like channel, for managing stormwater runoff, crossing the sloped yard. The architects developed a plan to fit a pool, but they called on their friend landscape architect Cameron Campbell to give them a second opinion on what they’d designed.

Campbell saw possibilities that Furman and Grabiel had not. He drew up a new plan that completely reimagined the contours of the yard, building the pool into the slope through a series of terraces. “It was so much better than what we were thinking about that we had to do it,” says Grabiel. While Campbell’s design would require significantly more site work, the couple knew it would ultimately improve the flow and increase usable space.

Campbell designed the terraces, which are built from reinforced concrete masonry blocks that have been covered in chukum, a type of Mexican plaster, so that the stormwater travels through four levels, slowing down and filtering into the planting beds as it does. “He designed it in such a way that there are a lot of planting areas that soften everything,” says Grabiel. He also recommended native and climate-adapted plants—like native dwarf palmetto, bamboo muhly, and silver pony foot—that could create the lush, layered feeling Grabiel craved. In the area closest to the dining area, Grabiel sowed native Texas wildflowers, including coneflowers, black-eyed Susans, and sunflowers to attract pollinators.

While Furman and Grabiel love how much more use they get out of the new yard, Grabiel is perhaps even more excited about how alive the garden is, buzzing with birds and bees. “Every little move we made, every plant, every tree–everything we did was a little invitation to insects and bees,” says Grabiel. “It just blows my mind how much better it got. Before it was just a hill of grass.”

Below, a tour of the reimagined, re-enlivened landscape.

#109. Exposed Pipes: How to Cover Them If You Want to—and What to Do With Them If You Can’t

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Published Oct 16, 2026 12:59 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Exposed pipes and air ducts running along ceilings can become an architectural eyesore, leaving homeowners wondering when it’s smart to conceal them, work around them, or leave them alone. While boxing in or painting exposed pipes and ducts can improve a room’s aesthetic and even offer insulation benefits against freezing temperatures, not every pipe or duct should be covered. In fact, fully enclosing gas lines or restricting access to essential shutoff valves can present serious safety hazards and code violations.

From choosing the correct paint to ensuring removable access panels are built into enclosures, find out what building design, HVAC, and plumbing professionals recommend so you can decide what to do about exposed pipes and ducts in your home.

Exposed pipes and air ducts can be covered, but never permanently conceal a component that must remain accessible for operation, inspection, maintenance, or repair, warns Andy Gibbs, an architectural engineer, building designer, and president of RemodX in Tucson, Arizona. “We commonly use drywall soffits, boxed-in framing, removable wood panels, or decorative slat panels,” adds Richard Golding, a general contractor, project manager, and founder of NYC Build Remodel LLC in New York City. “The best solution depends on ceiling height, available space, and maintenance requirements.”

HVAC ducts can generally be enclosed in soffits or ceiling cavities, provided required airflow, insulation, fire protection, and clearances are maintained, says Gibbs. Keep in mind that fire and smoke dampers, balancing dampers, and serviceable mechanical equipment may require access openings. “Enclosures must not obstruct required ventilation, combustion air, or equipment servicing,” Gibbs explains.

Water supply and drainage pipes can be enclosed in walls, ceilings, or soffits, but required drainage cleanouts, shutoff valves, and serviceable plumbing components must remain accessible, says Gibbs. Proper insulation and moisture protection must also be considered before enclosure. “In cold climates, insulate water pipes to prevent freezing, and in hot climates insulate pipes running through super-heated attics to prevent excessive water temperatures,” advises Gibbs. “Existing leaks, corrosion, or questionable piping should be corrected before covering.”

Gas lines should never be permanently enclosed inside a sealed soffit without ventilation, says Jon Graham, CEO of Element Plumbing, Heating & Air in St. George, Utah. “I have walked into homes where a previous owner had dry-walled completely over a gas line—no vent, no access, nothing,” he recalls. “You can’t smell a slow leak in there, and by the time someone notices something is off, the gas has had nowhere to go for a long time. That’s not a renovation choice; that’s a safety issue that puts everyone in the house at risk.”

Gas pipes can be safely enclosed in soffits or routed through walls and ceilings per gas codes. “While covering gas lines itself isn’t dangerous, gas shutoff valves must remain accessible, and certain fittings, unions, flexible appliance connectors, and other connections cannot be concealed in inaccessible spaces,” notes Gibbs. Gas pipes must also remain supported and protected per code, so be sure to check with local building officials.

The benefits of covering exposed pipes and ducts depend on what they are transporting. “Concealing gas piping in a soffit creates a cleaner appearance and offers opportunities to incorporate recessed or linear lighting as an intentional architectural feature, but natural gas does not freeze, so no thermal protection is required,” explains Gibbs.

On the other hand, enclosing water pipes in foam insulation sleeves can reduce heat loss and improve freeze protection but a decorative drywall box soffit won’t prevent freezing. In hot climates, attics can exceed 150 to 165 degrees Fahrenheit, which can heat water in exposed supply lines to extreme temperatures, says Gibbs. “Routing water pipes beneath attic insulation or wrapping them in foam insulation can reduce heat gain.”

Properly insulated HVAC ductwork reduces heating and cooling losses, particularly when ducts pass through unconditioned spaces. “Insulation with appropriate vapor protection helps prevent condensation on cold air-conditioning ducts, but decorative soffits alone don’t provide these benefits,” explains Gibbs.

If you choose to cover pipes or ducts with panels or sheet material, you still need to create an access point. “Building codes require access to certain utility components, even when concealed,” explains Gibbs. “Components requiring operation, inspection, adjustment, or servicing must remain accessible.”

Be sure to plan access panels and locations before installing drywall, decorative panels, or soffits. “I’ve seen jobs where a homeowner built a beautiful wooden soffit over a shutoff valve and then called us 2 years later with a leak they couldn’t stop,” recalls Graham. “We had to cut through the whole thing just to reach the valve, which turned into a half-day job and a ceiling that needed rebuilding.” His main recommendation is to include a removable access panel over every valve, damper, fitting, cleanout, and other maintenance points before you close anything up.

Disguising metal pipes or ducts with a fresh layer of paint is an affordable option to consider. Be careful not to paint plastic pipes, as paint can degrade plastic.

Designed for use on metal, this highly rated spray paint can cover unsightly pipes and ducts while also providing protection from corrosion.

Gibbs and Golding strongly advise against hanging anything from exposed pipes and ducts in your home. “Plumbing and HVAC systems aren’t designed to support decorative items, plants, or shelving,” explains Golding. “Additional weight can damage connections, cause leaks, or loosen ductwork.” Instead, they recommend using independently secured ceiling supports and approved hooks and hangers designed to carry the weight.

After months of scouring the market and putting products through their paces, we’ve named the best of the best in new tools. There’s something for everyone, from veteran pros to average Joes.

A thick layer of leaves can damage your grass, but there's no need to bag them up. Put nature's autumn bounty to work elsewhere in the garden.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fallen leaves start piling up in earnest in October, and a lot of homeowners rake every last one out to the curb as soon as they can. Honestly, it makes sense. A bare lawn looks tidy, and a soggy brown carpet of leaves isn’t much fun to look at all winter.

There’s a middle ground, though. Good fall leaf management means getting the thick stuff off the grass and finding those leaves a better home. Beds, borders, compost bins and vegetable plots can all use them, and whatever stays in the yard is mulch and compost you may not have to buy in the spring.

Some leaves need a little extra thought. Oak is slow to break down, and black walnut leaves contain juglone, a compound that can harm tomatoes and other sensitive plants, so it pays to know which trees are dropping what in your yard. Neither one has to go to the curb.

Why not just leave the leaves where they fall? Scattered leaves won’t hurt the grass – it’s the thick layer that causes trouble. After a couple of rains, leaves pack down into a wet mat that cuts off light and air, and left in place all winter, it can smother and weaken the turf underneath. That damp cover also favors snow mold. In snowier regions, you’ll usually spot it in spring as circular patches of matted, discolored grass, from either pink snow mold (Microdochium nivale) or gray snow mold (Typhula incarnata). Voles and mice like the cover, too, and a lawn buried under leaves can show more of their damage once things thaw.

So, you do need to keep on top of fall leaves – but there's no need to bag them. The rest of the yard can put them to good use with these clever ideas.

Firstly, you don't need to remove every leaf from your lawn. If there's only a light covering, mow over it with a mulching mower instead. The finely shredded leaf pieces fall between the grass blades, where they quickly break down, feeding the soil and returning nutrients to your lawn without smothering it. If you’re shopping for one, the Ryobi ONE+ 18V 13 in. Cordless Battery Walk Behind Push Lawn Mower, available at Home Depot, includes a mulch plug, making it easy to switch between bagging and mulching.

However, once leaves become too deep for the mower to chop up properly, rake them off. Thick layers of whole leaves can block light, trap moisture, and damage the grass over winter. Rather than sending them to the curb, use them elsewhere in the garden.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Whole leaves can make lousy mulch. They often mat into a slick layer that sheds water. Shredded leaves are another matter – they stay loose, let rain through and break down faster. Set the mower on its highest setting and run it over a low row of fairly dry leaves once or twice. That gets them small enough for most beds, though big piles go faster through a leaf shredder, like the WORX 13 Amp Electric Leaf Mulcher, available on Amazon.

Spread the pieces 2–4 inches (5–10 cm) deep around trees, shrubs and perennials and water them in. By spring, you’ll have fewer weeds and soil that stayed moister and steadier in temperature.

Leaf mold is what you get when a pile of leaves is left to rot down slowly, and the result is dark, crumbly, and earthy-smelling. Don’t expect much in the way of nutrients. It’s more of a soil conditioner, improving structure, helping soil hold water, and keeping it mostly weed-free.

Chicken wire bent into a ring makes an easy enclosure, though a vented plastic bin like the Redmon compost bin from Walmart works too, or even just a big plastic bag left loosely closed.

Wet the leaves as you go. Shredded leaves can be ready in about six months, while whole leaves take closer to a year, and a pile nobody touches may take two. Dig it into beds or stir it into potting soil when it’s done.

Leaves are a classic “brown” ingredient, full of carbon but short on nitrogen, so a pile of nothing but leaves needs some “greens” to get going. Grass clippings and kitchen scraps both work – with clippings, about two parts leaves to one part grass is a reasonable mix – and keep the pile about as damp as a wrung-out sponge.

A compost thermometer, like the Reotemp from Amazon, shows you when the pile has heated up and when it’s cooling off and ready to turn. Dry leaves keep well, so stash a few RISETEX reusable leaf bags full of them for next summer’s grass clippings.

Oak and magnolia leaves are slow, so shred them first or give them extra time, and keep walnut leaves for a hot, well-managed pile, where juglone breaks down.

Picture a January afternoon warm enough to thaw the soil surface, followed by a hard freeze that night. Repeat that often enough and shallow roots and crowns can get pushed right up out of the ground. Leaves piled on top won’t keep the ground from freezing, and they aren’t meant to. What you want is soil that stays frozen once it freezes, instead of flipping back and forth every time the sun comes out.

Hold off until temperatures have dropped well below freezing, then mound shredded leaves over the crowns of tender perennials. Tea roses need a little more fuss: a ring of chicken wire or burlap around the plant, filled with leaves packed just lightly enough for air to still move through. Soggy, matted leaves sitting on a crown can smother it.

Once the last tomatoes and squash come out, an empty vegetable bed has room for a deep layer of leaves. Spread 6–8 inches (15–20 cm) of shredded leaves over the soil and dig or till them in. They’ll keep breaking down through winter, and by spring the bed has more organic matter and microbes, better tilth, and better drainage to show for it.

It can take a lot of trips to haul that many leaves, and Home Depot's True Temper poly wheelbarrow has a roomy 6-cubic-foot (170 L) tub. On smaller beds, you can turn them in by hand with a fork – I like the Truper spading fork, available on Amazon. And don’t worry about oak leaves souring the soil. They’re acidic when fresh, but they break down to roughly neutral.

Want more fireflies and butterflies next summer? Then leave some leaves. Not every corner of the yard has to look raked and finished. Pile some leaves under a shrub or along a back fence and leave them there through winter, and you’ve made shelter for beneficial insects.

Mated bumble bee queens hibernate an inch or two (2.5–5 cm) down in the soil, and a layer of leaves on top gives them extra protection. Firefly larvae use leaf litter for cover as well. So do woolly bears, the fuzzy black-and-rust caterpillars that become Isabella tiger moths. Look closely at an old leaf pile in early spring, and you might spot a swallowtail chrysalis or luna moth cocoon that’s hard to tell from the leaves around it.

Lawns are the exception to all this leaf-saving. Any thick layer needs to come off before winter, and if you miss a spot and find a flattened, soggy mat in early spring, rake it up right away so it doesn’t hold back green-up. The True Temper 24-inch leaf rake from Home Depot has wide, clog-free tines that suit the job.

Keep an eye on the gutter out front as well. Leaves washed into a storm drain usually wind up in the nearest creek or lake, and rotting leaves there release phosphorus that feeds algae blooms.

In the beds, though, you can relax. Whatever falls under shrubs, around trees, and between perennials will slowly rot down and give nutrients back to the soil, just like leaves do in the woods. It’s kinder to the insects tucked in there, too, if you put off cleaning out beds until spring has properly warmed up.

I always remember what my grandpa always said. “That rake ain’t going nowhere, and neither are the leaves – there’ll be another round of them next October, and the October after that.” Each of those piles is free mulch and compost for the taking, so it seems a shame to send them to the curb.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.
