#112. Fireplace Tips To Keep Your Home Warm and Safe This Winter

A chimney sweep shares the cleaning and maintenance habits that keep your home safe all burning season long.

After working in the chimney industry for most of her life, Tracy Zarriello traded the office for the rooftop—and she’s never looked back. Now the owner of Queen Sweep Chimney, Plumbing, Air Conditioning & Heating Services, she has seen firsthand what causes the most common fireplace problems and knows exactly how homeowners can avoid them. Here are her top tips for a safe, warm and worry-free fall and winter.

The maintenance your fireplace needs depends largely on the type of unit in your home. While you may not always get to choose your fireplace—many homeowners simply inherit the one that came with the house—it pays to know how it works and how to care for it to avoid unnecessary service calls.

Wood-burning fireplaces create an undeniably cozy atmosphere with real flames and soothing crackling, but they’re also the most labor-intensive option. They produce ashes, require regular chimney maintenance, and mean hauling firewood and keeping fireplace tools nearby, including a poker, tongs, broom and ash shovel.

Gas fireplaces offer the convenience of an on-demand fuel supply and don’t produce messy ashes. They carry a much lower risk of chimney fires than woodburning fireplaces and require less care and maintenance overall, but regular inspections are still recommended to ensure the burner and venting system are working properly.

Electric fireplaces have simulated flames and produce no combustion byproducts. They’re primarily decorative, but most models also include a heating element and function as a space heater.

When it comes to heating efficiency, “many homeowners are surprised to learn that a traditional open wood-burning fireplace can actually pull heated air out of the house,” Zarriello says. “If your goal is heating, a gas insert or an EPA‑certified wood stove is usually far more effective than an open masonry fireplace.”

If you have a wood-burning fireplace, it’s important to understand creosote.

“Creosote is a highly flammable residue created when wood smoke cools and condenses inside the chimney,” Zarriello says. “Think of it like grease accumulating inside a kitchen exhaust hood.”

Creosote begins as light, flaky soot but can progress into crunchy, tarlike deposits and eventually a hard, shiny glaze. Zarriello says this last stage is the most dangerous because it’s much harder to remove and can ignite with only a spark or hot burst of exhaust.

A chimney fire can exceed 2,000 degrees, Zarriello says, and sound like a roaring freight train. But some of the fires aren’t so dramatic.

“Many homeowners don’t realize they’ve had a chimney fire because some are slow-burning and occur inside the flue,” she says. Yet even an unnoticed chimney fire can cause a cracked flue liner, structural damage and the potential for dangerous levels of carbon monoxide to enter your home.

Preventing creosote buildup starts with smart burning habits and regular maintenance.

Zarriello recommends burning only seasoned hardwoods such as ash, maple and oak. “Wood should generally be dried for 6 to 12 months or longer and have a moisture content below 20 percent,” she says. Burning wet or green wood produces more smoke and creosote.

Make sure the damper is fully open before lighting a fire, and leave it open while the fire burns. “Airflow is everything,” Zarriello says. “A properly drafting chimney pulls smoke upward and out of the home.” That airflow helps create a hotter, more efficient fire.

Use a fireplace screen to contain sparks, and remove excess ash from the firebox only after it has completely cooled. Once a month during burning season, inspect the firebox for cracked bricks or deteriorating mortar joints. Test the damper to make sure it opens and closes properly, then go outside and look at the chimney cap from the ground. A missing or broken cap lets in rainwater and gives animals an opening to nest in your chimney.

“A properly installed chimney cap is one of the best investments a homeowner can make,” Zarriello says.

Have your chimney professionally inspected at least once a year. “While homeowners can perform visual checks, they cannot see most of the flue system without specialized equipment,” Zarriello says. A qualified professional can inspect the flue liner and other parts of your chimney; check for creosote buildup, water damage and masonry problems; and confirm proper ventilation.

“A fireplace should provide warmth and enjoyment—not become a hidden fire hazard,” Zarriello says. “A yearly inspection helps protect your home and your family.”

Commonly sold at home centers and online, chimney-cleaning logs (also called creosote-sweeping logs) release chemicals as they burn and are marketed as an easy way to reduce creosote buildup. Simply burn the log like a piece of firewood, then sweep out any loosened debris after the fire goes out.

But Zarriello warns they aren’t a substitute for professional chimney maintenance. As she puts it, “Don’t be fooled by chimney-cleaning logs!”

“While some products may help loosen light deposits, they do not eliminate the hardened creosote that sticks to the inside walls of your chimney,” she says. “The only way to properly remove creosote is through a chimney inspection and a cleaning using the proper equipment.”

Creosote is a serious fire and safety hazard, and relying on a cleaning log alone can create a false sense of security. “Protect your home and your family—don’t rely on a log when your chimney needs a real cleaning.”

#115. Smart Ways to Use Citric Acid Around the Home

Discover the deep-cleaning power of this all-natural cleaning powder.

Citric acid is a surprisingly powerful natural cleaner. Popular in Europe, this versatile product is great for removing limescale, hard water stains and mineral buildup. “Citric acid can descale an electric kettle, remove spots from glass and even shine up stainless-steel sinks,” says Sofia Martinez, cleaning expert and owner of Sparkly Maid Austin.

It’s inexpensive, too, and safe for use on most surfaces. Read on for some of the best ways to use citric acid around the house, with expert-backed tips from professional cleaners Martinez, Enrique Gonzalez of Seattle Green Cleaning Fairy and Terry Klymkiv of Alpha Cleaning Company.

Citric acid is a naturally occurring acid found in citrus fruits, that can also be manufactured for use as a preservative, food ingredient and cleaning agent. Purchase it at your local grocery or hardware store in powder or crystalline form.

Citric acid’s superpower is removing water mineral deposits, but it has a host of other uses as well. It is an acidic cleaner, so test it first in an inconspicuous place and consult the manufacturer’s instructions before using it on metal-finish fixtures.

Coffee makers develop scale as minerals separate from heated water through and build up to form a white crust over time. Use citric acid to easily descale and return back to its original condition. “Add one to two tablespoons of citric acid to a full tank of water. Run one brewing cycle and then two cycles using just plain water,” Gonzalez says. Descale an Electric Kettle

A useful countertop appliance to quickly boil water, electric kettles also develop scale over time. To descale, fill the kettle with water, then add one to two tablespoons of citric acid. Bring the water to a boil, then let it simmer for 15 to 20 minutes. To rinse the citric acid from the kettle, Gonzalez says to empty,, rinse, then boil clean water again and discard.

Keeping hard water stains off of bathroom and kitchen faucets can feel like a full time job, but use citric acid for faster work times. Mix one to two teaspoons of citric acid to one cup of warm water, then apply with a soft, damp cloth. Martinez suggests leaving it to sit for three to five minutes before wiping away, and dry when done to avoid new spots. A word of caution:

Remove mineral build-up from shower head spray holes by soaking showerheads in a citric acid solution. “Dissolve a tablespoon of citric acid in two cups of warm water and soak your shower head,” Martinez says. Rinse with clean water when finished, then run hot water through the showerhead to remove any remaining deposits.

Soap scum deposits can be challenging to clean, so let the citric acid mixture sit for best results.  Mix one teaspoon of citric acid in one cup of warm water. “Place cloth or sponge soaked in the solution over the area where mineral deposits have formed,” Gonzalez says, then allow it to sit for five to 10 minutes before rinsing thoroughly. After rinsing, dry the surface completely. Gonzalez recommends avoiding using this technique on marble surfaces.

Hard water spots are notoriously difficult to remove from glass shower doors, but citric acid cuts through them for easy cleaning. “Mix one tablespoon of citric acid to two cups of warm water and apply to hard-water spots with a spray bottle, Martinez says. “Allow the citric acid to sit on the hard-water stains for up to five minutes without letting it dry, then wipe away with a clean, damp, nonabrasive rag or sponge.” For a streak-free finish, squeegee or buff the glass right away.

Hard water stains, food build-up and detergent films can make a mess of any dishwasher. Gonzalez recommends first cleaning the filter at the bottom of the dishwasher tub, then running a cycle with citric acid. “Place a couple of tablespoons of citric acid in a small bowl and place the bowl on the uppermost rack in your empty dishwasher,” he says. “Then run it on a hot cycle.”

Rust stains develop from high levels of iron in your water or from wet metal objects left on bathroom surfaces. For these tough to remove stains, you’ll want to make a paste of citric acid and water. “Apply the paste to the rust stain and let it sit for twenty minutes,” Klymkiv says. “Scrub gently with a soft brush and rinse.” Repeat these steps until the stain is removed.

Citric acid removes hard water stains or even small rust spots on stainless steel sinks and appliances. First, mix one teaspoon of citric acid in one cup of warm water. “Apply to hard-water spots with a dampened microfiber cloth, wiping in the same direction as the grain of the stainless-steel,” Martinez says. “Allow to sit for two to three minutes, rinse and immediately dry to prevent new spots from forming.”

“This is the easiest and probably my favorite tip,” Klymkiv says. “Add two to three tablespoons of citric acid powder directly into the toilet bowl. Let it sit for at least thirty minutes or even overnight. The acid dissolves mineral deposits without unpleasant fumes of chemical bowl cleaners. Scrub with a toilet brush and flush.”

While citric acid is an amazing cleaning agent, it is corrosive so use it with care. Avoid using it on:

Patience is a virtue when cleaning with citrus acid, as it does take time to work its cleaning magic. It’s not a product to apply and immediately wipe away. When applying to vertical surfaces, mix a thicker paste that will resist dripping and try to prevent it from drying out during wait times. For the best results, always dissolve citric acid in warm or hot water and only mix as much as you can use in a two-week period, as it will mold if left to sit for too long. “Citric acid should be handled with gloves and without inhaling the powder,” Martinez adds.

You can, but pre-mix the water and citric acid first to ensure it’s fully dissolved. “Label and date the spray bottle, store it out of reach of children and pets, and never store it in a former beverage container,” Martinez says.

“Stronger concentrations of citric acid or leaving it to sit for long periods of time can discolor or damage some types of stainless-steel surfaces,” Martinez says. “Always check with your manufacturer if your appliance or fixture is coated or has a fingerprint-resistant finish.”

Citric acid should never be mixed with bleach as it creates toxic chlorine gas.

#117. Martha Stewart’s Annual Homegrown Pumpkin Display Is Iconic – and It’s So Easy to Copy It This Fall

Martha Stewart's pumpkin stair display looks effortless, and it nearly is. Here's the variety guide, design principles, and growing tips to recreate it at home.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There are two types of people in this world: those who put one pumpkin outside in October and feel good about it, and those who aspire to be like Martha Stewart. Every autumn, her entire staircase is lined with pumpkins and gourds that look like they were grown by expert garden design fairies. And, as usual, her comment section collectively decides to give up and beg for a tutorial on how to create a fall porch display.

Well, I consulted with a couple of experts to give you that tutorial, so just call me a younger, dark-haired Martha Stewart. If you squint, you won’t even see the difference.

A post shared by Martha Stewart (@marthastewart48)

Before you even think about raiding a pumpkin patch, you’ll need to understand what makes this display look planned rather than like Halloween decorations set out at HomeGoods in July.

Preeti Shah, founder of Spotlight Style and luxury event producer of over 20 years, is clear on this: "A pumpkin display looks designed when it has a plan. Choose a tight palette, such as creamy whites, soft sage and one deep orange, and repeat it from the bottom step to the door. Vary the sizes, but group them in odd numbers, with the biggest pieces anchoring the corners and the smallest at the front edge. Leave breathing room between groups so the stairs still read as stairs. Then step back and squint. If one spot grabs your eye, move it."

According to Heidi Grasman, gardening expert and co-owner of Garden Crossings, the difference between an autumnal display that looks well-planned and one that looks thrown together on a whim comes down to one thing. She says, "Just throwing pumpkins on a porch is very Halloween-looking – adding in flowers and foliage makes it look decorated." Pumpkins are the supporting cast, not the main event.

If you’re new to decorating and gardening in autumn, you might be surprised to know there are actually different varieties of pumpkins you can choose from. If you're interested in growing your own, you can even buy a Spooky Pumpkin Seed Mix from Seed Needs on Amazon.

The cream and white pumpkins that really anchor Martha’s display are usually Casper, Lumina, or Baby Boo. These all have smooth skin, clean color, and look exceptionally striking against a dark door or stone step.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If you prefer the classic deep orange, Howden or Cinderella (Rouge Vif d'Etampes) will give you that saturation that looks beautiful in fall photos and holds on to its color for several weeks. If you like things to be a little more unique, Galeux d'Eysines has tiny little wart-like skin, while Jarrahdale is a flat, bluish-gray variety. And if you love a good gourd mix as I do, these quirky, unique shapes will fill in the gaps in your display and can add extra interest to the front of each step edge.

If you're trying to get a similar display to Martha Stewart’s, think outside the box (or pumpkin) with some fall foliage. Grasman recommends using chrysanthemums as the focal point, with foliage doing the structural work. She says, “I like to use coral bells for foliage color, ornamental grass as a thriller or spiller, and then mix the mums in for flower color."

On choosing the right mum: "It's not so much about what variety to choose but where it is at in its bud or bloom stage. If they are looking for instant color, choose one that is more in bloom. If they are looking for the color to last a while, choose one that is just in bud."

Her advice on pumpkins within a planting scheme is useful too. She adds, "Let the pumpkins and vegetables be an accent, not the main show of color. Tucking some ornamental peppers, kale, cabbage into your fall combination planters can add a pretty touch. Let the mums be the focal point."

If you’re a purist and want to grow your own pumpkins and gourds for next year, sow them outdoors in late May or early June, or indoors 4 to 6 weeks before your last frost. They need a lot of space (at least 6 feet in each direction for most varieties), but even a small patch can give you enough for a full stair display.

Sow two seeds per station, and once both have germinated, remove the weaker seedling by snipping it at soil level so only the strongest plant remains; then keep it well-watered once the fruits start to develop.

They are ready to harvest when the skin is hard and the stem is dry. Then leave them to dry in a warm spot for 10-14 days. This helps harden the skin, make the orange even orangier, and extend how long they’ll last in your display.

Remember this TL;DR version from Martha Stewart when creating your own autumnal porch display: Same palette, odd numbers, a little foliage, and enough breathing room between the pumpkins.

#119. Room to Grow: Kai Avent-deLeon Turns a Mobile Home Into a Modern Sanctuary

From house tours and expert advice to favorite finds and DIYs.

Design-forward shops, hotels, and restaurants for your itinerary.

Renovating? Start here for expert advice, deep dives, and helpful tips.

Our catalog of more than 10,000 products featured on Remodelista.

Remodelista’s members-only directory of architects, designers, and landscape professionals.

We’ve been following artist/designer/entrepreneur Kai Avent-deLeon’s moves since 2019. Back then, we photographed her one-bedroom railroad apartment in Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn. A year later, we reconnected when she moved into a larger duplex in the same neighborhood, and we shot it for our newest book Remodelista: The Low-Impact Home. Not long after that, she found a weekend home far from the city, in Sullivan County, New York—and today, we’re sharing it with you.

Kai’s roots in Bed-Stuy run deep (she was born there and both her grandmother and mother live in the neighborhood), but she longed for land to call her own and more space—both literal and metaphorical—for her and her now four-year-old son to roam freely. She found it upstate when she stumbled upon a property (3 acres of mostly woods) on which stood a run-down 1960s mobile home. It was perfect.

Kai quickly drew up a plan—double the size of the original 700-foot structure; concrete floors; a simple, basic kitchen made up of workbench-style pieces; lots of pottery and baskets; a smattering of antiques; impactful furniture; and quiet moments of beauty everywhere—and hired a contractor to exact her vision. Soon enough, she was making weekend trips to the bucolic property, feeling the tension of city living ease with every mile. “When I’m here, I’m at peace,” she says. “My daily routine is much more structured, but not in the way you think. I can wake up and meditate and work out. And I do stuff around the house. I feel way more relaxed here versus in the city, where I’m trying to get those things in but am in more response mode.”

She’s grateful for the open space and what that can do for one’s sense of wellbeing—so much so that she wants to share it with others. “This property feels intended to be more than just a weekend home. I have all these friends who work in different practices that connect to wellness. We just came together and start doing these retreats—three last summer, each with a theme,” explains Kai (like “Sensuality and Sensitivity: Connecting to Your Senses Through the Four Elements”).

“It started last year when I was going through some personal transitions. I find that part of my healing comes from [being] surrounded by women going through similar transitions.” Today, as we speak by phone, she’s preparing for another retreat here, this time for a group of 9-year-old girls from her son’s school in Brooklyn. The theme: Rites of Passage, fitting for a property bought with the express purpose of personal growth and exploration.

Below, Kai walks us through her special place. (Follow her on Instagram @kaiaventdeleon for news of future retreats.)

N.B.: This story originally ran on May 26, 2023, and has been updated.

#121. The Best Electric Wall Heaters of 2026, Picks from Our Editors

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Published Oct 16, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Despite its size, an electric wall heater is a great way to provide your home with extra heat—whether you’re in a multifamily house or a tiny apartment. What’s more? Electric wall heaters are cost-effective, energy-efficient, and safer than most portable heaters.

If you’re interested in learning more about how a wall-mounted heater could help keep you and your family warm and toasty throughout the winter months, this in-depth buyer’s guide covers everything from the type of heater to the installation process, as well as our favorite models. Out of all the options we researched and tested, we think the Heat Storm HS-1000-WX-WIFI Infrared Wall Heater will be best for most users due to its ample coverage area, easy remote controls, and child-safe features. Read on to learn more about it and the rest of the best electric wall heaters available today.

Bottom line: Electric wall heaters provide a practical and stylish solution for supplemental heating, with various models offering advanced features and safety options.

Choosing the best electric wall heater requires a bit of research to make informed purchasing decisions. To help you make an informed purchasing decision, we’ve listed a few top-notch options (that are easy to install, have low noise levels, and have safety features) below. Here are our top picks for the best electric wall heater.

The infrared electric wall heater from Heat Storm offers 3,400 BTUs controlled by a Wi-Fi–enabled mobile app. This wall-mounted unit offers a child lock, overheat protection, a safe-touch grille, and an operating schedule that can be adjusted via the app, or quick adjustments can be made with the included remote control or the digital display located on top of the unit.

This heater offers 1,000 watts of power and can heat up to 100 square feet as the primary heat source; it can be a supplemental heat source for up to 500 square feet. For added user-friendliness, this Heat Storm wall heater has a noiseless operation volume, tip-over protection, and an air filter for cleaning the air while heating.

Get the Heat Storm HS-1000-WX-WIFI electric wall heater at Amazon.

The fast-heating coil element of this electric wall heater from Cadet can heat up to 200 square feet quickly with a centrifugal fan, which quietly spreads the air around the room. At only 10.75 inches high by 7 inches wide by 4 inches deep, this heater can recess back into the wall and won’t take up a lot of space. The heater also comes with a wall can for recessing, a grille for safety, and a thermostat for hardwired installation.

Durable metal surfaces and a white powder-coated paint job make this 1,500-watt heater safe and reliable while offering a vintage look. The recessed nature of this electric wall heater makes it a bit more difficult to install than other brands. Those who aren’t handy might require the help of a contractor.

Get the Cadet electric wall heater at Amazon or The Home Depot.

This recessed fireplace from PuraFlame offers a 50-inch length, which is suitable for installation on 2-by-6 studs in the wall. Flush mounted and with 1,500 watts of power, this fireplace has a dancing flame created by LED lights and several options for whatever look suits the home—the ember bed can be a log set or crystal stones.

The flame can be adjusted to include four blends of yellow and blue colors. The flame can be operated with or without heat, making this a year-round feature of the home. A countdown timer sets the flame from 30 minutes to 9 hours, and the other settings can be adjusted with the included remote control or touch panel. Keep in mind that though this can heat up a room, it should not be used as a primary heat source.

Get the PuraFlame Alice electric wall heater at Amazon.

Users who are interested in a versatile, high-tech model that can be mounted to a wall and out of the way will want to take a look at this option from Heat Storm. Made to heat rooms of up to 1,000 square feet with its quartz bulbs, this Heat Storm wall heater runs between 750 and 1,500 watts at 5,200 BTUs and comes with brackets for wall mounting or legs for floor-standing use. If users opt for the floor-standing option, children and pets are safe due to the always cool-to-the-touch grille and tip-over switch.

However, one of the most notable features of this model is its Wi-Fi capability. With this high-tech function, the Heat Storm integrates with Google Assistant and Amazon Alexa or can be controlled with the included remote control. If all else fails, this unit has a backlit control panel that can be used for quick and easy adjustments, including a convenient child lock. To ensure the air quality is also on par, this model comes with a washable air filter. One of the only downsides to this model is that it requires installation near an outlet when wall-mounted.

What our tester says: “This was a definite favorite during testing. It’s compact and hangs on the wall without being obtrusive, but it also comes with legs and a tip-over switch to make it a suitable freestanding model. It was powerful enough to heat one of our uninsulated offices quickly and comfortably in the dead of winter. We could set timers and program settings using our smart devices as well.”—Tom Scalisi, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Heat Storm HS-1500-PHX-WIFI electric wall heater at Amazon or The Home Depot.

This electric wall heater from De’Longhi uses convection panel heating, releasing up to 1,500 watts of power with a two-fan lateral system. At only 3 inches in depth, this heater sits flush against the wall and blends in with different decors, from traditional to modern. Hardware is included, making installation a breeze.

This convection heater also has an adjustable thermostat, timer, multiple heat settings, and an LED display. The thermal cutoff prevents overheating, and the tip-over protection is good for those who choose to use this as a freestanding option. It’s designed to heat 300 square feet.

Get the De’Longhi electric wall heater at Amazon.

Those looking for a powerful heating option might want to go with the 2,000/4,000-watt high-capacity wall heater from Broan-NuTone. This heater is designed to be recessed into the wall and hardwired for maximum heating; it can also be attached to the wall and used at half-power through connection to a 120-volt outlet. But, when used with full 240-volt power, this option emits over 13,653 BTUs. This white traditional grate-style heater includes an adjustable, front-mounted thermostat control and an 18-gauge steel grille for gentle release of heat.

A high-efficiency blower wheel, permanently lubricated motor, thermal overload protection, UL listing, and heavy-duty sheathed element help ensure safety and solid operation for years. This can serve as the primary heating source for an area between 265 and 400 square feet.

Get the Broan-NuTone electric wall heater at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Walmart.

With a variety of wattage options and the company’s original “Pic-A-Watt” element, this wall heater from King allows tailoring to a room’s specific requirements, heating up a maximum of 500 square feet. At 13.5 inches wide by 7.5 inches high and designed to recess into the wall with simple tools, the whisper-quiet “squirrel cage” blower is quiet enough for bedrooms.

To choose the wattage, simply unplug the appropriate wires during installation using the color-coded instructions. Use it with a built-in or wall-mounted thermostat. The Patented Smart Limit Protection will shut off the heat to avoid a thermal event and must be turned on manually to reset the heater.

Get the King Electric wall heater at The Home Depot or Walmart.

For a more high-end wall heater, consider the PuraFlame Klaus electric fireplace insert. Though it may take a little more work to install, this model is made for heating over 400 square feet while creating the classic, luxurious look of a real fireplace. It has a heating output of over 4,600 BTUs with its 1,500-watt heater, and the heat can be adjusted with the included remote control.

This model uses LED flames and embers to create its scarily realistic look of an actual fire while also including six crackling sound choices. Plus, there is a spark-arresting curtain for even more authenticity. All in all, this wall heater provides all the heat and luxury one could hope for with a midrange price tag that won’t break the bank.

What our tester says: “There are things we really enjoyed about the PuraFlame Klaus electric fireplace insert. It was the most realistic-looking electric heater we tested, from the spark-arrest curtains to the log glow and the flames.”—Tom Scalisi, Product Reveiws tester and writer

Get the PuraFlame Klaus wall heater at Amazon.

We researched the most sought-after wall heaters in their respective categories and discovered that the best models are determined by their type, wattage and British thermal unit (BTU) output, settings, and other special features included by reputable brands.

After extensive product research, we included options in our list of top picks that were made with infrared, convection, and fan-forced electric constructions that run at 500 to 4,000 watts and emit up to 13,600 BTUs of heat. We also wanted to include a versatile range of heaters, so many of these picks are capable of functioning as either a primary or secondary heat source.

As for user-friendly features, these top picks come with Wi-Fi connectivity, remote controls, digital control panels, dial thermostats, tip-over or overheat protection, child-lock functions, and even air filters for cleaning the air while heating. Many of these picks are also capable of being wall-mounted or used as floor-standing units.

While you’re browsing for an electric wall heater, there are a few things you will want to keep in mind. To ensure your heater can do what you need it to (i.e., keep you comfy and cozy on cold, wintry nights), here are a few shopping considerations to factor in when making a purchase.

There are several types of heaters out there. When it comes to space heaters, you can choose between convection heaters, ceramic fan-forced heaters, radiant and infrared heaters, and mica thermic space heaters. Unlike portable heaters, electric wall heaters are recessed inside a wall—which means they’re hardwired into an electrical branch circuit.

Electric heaters come in a variety of styles, including wall heaters, toe-kick heaters, baseboard heaters, and cove or panel heaters. Wall heaters, sometimes referred to as “forced fan heaters,” combine a fan (as the name suggests) and a heating element to circulate heated air throughout the room. If you’re worried about noise, infrared electric wall heaters use radiant heater panels instead of fans.

Electric wall heaters are designed to heat small spaces and shouldn’t be used as a primary heating source for large rooms or spaces. Electric wall heaters can work as a supplement to a larger unit. For example, the Broan-NuTone, White 198 High Capacity Wall Heater is packed with 4,000 watts of power but was designed to heat up to 400 square feet max. Heating an entire home with electric wall heaters would most likely mean you’d need one heater per room, which could make for an outrageously expensive utility bill.

The heat settings of a standard electric wall heater can range from 750 watts, which is usually the minimum, to 4,000 watts. (Though there are high-wattage heaters built to heat larger areas.) Wall heaters can be powered by 120V or 240V electricity and usually include a built-in thermostat. Some wall-mounted heaters, however, come with a detached thermostat that allows the user to control the temperature of one or more heaters at a time.

Many 1,500-watt heaters offer a 750-watt option. This allows users to turn the heat down whenever they’re not in the room (or if they’re warm and comfortable with the heater set to a lower setting). This is just one of the ways electric heaters can be energy efficient.

Some electric heaters come with an automatic shut-off switch (auto shut-off switches are often found with wall-mounted fireplaces, too). The use of LED lights for fireplaces, as well as energy-saving options that drop the heat with a programmable thermostat or a timer, are all good options to keep the electric bills low.

Choosing an electric wall heater depends on function and aesthetics. When shopping, think about your home’s decor and your personal style. The best electric wall-mounted heater will offer a balance of looks and utility. Some might choose an electric wall heater that looks like a traditional grate, thus lending a vintage air. Others may prefer a sleek, flat heater that blends into the room or fits well with modern décor.

The choice for a heater in the living room might look entirely different from the garage heater. Fortunately, electric wall heaters are available in a variety of designs and styles, so finding one that suits a particular home shouldn’t be a difficult task.

When it comes to heating the home, safety is always paramount. Look for features such as a timer or an overheat shut-off function, which will cut the power if the heater becomes too hot. An automatic shut-off function, in which the electric heater shuts down after a certain period of time, might be helpful for those who need it for only a small space and aren’t worried about preventing pipes from freezing or other cold-weather catastrophes. A cool-to-touch casing is also a good idea, especially in a home with small children, as well as on-off buttons or switches that are hard for kids to reach.

For those who are worried about noise, a radiant heater may be the way to go, as fan-forced heaters can be noisy. Though most modern heaters have a noise level that is acceptable for even a bedroom. If there’s any question about a fan being too loud, it’s important to go with radiant heat for a very quiet experience.

Electric wall-mounted heaters are designed to be recessed into the wall, which requires careful cutting of drywall to insert the “can” or box that the heater uses for safe installation. Even so, once the hole is prepared, installation is a matter of a few screws. Those who aren’t very handy with household tools should hire a contractor to handle the installation of a recessed heater.

Though you’ve already got plenty of information on electric wall heaters, you might still have questions about which one is the best for you. Here are some other considerations to keep in mind when choosing the best electric wall heater.

A typical rule of thumb is that every 500 watts heats up to 100 square feet of space. Therefore, a 1,000-watt heater can handle up to 200 square feet while a 1,500-watt heater can heat up to 300 square feet. Keep in mind this is if the heater is the dedicated heat source. As a supplemental heater, it can cover more square footage.

Some electric wall heaters have a fan that forces heated air into the room. This fan makes some noise. Other wall heaters use radiant heating, which is silent.

As long as you follow all the safety instructions that come along with the manual, an electric wall heater can be just as safe as any other heater. In fact, it might be safer than a space heater, as there is no risk of carbon monoxide poisoning associated with electric heaters.

Though the electric wall heater might cost less for the initial purchase and installation, the cost of electricity is often higher than that of gas, meaning the electric option will cost more in monthly costs.

#122. 7 Underused Shrubs and Perennials to Plant in October for Extraordinary Fall Color that Lasts into Winter

Looking beyond standard mums and burning bushes for dazzling fall color? These hidden gems bring vibrant foliage, berries, and lasting winter tone and structure to your yard

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sugar maples and burning bushes may be spectacular sources of fall color, but they are far from being the only examples of shifting seasonal hues. In many cases, the most popular fall plants offer only a brief burst of red or copper before dropping their leaves almost overnight. If you’re looking for something a little less predictable or fleeting, a few lesser-known options offer unique elements like berries and bark.

October presents a golden opportunity to show some love to these tough perennials and shrubs for fall color. Thanks to a combination of warm soil temperatures and crisp, cool air, they will hit their stride that much quicker. Shrubs and hardy perennials planted now can settle in with minimal stress, developing deep, healthy root networks long before the ground freezes.

Make some room for golden, swaying grasses, deep burgundy bark and stems, and bright berries to feed local wildlife. By expanding your palette, you’ll create a mult-layered and multiseasonal array of tone and texture. Hopefully, these shrubs and perennials will inspire you with diverse visuals that often sustain well into winter. Make more of these dazzling hidden gems for effortless fall color that can keep your garden glowing for months.

Getting plants into the ground in October is one of the smartest moves you can make. Unlike spring planting, where young roots must cope with rising heat and drought, fall soil holds abundant summer warmth while rains keep moisture levels consistent. This allows young roots and crowns to focus their energy underground.

Just make sure you select plants that will grow well in your USDA hardiness zone. In northern zones (zones 3-6), aim to complete planting by the third week of the month, so roots can anchor before soil temperatures drop sharply. However, in the south (zones 7-10), you can plant comfortably well through November.

Prepare your planting holes by top-dressing with rich organic compost. This gives young roots a gentle nutrient boost without forcing tender growth that could be damaged by early frosts. A little mushroom compost makes an excellent soil amendment for these fall plantings. Either add a little aged natural mushroom compost, or a handful of Espoma Organic Natural Mushroom Blend, available from Walmart. This is ideal for conditioning planting holes and encouraging deep roots.

Once planted, water your tough perennials and fall shrubs deeply. Apply a 2-3-inch (5-8cm) blanket of organic wood mulch or shredded leaves, as this will help to insulate the roots against winter freeze-thaw cycles. Then sit back and enjoy the lovely spectacle of color and texture these hidden gems bring all season long.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If you were to choose just one underused native shrub for fall color, fothergilla (Fothergilla spp.) deserves the top spot. While famous for its honey-scented, brush-like spring flowers, autumn is when this compact shrub can really steal the show. Beginning in October, its leathery, witch-hazel-like leaves undergo a mesmerizing transformation, mixing vibrant shades of electric yellow, fiery orange, deep crimson, and rich violet on a single branch.

Hardy in zones 4-8, fothergilla grows 3-5 feet (90-150cm) tall with a neat, mounded habit. It flourishes in full sun to partial shade, though full sun produces the most intense colors. Fothergilla prefers moist, acidic, well-draining soil. Add mulch annually with pine needles or acidic leaf compost to maintain a low soil pH. Alkaline, chalky soils can cause leaf yellowing. Pair this shrub with blue-toned dwarf conifers or Japanese forest grass for gorgeous contrast. To enjoy these dazzling tones in miniature, you can buy Mount Airy Dwarf Fothergilla from Nature Hills.

Virginia sweetspire (Itea virginica) is a native deciduous shrub that can even put traditional burning bushes to shame. Forming arching mounds 3-5 feet (90-150cm) high, Henry's Garnet produces fragrant, cascading flower spires in early summer. As autumn arrives, its glossy leaves shift to a saturated garnet-red and port-wine purple that survive further into late autumn than almost any other shrub. You can buy Henry’s Garnet from Plant Addicts for long-lasting shocks of crimson and purple.

Hardy in zones 5-9, it is highly adaptable. It thrives in full sun, partial shade, and even heavy shade (though sun yields the brightest red tones). It is tolerant of wet, clay soils, making it perfect for rain gardens, low-lying garden spots, or erosion control on slopes. Just water consistently during its first year. Don't worry about heavy pruning, as its natural arching habit is part of its charm. Plant it alongside yellow-foliaged shrubs or golden grasses for a rich border display.

For structural elegance that combines dazzling fall foliage with year-round visual interest, the paperbark maple (Acer griseum) is well worth a spot. Growing slowly into a small, well-behaved specimen tree or large shrub, reaching 15-20 feet (4.5-6m) tall, its trifoliate leaves turn copper, ruby-red and scarlet in late October. After the leaves drop, its cinnamon-brown bark peels back to reveal polished mahogany wood that glows in winter sun. It may take a few years to develop those distinctive colors, but you can buy Paperbark Maple Container Trees from Amazon.

Hardy in zones 4-8, paperbark maple grows best in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, average-to-rich soil. It is virtually pest- and disease-free, and requires no complicated pruning. Just don't allow newly planted specimens to bake in severely dry, compacted clay without moisture. Underplant with evergreen groundcovers like vinca or dark hellebores to accentuate its cinnamon trunk.

While most fall plants deliver on leaf color, Coralberry Magic Berry (Symphoricarpos) adds a pop of vibrant fruit. Growing into a rounded shrub 3-4 feet (90-120cm) tall and wide, in October its stems are filled with vivid clusters of pink-purple berries. These jewel-like berry clusters remain on the bare branches well into winter, providing valuable food for songbirds. For a softer bubblegum berry tone, buy Proven Winners’ Proud Berry Pink Coralberry from Walmart for exquisite late-season color.

Hardy in zones 4-9, coralberry handles full sun to partial shade and adapts to a wide variety of soil types, including lean or clay soils. Cut back stems lightly in early spring to encourage fresh, fruit-bearing new growth. Avoid high-nitrogen feeds now, which encourage leaf growth at the expense of berries. Interplant with dark purple ninebark (physocarpus) or golden panic grasses for a lush fall tonal contrast.

Don’t forget flowers for autumn joy! For late-season color just as frost approaches, pineapple sage (Salvia elegans) is an unexpected treat. True to its name, rubbing its soft leaves releases an irresistible pineapple fragrance. Rising 3-5 feet (90-150cm) tall, this fast-growing plant erupts in October with tubular scarlet flower spikes. These act as a magnet for hummingbirds and pollinators. You can buy Greenwood Nursery Store’s Pineapple Sage from Amazon as double starter pots.

Hardy as a perennial in zones 8-11 (and grown as a late-season annual or overwintered indoor pot in zones 3-7), pineapple sage loves full sun and well-draining, fertile soil. Plant in a warm, sheltered spot near patios – don't let it sit in waterlogged soil. In colder zones, take softwood cuttings in October or bring potted specimens indoors before freezes. Pair its scarlet blooms with purple salvias or dark sweet potato vine for a fall finale.

This unique perennial is native to Arkansas and Oklahoma, but easy to grow anywhere in zones 4-9. Arkansas blue star (Amsonia hubrichtii) is regarded as one of the finest native perennials, thanks to its fall transformation. Through summer, it forms a dense, feathery 3-foot (90cm) mound of needle-like foliage, topped with soft blue spring blooms. But in October, it turns a brilliant, glowing butter-gold and amber-orange, holding its color for over a month. Buy Perennial Farm Marketplace’s Arkansas Blue Star from Amazon as live plants for fine-textured, golden foliage.

Hardy in zones 4-9, Arkansas blue star is long-lived, drought-tolerant, and deer-resistant. It performs best in full sun and well-drained soil, but otherwise this plant is not picky and is easy to grow. Plant in full sun to prevent flopping and don't disturb established clumps unnecessarily. Shear foliage back by one-third after spring flowering to encourage a dense shape. Combine its glowing plumes with purple asters or blue sedums for a classic, high-contrast fall border.

You may consider ornamental grass for texture and movement, but certain native grasses are also excellent for dynamic fall tone. Little bluestem is a gorgeous fall prairie grass option. Growing in neat tufts 2-4 feet (60-120cm) tall, its blue-green summer blades transform in October into rich shades of mahogany, coppery-orange, and warm purple, topped with fluffy, silvery seed heads that catch the light. For playful streaks of purple, Plants That Work’s Twilight Zone Little Bluestem Grass from Nature Hills is a gorgeous drought-tolerant native grass.

Hardy in zones 3-9, little bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium) thrives in full sun and dry, lean soils where other plants struggle. Don't overwater or plant in heavy shade, which causes stems to flop. Otherwise, you can leave the coppery foliage standing in winter to provide food and shelter for songbirds and winter interest. Interplant with goldenrod, coneflowers and amsonia for luxe designer accents.

You may remember Lisa Przystup from our 2017 post on her rustic-meets-minimalist Catskills home (the one with that clever DIY brass backsplash) or our 2021 story on the updates made since then. Or perhaps you’ve heard of her because you read and loved her book on the chic homes of chic Upstaters. But even if her name doesn’t ring a bell, you’d definitely recall her gorgeous holiday decorations that captured every design-minded professional’s attention last year (a hard thing to do these days).

That festive dreamscape that birthed a whole new palette for the holidays (blue and red? yes!)  is featured in her newest book, Once Around the Sun (dropping Oct. 14), a visual diary of the 1893 farmhouse she shares with her husband, Jonathon, as it moves through the seasons. Inside its pages are beautiful images of the interiors as well as the land, water, and sky just outside its doors—all of it evolving as the months go by.

Of course, the garden is where the seasonal effects are felt most acutely. Today we share Lisa’s garden-centric quick takes, with thoughts on cultivating the land, “the sort of miracle that never ever gets old.”

Photography by John  Hesselbarth + Kate Foster, unless otherwise noted.

Less a garden memory and more a plant-related memory: pulling the stamen through the base of honeysuckle blooms to drop the nectar onto my tongue. I remember feeling like I had discovered the most incredible secret.

Orwell’s Roses by Rebecca Solnit (a very good reminder on so many levels, in so many ways). The Garden Against Time by Olivia Laing (I can’t technically say I return to this time and time again as I started reading it last year and have yet to finish it, but I can say that I’ve loved it so far and my inability to complete it has more to do with me than it has to do with the quality of writing or storytelling). And this wonderful essay, “Autumn, It’s No Garden Party,” by Michael Pollan.

@saipua: the OG, the G.O.A.T, all the superlatives. Her floral design is art of the highest order, her color palette game is next level.

Oh, there are so many, for so many different reasons…. I’m obsessed with the size and grandeur of angelica and mullein, garden roses and gardenias for their heady scent, foxgloves and Turk’s-cap lilies because there’s just something about them isn’t there?

Honestly, I don’t think I have one! I really thought about this, I was sure that I did, but as it turns out, not so much. Maybe this is why I’m still trying to figure out the great puzzle of our flowerbeds…

Everything about gardening is the hardest lesson: the patience it asks for, the ability to keep trying despite failure year-over-year, the fact that the thing that does you in one year will be different from what does you in the next. Sometimes it’s too much rain, sometimes it’s too little, sometimes it’s the slugs, sometimes it’s the beetles, too much sun, too little—the list goes on and on.

This is something I’ve only noticed in certain places, but there seems to be this strange trend of fake flowers in planters that I just cannot wrap my mind around.

Putting shallow dishes of beer out to help mitigate slugs.

I still have yet to learn one…I asked my husband who, as I mentioned, captains the ship of our garden and he said “What’s a gardening hack? It’s all work. Always.”

This question is making me realize we have no hardscaping in our lives, but I do have a soft spot for pea stone (in theory).

Whatever I’m wearing that day, which is usually jeans and a t-shirt/sweatshirt.

Locally: Barkaboom Native Plants—Chris is an incredible source of knowledge when it comes to native plants in our region and is a big proponent of using locally adapted ecotypes to help conserve local flora and the animals that rely on native plants, something we can all get behind. A little further south: Catskill Native Nursery in Kerhonkson is incredible; they carry the largest selection of North American native plants in New York with a focus on regional species. Story’s Nursery in Freehold is also a favorite.

Mullein, nicotiana, turk’s cap lilies, more bearded irises and hollyhocks too.

Wave Hill in the Bronx. The Landcraft Garden Foundation in Mattituck, NY.

Because I love beautiful things. Because the thrill of walking out your door and down to the garden to pick ingredients you grew to cook dinner with is unmatched. Because pushing a seed into the ground and watching it become something is the sort of miracle that never ever gets old.

Thanks so much, Lisa! You can follow her on Instagram @brass_tacks.

#124. Car Dealers Probably Don’t Want You to Know This Magnet Trick When Buying Used

A small magnet can reveal signs of body filler and past repairs on a used car, but the test has limits every shopper should know.

It can be nearly impossible for an untrained eye to know if they’re getting a safe and reliable car when shopping at a dealership or from a private seller. Bringing a magnet when buying a used car can give shoppers one quick way to spot signs of previous body repair.

Cosmetic repairs can make a used car look better than its condition suggests. A fresh coat of paint can make an older vehicle look surprisingly clean. There’s one simple trick shoppers should be aware of to help check for signs of previous repair work: bring a magnet.

The test takes only a few minutes, but it works best when shoppers understand its limits. Learn how the magnet test can reveal signs of hidden bodywork, where the trick can mislead, and what else deserves attention before purchase.

Many car body panels contain steel, so a small magnet should stick to them. Body filler isn’t magnetic, however, which means the magnet may feel weaker or fall away over an area with a thick repair.

“Bondo® Body Filler shapes in minutes and will accept as many reasonably applied applications as required to fill holes and deep scratches or dents,” according to 3M, the manufacturer that makes Bondo.

Finding filler doesn’t necessarily mean the car has serious damage, but it does show that the panel has been repaired. In a YouTube Short, mechanic Scotty Kilmer demonstrates the test by moving a magnet across a repaired panel. He also checks the gaps between body panels, since uneven spacing can point to previous bodywork.

Shoppers can gently place it against a steel section of the car, then move it across the same panel to compare how strongly it sticks. It can also help to compare matching panels on opposite sides of the vehicle. A noticeable change in the magnet’s pull may be a reason to look more closely at the paint, panel gaps, and repair history.

The magnet should only touch clean paint, and shoppers should get the seller’s permission before placing anything against the car.

A magnet can’t reveal every repair. Some vehicles use aluminum, fiberglass, or plastic body parts, so a magnet won’t stick to those areas even when they’re original. 3M also makes body fillers that work on several materials, including steel, aluminum, and fiberglass.

A thin layer of filler over steel may still attract a magnet. A replacement steel panel may also pass the test even if the car has been in a collision. Repainted panels and repaired plastic parts may not show up at all. For that reason, the magnet test works best as an early warning sign. A weak or missing magnetic pull can prompt shoppers to inspect that area more closely.

A magnet can point out areas that deserve questions, but it can’t show the quality of a repair or the car’s mechanical condition. A vehicle history report also has limits.

“A vehicle history report is not a substitute for an independent vehicle inspection,” according to the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC).

The agency recommends having a used vehicle checked by a mechanic before purchase. “That’s why it’s always a good idea to pay for an independent mechanic to conduct a mechanical inspection of a used car,” according to the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC).

Paint differences, uneven panel gaps, unusual magnet results, or unclear repair records can all give shoppers a reason to request a professional inspection before buying.

#125. How to Give Your House a Cinematic Halloween Makeover With Smart Lighting

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Published Oct 15, 2026 6:41 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

With customizable, easy-to-install outdoor lighting from Govee, you can create a more atmosphere that goes from haunted to holiday.

When Halloween rolls around, turning your front yard into a neighborhood highlight usually comes down to lighting. Lawn skeletons and inflatable decorations can be fun, but lighting is the real star when it comes to creating a moody scene at home. Borrowing a few lighting tricks straight from Hollywood horror movie sets, anyone can transform an everyday home into a cinematic Halloween display.

To show how easy it is to bring professional set design tricks home, smart lighting brand Govee teamed up with filmmaker Ryan Connolly, the founder of filmmaking channel Film Riot who is known for breaking down professional techniques into practical how-tos. Connolly used smart outdoor lighting to turn normal houses into haunted movie-worthy sets in his Halloween short film Last Light.

“For me, Halloween spookiness is about making the familiar unfamiliar in fun ways,” says Connolly. “And we got to toy around with that throughout Last Light, with my mind always on two things you can bring to your Halloween lighting at home: contrast and color.”

Lighting directors never blast a set with just one solid color as this can make it look flat and washed out. Instead, pick one main color to set the mood and add an accent color to highlight details and catch people’s eyes.

“I like to start with a lead color, then add contrasting colors as accents,” explains Connolly. “Even a small amount can give your main color more punch and presence. It’s sort of like the color version of scale; it’s hard to tell how big something is unless you see something familiar next to it.”

Every great horror scene needs shadows just as much as it needs light. Highlighting certain parts of a house while letting the surrounding spots stay dark creates unease and mystery.

“Use light to accent hero areas, whether that’s a decoration or a portion of the house,” Connolly advises. “Give those areas their own pockets of light, and let some of the surrounding space fall into shadow.”

The glowing window effect is one of the easiest movie tricks to copy at home. To get an eerie glow in the windows, hang a white bedsheet on the inside and position a light behind the sheets, like the Govee Strip Light 2 Pro. Set the light to a bold color to match your vibe, like a deep red or ghostly green. The fabric diffuses the light so it glows evenly without revealing its source to trick-or-treaters outside.

Adding motion to your lighting setup—like a flickering candle or a passing shadow—can make a scene feel alive. Govee smart lights make it easy to add subtle motion without manually turning on and off switches:

“The thing I love about Govee lights is how versatile they are,” Connolly explains. “I don’t feel like I have to lock them into just one use… move them around and see how the same light changes the space when it comes from a different direction.”

A huge benefit of smart lighting is that it can work as an all-occasion outdoor lighting solution, rather than something that only comes out for Halloween. Durable, weather-ready lights like Govee Permanent Outdoor Lights 2 Pro and Govee Permanent Outdoor Lights Prism stay mounted year-round, saving you the hassle of hanging and taking down temporary strands every season.

Once Halloween wraps up, changing the look and vibe of a home for Thanksgiving and the holiday season is quick and easy. By November 1, swap out spooky Halloween purples for warm ambers, rust oranges, and cozy yellows for a warm seasonal feel. For the holidays, introduce a festive red and green or icy blues to your lighting. And when the new year rolls around, keep your outdoor lights set to a warm white light along the roofline for clean, everyday curb appeal.

By using Film Riot’s tricks, like mixing contrasting colors, utilizing shadows, diffusing window lights, and adding subtle motion, anyone can use smart lighting to turn their front yard into a professional cinematic Halloween display that neighbors will remember.

We all know and love the Japanese maple, true, but this native tree deserves your adoration this fall...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Japanese maples are deservedly popular for their spectacular autumn foliage, but there’s actually a native tree that deserves a place in the fall color spotlight.

Oh sure, it may not have the same name recognition as Japanese maple, but this little beauty certainly knows how to put on a show with its dazzling display of red, burgundy, orange, and yellow leaves each fall.

And, better still, this North American native's good looks aren’t just limited to the season of mist and mellow fruitfulness, either: its fragrant summer flowers make it a favorite with bees and other pollinators, and that strongly patterned bark makes it a standout feature every time winter rolls around, too!

If you love the idea of a native tree that brings several seasons of interest to your yard (and all while supporting local wildlife, no less), than sourwood might be just the plant you’ve been looking for.

Unlike Japanese maples, which are often grown for their distinctive leaf shapes and elegant branching, sourwood (Oxydendrum arboreum) offers a different kind of beauty. Its elongated leaves and naturally graceful branches give it a softer, woodland-inspired appearance that works beautifully in a naturalistic garden.

And the seasonal show doesn't end when summer arrives. In early to midsummer, sourwood produces drooping clusters of fragrant bell-shaped flowers that resemble lily-of-the-valley flowers (giving you yet another reason to buy yourself a sourwood from Nature Hills).

Now, its flowers aren't just pretty to look at; they also provide a nectar that is beloved by pollinators and beekeepers alike (no surprises there, considering how famous sourwood honey is). Then, after flowering, this native tree's blooms give way to small seed capsules that can persist into the colder months, providing additional visual and wildlife-friendly interest after the leaves fall.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Before you rush to plant one, though, it's important to note that sourwood naturally grows in woodland habitats in the eastern United States and generally prefers acidic, well-drained soil. In fact, it can struggle in alkaline soil and in ground that stays waterlogged, so be sure to check your soil conditions before bagging one for yourself. (It's easily done with something like Amazon's Rapitest Soil Test Kit for Gardens).

Aim for acidic soils with a lower pH of 5.5 to 6.5 (or a netural soil).

Be sure to prune only when dormant (and only to remove damaged branches).

Don't dismiss Japanese maple entirely, of course; it remains a wonderful choice for ornamental gardens, especially if you want finely divided foliage, a sculptural silhouette, or a compact specimen for a carefully designed landscape. If you want a tree that offers more than a single season of interest, though? Well, then sourwood is well worth considering.

This native tree's glossy summer foliage, fragrant white flowers, spectacular autumn colors, and attractive winter structure give it plenty to offer throughout the year, especially if you want to support pollinators without sacrificing ornamental impact.

Plant it for the fall foliage, then, and let the bees benefit along the way. And maybe pick up a jar of local sourwood honey, knowing your garden probably helped make it taste all the sweeter.

#128. Autumn To-Do: DIY ‘Baskets’ for Fallen Leaves

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

This is part of a series with Perfect Earth Project, a nonprofit dedicated to ecological gardening, on how you can be more sustainable in your landscapes at home.

Firefly fans, luna moth lovers, woolly bear worshippers: Now is the time to take action. Leave the leaves! It’s crucial to biodiversity. Fallen leaves host these beloved insects and more who overwinter in them. They also enrich the soil when they decompose. And they reduce waste by staying out of landfills. The EPA estimates that the U.S. sends about 35 million tons of yard waste to the landfill annually, which adds to already high levels of methane, a potent greenhouse gas. According to the National Wildlife Federation, “solid-waste landfills are the largest U.S. source of man-made methane.”

While it’s best to leave the leaves where they land in your yard, we know it’s not always possible. Rake them under trees, shrubs, and in beds to use as free—and beneficial—mulch. Just don’t chop or mulch-mow them, which was once a recommended practice. (Mulch-mowing can kill all insect life, so leave the leaves whole.) Or store leaves in a leaf basket you create out of fallen branches. Perfect Earth Project founder Edwina von Gal has created chic “baskets” at her property to store fallen leaves and keep them out of the landfill. Here’s how you can do it at home.

Photograph courtesy of Perfect Earth Project.

We’re having more storms. Big storms—just ask anyone in the Northeast after last weekend’s Nor’easter. But don’t despair. Gather those fallen branches and put them to good use.

Using larger branches, map out the shape of your basket. The size is up to you. Create a cluster of smaller baskets or build one large one. Do you have a spot full of invasive plants or an area you want to prep for future planting? Place your leaf basket there. The leaves will smother whatever is growing beneath it and get it ready for new growth in the future.

Now start building. Lay down branches, overlapping and tucking them into each other to form a cohesive unit. Trim branches as you need to make them fit. Keep adding more branches, building layer after layer, until you reach your desired height. You can continue adding branches as you find them throughout the year to reinforce the structure. Just make sure to weave them into other branches so that they’ll stay in place.

Rake leaves off of paths and driveways and place them into your basket. The basket will keep them contained and the leaves and branches will decompose over time, enriching the soil beneath it.  “It might look like a lot of leaves and a full leaf basket this fall, but by next summer the mass of leaves will have drastically shrunk,” says Perfect Earth Project’s Tim Wheeler.

#129. The Weed Killer Cheat Sheet You Need Before Going to the Hardware Store

A viral hardware-store trick uses package colors to sort weed killers by purpose, but the product label still matters most in the aisle.

Not all weed killers are the same, and picking the wrong one can cost more than a wasted purchase. A formula meant for driveways, for example, can kill the lawn or landscaping you were trying to protect.

Bottles from Ortho, Roundup, Spectracide, BioAdvanced, and other brands can look similar from several feet away, even though the formulas may serve very different purposes. A hack social video pointed out a simple shortcut to cut through some of the confusion.

Learn what shoppers may spot in the aisle, where the shortcut has limits, and what matters most before a weed killer goes into the cart.

In a T&M Hardware video, an employee explains that orange, yellow, green, blue, and black packaging help shoppers tell different types of weed killers apart.

A post shared by T & M Hardware & Rental (@tandmhardware)

In the video, Orange often points to products for crabgrass and other grassy weeds. Yellow can mark products made for poison ivy and tough brush. Green often appears on weed killers made for established lawns. Blue is marked to only kill weeds and black points to products that kill everything.

The colors can narrow the choices, but shoppers still need to compare the labels before buying.

Weed killer colors aren’t a standard system across every brand. Two products with similar packaging may have different uses, while one brand may use several formulas that target some of the same weeds. A shopper relying on color alone could easily put it in the wrong category.

Packaging colors also shouldn’t be confused with temporary spray dyes. Those dyes simply show where a product has already been applied and don’t indicate what the weed killer does.

The viral color guide can help shoppers scan the shelf faster, but the wording on the bottle provides the more reliable answer.

The product label matters most when weed killer will be used on a lawn.

A weed killer that’s suitable for one grass type may not work for another. Lawn products list the grass types they can treat, the weeds they control, and any limits on where or when they should be used.

Shoppers should also distinguish between lawn weed killers and products that kill both weeds and grass. A formula intended for a driveway, walkway, or bare area can damage nearby lawn and landscaping. The same goes for brush and poison ivy killers, which may harm desirable plants they touch.

“Pesticide product labels provide critical information about how to safely and legally handle and use pesticide products,” according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

That includes directions on where and how a product can be used, so the label’s approved use sites and application limits are worth checking before the product leaves the shelf.

T&M Hardware, “Instagram Video” U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, “Introduction to Pesticide Labels”

The most striking aspect of Pensión, the Mexico City guesthouse by Rafael Prieto and Bernardo Dominguez of Savvy Studio, is that it looks unlike any other design-forward hotel on your Instagram feed. It feels as though it were conceived entirely outside of the internet design vernacular. Salmon wall-to-wall carpet, large-scale photographic wallpaper, a bathtub in a bedroom—there are unexpected twists and surprises at every turn as Prieto and Dominguez subvert your expectations.

What began as a small three-room project has recently expanded to ten rooms, each with its own distinct design that feels like a little private world, alongside the launch of Café Ideal, a restaurant-bar on the ground floor with a menu by Prieto’s friend and frequent collaborator (and Remodelista favorite) Laila Gohar. On the second floor is Prieto and Jorge de la Garza’s bookstore, Librería, where you can pick up rare art books from independent publishers.

Eat, sleep, and shop all under one (sublimely designed) roof. Here’s a tour of the three spaces.
