#131. 11 Strange Sounds That Could Spell Trouble for Homeowners

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Updated Oct 15, 2026 4:56 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Homes often make strange noises. They’re built of many different materials—glass, concrete, wood—that expand and contract at different rates, causing friction that results in those odd spooky sounds.

But still, “The most noise your house should make is a popping sound, like your knuckles cracking, and only once in a while,” says Bill Richardson, former president of the American Society of Home Inspectors and owner of Responsive Inspections in Bosque Farms, New Mexico.

If your home is making noises that make you jump in the night (or sounds that rival Metallica’s greatest hits), then it may be sending you signals that there’s a problem. We asked the experts to catalog some of the more worrisome pops, hisses, groans, creaks, and knocks and tell us what they mean and how they can be remedied. Read on to find out how 11 spooky house sounds are diagnosed and how each can be resolved.

The problem: When most homeowners first turn on their heating system in the fall, they’ll often hear a little moaning and groaning as the heating system expands and rubs against the frame of the house, says Mike Kuhn, the New Jersey owner of a HouseMaster inspection service and coauthor of The Pocket Idiot’s Guide to Home Inspections.

With a baseboard hot-water system, you can also expect “normal clinking and knocking,” says Kuhn. The circulator pump or pumps to the system, however, “should be silent when they run,” says Kuhn. If you hear knocking or clanking, typically located at the boiler itself, it might be a sign of impending failure of the circulator pump, he says.

The solution: Get a repairman out to check on it, pronto.

The problem: If you hear strange noises like scratching and possibly chittering coming from places where no human or beloved pet lives in the house, you probably don’t have ghosts. You may have mice, squirrels, raccoons, or even bats sharing your quarters, says Richardson. “Any kind of wild critter could be up in the attic,” he says.

And these freeloaders aren’t just a nuisance; bats can carry deadly rabies. In the Southwest, the droppings of mice can spread hantavirus. Some animals will tear up insulation to nest, or chew through siding or even electrical wires, causing fires.

The solution: As soon as you suspect an intruder, get on it: Set traps or a bat repelling system. (Call in a pro if the animal is stubborn or large.) Finally, prevent the problem from reoccurring by sealing up the entrances to your house with steel wool, metal sheeting, caulk, and/or hardware cloth.

To keep raccoons away, put garbage in sealed, secured metal cans that can’t be tipped. Bring pet food inside. After pests have been removed, make sure vents and chimneys are securely covered with a grille or mesh chimney cap so those spaces can still breathe.

The problem: “You definitely don’t want to hear water running if nobody’s using anything,” says Richardson. The sound could indicate many things: a busted pipe in a wall, under the floor, or even in the irrigation system.

If you hear running water when you shouldn’t, “Shut the main off and see if the noise goes away. If it does, you’ve got a [water] leak somewhere,” says Richardson, and a plumbing problem in need of fixing.

The solution: Unless you’re really handy and ready to do surgery on your home, call in a plumber.

The Shelly Flood Gen 4 uses a 2-meter (about 6.5-foot) sensing cable that can detect moisture along its entire length. Read the review.

The problem: A gas-fired hot water heater works pretty much like boiling a pot of water: A fire is lit and the water inside is heated until it’s ready for use. “A lot of sediment builds up at the bottom of a hot water tank, and that sediment works like an insulator,” forcing the burner to work harder, Kuhn says. The strange noise you hear is the bubbling sediment—and a sign that the tank is probably experiencing fatigue and may be facing premature failure, says Kuhn.

The solution: Ideally, you should flush out your hot water tank every few months, using the drain valve near the bottom of the floor. “However, nobody does it,” says Kuhn, because it can be a pain to do.

If your water heater is already making these noises, draining it might help. “It could [work] a little bit longer, it could go a lot longer,” but the damage is probably done, says Kuhn.

The problem: “What that can connote is that your filter hasn’t been changed,” says Richardson, “and your furnace is trying to pull in air from around it.” That’s not good, he says; the furnace is working too hard. “What it will do is start sucking exhaust gases from the furnace into the house.”

The solution: Install clean filters regularly, “anywhere from 3 months to monthly, depending on atmospheric conditions,” says Richardson. Consider lessening the impact on the planet by trying cut-to-fit filters that can be cleaned and reused.

The problem: If you’ve got a well for your water, you’ve got a well pump that has a switch, either in the house or above the well in your yard. “If you are sitting in your house and hearing the pump switch click on and off, you may have a problem,” says Kuhn.

The pump pulls water from the well and into a holding tank, where it’s stored for your use. If you’re hearing it when you, say, turn on the faucet, something may be wrong. The pump “should not operate every time there is a call for water. The wear and tear would cause the pump to fail prematurely,” Kuhn says. It’s likely that you have a leak in the system. “The leak is either going to be in the well equipment itself, or in a fixture”— a leaky toilet, for example— that is causing the holding tank to drain, says Kuhn.

The solution: Check your fixtures for leaks. If there’s a small leak, try a quick repair with an epoxy like J-B Weld’s WaterWeld. If it’s a bigger issue, call a plumber familiar with well systems.

The problem: Hissing sounds can happen for a variety of reasons, and some can be spookier than others. If the hissing sound happens when the HVAC system is running, there may be a leak somewhere in the system. Leaks can happen at the compressor, in radiators, or inside air ducts.

However, if your home uses natural gas, the strange noise that sounds like hissing could indicate a bigger problem like a gas leak, says Richardson. Sometimes you can hear a hissing outside at the gas meter or at a home’s outdoor gas light post—places where the line could have corroded, he says. “You should be able to smell it, but you never know.”

The solution: If you smell gas around the gas main, don’t mess with the gas shutoff unless you absolutely know what you’re doing, because any mishandling or spark could make things much worse, says Richardson. If you hear the noise and smell the gas, immediately evacuate the house and call the gas company.

To fix air leaks in an HVAC system, check the valves on the different components for obvious leaks and call in an HVAC professional to find bigger issues and make sure the system is in good working order.

The problem: A squeaking wood floor is a common old house noise, but don’t dismiss it out of hand. While some squeaky floor noises are just wood boards rubbing against each other as temperatures change and the house settles, there are other reasons to investigate the sound. One big concern is termites. If there’s also a low point in the floor, it’s an even bigger sign that termites might be munching away at the wood structure.

The solution: Fixing a squeaky floor takes a bit of detective work to diagnose the cause. If it’s part of a subfloor that has settled or a nail that is rubbing against a wood board, those issues can be fixed with wood shims or a few extra fasteners to secure the connections. If it’s termites, it’s time to call in professionals to assess the damage and make sure the structure is still sound.

The problem: Plumbing pipes can create a variety of spooky noises to alert homeowners that something’s up. Banging noises heard after running a sink or flushing the toilet may be due to water hammer, which is pressure inside the pipes caused by air or excess water.

Tapping noises heard when a dishwasher is running can be caused from a clog inside the system. Its drain hose sometimes can get clogged with debris, making it tough for the water to flow, which can cause that tapping noise.

The solution: To get rid of the air pressure causing banging noises in the pipes, it’s helpful to drain the system. This will help eliminate the pocket of air, so it can run smoothly. For the dishwasher, it’s time to clean the drain hose, which is usually a job for an experienced DIYer or professional plumber.

The problem: If it sounds like there’s something in the washing machine banging around and trying to escape, it’s probably due to an unbalanced load or an issue with the balance ring. If it’s an unbalanced load, you won’t hear the thumping every time you wash clothes. An unbalanced load usually happens with heavier and thicker items, and it can be fixed by just redistributing the items in the washer.

If the thumping and banging happen every time the washer runs, it could be the balance ring. A washer’s balance ring helps keep the washer in balance when washing a load of laundry. If the thumping isn’t fixed, then the washer could really go out of balance and cause a bigger problem with the electrical system of the machine.

The solution: Before attempting to investigate or do anything to fix a banging washer, make sure it is unplugged and the water to the machine is off. When a balance ring is depleted of fluid, the washer tub can shake. This is usually a job for a pro to fix.

The problem: Worn weatherstripping or windows that aren’t fitting quite right due to temperature fluctuations and age can cause a whistling sound, heard more in colder weather when it’s quiet at night. While it’s annoying, it’s also an energy waster and could lead to bigger problems.

If the windows are also rattling, then there’s usually something not fitting quite right and bumping into another part of the window system. Either of these issues could eventually lead to cracks in the glass.

The solution: Figuring out where the leaks are happening can be as easy as feeling around the window for cold air and looking at the weatherstripping around the window. If there are any cracks or gaps in the seal around a window, replace the weatherstripping. It’s a fairly easy DIY project that most homeowners can tackle.

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned and Loved About Them

From crown molding and built-ins to creaky floors and drafty windows, old houses are full of charm and challenges. So we’re celebrating all the things that make old homes worth loving, living in, and fixing up. Learn about historic house styles; find practical advice for maintaining your old home; and discover quirky, forgotten features you simply won’t find in new builds.

#132. These Cheat Codes to Identify Paint Went Viral — But Do They Work for All Paint?

A viral hardware-store paint trick can help shoppers read certain cans faster, but the colors don’t mean the same thing for every brand.

Whether you’re a tradesman, a savvy DIYer, or beginner, finding exactly what you’re looking for in a hardware store can be overwhelming. That’s especially true in the paint aisle. A wall of paint cans can look nearly identical, but thankfully, one recent viral hardware-store paint cheat code revealed that some of those cans contain a much quicker visual cue. Shortcuts like this can make a crowded paint aisle easier to navigate, but they don’t work in all cases.

Learn how the viral paint-can code works, what each color means, and why shoppers should still read the label before heading to the register.

The trick comes from a T&M Hardware & Rental video showing colored sections on certain Do it Best paint cans.

A post shared by T & M Hardware & Rental (@tandmhardware)

The colors give employees and shoppers a quick way to spot the right type of paint before reading the full label. Do it Best currently sells Best Look interior paint in flat, eggshell, satin, and semi-gloss finishes, as well as separate exterior paint products.

No. Paint can color codes aren’t universal.

Manufacturers use their own packaging systems, so a colored band on one brand may mean something different on another. Some brands use color to separate product lines rather than sheen.

That makes the viral T&M Hardware trick most useful for the same Do it Best paint line shown in the video. Shoppers should still check the sheen on the printed label and confirm whether the paint is intended for interior or exterior use.

Paint labels can also include tint-base terms such as white, neutral, or deep base. Those terms describe the paint base rather than its sheen. Anyone matching an old can should check the brand, product line, sheen, base, and color formula instead of relying on a colored band alone.

Paint sheen affects how much light the finish reflects and where the paint usually works best.

Flat paint has very little shine and can make small wall flaws less noticeable. Eggshell has a slight sheen. Satin reflects more light and works well in many frequently used rooms. Semi-gloss has a shinier finish and often appears on trim or surfaces that need regular cleaning.

Paint brands don’t always use the same names or group their sheens in the same way. Sherwin-Williams and Behr, for example, list finishes including flat, matte, satin, and semi-gloss, and eggshell.

The color code can help narrow down a choice, but the printed sheen on the can remains the most reliable guide.

#133. The Fall Garden: 7 Vegetables to Start Growing Now

For cooks and gardeners, colder weather is something of a second spring. It is our Greens Season.

In hot summer climates, there is no hope of growing crisp salads and chewy kales from June to August. And cilantro bolts while your back is turned. But as the nights grow longer and chillier, we can begin to look forward to a fall salad strategy, and order seeds, and dig, and wait.

Here are seven of our favorite autumn vegetables to start growing now:

Thanks to heirloom seed saving and clever breeding, lettuce is no longer just lettuce. There are dozens of cultivars from which to choose, Flashy Trout Back Lettuce (also known as Spotted Trout and Speckled Trout) is a charmer, with freckled pale green leaves and an open habit. Sow it every week for a succession of salads till frost.

Arugula’s peppery bite might be ubiquitous in supermarket clamshells by now, but nothing beats a spicy leaf picked straight from the pot on your terrace or from the row you dug three weeks earlier. Allowing your arugula or mustard plants to bolt is rewarding, too, because their buds and flowers are as hot as their greens, and perk up mild salads.

A microgreen is the immature form of any edible leaf, snipped while it has just two cotyledons or the first two true leaves to its name. These miniature leaves can be grown in windowsill trays if you are an apartment dweller, or in outdoor pots in full sun. Sow every week for repeated harvests. Collect them when their stems are about an inch long.

Dwarf kale is a container gardener’s delight, providing the full kale taste and health experience packed into a small and sturdy leaf which is mature before its full-size cousins. If you plant it in full sun, you might be lucky enough to be eating your crop well into the frosty weather—I have seen the plants withstand inches of snow and become sweeter in the process.

Chards and spinaches love cold nights and like kale and other cool greens can be harvested well after the first frost. Rainbow chard may taste the same as regular chard, but its prettiness factor is so high that it can be included as a fall crop for aesthetic pleasure alone.

Waiver: fall-planted peas will not set pods in cold climates. Instead, the goal is gather as many bunches of tender pea shoots as possible. The tender stems and leaves are as sweet and pea-ish as the pods and are wonderful in salads, or gently steamed and dressed with soy and sesame oil. The seeds must be soaked for 12 hours before planting, and full sun is optimal for the most prolific growth. Pinch out the tender growing stems as soon as the plants are about four inches tall, and keep picking until successive frosts close your pea season.

This is one bean that loves the cold. Sow favas (also known as broad beans) in late winter and in early fall. As with peas, you will not see pods form after a fall planting–the days are too short. The autumn  crop is grown for the tender leaves and stems only, and these can be harvested about three weeks after planting and for a month or more beyond. The youngest silky leaves make unusual salad ingredients and are good cooked, too.

This root vegetable works while the winter world sleeps. Plant parsnips straight into deep pots (about 16 inches or more) in mid-fall for February or March harvest. Their leaves will appear before winter, and over several months the sweet tap roots will grow fat for harvest. Pulling vegetables from your garden in the middle of winter is a bit of a party piece–plan a celebratory salad with quick-pickled beets and kale greens and apple, and invite your friends.

It is ironic that the herb so closely associated with hot climates and spicy food evolved in cool Europe, where it was largely shunned. Cilantro, which gets a bad rap for bolting in a heartbeat, grows best before and after summer. Spring and autumn are the best times to sow this pungent herb. It will withstand a couple of frosts before it gives up for good.

#134. Brittany and Patrick Mahomes’ Fall Porch Proves You Don’t Need Much to Create a Gorgeous Seasonal Display

Recreate Brittany and Patrick Mahomes’ fall entrance with mums, pumpkins, and warm lighting for a beautifully cohesive seasonal display.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes and his wife, Brittany, have a fall entrance that’s just perfect inspiration for the season. Brittany, a former soccer player and co-owner of the Kansas City Current, shared a series of charming family snaps of their Halloween display on Instagram (see below). It suits the season without going over the top, looking like an extension of the landscape rather than decorations thrown together at the last minute.

Chrysanthemums, pumpkins, and integrated lighting make the entryway feel warm and inviting – exactly what you want if you’re welcoming trick-or-treaters or simply hoping to boost curb appeal in the fall.

The secret is to build on the garden you already have. Add the right plants, complementary colors, and strategically placed lighting for an autumn display that lasts until the frosts set in. Here are my five simple steps to help you recreate the look.

A post shared by Brittany Mahomes (@brittanylynne)

Mums – or chrysanthemums – are really the star of Brittany and Patrick Mahomes’ entryway, and they’re a classic choice for autumn containers. However, believe it or not, you can actually choose the wrong ones. You’ll want to choose hardy ones that last much longer and are suited to your climate rather than florist varieties intended for short-term indoor displays.

Choose plants with plenty of unopened buds for a longer succession of flowers than ones that are already in full bloom. Choose two or three complementary shades, like bronze, burgundy, cream, and golden yellow, and repeat these throughout your entryway.

Timing matters, too. Wait until nighttime temperatures begin to cool before adding chrysanthemums, and let pumpkins and gourds form the foundation of the display first.

Rather than spending a lot of money on replacing all the planting you did in summer, look for porch plants that add interest throughout the whole year. Ornamental grasses, heucheras, and sedums add some texture and color, even as summer flowers are fading, while shrubs and small trees with fall foliage can give the entrance a more established look.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Keep some of your existing summer plants if they still look healthy. A summer perennial can bloom early and then leave behind attractive foliage or seed heads that carry the garden into autumn.

Additionally, a trailing plant spilling over a container or a few late-flowering perennials can help bridge that between-season gap.

Pumpkins and gourds can look just as at home in a garden border as they do on a porch. The trick is to treat (did you like that pun?) them as part of the planting design rather than scattering them randomly around the entrance.

Interior designer Preeti Shah, founder of Spotlight Style, recommends grouping pumpkins in odd numbers at different heights, anchored by one or two large containers. Place larger pumpkins toward the back or at the base of a display, then use smaller varieties to lead the eye toward the front door. “The difference between planned and decorated is restraint,” Shah says. “Pick two or three colors from your house, repeat them, and use natural materials.”

Look for colors already found in your brickwork, front door, or foliage to really help the display feel like part of your landscape.

Lighting can bring out the texture of ornamental grasses, highlight colorful chrysanthemums, and create a welcoming glow after dark. Rather than illuminating every part of the entrance equally, focus on a few key plants or architectural features.

Jarald Patterson of Christmas Light Supplier recommends aiming low uplights or small spotlights into the planting, rather than making the path edge the main attraction. He also suggests choosing warm-white lighting around 2,700K to complement autumn shades.

“Pools of light with dark gaps between them look intentional; even, bright coverage looks like a parking lot,” Patterson says. Where practical, hide fixtures behind containers or within planting beds, and ensure cables are safely installed and rated for outdoor use.

The most convincing autumn entrances develop gradually; it’s all in the phases. Begin with existing plants and containers in late summer, introduce pumpkins as autumn approaches, and add chrysanthemums when temperatures cool. Ornamental grasses, seed heads, and evergreen foliage can help maintain the structure as flowers start to die.

As Shah advises, “Add a few pieces each week, and the entrance keeps changing all season without a big redo.” That’s a relief for those of us who don’t have time for a big, sweeping redo of the entryway for every holiday and season.

By working with the garden instead of starting from scratch, you can create an autumn entrance that feels cohesive, seasonal, and inviting long after Halloween has passed.

#135. Kitchen of the Week: Frama’s Freestanding Components Made By Top-Drawer Swedish Cabinetmaker Kvänum

A decade or so ago, when Niels Strøyer Christophersen founded his celebrated Copenhagen design firm, Frama, he used his living quarters in a restored 1905 watchmaker’s shop as a showcase for his studio’s work. Extolling natural, unpretentious materials, ease of use, and reverence for the old, Christophersen went on to created refreshingly simple elements for the home, including his own kitchen out of parts found on the street. It served as a model for Frama’s initial kitchens composed of freestanding, wood-framed components.

“The first Frama kitchen was based on principles refined to their most essential,” explains the company. “The aim was to celebrate the essentials of cooking and being.” Frama has now taken its kitchen offerings to the next level: collaborating with Swedish cabinetmaker Kvänum, a century-old kitchen maker and supplier to the Swedish royal court, it offers Frama Modules by Kvänum, a line of kitchen components in two wooden frames.

The modules are made of birch, here stained a warm hue they’ve dubbed Ginger, with milled stainless steel pulls.

Here’s Frama’s former kitchen system, pop-up in Brooklyn, and 2024 Rivet collection of Shiny Aluminum Shelves and Side Tables.

#136. 9 Quick Fixes for a More Refreshing Shower

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Updated Oct 15, 2026 4:20 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Nothing kills the mood of a refreshing bath after a long day (or for that matter, an energizing shower to start one) faster than the sight of mold. Or a delay in warm water. Or a damp towel. The fact is this: So many factors can cramp what should be a relaxing retreat. Fortunately, the following quick fixes can help you go back to enjoying your next shower—and maybe even make it a long one.

For better water pressure, first loosen mineral deposits that could be clogging the flow. Unscrew the shower head and soak in a bowl of boiling water and ½ cup of vinegar for 10 minutes. If you can’t remove the head, ﬁll a plastic bag with full-strength vinegar and tape it over the ﬁxture. Let it sit for an hour, then remove.

For all of the amplification power without any of the additional tech, slip your smart phone (speaker end down) into a ceramic mug and sit it on a ledge in the bathroom. The sound will fill the room, and you’ll be ready to rock with accompaniment to your favorite tunes.

The days of shower curtains blowing in during a shower are over. Switch to a weighted curtain—or DIY one of your own. You can use heavy-duty magnets (smaller ones will slide) to hold the bottom of the curtain to the side of your tub, or take a handful of binder clips and attach them, evenly spaced, along the edge.

The neck of your shower head is the obvious place to hang a basket of shampoo and body wash, but leaves your supplies sopping wet—and you with an eyeful when going in to grab face wash. No more. Install a towel hook at the opposite end of the shower for a more convenient spot to hang your basket.

A second rod outside your shower curtain puts your towel in better reach and frees up wall space for additional storage. Create this placement using an extra tension rod, or replace your current rod altogether with a double rod.

Follow every shower with a splash of this natural, aromatic cleanser and say goodbye to mildew. Mix up 1 tsp. tea tree oil with 1 cup of water, fill a spray bottle, and spritz around the tub. Let air-dry, and enjoy the lingering pine smell. Also leave the bathroom door open to promote better air circulation.

Spot rust rings leftover where a metal can of shaving cream often sits? Remove all bottles from the area, then dip half of a cut lemon in salt and use it to scrub the affected area—you’ll soon see it disappear. When moving items back into place, flip your shaving cream can on its head to store without leaving future rings.

Mix equal parts hydrogen peroxide and baking soda, then scrub into tile grout using a sturdy toothbrush. Covering a lot of ground? Consider fixing a small wooden scrub brush to the end of your electric drill for serious power. When your work is dry (and now bright), seal the grout.

Help your bathroom’s exhaust fan do its job sucking moisture out of the air post-shower (and preventing mold) by wiping out collected dust and towel lint once in a while. Flip off the circuit breaker to the bathroom, then remove and suds up the vent cover. Vacuum any excess inside the fan using your machine’s brush attachment.

#137. What the Octane Numbers on the Gas Pump Really Tell You

Everything you need to know about the numbers on the gas pump.

If you have ever stood at a gas pump and wondered whether your car really needs that expensive button marked “Premium,” you are not alone. Gasoline pumps offer a small menu of numbers ranging from 85 to 93 and then politely wait for you to make a decision that could cost anywhere from a few cents to a dollar or more per gallon.

Those numbers are octane ratings. They do not tell you how much energy is in the gasoline, how “powerful” the fuel is, or how clean it will make your engine. What they primarily tell you is how resistant the fuel is to knock, also called pre-detonation. And understanding that distinction can save you money.

Let’s dive into what the octane numbers actually stand for and why it’s important to know which one you should be using in your vehicle.

A gasoline-powered engine requires three things to operate: air, fuel, and spark. Air is all around us, so it’s easy to get. It enters the engine and is mixed with vaporized gasoline. A spark ignites the fuel and air mixture, and the resulting combustion presses a cylinder down to rotate a crankshaft, producing the power that makes the car go.

Under certain conditions, some of the unburned mixture ahead of the flame front can become hot and pressurized enough to ignite on its own. Instead of one controlled combustion event, the engine gets multiple combustion fronts colliding inside the cylinder. That creates the characteristic metallic knocking or pinging sound heard as the vehicle rus, especially when accelerating. Usually referred to as “knock.” This misfire causes the piston to move prematurely or not enough, depending on when it occurs, resulting in incorrect engine timing.

Modern engines are generally pretty good at detecting and managing knock, but that doesn’t mean you want it happening constantly. Persistent severe knock can damage pistons, bearings, spark plugs, and other critical engine components.

Octane rating essentially tells you how resistant gasoline is to this unwanted self-ignition. Higher octane fuel is more resistant to knock. The more resistant to knock a fuel is, the harder it is to get it to combust. That creates a careful balance in fuel requirements between knock resistance and ease of ignition.

In general, gasoline engines in the U.S. are made to use fuels between 85 and 93 octane. Some require a specific rating while others are largely indifferent. The reasons for this are a combination of air mixture and engine compression. Higher air pressure (through induction, turbocharging, and so forth) often coincides with higher pressure before ignition in the engine. Higher pressure before combustion increases the chance of pre-ignition knock. This is why many turbocharged engines require higher octane fuel.

When at the gasoline pump, you’ll see anywhere from two to four options for octane ratings. These numbers are standardized by ASTM International for North America and enforced in the U.S. by the Federal Trade Commission, with the octane rating listed on the pump given as the Anti-Knock Index (AKI) number. Below that number, you may have noticed some pumps add the label “(RON+MON)/2” or “(R+M)/2”.

That’s the formula used to calculate the AKI rating for the fuel. The “R” or “RON” is the Research Octane Number, while the “M” or “MON” is the Motor Octane Number. Adding those together and dividing by two to get an average returns the AKI.

That means 87-octane gasoline isn’t 87 percent octane. It is a rating based on the fuel’s resistance to knocking compared with standardized reference fuels. This is why the numbers can be confusing when comparing American gasoline with fuel ratings used in other countries. Many countries advertise RON rather than the AKI number used in the U.S.

The test procedure for getting those RON and MON results is very similar. The RON is achieved by running an engine at low revolutions per minute (RPM), with valve timing varied throughout the cycle to increase the likelihood of inducing knock. The MON is tested the same way, but at higher RPM and with variable ignition timing added to further raise the chance of knock. Generally, the MON will produce a lower average result than the RON. The results of the RON and MON are then compared to a baseline and given a rating. Those two ratings are then averaged.

Higher octane does not equate to more power. This is probably the biggest misconception surrounding premium gasoline. Putting 93-octane fuel into a Toyota Prius, which was designed for 87 octane, doesn’t magically turn it into a NASCAR winner. If the engine’s computer isn’t designed to take advantage of the higher octane, you may notice absolutely no difference other than your wallet becoming slightly lighter.

However, there is an important exception. Some engines are specifically calibrated to take advantage of higher-octane fuel.

Many high-performance, high-output, or highly efficient engines frequently use higher compression ratios, turbocharging, supercharging, aggressive ignition timing, or combinations of these. Those characteristics can increase cylinder pressures and temperatures, making knock more likely. Using higher-octane gasoline gives those engineers more room to operate without encountering destructive levels of knock.

In those engines, premium fuel can allow the engine to produce its intended power and efficiency. Many turbocharged, high-efficiency engines require higher octane fuel to operate. This is much more common now, as newer vehicles use smaller, more compact, and more efficient engines that employ turbocharging, higher compression ratios, etc. This is true of vehicles that are not performance or sports-oriented, like pickup trucks, sport utilities, and minivans.

This depends on the vehicle, but for the most part, higher-octane fuels are unlikely to benefit engines not designed to use them. Some vehicles can use higher octane to improve performance. Mazda, for example, often lists horsepower ratings alongside fuel octane ratings because the SKYACTIV engine family can vary valve timing more or less based on the amount of knock sensed. More knock likely means a lower-octane fuel, so the engine’s computer will adjust timing less often to prevent knock, thus reducing potential power output. And vice versa.

Most modern engines are designed to do something similar, though how much adjustment will depend very much on the engine’s design. The majority of hybrid vehicles, for example, will not benefit from higher-octane fuels because they use a less varied timing cycle to improve efficiency at the lower rpm rates at which they are most often running.

For most vehicles and the way we drive them, the answer is yes. Most of the time, paying more for the premium fuel isn’t going to improve your efficiency or clean your engine better. Most of the “cleaning” of your engine during operation, including the carbon buildup that is often talked about, happens despite the fuel, not because of it. The obvious caveat being that if your vehicle’s owner’s manual or the manufacturer recommends or requires higher-octane fuel, that is what you should use.

An efficiently burning engine free of knock will also burn nearly everything that would otherwise coat the cylinders and cylinder heads. The cleansers in fuel at the pump do very little cleaning inside the engine. Fuel additives, however, can have a bigger effect on carbon buildup, but are still limited as to how much they can accomplish.

The octane rating of fuel does not equate to its power output or performance level. It is a measure of how resistant the fuel is to early combustion under pressure, or knock. If your engine requires higher-octane fuel, you should pump high-octane fuel. Most engines do not benefit from raising octane levels unless the manufacturer specifically lists a benefit.

For these reasons, you can save money at the pump by using minimum octane fuel (usually 85 or 87). There is very little benefit to using high octane fuels in a vehicle that cannot utilize it.

#139. What to Do With Clematis in October – 5 Fast Tasks to Prep This Hard-Working Vine for Winter

Treat your clematis vine to some TLC in fall and your stronger, healthier plant will sail through the cold season to bring abundant blooms next year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Giving a clematis the right care in fall makes a real difference to how well the vine will perform next year, so gift this hard-working plant an hour of your time now for big rewards. We gardeners love the vast range of clematis varieties, some with huge blossoms and others with a froth of tiny flowers, with glossy green foliage providing the perfect foil for the generous blossoms. And as October rolls in, it’s time to tend to this favorite plant and get clematis ready for winter to ensure a great repeat show.

Clematis care in October is neither difficult nor time consuming, but it’s well worth your time. Give your vine a tidy-up, tie in new growth, water and mulch the soil and look out for powdery mildew which saps a plant's strength, and your clematis will be prepped to sail through whatever the winter weather throws at it.

There are clematis varieties to suit every spot, and plenty of vines that grow quickly without scrambling our of control to cloak bare fences and cover awkward structures in the landscape. And giving these useful garden plants the right care now will mean a healthier vine that'll survive winter well and produce plenty of flowers next year.

While no clematis should be heavily pruned in fall, it’s never a bad idea to do the 3-Ds trim, cutting back dead, diseased or damaged stems. If this fast-growing vine is swamping another plant or reaching into places it shouldn't, don't be afraid to remove unwanted stems now either.

Don't just jump in with the pruners though, as how much you snip off depends on which clematis group the plant belongs to. While pruning a clematis in October should always be limited, whatever type you're growing, it’s really useful to know which group it belongs to so you don't risk cutting off too many of next year’s flowers.

There are three types of clematis: some bloom on old wood in spring, others flower on both old and new wood, and a third group blooms on new wood in autumn. Don’t let this confuse you. Clematis are a little like hydrangea: you simply need to know which group yours belongs to, so you can prune it at the right time, confident that you’re not snipping off next year’s flowers.

Now you know which group your clematis belongs to, you can decide just how limited this health-giving tidy-up prune should be.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If you have sweet autumn clematis, once its lush froth of tiny white flowers is finished, consider deadheading the plant if you are worried about self-seeding. Beautiful as its seedheads are, this vine self-seeds aggressively.

Tying new growth to its support is an esssential task to get clematis ready for winter. Clematis may be the optimal flowering vine, but these plants gets heavier every year so it's vital to give plants the right support. It's also important to check the ties already attaching older stems to the trellis are in good order before fall and winter storms arrive, and secure loose vines so they’re not snapped by high winds. This is about much more than aesthetics because a snapped stem invites fungal spores to settle in for the winter.

Velcro Garden Ties, available from Amazon, work well for clematis vine as the cut-to-length hook and loop tape holds firm but is quick and easy to adjust, and is endlessly reusable.

Powdery Mildew is a common issue for clematis in fall and while a late-season outbreak is rarely fatal, it can significantly sap the strength of the plant. It’s easy to deal with powdery mildew if you spot a dusty white coating on leaves by removing and disposing of the affected foliage. Make sure you disinfect your pruners with isopropyl alcohol, available from Amazon, so you don’t inadvertently spread this disease.

A garden waste bag with a top closure such as this Collapsible Garden Waste Bag from Walmart makes it easy to safely transport infected leaves to the trash can or tip – because you don’t want to add these fungal spores to your compost heap. A small rake like Fiskar’s Xact Hand Rake, available from Lowe’s, helps you get rid of infected plant material that’s fallen to the ground.

Plants need water even in winter but once the ground freezes, there really is no way to get water to the plant roots. So, add ‘water deeply’ to your list of gardening jobs to do in October and if fall rainfall is very sparse, deep-soak the roots once a week until the first freeze.

Clematis plants are tough vines but their roots are surprisingly fragile, growing out in a shallow network rather than diving deep into the ground. Protect them from winter’s worst by layering a 2-3-inch-thick layer of mulch such as Back to the Roots Premium Mulch, available from The Home Depot, over the soil at the base of the plant. Clematis roots extend to around 2-3 feet wide, so be generous with the mulched area, but be careful not to pile material against the stems which will cause them to rot.

Depending on your USDA zone, there are a couple of extra tasks to put on your October to-do list.

All clematis species are vulnerable to clematis wilt, a fungal disease that can kill the vine. While it’s more of a problem in late spring and early summer, if you live in a zone with warm, humid days and cooler nights, clematis wilt can flare up in fall. Look for dry and withered leaves – some may even blacken – that doesn’t look like seasonal dieback. All this foliage should be trimmed out with pruners that are disinfected with isopropyl alcohol, available from Amazon, and thrown out. Get all of the diseased material, and your vine should be okay in spring.

In colder regions (USDA zones 3-5), prepare your clematis well for harsh winter freezes. Wait until after your first hard frost before mulching, as without this cozy fall duvet, the plant will naturally prepare better for winter cold. Then apply a deeper 3-4-inch-thick mulch to protect roots. Mulching will also reduce the soil’s freeze-thaw cycle which can heave a clematis’ shallow root system out of the ground in cooler zones.

Pay extra attention to ensuring this season’s growth is tied in to a trellis or support, as heavy snow and ice loads are likely to collect on the dense tangle of stems.

Do these fall clematis care tasks and your plant will go into the winter strong and healthy, full of sensational seedheads and ready for another great season next year. One task you should definitely leave off your fall to-do list, however, is fertilizing your clematis. This vine is fast-growing and tough so doesn’t routinely need fertilizing to begin with, and certainly doesn’t need feeding in October with winter fast approaching. Instead, the plant needs to slow down its growth and harden off naturally before harsh weather arrives.

#140. Quick Takes With: Lisa Przystup

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

You may remember Lisa Przystup from our 2017 post on her rustic-meets-minimalist Catskills home (the one with that clever DIY brass backsplash) or our 2021 story on the updates made since then. Or perhaps you’ve heard of her because you read and loved her book on the chic homes of chic Upstaters. But even if her name doesn’t ring a bell, you’d definitely recall her gorgeous Christmas decorations that captured every design-minded professional’s attention last year (a hard thing to do these days).

That festive dreamscape that birthed a whole new palette for the holidays (blue and red? yes!)  is featured in her newest book, Once Around the Sun (dropping Oct. 14), a visual diary of the 1893 farmhouse she shares with her husband, Jonathon, as it moves through the seasons. Inside its pages are beautiful images of the interiors as well as the land, water, and sky just outside its doors—all of it evolving as the months go by.

Of course, the garden is where the seasonal effects are felt most acutely. Below, Lisa shares her thoughts on cultivating the land, “the sort of miracle that never ever gets old.”

Photography by John  Hesselbarth + Kate Foster, unless otherwise noted.

Less a garden memory and more a plant-related memory: pulling the stamen through the base of honeysuckle blooms to drop the nectar onto my tongue. I remember feeling like I had discovered the most incredible secret.

Orwell’s Roses by Rebecca Solnit (a very good reminder on so many levels, in so many ways). The Garden Against Time by Olivia Laing (I can’t technically say I return to this time and time again as I started reading it last year and have yet to finish it, but I can say that I’ve loved it so far and my inability to complete it has more to do with me than it has to do with the quality of writing or storytelling). And this wonderful essay, “Autumn, It’s No Garden Party,” by Michael Pollan.

@saipua: the OG, the G.O.A.T, all the superlatives. Her floral design is art of the highest order, her color palette game is next level.

Oh, there are so many, for so many different reasons…. I’m obsessed with the size and grandeur of angelica and mullein, garden roses and gardenias for their heady scent, foxgloves and Turk’s-cap lilies because there’s just something about them isn’t there?

Honestly, I don’t think I have one! I really thought about this, I was sure that I did, but as it turns out, not so much. Maybe this is why I’m still trying to figure out the great puzzle of our flowerbeds…

Everything about gardening is the hardest lesson: the patience it asks for, the ability to keep trying despite failure year-over-year, the fact that the thing that does you in one year will be different from what does you in the next. Sometimes it’s too much rain, sometimes it’s too little, sometimes it’s the slugs, sometimes it’s the beetles, too much sun, too little—the list goes on and on.

This is something I’ve only noticed in certain places, but there seems to be this strange trend of fake flowers in planters that I just cannot wrap my mind around.

Putting shallow dishes of beer out to help mitigate slugs.

I still have yet to learn one…I asked my husband who, as I mentioned, captains the ship of our garden and he said “What’s a gardening hack? It’s all work. Always.”

This question is making me realize we have no hardscaping in our lives, but I do have a soft spot for pea stone (in theory).

Whatever I’m wearing that day, which is usually jeans and a t-shirt/sweatshirt.

Locally: Barkaboom Native Plants—Chris is an incredible source of knowledge when it comes to native plants in our region and is a big proponent of using locally adapted ecotypes to help conserve local flora and the animals that rely on native plants, something we can all get behind. A little further south: Catskill Native Nursery in Kerhonkson is incredible; they carry the largest selection of North American native plants in New York with a focus on regional species. Story’s Nursery in Freehold is also a favorite.

Mullein, nicotiana, turk’s cap lilies, more bearded irises and hollyhocks too.

Wave Hill in the Bronx. The Landcraft Garden Foundation in Mattituck, NY.

Because I love beautiful things. Because the thrill of walking out your door and down to the garden to pick ingredients you grew to cook dinner with is unmatched. Because pushing a seed into the ground and watching it become something is the sort of miracle that never ever gets old.

Thanks so much, Lisa! (You can follow her on Instagram @brass_tacks.)

#142. I Tried the Anker Solix Smart Tri-Fuel Generator and I’ll Never Lose Power Again

The Anker Solix 5500 is a smart generator that can run on three types of fuel to keep your home running during an outage. We tested it in Florida during hurricane season.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Living in Florida, backup power is a serious consideration. Hurricanes and severe storms can knock out electricity for hours or days, and I wanted a system that could keep my home running without relying entirely on stored battery power or sunshine.

That led me to the Anker Solix Smart Generator 5500, a tri-fuel generator designed to work both as a standalone portable generator and as part of Anker’s Solix home-energy ecosystem. I’ve spent over a month testing it with gasoline and propane, both on its own and connected directly to my Anker Solix E10 whole-home battery system.

The biggest surprise was how easy Anker made practically everything about using a gas-powered generator. Setup took around 20 minutes, the app controls are excellent, moving the 110-pound unit is surprisingly manageable, and when paired with my E10 system, the generator can essentially take care of itself.

There are some caveats, particularly the noise and the considerable cost of building out the complete Anker home-backup ecosystem. But as someone who wanted a generator that could complement solar and battery storage during an extended outage, this is an exceptionally well-thought-out setup.

A tri-fuel inverter generator that delivers up to 3,600W of AC power and 4,500W of DC power, with smart app controls and seamless integration with Anker’s home-energy systems.

The Anker Solix Smart Generator 5500 is a 224cc, four-stroke portable generator that can run on gasoline, propane or natural gas. It produces up to 4,500 watts of DC output on gasoline or propane and 4,000 watts on natural gas. For conventional AC use, all three fuels provide up to 3,600 rated watts through one NEMA TT-30R and one NEMA 5-20R outlet.

That DC output is particularly important if you own compatible Anker equipment. Rather than converting the generator’s output to AC and then back to DC to charge the batteries, the generator can feed up to 4,500 watts directly into an E10 system. The E10 itself is designed to accept that full 4,500-watt DC generator input.

You don’t need an E10 to use the generator, but after testing the two together, I think that integration is the strongest argument for buying this particular model.

I’ve been testing the Anker Solix Smart Generator 5500 for just over one month at my Florida home. I tested gasoline and propane operation, manual and app-based starting, Eco and higher-output operating modes, portability, noise, controls and its integration with my whole-home Solix battery system.

My longest continuous test lasted about two hours. I also tracked generator output through the Anker system while my home was actively drawing power.

I have not yet tested the generator on natural gas. That requires a professionally installed connection to my home’s gas supply, which I plan to add in the future.

My house already has rooftop solar and an Anker Solix E10 whole-home battery system. The system includes two E10 power modules and three battery expansion modules, along with the equipment necessary to manage backup power for the home.

Electricians Arcenio Garcia of Firstline Electric & Energy and Oswin Fernandez of Future Electric Solutions performed the installation. The battery equipment itself cost me around $14,000, with the pro installation adding approximately $4,500.

That makes my complete setup much more expensive than the generator alone, and it’s an important distinction for anyone considering the same configuration.

During an outage, the batteries are responsible for powering my house. My rooftop solar can replenish those batteries during sunny daytime hours, while the generator serves as another charging source when solar isn’t sufficient, including at night.

This distinction matters because when I say the generator supported my entire house during testing, the generator wasn’t directly supplying every appliance. It was providing up to roughly 4.5 kW of DC charging power to the E10 system while the batteries handled the home’s actual electrical loads.

Getting the generator ready for its first run was super simple. It arrived in pristine condition inside a thick, sturdy box with dense packing foam protecting the unit.

There’s almost no assembly. I removed a side panel to connect the generator’s startup battery, added engine oil and was ready to go. The entire process took me about 20 minutes (not including the trip to Home Depot for the oil).

Starting it is just as straightforward. After selecting the desired fuel with the physical selector, I could hold the start button for three seconds and let the electric starter do the rest. I also started it remotely through the Anker app. Both methods worked flawlessly throughout testing. There’s also a traditional manual pull start on the side of the generator, which is a great backup in case there’s any issue with the app or the electric start.

For fuel, I alternated between gasoline and propane, and switching between them required little more than selecting the appropriate fuel setting and connecting the fuel source. I had no starting problems, overloads, connection failures or app glitches during my month of use.

Under DC charging, I saw output reach around 4.5 kW, which is right in line with Anker’s advertised maximum. That’s often more electricity than my home happens to be consuming at a given moment, allowing the system to run household loads from the batteries while putting excess generator power toward replenishing them.

The closest alternative I’ve found is the EcoFlow Smart Generator 4000. Like the Anker, it’s designed not just to operate as a conventional generator but to communicate with and directly charge compatible battery systems.

EcoFlow’s model is less expensive at a current starting price of $1,259, compared with $1,999 for the Anker. It is also lighter at 83 pounds versus Anker’s 110 pounds.

But there are meaningful differences. The EcoFlow is dual-fuel, supporting gasoline and propane, whereas the Anker adds natural gas. EcoFlow provides up to 3,200W of DC charging output, while Anker reaches 4,500W on gasoline or propane.

If I were shopping primarily for an inexpensive standalone generator, I wouldn’t automatically spend $1,999 on the Anker. There are plenty of generators that produce considerably more AC wattage for less money.

This changes if you’re shopping for a hybrid battery-and-generator backup system. That’s where the Anker makes considerably more sense to me. The fast DC charging, automatic E10 integration, app controls and third fuel option are exactly the features I’m paying for.

The generator is the focus of this review, but my experience with it is inseparable from the Solix E10 because that’s how I expect to use the generator during a real outage.

And the combination is much more interesting than either component on its own.

My setup includes two E10 power modules and three expansion batteries, along with Anker’s whole-home power-management equipment. Arcenio Garcia of Firstline Electric & Energy and Oswin Fernandez of Future Electric Solutions installed the system.

The E10 is a modular platform. Anker says systems can scale from 6kWh up to 90kWh of battery capacity, while output can also be expanded by adding E10 units.

My own configuration cost around $14,000 for the equipment, plus another $4,500 for professional electrical installation. Add the $1,999 generator and you’re talking about approximately $20,500 for my particular setup. That’s clearly not cheap.

Still, one of the electricians working on my installation told me that he considers Anker one of the strongest brands he’s currently seeing in the home-energy space. I didn’t treat that as a substitute for testing, but it was reassuring to hear from someone who installs electrical equipment professionally. After living with the finished system, I understand where that enthusiasm comes from. The hardware feels extremely polished, and the individual components work together really well.

This is where the Smart Generator 5500 went from being a nice generator to one of my favorite parts of the system. The generator plugs into the E10 using a dedicated DC charging cable. Once connected, the E10 can monitor its battery level and automatically call on the generator when additional power is needed.

I can configure when I want the generator to start and when I want it to stop charging. That means I don’t necessarily need to keep a fuel-burning generator running continuously through an outage.

My batteries can quietly power the house. Solar panels replenish them when conditions allow. Then, if battery capacity falls too far, the generator can start automatically, feed as much as 4.5kW back into the batteries and shut itself down once the desired charge level is reached.

During testing, watching this work was a thing of beauty.

It’s also why I want to eventually connect the generator to my home’s natural-gas supply. In that configuration, the system could theoretically have access to three layers of backup: stored battery energy, rooftop solar and a generator connected to the home’s gas supply.

If you’re considering spending roughly $2,000 specifically on this generator, I think the E10 compatibility is one of the biggest reasons to choose it over another portable model. But I wouldn’t suggest that everyone buying the generator should immediately go spend tens of thousands of dollars on batteries.

The E10 makes sense for someone who wants a much broader home-energy system, particularly if you already have or plan to install solar. It gives you silent battery backup, automatic switching and the ability to use generator power much more strategically.

The downside is obvious: cost. The generator itself feels reasonably priced to me for its feature set. The complete Solix ecosystem is a major home investment.

I also spoke with Matt Kovalik, a licensed electrician and founder of NailThePrice, who maintains 24 commercial Generac and Cummins generators as part of his day job.

Kovalik hasn’t personally worked with the Anker Smart Generator 5500, so I didn’t ask him to evaluate this particular model. Instead, I asked him about the broader considerations involved in using portable and tri-fuel generators for home backup.

The natural-gas option immediately stood out to him. “The most intriguing part to me is the natural gas hookup,” Kovalik says. Being able to connect a generator to an existing home gas supply means you aren’t solely dependent on stored gasoline or propane during a long outage. You need a pro to install it, though. “Just like an interlock kit on a panel, tapping into your home’s gas line is not a DIY job,” Kovalik says. PAUL RANKIN FOR FAMILY HANDYMAN

That’s something I’ll have to factor into my own setup when I add natural gas. A qualified professional will need to determine whether my existing gas supply is adequate and install the appropriate connection.

Kovalik also stressed that homeowners shouldn’t treat connecting a portable generator to household wiring as a DIY shortcut. “Back feeding power onto the grid can kill a lineman working your street and it’s a code violation,” he says.

If you’re planning to power household circuits from a portable generator rather than simply plugging equipment into its onboard outlets, Kovalik recommends having the proper interlock or transfer equipment professionally installed.

He also emphasizes sizing. A bigger generator isn’t automatically better. Homeowners who haven’t calculated their actual loads can end up paying for capacity they don’t need or buying a generator that can’t handle the loads they expect it to run.

That’s another reason I like my battery-based configuration. In my setup, the generator doesn’t have to independently handle every load or the startup surge of my central air conditioner. The E10 handles those household demands while the generator concentrates on charging up the battery.

After a month of testing, the Anker Solix Smart Generator 5500 has turned out to be one of those products where the mundane details have impressed me as much as the headline features.

Yes, tri-fuel operation is useful. And yes, reaching the advertised 4.5kW DC output during my testing matters. But what I appreciate most is how little effort the generator requires from me.

Setup took about 20 minutes. Gasoline and propane both worked without drama. The electric start has been flawless. The app is excellent. The controls make sense. Moving a 110-pound generator is surprisingly easy. The cables and connectors feel unusually well designed. And when I connect it to the E10, I can automate much of the process that would normally require someone to go outside and babysit a generator.

My biggest complaint is noise. For a relatively compact machine, it makes itself heard when it’s working hard. Fortunately, Eco mode helps, and I couldn’t hear it running on my driveway from inside the house.

I also think buyers should consider the $1,999 price in context. If you simply want maximum AC wattage per dollar, this wouldn’t be my first recommendation.

If you want a generator that can run gasoline, propane or natural gas while also serving as an intelligent range extender for an Anker battery system, that’s an entirely different story. That combination is what makes the Smart Generator 5500 special.

A tri-fuel inverter generator that delivers up to 3,600W of AC power and 4,500W of DC power, with smart app controls and seamless integration with Anker’s home-energy systems.

At the time of writing, the Anker Solix Smart Generator 5500 is available directly from Anker or Amazon. Anker also sells the generator bundled with various E10 configurations for buyers building a larger home-backup system.

Probably not the entire home. A 5,500-watt generator can keep many of your home’s essentials running during an outage, but it usually won’t be able to power everything at once. The Anker Solix Smart Generator 5500 provides 3,600 watts of continuous AC power, which is enough for necessities such as a refrigerator, lights, electronics and select small appliances, provided their combined demand stays within that limit.

Based on my testing, the Anker Solix Smart Generator 5500 is a very capable generator, particularly if you already own or plan to purchase an Anker Solix backup battery system. I liked its gasoline, propane and natural gas compatibility, along with electric and app-based starting, remote monitoring and automatic operation when paired with the E10.

A generator in this class can typically handle several household essentials at once, including refrigerators, freezers, lights, TVs, computers, fans, battery chargers and some microwaves or small air conditioners. You’ll need to add up the running watts of everything you plan to use and account for the higher starting wattage of appliances with motors or compressors.

The Anker Solix Smart Generator 5500 has one standard NEMA 5-20R outlet and one 30-amp TT-30R outlet. Its AC output is rated at 3,600 continuous watts, so don’t assume the “5500” in the name means you can continuously plug in 5,500 watts worth of appliances.

Generator runtime depends heavily on the load, fuel type and operating mode, so there isn’t one runtime that applies to every 5,500-watt generator. Anker says the Smart Generator 5500 can produce up to 17 kilowatt-hours of energy from its 10-liter (2.64-gallon) gasoline tank.

Don’t connect appliances that push the generator beyond its continuous or starting-watt limits. With the Anker Solix Smart Generator 5500 specifically, you should also remember that its AC outlets supply 120-volt power, so it isn’t intended to directly run 240-volt appliances like many central air conditioners, electric dryers and electric water heaters.

You should also never plug a portable generator directly into a household wall outlet to power the home (which is called backfeeding and is very dangerous). Whole-home connections should use the appropriate transfer equipment and be professionally installed. Follow the manufacturer’s requirements for sensitive or critical equipment and always operate a fuel-burning generator outdoors, well away from doors, windows and other openings.

I’ve spent several years testing and reviewing home improvement, power equipment and smart-home products for publications including Family Handyman and BobVila. For this review, I spent more than a month testing the Anker Solix Smart Generator 5500 at my Florida home, where backup power is an important consideration during hurricane season. I tested it with both gasoline and propane, ran it as a standalone generator and connected it directly to my existing Anker Solix E10 whole-home battery system. I evaluated setup, portability, controls, app connectivity, noise, power output and how well the generator integrates with solar and battery backup.

I also drew on the expertise of licensed electricians throughout the project. Arcenio Garcia of Firstline Electric & Energy and Oswin Fernandez of Future Electric Solutions professionally installed my Solix home-backup system and provided firsthand perspective on the equipment and installation. For additional generator-safety and home-backup guidance, I spoke with Matt Kovalik, a licensed electrician and founder of NailThePrice who maintains 24 commercial Generac and Cummins generators as part of his day job. His input helped inform our guidance on natural-gas connections, proper transfer equipment, generator sizing and the dangers of backfeeding a home.

#143. Divide These 8 Perennials in October – It's the Easiest Way to Make More of Your Favorite Plants for Free

Every method of plant propagation has its bit of magic. It’s amazing to see a little green shoot emerging from a tiny seed or to watch roots appearing on the lower end of cuttings. But division has a huge advantage that seeds and cuttings lack: you start with one perennial, then, presto chango, you have two, or three, or four.

Dividing plants is a simple, highly effective method used to propagate perennials. It doesn’t require any technical or botanical knowledge. All you need to do is lift a mature perennial from the ground, then divide its root system into two or more distinct sections to be replanted.

But timing is important when it comes to division. Never try this in the heat of the summer, nor in the heart of the winter. Along with early spring, October is one of the very best times to propagate your perennials by division, as the soil is still workable. You want to dig the plant up, divide it into several rooted sections, and get the roots of the sections established before the first frost.

It’s a good idea to get an overview of the division process before trying it on a perennial. The first rule to remember is that you can’t divide annual plants – only perennial plants have the established root structure that allows for this type of propagation.

Use a sharp spade or garden fork to dig a circle around the perennial before prying out the rootball. Then you might use two garden forks to divide the roots, although I personally find it easier to do by hand. Finally, do the actual division with something sharp, like a garden knife, a pruning saw, or a spade. Alternatively, a Root Slayer Perennial Garden Shovel, available on Amazon, is a multipurpose tool that lets you cut neatly around the plant, ease it out, and slice it into divisions.

Can you pause once the plant is out and divided? Nope, no rest for you at this stage. Immediately replant each division, and do so at exactly the same depth at which it was previously growing. Use your fingers to press down the soil and eliminate air pockets, then water thoroughly. If you're potting up divisions before planting them elsewhere, use a high-quality potting mix, such as Miracle-Gro Potting Mix from Walmart, to help the roots establish quickly before winter.

The newly created divisions will need adequate water until they establish. Water the soil around the plant several days before dividing, then deep water the sections immediately after they are in the ground. Keep the soil consistently moist for several weeks to allow the roots to re-establish.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Now, let's dive into the best plants to divide in October.

Hostas are shade garden favorites, but they can grow larger than you might expect. One great way to control plant size is division. Not only can you cut back the size of the clumps, but you get new ones as well.

If you decide to divide hostas in the fall, do it in October. Using a sharp spade or shovel, dig out the entire plant and place it carefully on the ground. Separate tuber clumps.

Sedums, also known as stonecrops, are clump-forming succulents that are easy to divide. You can divide sedum plants in autumn, right after they finish blooming. Use a garden spade or fork to dig out the plant with its entire root mass, then clip back the tallest stems to several inches. This makes them easier to handle. Chop the clump into smaller sections, each one with healthy green stems on top and a root cluster on the bottom. Plant each division in a sunny location at the same depth it was growing previously. Firm the soil and water thoroughly.

If your peonies are overgrown, divide them in the fall. They are somewhat picky about division, so be sure to walk through all the steps.

First, cut back your peony stems, then dig out the plant, including the thick roots. Set the plant on the ground, then hose down the root ball. This is important because you need to see the peony's “eyes”, which look like pink buds at the crown, and make sure each division has at least three eyes and strong roots. Replant the divisions immediately, placing the eyes no more than 2 inches (5 cm) below the surface of the soil.

Bearded irises are among the easiest perennials to divide. All you need to do is dig up the clump, prune down the foliage to about 6 inches (15 cm) long, then chop up the clump into smaller divisions. Afterward, let the plant dry for a full day, then replant the divisions. The top of the rhizomes should end up just at the level of the soil surface.

Divide established astilbe plants every few years. Just dig them up, trim back the foliage, and divide them with a sharp shovel or spade. If the plant is too big to dig up, just cut out sections from the standing plant. Replant astilbe segments in a new site, watering generously.

Divide bee balm in fall after flowering ceases but before the first frost. Use a spade to dig around the clump, leaving plenty of room to make sure you don’t dig through the root system. Dig up the clump, lift it up, and shake out extra soil. Toss the center of the clump – it will be woody, hollow, or dead, and it won’t flower well again. Divide the plant with hand pruners, making sure each section has three shoots or growing buds. Replant bee balm plants at the exact same depth as they were planted before, tamping down the soil. Water well.

Divide bleeding heart plants in October, after the plant’s foliage has naturally died back. Dig out the root clump, then use a sharp knife to divide it into sections, each one with at least one growth bud. Replant immediately and water well.

Divide phlox at least four weeks before the first hard frost. October is generally a perfect time to do the deed. First, cut back the foliage. Then, use a sharp spade to dig up the entire phlox plant and chop the root clump into sections. Each section should have at least three shoots and some sturdy roots. Replant immediately and water generously.

The watering you give your divisions after replanting is very important. Be sure to water each one well, then water regularly to keep the soil moist.

Mulch the area around each division to help protect the new plants from winter chills. Apply a 2–3 inch (5–8 cm) layer of organic mulch, such as straw or pine bark, like these Timberline pine bark nuggets from Walmart, to insulate the soil and protect the roots from temperature fluctuations. Keep the mulch clear of the plant's crown to prevent rot.

#144. Is Perishable Food Safe to Eat After a Power Outage? Here’s How to Know.

Published Oct 15, 2026 1:43 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

“Power outages are more than an inconvenience. They can create food safety hazards that families cannot see, smell, or taste, and they can also put hundreds of dollars’ worth of food at risk at a time when families are already dealing with high grocery prices,” says Dr. Darin Detwiler, food safety advocate, author, and educator at Detwiler Consulting Group. “Preparation matters both for protecting health and for protecting the value of the food we bring into our homes.”

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), foodborne disease sicken an estimated 1 in 6 Americans (or 48 million people) every year; 128,000 are hospitalized, and 3,000 die. Knowing how long food in the fridge remains safe to eat during a power outage depends on the type of food and duration of the outage. The vital information in this guide can both help keep your household healthy and minimize the cost of replacing thrown away frozen and refrigerated foods. Here is what you need to know about food safety during a power outage.

The temperatures inside your refrigerator and freezer is key when determining whether your food is safe to eat after a power outage. According to the CDC, refrigerators should be kept at or below 40 degrees Fahrenheit and freezers should be kept at or below 0 degrees Fahrenheit. However, because many refrigerators and freezers do not have a thermostat, and those that do may not provide accurate temperature readings, it can be difficult to know exactly how cold it is inside the appliance’s compartments.

A couple of inexpensive appliance thermometers will let you easily monitor the temperature of your refrigerator and freezer to determine if the food stored inside is still safe to eat. Choose a wireless refrigerator thermometer with a tabletop display or an analog model with an easy-to-read temperature dial, like this Rubbermaid refrigerator thermometer. Fridge and freezer thermometers can also cue you into issues with your appliances even when the power is running, such as if your fridge isn’t cooling and needs to be repaired or replaced.

If you want to go old-school with a monitoring method that’s also a good idea pre-vacation, use the frozen penny trick: Fill a cup with water, freeze it, and then place a penny on top of the ice. If the penny is frozen in the middle of the cup, that means there was a power outage and your food may not be safe to eat.

Keep in mind that the longer the power is out, the more refrigerated and frozen foods will become unsafe to consume. “During an emergency, we are protecting more than groceries. We are protecting the health of the people we love, particularly those most vulnerable to serious illness, while also protecting the economic value of food that families worked hard to purchase,” says Detwiler.

Here are general guidelines for food safety during a power outage based on elapsed time.

What’s the most important food safety rule when the power goes out? “Do not open your refrigerator or freezer,” says Jill Roberts PhD, MS, MPH, CPH, Professor at the College of Public Health, University of South Florida. “Both can maintain safe temperatures for about 4 hours with no power.”

When the doors are left closed, the food inside a standard refrigerator should stay cold for approximately 4 hours. Since a full fridge and freezer maintains its temperature longer, Detwiler suggests that if you know that a power outage is possible, “containers of frozen water can fill unused space and provide additional cooling capacity.” If the power outage lasts longer than a few hours, move milk, meats, eggs, and other perishable items to a cooler filled with ice to keep them cold.

The Bluetti Elite 200 V2 is the best portable power station we’ve tested to date—it runs a full-size fridge for about 30 hours. Read the review.

If your freezer is at least half full and remains closed, it should be able to maintain its recommended 0-degree Fahrenheit temperature for about 24 hours. If your power has been out for a full day, purchase a block of dry ice from a grocery or big box store and place it in the freezer to help the compartment maintain 0 degrees Fahrenheit. If you have a wireless thermometer, check the tabletop monitor periodically to monitor the temperature, but avoid opening the door to check an analog thermometer often as opening it will raise the temperature. Detwiler says: “Think of the cold air inside as a limited resource: every time the door opens, some of that protection is lost.”

When the door remains shut, a full freezer should maintain the recommended 0-degree Fahrenheit temperature for about 48 hours, or 2 days. However, if you still have no electricity after 2 days, the temperature inside the freezer may rise, causing frozen items to begin defrosting. If the power has been out for a while—or you know that a long outage is likely—purchase some dry ice before you reach 48 hours. About 50 pounds of dry ice will help a fully stocked,18-cubic foot freezer cold for about two days.

“Preparation should happen before the lights go out,” says Detwiler. “Preparation before an outage gives households the information and tools to make safer, more confident decisions when the power goes out.” Here’s what you can do today so you are ready for the next power outage.

Keep refrigerated and frozen food cold and safe with food safety recommendations from FoodSafety.gov so you are ready when the electricity cuts out.

“Families should also think ahead about what they would eat if refrigeration and normal cooking were unavailable,” says Detwiler. “Shelf-stable foods and a supply of safe drinking water can reduce the temptation to repeatedly open the refrigerator or freezer.” Roberts agrees: “I would highly recommend keeping a stash of non-perishable foods. Store them in a cool, dry area.”

Here are more emergency food prep tips from FoodSafety.gov:

Not sure what to buy? Here are suggested emergency food supplies from Ready.gov.

During a power outage, help maintain food safety and decrease the likelihood of food spoilage and foodborne illnesses with the following.

Perishable refrigerated food that has been stored at a temperature greater than 40 degrees Fahrenheit for 4 hours or more must be thrown out. While it may be tempting, Detwiler warns: “Never taste questionable food to determine whether it is safe. Unfortunately, the pathogens that cause foodborne illness do not necessarily change the appearance, smell, or taste of food. Something can look perfectly normal and still be unsafe.”

Food in the freezer that is still covered in ice crystals can be refrozen or cooked. If you have an appliance thermometer in your freezer that reads at or below 40 degrees Fahrenheit once the power is restored, you can also safely refreeze or cook any of the freezer contents.

If you aren’t sure, Detwiler advises: “When there is genuine uncertainty about the safety of a perishable food, the appropriate message remains: When in doubt, throw it out.”

When cleaning out the refrigerator after a power outage, any perishable food items that have been stored at temperatures above 40 degrees for 4 or more hours need to be thrown out.
