If you love growing peppers and fancy squeezing a little more life out of them over winter, this indoor trend makes it possible to appreciate them in a whole new way

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’ve been growing productive pepper plants outdoors this summer, fall usually signals a sad goodbye. Because peppers are tropical perennials that cannot tolerate frost, autumn’s temperature drops generally mean it’s time to let them go. They aren’t hardy in most growing climates, so they tend to succumb soon after the first frost. However, there is a brilliant, creative indoor alternative: turning your favorite summer chili into a bonchi: a miniature bonsai chili tree.

This style of growing chilil peppers is about more than just overwintering. Bonchi (short for bonchili, aka bonsai chili) culture transforms your productive outdoor plants into stunning, living indoor sculptures that sit comfortably on a sunny windowsill. By hard-pruning the top growth and trimming the root mass to fit a shallow bonsai pot, you reduce the size to create a mini tree form.

So, not only does this fun project save your hard-earned plants from freezing weather, but it also gives you a fascinating head start for next year. Come spring, it's possible for your established bonchi to be kept as a productive, fruit-bearing indoor houseplant for years to come. This step by step guide shows you how to create your own pretty miniature chili tree. So grab your pruning snips, clear a spot on the windowsill, and let’s turn this season’s harvest into a lasting masterpiece.

While all peppers (Capsicum spp.) are tender perennials, certain varieties adapt much better to bonsai cultivation. Capsicum chinense species (such as habanero, Scotch bonnet and ghost peppers) and Capsicum frutescens (like tabasco) naturally develop thick, gnarled, woody main stems early in their growth cycles, giving them an instant ancient tree aesthetic. Compact Capsicum annuum varieties like jalapeño and cayenne, plus ornamental varieties like 'Black Pearl' or 'Numex Twilight' are also stellar candidates thanks to their small leaves and abundant, colorful pods.

When selecting a candidate, look for a plant that has demonstrated outstanding vigor and heavy fruit production throughout summer. Choose a specimen with a thick main stem (at least thumb-width) near the soil line and balanced lower branching. Avoid weak, leggy plants or those showing signs of viral infections, such as mottled leaves or stunted stems. Healthy roots are important, too.

Remember, smaller-fruited varieties look much more proportionate on a miniature tree than massive bell peppers, creating a far more harmonious visual balance once your bonchi starts setting fruit indoors. It’s also worth grabbing a soil meter, such as the Raintrip Soil 4-in-1 Meter from Amazon, to give the soil a quick read as you assess the healthiest candidates.

Timing is everything when transitioning outdoor peppers indoors. You must lift your chosen plant before the first hard frost, and ideally before night temperatures consistently dip below 50°F (10°C). Chilly winds slow down the plant’s metabolism, making root recovery much harder once brought inside. Water your pepper plant deeply 24 hours before digging. Damp soil clings to the root ball, reducing transplant shock and making extraction easier. Just make sure it is damp, not soggy.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Cut a wide circle roughly 6-8 inches (15-20cm) away from the main stem, slicing down deep to free the root ball. Lift the plant gently, shaking away excess soil to expose the roots. Before taking your plant inside, conduct a strict pest inspection. Outdoor peppers frequently harbor aphids, whiteflies, or spider mites under leaves. To help with pest inspection, grab a magnifying glass or loupe such as the Carson LumiLoupe 10x Stand Magnifier, available from Walmart. This handy pocket magnifier lets you inspect leaf undersides for tiny aphid eggs or spider mites before bringing plants inside (and they are really good value to have around the house).

Rinse the plant with a gentle spray, or apply a mild insecticidal soap drench to prevent unwelcome hitchhikers from invading your indoor setup.

Now comes the bit that might scare you if you are a beginner grower, but it is important: severe pruning. Don’t panic, peppers are resilient, and aggressive pruning is essential to force the plant into its compact bonsai habit. For this, you need the sharpest snips or scissors you can find. One team favorite is a set of Fiskars Micro-Tip Pruning Snips,available from Amazon. Alternatively, dedicated bonsai shears such as Garden Guru Professional Butterfly Bonsai Shears, available from Walmart, give precise cuts without harming the plant.

You need to cut the main trunk back to a height of just 4-8 inches (10-20 cm) above the soil line. Strip off all remaining large leaves and thin out weak or crossing side branches, leaving just 2-3 short, structural branch stubs to serve as your new tree framework. You’ll need to leave a few side stems in place to become branches.

Next, turn your attention to the roots. You’ll need to be able to see the taproot and side feeder roots. Trim the root ball down. reducing the volume by around 60-70 percent. Prune away thick taproots and long, straggly roots, preserving a compact, dense pad of fine feeder roots close to the base. This might seem drastic, but it balances the root volume with reduced top growth, preparing the plant for effective bonsai container gardening and allowing the plant to easily fit into a shallow dish.

Selecting the right container can transform your pruned pepper into living art. Traditional bonsai containers are shallow, ceramic dishes featuring generous drainage holes. Choose a pot that can comfortably house your trimmed root mass with an inch of clearance around the sides. Ensure the container has adequate drainage, as standing water will rot pruned roots rapidly. Position the plant so the primary root flares sit slightly above the soil line, exposing the top of the root system to give your mini tree an established, aged appearance.

Soil choice is vital for long-term health. Avoid dense potting mixes, which retain too much water in shallow pots. Instead, use a free-draining bonsai mix, or mix 60% high-quality potting soil with 40% perlite or horticultural sand. If you need perlite, lightweight Legigo Organic Perlite from Amazon is an excellent choice, helping to prevent compaction in shallow bonsai potting mixes. Pack the substrate firmly around the roots, using a chopstick to eliminate hidden air pockets. Water thoroughly until water streams freely from the drainage holes.

After the shock of severe pruning and repotting, your new bonchi needs a bit of time to rest and recuperate. Place in a warm, sheltered spot, away from direct, scorching sunlight and leave for one week to recover. Once new green buds begin pushing out along the trunk, move to your sunniest south-facing windowsill, where it can receive at least 6 hours of bright light daily. If winter light is weak in your region, supplement with a grow light.

Watering requires a careful touch during dormancy. Allow the top inch (2.5cm) of soil to dry out between waterings, as overwatering cold roots is the fastest way to cause root rot. Skip heavy feeds for the first month. Once active leaf growth is established, you can feed bi-weekly with a gentle seaweed drench diluted to half-strength. I recommend TPS Seaweed Fertilizer, available from Amazon, to encourage healthy root recovery. As fresh shoots expand, lightly pinch back overly long stems to encourage dense branching and maintain a mini tree silhouette.

One of the most rewarding moments of bonchi cultivation is watching delicate white or purple flowers blossom during the depths of winter. However, because your living room lacks natural outdoor pollinators, like bumblebees and wind breezes, you’ll need to step in as chief pollinator to help set fruit. Fortunately, pepper flowers are self-fertile, meaning each bloom contains both male and female reproductive parts.

Once flowers open fully, gently tap the trunk or flick the flower stems with your finger to release pollen. For higher success rates, use a small, soft watercolor paintbrush to gently swirl inside each flower, transferring pollen from the outer anthers to the sticky stigma. You can pick up Royal & Langnickel Taklon Art Brushes from Walmart for just a few dollars. These fine-tipped brushes are ideal for delicate pollination. Within a week, the petals will drop away, revealing tiny green pepper pods. You can then enjoy seeing fresh peppers ripening indoors while snow falls outside your window.

Need more ideas for getting the most from your plants, indoors and out, and looking for the best seasonal expert advice delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for the free Gardening Know How Newsletter!

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

Overhauling their previous place, an apartment in Brussels, gave Arthur and Kelly the courage to take on a needy house. #149. The Best Home Safes of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

By Michelle Larson, Additional research provided by Michelle Ullman, Jasmine Harding

Published Oct 15, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Home safes provide peace of mind when you’ve got cash, important documents, jewelry, and other valuables in the house. We recently tested the durability, security, and water resistance of 10 top options to see which protected best. We evaluated basic models that shield against theft as well as higher-end options that offer fire protection and water resistance to keep precious belongings safe during disasters.

Since home safes are meant for some of your most prized possessions, it’s important to look at lock type and protective capabilities when choosing one. Our favorite home safe, the SentrySafe Digital Fire/Water Safe, was best in both these regards. It has great basic features like a digital keypad, backup key, lighted interior, and bolt-down hardware. But what earned it our award for best overall was its ability to withstand fire, heat, and smoke for up to 1 hour and keep contents dry for up to 24 hours in 8 inches of water.

To see which home safe is right for you, consider the items you intend to store and the security the safe offers, as well as a host of other features and potential upgrades. Read on to learn the pros and cons of the best home safes and see how each performed in our hands-on tests.

Bottom line: Choose a home safe based on your specific needs, balancing security features with budget and intended use.

Home safes keep their contents safe from perils like theft, fire, and water damage. They provide owners with peace of mind by protecting valuable items, irreplaceable heirlooms, and important documents from such threats. Keep your prized possessions secure in a home safe suited to your needs and preferences.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Water Resistance 4.5/5; Durability 5/5; Security 5/5; Value 4.8/5

Deter theft and enjoy protection from both fire and water with this highly rated and reasonably priced waterproof and fireproof safe. Sturdy steel, four live-locking bolts, a pry-resistant hinge bar, and bolt-down hardware keep valuables and important documents safe and secure.

SentrySafe claims this safe is water-resistant in 8 inches of water for up to 24 hours. We placed a sprinkler on top of ours and let it run for over an hour. When we opened the safe, the toilet paper inside was bone-dry.

Its 1.23 cubic-foot capacity is large enough for stacks of sensitive materials like USB drives, file folders, and jewelry boxes. In addition to protecting from water, it can withstand fire, heat, and smoke for up to 1 hour at 1,700 degrees Fahrenheit. It also has a digital keypad with a backup key, an interior light, and a locking drawer.

Read our review: SentrySafe SFW123GDC Digital Fire/Water Safe

Get the SentrySafe SFW123GDC home safe at Amazon, Lowe’s, The Home Depot, or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5;Water Resistance N/A; Durability 3/5; Security 5/5; Value 4/5

Thanks to the included instruction booklet, setting up the Amazon Basics electronic safe was simple, though it did not come with the required four AA batteries for the digital keypad. The interior is just large enough to fit an A4 document without bending or folding it, so you can store important certificates and other files without worry. The safe’s bottom shelf has a felt liner, but there is nothing to soften the removable shelf, so users will want to package delicate items before storing them there.

At over 33 pounds, the Amazon Basics safe is heavy for its dimensions, making it feel quite sturdy, which is a plus for such an affordable model. To test durability, we dropped it onto a concrete surface, and it came out unscathed. Its heavy carbon-steel construction actually chipped the concrete!

One small complaint we had with this safe is the removable panel to access the keyhole, which felt a little flimsy—like it could easily come off and get lost. That aside, the Amazon Basics safe is a well-built, moderately sized model that comes with mounting hardware to bolt it into place. Shoppers should note, however, that this safe is not water-resistant, so a flood would certainly creep into your valuables here.

Get the Amazon Basics steel home safe at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5;Water Resistance 5/5; Durability 5/5; Security 4/5; Value 4/5

With interior dimensions of 4.4 inches high by 12.8 inches wide by 8.5 inches deep, this safe for documents, valuables, USB drives, and other small items is built to withstand fire and water. Its simple key-lock design features one main compartment with in-lid organizer straps. It also has a carrying handle that makes it easy to grab in an emergency or as a travel safe.

During testing, we found the tubular key lock a little sticky. While momentarily frustrating, the system actually adds a layer of security by preventing the lid from opening in a fire. The thick walls of this Underwriters Laboratories–rated safe box can withstand 30 minutes of fire at 1,550 degrees Fahrenheit, and its Electrical Testing Laboratories (ETL) verification ensures its waterproof gasket will keep water out for up to 72 hours of submersion. For those with limited space or who want to be able to quickly grab valuables and go, this small lockbox is a great option.

Get the SentrySafe CHW20221 home safe at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5;Water Resistance N/A; Durability 4/5; Security 3/5; Value 4/5

Looking to hide small holiday gifts from snooping kids? Want a spot for jewelry and other valuables while repair people are in your house? This Stalwart safe with electronic lock might work well for you. At about a foot wide and 8 inches high by 8 inches deep, it’s roughly the size of a bread box—room enough for passports, jewelry boxes, or folded papers. Its steel construction feels fairly durable, and it comes with bolts (and drilled holes in the sides of the safe) for affixing it to the wall or floor. At just over 9 pounds, it’s heavy enough that you won’t want to schlep it while traveling but not so heavy that a burglar couldn’t simply steal it rather than attempt to crack it.

During testing, we were happy to see we couldn’t access the safe’s interior reset button by poking a stick through the bolt holes in the back and bottom of the unit. If you or a would-be thief enter an incorrect code three times, its automatic keypad-disabling function activates a warning beep that only stops by removing one of the batteries. Just be aware that powering it down erases the user code, making the safe key your only option until it’s reset.

Bottom line? This is a decent unit for the back of your closet or the top of your dresser—but for heaven’s sake, don’t lose the keys.

Get the Stalwart home safe at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Wayfair.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5;Water Resistance N/A; Durability 5/5; Security 5/5; Value 4.5/5

With a virtually flat profile, a wall safe is a great way to hide valuables behind artwork or furniture. Though it requires some tools and a little effort to install, this option from Paragon Lock & Safe comes with the necessary mounting hardware and is sized right to fit between studs. Just be sure you insert the included batteries and set up your user and manager codes first. This process is much easier when the safe is still on the ground.

Also, be aware that, like many safes, the Paragon safe is shallow, measuring just 4 inches deep. It has three interior shelves, but the housing of the locking mechanism takes up most of the middle shelf. Still, the other two shelves provide ample space for cash, jewelry, folded documents, and small heirlooms. While this wall safe is not fire- or water-resistant, it does include an extra theft-busting feature: an automatic 5-minute alarm that sounds after three incorrect code entries, alerting everyone nearby of the failed entry.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5;Water Resistance N/A; Durability 5/5; Security 4/5; Value 4.8/5

Measuring 4.4 inches high by 11.8 inches wide by 8.6 inches deep, this mini safe is slim enough to fit inside a standard desk drawer. It features heavy-duty alloy steel construction and unlocks via a convenient electronic keypad or backup keys. One word of caution on this particular option, however: Be careful as you move it around. During testing, we found that even drops of around a foot sometimes dislodged the batteries enough to disrupt the keypad’s functionality. Also, like many electronic keypads, the batteries’ housing takes up a portion of the internal space. For this small safe, that means about half the interior area is unusable.

If you’re looking to store passports, folded papers, or small jewelry boxes, however, rest assured they’ll be protected by two secure door bolts and pry-resistant, concealed hinges. At just over 10 pounds, you could use this mini safe as a portable option for travel or employ the included mounting hardware to install it in a drawer, closet, or other hidden space.

Get the Amazon Basics desk drawer home safe at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5;Water Resistance 4/5; Durability 4/5; Security 5/5; Value 5/5

During testing, positioning the big 217-pound SentrySafe EF4738E safe was the most difficult part. Once in place, the installation hardware, keypad, locking mechanism, and setup instructions worked as smoothly as we wanted. Also, the digital keypad allowed us to create and erase as many custom access codes as we needed.

From a security standpoint, this safe excelled. Its five live-locking bolts and four deadbolts created a super-strong barrier to unauthorized access, leaving us unable to crack the safe with any of the well-known internet hacks we tried. As a large home safe, its roomy 4.71 cubic feet of interior space and three carpeted shelves make it a great option for home storage of larger valuables.

Though described as a fire- and waterproof safe, it offers only modest protection from these elements. It passed our overhead sprinkler and 12-inch flooding tests with no detectable moisture infiltration, but the door seal is not designed to protect against submersion. Likewise, it offers just a half hour of fire protection at 1,400 degrees Fahrenheit. If a fire reaches hotter temperatures or burns longer than a half hour, any papers or cash inside the safe could combust.

Get the SentrySafe EF4738E home safe at Amazon, Lowe’s, or The Home Depot.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5;Water Resistance 1/5; Durability 4/5; Security 4/5; Value 4/5

Master Lock’s clamshell-style personal safe is designed to neatly fit and guard a smaller set of valuables, such as a slim wallet, cash, or jewelry. We tested it on an overseas trip for passports and keys, but it will also fit travel items like a GoPro or digital camera. Since it weighs just over a pound, this portable safe was hardly noticeable in our carry-on bag.

While Master Lock markets this safe as water-resistant, it filled with water when we left it in a shower to simulate a storm, so we don’t recommend leaving it outdoors on a camping trip. Otherwise, the hard plastic was durable enough to survive our smash tests but could probably be cut open with the right tools. And though it’s small, it’s not easy to walk off with when you wrap the braided cable around a stationary object.

Several years back, a lock picker posted a YouTube video of how he opened this version in minutes without tools by simply spotting the gates in the combination locking mechanism. We tried replicating his trick without luck, so it looks like Master Lock has improved the design. Even so, we locked it down in a hidden spot or kept it somewhere we had an eye on it during a day trip.

Get the Master Lock home safe at Amazon, Ace Hardware, The Home Depot, or Master Lock.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Water Resistance N/A; Durability 4/5; Security 2/5; Value 3.5/5

The Jssmst book safe is a small concealment safe that comes with a combination lock inside a dictionary facade. The safe is meant to tuck small valuables out of sight at home or in the office. In our tests, we found this safe extremely convenient to use and store as well as excellent for concealment, but lacking in actual security.

Setting up the safe was straightforward: Set the code, put valuables inside, lock the safe, and place it on a shelf. In its “stealth” mode, the safe looks like a real book, particularly when sitting on a shelf with other hardcover books.

However, for actual security, a lot remains to be desired. We found the safe to be obvious when actually picking up and handling it, meaning it won’t fool any would-be thieves if they get their hands on it. More importantly, we broke through the lock by trying every possible combination in just under 20 minutes. The safe is likely also not strong enough to survive a more forceful entry using tools.

When choosing which home safes to test, we considered basic features like build, wall thickness, and locking mechanisms. We looked at safes of various sizes, weights, and intended purposes, such as travel or concealment. We included options rated for fire resistance and water resistance since they provide an added layer of protection in the event of a natural disaster. We also looked for models with extra features like protective carpet, lighting, and adjustable shelves.

Once we had our safes, a team of Bob Vila writers and editors across the country each performed a series of tests. We used common safe-cracking methods to check basic security and repeatedly dropped the safes against hard surfaces to measure durability. For safes claiming water resistance, we put them in a shower for at least 15 minutes with a roll of toilet paper inside. If waterproof, we submerged the safes storing TP in a bathtub full of water for a minimum of an hour. If the toilet paper showed even the slightest hint of moisture in either test, the safe lost points on our rubric.

Home safes keep your valuables safe from individual dangers like theft, fire, or water, but not every model safeguards against all of these threats. If you are most concerned about one particular type of threat, consider that as you choose the best safes for home use. Also, look at what you plan to store in your home safe. Different designs work better for specific items, such as a gun safe for storing firearms.

Secure safes hold some of the most valuable items in your home, so it’s important to find a reliable option. When choosing the best home safe for your home, consider its protective capabilities, size, weight, lock type, and any additional convenience or security features that are important to you.

Before you choose a secure storage space for your valuables, consider the type of safe that will work best for you and learn about the features offered with each type.

Heavy insulation in fire safes protects their contents from heat, smoke, and sometimes water. Often small and portable, many fire-resistant safes open with a simple key or combination. Fire safes are rated by the global safety consulting and certification company UL and other agencies based on the length of time the interior of the safe can remain below a certain temperature when the exterior has reached fire-level temperatures.

UL-classified fire-resistant safes are built to withstand peak temperatures ranging from 1,150 degrees Fahrenheit to 1,850 degrees Fahrenheit for up to 2 hours. They should be stored on concrete, such as a garage or basement floor, and away from flammable materials.

The most secure residential safes are tough enough to keep both thieves and fire out. A burglary safe, constructed with thick, insulated walls; a heavy door; and other safety features, may provide both theft protection and fire resistance. Some also include water-resistant features. Burglary safes are available in two main forms:

A gun safe is a must-have for safe gun storage at home. A sturdy lock keeps contents from curious little fingers. Consider the safe’s intended use when making your pick, since some gun-specific safes place less focus on theft, fire, or water protection.

For keeping guns safely out of reach of children, a simple locked gun safe is a suitable choice. If burglary is your main concern, look for a gun safe with an anti-pry design intended to prevent theft.

Gun safes come in a range of sizes, from bedside handgun boxes to large rifle safes. Keep in mind that it’s always best to keep the safe out of reach of young children. Also, consider the lock type. A safe with a combination or biometric lock means no keys to hide (or lose), which also means no keys for curious kids to stumble across.

Jewelry is easy fodder for burglars. Keeping jewelry tucked away in a home safe adds an extra layer of security.

While most jewelry fits in any home safe, certain features help protect precious pieces while they’re in storage. Protective shelving, such as soft carpeted or felted shelves, helps prevent scratches and dings on expensive jewelry. Hanging hooks prevent tangles in chains and other baubles.

While less secure, a locked jewelry wall armoire is one alternative. These units mount to the wall and include plenty of organizers and hanging spaces to keep jewelry beautifully displayed inside. To secure jewelry, locking armoires may deter curious children or opportunistic burglars.

Home safe ratings take into consideration both the safe’s construction and its ability to thwart forced-entry attempts. UL rates some safes, but not all safes on the market come with ratings.

Generally, the heavier and thicker the safe’s walls and doors, the higher the rating. The higher the rating, the higher the price for the safe. Common burglary ratings for safes without alarms are as follows:

Home safes range from small, portable options to large, freestanding units capable of being bolted down. The ideal home safe should offer enough room for the items you plan to store plus a bit of wiggle room for valuables you may acquire in the future. Stack the items you plan to store and measure the stack’s dimensions to determine the appropriate size for your home safe.

Home safes generally measure around 0.5 to 1.3 cubic feet, with smaller and larger options available. An average-size 1.2-cubic-foot safe will probably weigh around 100 pounds. Although they may be tougher to set up and move around, the heavy weight of a permanent safe adds an extra layer of security against theft.

A portable home safe can be a useful accessory for renters or frequent travelers. These smaller safes are usually made to hold a few important items like passports, cash, important documents, and other small objects. A good portable safe will be reasonably lightweight, usually under 30 pounds, for easier transport.

Portable home safes have one downside, which is that they’re easier to steal. But these safes still provide a layer of protection against theft, plus many users have them for fire and water protection. If you don’t plan on moving the safe anytime soon, though, you may want to look for a more secure option. A heavy-duty safe that bolts down will be harder for robbers to take advantage of and, therefore, a better option to protect against theft.

Home security safes may require a key, a combination, an electronic keypad code, or biometric data to access their contents.

Classic key or combination locks don’t require a power source. Just insert the key or enter the combination to unlock the safe. As with padlocks, one downside of a key lock is the risk of losing the key. If you choose a safe with a combination lock, look for an option with a backup key to prevent locking yourself out.

The next step up in complexity is a home safe with an electronic keypad, for which users enter their access code into the keypad rather than turning a combination dial. Lastly, biometric locks have an advanced fingerprint sensor that reads your fingerprint and unlocks if it matches a print in the fingerprint library. Electronic keypads and biometric scanners need a power source, such as batteries or an AC outlet.

Water-resistant safes protect valuables from flooding, leaks, and other costly water damage. Consider whether waterproofing is necessary for your needs depending on your location and where the safe is stored. Water exposure may be more of a concern in flood-prone areas or for a safe stored in a basement.

Some safes protect against minor water exposure, like splashes or shallow water, while others can be completely submerged for a specified length of time. For submersion protection, consider a safe with an ETL Waterproof Verification. The ETL gives its seal of approval to safes that can withstand a certain level of water exposure for a specified time frame.

Home safes may include a range of extra features for added security, convenience, and accessibility, including bolting hardware, adjustable shelves, protective carpet, and lighting.

A home safe is one part of a robust home security plan to keep you and your valuables safe. These relatively inexpensive units can give you peace of mind against theft, fire, and water damage. Read on for frequently asked questions about choosing and using your new home safe.

The top home safes are made of heavy steel, a half-inch-thick door, and quarter-inch-thick walls.

The SentrySafe SFW123GDC waterproof and fireproof home safe is one of the most secure options, providing excellent protection against theft, fire, and water.

Choose a spot that is as hidden as possible to prevent theft but that is also accessible enough so you can grab items when you need them. Try to avoid placing the safe in an area that is at high risk for humid conditions or flooding.

Most safes include a digital keypad or biometric technology for opening and a backup key. If you can’t get into your safe, start by contacting the safe manufacturer—the company should have a process in place so you can regain access to your safe.

Yes, a home safe can be breached with enough time and effort. To deter burglars as much as possible, look for a quality safe that is difficult to remove from the home or that will take a long time to break into.

If a home safe is stolen, it is treated like other stolen property and may be difficult to recover. File a police report and contact your home insurance broker to assess next steps.

Jerry Hall may be making headlines for The Celebrity Traitors, but when it comes to her garden, she's certainly no traitor to her favorite color...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of the best things about The Celebrity Traitors right now? Jerry Hall, who is proving to be almost as delightfully kooky as her neighbor, Richard E. Grant.

Between the unexpected personalities and the wonderfully eccentric energy, many of us have found ourselves wanting to know more about the supermodel beyond the castle walls. Naturally, that led us down a little Instagram rabbit hole, and straight into her rather spectacular garden.

Now, I have to admit, I’m a little jealous of Jerry’s garden. Not only does the supermodel and actress have an enviable collection of plants, but she appears to have landed on one of the most effective garden color planting palettes without making it look overly designed: purple, purple, and a little more purple.

That's right; Jerry Hall’s garden, which features wisteria and lilacs among its purple blooms, is a lovely example of what happens when you commit to one color family rather than trying to squeeze every shade of the rainbow into a border.

And while purple might seem like a purely aesthetic choice, there’s actually some very good garden-design thinking behind it. Before we get into that, though, check it out for yourself:

A post shared by Jerry Hall (@jerryfayehall)

If you’re looking at Jerry Hall’s garden and wondering why all that purple flowers work so well, take a closer look at what’s surrounding them: green.

Now, green and purple are a favorite combination among professional gardeners, and it’s easy to see why; the contrast is strong enough to give a planting scheme some definition, but it isn’t so dramatic that it becomes overwhelming. Purple also has a slightly receding quality in the landscape, which can help garden beds feel deeper and more spacious.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

That makes purple flowers particularly useful when you want a garden to feel abundant and interesting without looking chaotic. Rather than competing with every other color, a purple-and-green scheme gives the eye a clear thread to follow. And there’s another benefit: purple flowers can be particularly attractive to bees and butterflies, making them a valuable food for pollinators.

Catmint blooms forever, looks beautiful, and doesn't go woody!

Another fragrant perennial, salvia is an absolute pollinator magnet.

A classic upright rosemary boasts a fabulous scent and purple hue.

Tempted to try it for yourself? Of course you are, and I have good news for you on that front: you don’t need acres of garden – or a supermodel’s landscaping budget – to borrow the idea. Because... well, because you don't have to go full Jerry Hall

The easiest way to try the look at home is to think of purple as a thread running through your planting rather than a rule you have to follow religiously. Lavender (like this Grosso Lavender from Nature Hills) is an obvious starting point, while salvias, catmint, alliums, geraniums, pansies, purple-leaved heucheras, hellebores, and aquilegias can all bring different versions of the shade into a border.

Soft pinks can make the scheme feel romantic, blues can deepen the cool tones, and even brighter shades can work when they're anchored by plenty of green. All of which means that, no, you don't need to turn your entire garden into a purple paradise.

But after seeing Jerry Hall's? Well, I can certainly understand why you might want to.

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

#154. The Best Cordless Leaf Blowers of 2026, Tested In Real Yards

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Updated Oct 15, 2026 4:37 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

A cordless leaf blower is one of the most useful tools a homeowner can own. It makes quick work of seasonal messes, from fallen leaves and grass clippings to storm debris and light snow. To find the top performers, we’ve spent the past couple of years testing 26 of the most popular and powerful models while cleaning up our own yards.

Battery-powered options keep multiplying as gas blowers fall out of favor, so shopping for one can be confusing. The wrong model can make yard work harder: a unit that’s weak, awkward, or quick to drain turns a 15-minute chore into an hour-long slog.

Our favorite is the Toro 60V Max 900 CFM cordless leaf blower. It delivers tremendous blowing force, has the battery life to clear large properties, and pairs a well-balanced, comfortable handle with intuitive controls. It isn’t the cheapest or lightest pick, though, and it may be more power than a small yard needs.

Read on for our shopping tips and hands-on reviews of the best cordless leaf blowers for every yard size and budget.

Cordless leaf blowers come in many shapes and sizes. Whether you need a compact blower or a heavy-duty backpack model, the lineup ahead has you covered. Check out these reviews to find out more about each model and why we recommend it.

Not everyone needs top-end blowing force from a handheld leaf blower, but it’s nice to have a little extra power at your disposal when you need it. The Toro 60-volt MAX 900 CFM cordless leaf blower delivers massive air-moving power to maintain landscapes up to 1 acre or larger. It’s also built to take on heavy-duty cleanup projects. It comes with a charger and a 4 Ah battery that delivers up to 120 minutes of runtime and recharges in 120 minutes.

In addition to air movement that rivals some of the best gas-powered leaf blowers, we really like the design of this model. Although this battery leaf blower was the heaviest handheld we tested, it was perfectly balanced, so the blow tube naturally rested at the right working angle with zero effort. The handle was comfortably shaped, with a secondary forward handle for two-handed operation, and covered with a slip-resistant overmold that provided a little bit of cushion.

To us, the benefit of a comfortable, balanced design outweighed the slightly heavier weight. And the massive air-moving ability allowed us to do the same amount of work in as little as half the time it would have taken with a lightweight leaf blower. Since this blower shares a battery platform with the Toro TimeCutter electric zero-turn mower and the 60V MAX Recycler self-propelled lawn mower, users have options to share batteries with lawn equipment that best fits their yard.

What our tester says: “I like that the Toro brand introduced a top performer right out of the gate. This blower gives midsize yard owners the required power and runtime to fully embrace battery power. The Toro battery-powered lineup may be narrower than others on this list, but it is well worth the investment for premium performance.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and multimedia reporter

Get the Toro cordless leaf blower at Lowe’s, Acme Tools, or Toro.

One of the best lightweight blowers we tested, the Greenworks PowerAll 48V blower sells for the lowest price in the group. This blower runs quietly and cleans remarkably well with its outstanding power-to-weight ratio. It operates at 68 decibels, pushes 600 CFM at 150 mph, and only weighs 8.5 pounds. It was comfortable and well balanced, and its performance exceeded most handheld gas blowers.

The controls were simple and intuitive to operate, including a variable trigger, a right-handed speed-lock lever, and a turbo button. The trigger had just the right level of sensitivity, and accelerated smoothly from “off” to full power. The blower worked as well as any of the others, (and better than some) on light- and medium-duty cleaning, including grass clippings, dry leaves, sawdust, and drying a car or wet patio furniture.

The battery system uses tabless cell technology to deliver faster charging and a longer working life than regular rechargeable batteries. They pack about 20 percent more wattage than 18V batteries, and it shows in the blower performance. As a bonus, this system features bi-directional USB-C charging. The kit includes a space-saving 100 watt dual USB-charging block that tops up both batteries from zero to full charge in just 60 minutes. The batteries can also be used to power up small electronic devices.

The tool requires two 24V batteries to achieve 48V power, which means that both of the kit batteries are depleted at the same time. If you need backup batteries for extra runtime, you’ll need to buy those separately. That should not be a problem though, since the same batteries work in more than 200 tools within the Greenworks 24/48-volt ecosystem.

What our tester says: “There’s so much to love about the Greenworks PowerAll leaf blower: cutting-edge battery tech, remarkable power-to-weight ratio, fast charging, and dual-purpose batteries to name a few. The affordability factor almost makes it an unfair competition.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and multimedia reporter

Get the Greenworks PowerAll cordless leaf blower at Amazon, Walmart, Lowe’s, or Best Buy.

The most powerful cordless leaf blower on our list, this beast from Ego beats our top pick statistically in blow force and weighs nearly 1.5 pounds less. But it also costs more. In our tests, the actual performances of the two were very similar. In addition to the blower, battery, and charger, this kit includes a second 4 Ah battery, shoulder strap, and two nozzle extensions.

In terms of blowing power, the Ego cordless blower delivered the muscle needed to clean up tough messes. It had no problems with wet, matted leaves, pine cones, and other heavy debris that traditionally call for a gas-powered backpack blower. We mostly used it without the shoulder strap, which we found to be more restrictive than helpful. This model is better balanced and felt less fatiguing than earlier Ego models that we tested. We won’t describe it as “lightweight,” but using it for 30 to 40 minutes at a time was not overly taxing.

We really liked the wide support base on this blower. It enabled us to set the unit down on the ground without worrying about it rolling over. The digital display made it easy to monitor battery life while operating as well.

On the downside, we didn’t love the awkward speed lock; setting it requires squeezing the trigger with your forefinger while simultaneously pressing a button with your thumb. Not impossible, but not well refined either. We also found ourselves tapping into the second battery earlier than expected, after only 20 minutes on “high.” All that being said, for raw power, and with two batteries that combine for at least 40 minutes of runtime per charge, you’ll want to consider this one.

Get the Ego cordless leaf blower at Amazon, Lowe’s, Ace Hardware, or Northern Tool & Equipment.

When you have a yard full of leaves to clean up, a leaf blower with plenty of power and an extended range makes the job manageable. In our tests, the Husqvarna 350iB Leaf Blaster, one of the most powerful handheld cordless leaf blowers available, delivered an average of 38 minutes of runtime per charge on the included 7.5 Ah battery.

This blower felt lighter than its actual weight thanks to its balanced design. It was easy to maneuver and less tiring than some of the models with similar blow force ratings. It also includes a handy scraper built into the tip of the blow tube that helped dislodge wet, matted leaves. From an operational standpoint, we didn’t love the push-button cruise control–a thumb lever would have been simpler and more intuitive.

After clearing the yard, we finally had to recharge the battery while we shredded and bagged the mountain of leaves. The only mediocrity we found with this kit was the modest charging rate. Although the blower runs a long time, when the battery finally runs down it needs to sit on the charger for about 90 minutes to recharge.

Get the Husqvarna cordless leaf blower at Amazon, Lowe’s, Walmart, or Tractor Supply Co.

If you’ve ever tried to use a leaf blower in a small space, you’ll appreciate the quiet, easy-to-control performance of the new 3017-21HD blower. With the included 18V, 12 Ah battery installed, the unit only weighs 8.5 pounds. It also features a comfortable handle and balanced design for easy maneuverability. At full power, it produces 12.2 newtons (N) of blowforce, and emits just 54 decibels–significantly quieter than any of the others we’ve tested.

This lightweight unit excelled when it came to controlled cleaning inside the garage and basement. Instead of blasting a cloud of debris into the air, it pushed dirt and sawdust across the floor and out the door. It also did a great job clearing grass clippings from the front porch and dried flowers and leaves off the deck. The sound was so quiet that we were able to use it early in the morning and late at night without disturbing the neighbors.

One of our favorite features was the sliding airspeed lock. No need to squeeze the trigger and operate the lock at the same time–simply slide the control forward with your thumb and it stays in position. The slider worked equally well for right- and left-handed users, which was unique among the models we tested. The 3017-21HD blower is part of Milwaukee’s popular M18 Fuel battery ecosystem, featuring interchangeable batteries among hundreds of power tools.

Get the Milwaukee cordless leaf blower at The Home Depot, Ace Hardware, or Northern Tool & Equipment.

No need to blow your budget on a cordless leaf blower for small yard maintenance. This Skil 40V 650 CFM model delivers plenty of air power and runtime to do all the chores without breaking the bank. The kit includes a 40V, 6 Ah battery that powers up to 20 minutes of full blowforce.

For nearly the same price as our “Best Bang For The Buck” pick, this blower moves more air (650 CFM compared to 600 CFM) faster (170 mph versus 120 mph), which equates to a much higher blowforce rating of 19 N. That power is good for clearing all kinds of messes, from moving heavy wet leaves and debris to clearing snow.

Since this blower is a bit heavier, even with its balanced construction, we especially liked the dual-handle design. The supplemental forward handle proved helpful whenever we needed to handle the blower overhead or at any odd angle (drying the car roof, cleaning gutters, blowing cobwebs from window exteriors, etc.).

Another handy feature, the quick-connect stubby nozzle, concentrated the airstream for maximum power. It helped with heavy debris, and the connection held securely, unlike the nozzles on other blowers that didn’t always stay in place.

Get the Skil cordless leaf blower at Amazon, Acme Tools, Ace Hardware, Walmart, or Best Buy.

A good battery system offers an expertly balanced combination of power, runtime, and flexibility. With the DeWalt FlexVolt battery system, the same battery can be used to power any of DeWalt’s 60V or 20V cordless tools. The 60V MAX brushless blower kit comes equipped with a charger and a 4-Ah battery that provided 30 minutes of full-force runtime per charge during testing. That was not the longest-running battery overall, but arguably the best performance per available watt-hour.

The blower itself produced airflow powerful enough to move heavy, wet debris and large quantities of dry material. And it ran relatively quietly for the amount of power. We recorded 86 decibels at the operator’s ear level on the high setting–significantly lower than other high-powered models.

This DeWalt cordless electric leaf blower had the highest price among the handheld units we tested, but not by much. Brand popularity and the unique battery system might justify the price. The only real drawback we experienced was that the weight of the blower was balanced too far rearward so that it naturally rested parallel to the ground. We had to exert constant effort to angle the blow tube downward toward the debris. A lighter battery pack or longer blow tube could fix that.

Get the DeWalt cordless leaf blower at The Home Depot or Ace Hardware.

Operating a handheld blower gets tiring after a while. DeWalt’s Flexvolt backpack blower eliminates the hand, arm, and shoulder strain that comes with extended use, and it provides up to 82 minutes of cleaning power per charge. The kit includes the blower, a removable nozzle, a pair of 60-volt 5 Ah Flexvolt batteries, and two chargers.

To get started, you’ll have to assemble the lower blow tube and control unit to the rubber boot with an included clamp. The instructions could have been more clear. We had a little trouble determining how the parts should be aligned, but after a first failed attempt, we figured it out.

In normal yard cleanup duties, the DeWalt backpack blower quickly cleared grass clippings and debris from the driveway, curb, deck, and lawn equipment, with battery life to spare. The harness felt secure and comfortable while we moved, with plenty of padding in the shoulder straps and hip belt and lots of room to adjust the straps. When we were not trying to conserve battery life, it consistently delivered 40 to 45 minutes of runtime per charge.

One of the unit’s standout features was the option to select from three different performance modes in order to limit or boost the base powerload. When we dialed in “eco mode”, we were easily able to push dry leaves, grass, and sawdust for up to the listed 80+ minutes per charge. Switching to turbo mode reduced working time to about 20 to 25 minutes, but allowed us to move substantial quantities of heavier material.

Get the DeWalt cordless backpack leaf blower at The Home Depot, Acme Tools, or ToolUp.

For small and midsize yards, there’s no need to spend a small fortune on lawn equipment. This Greenworks cordless electric leaf blower delivers ample blowing force and runtime for cleaning up grass clippings and collecting fallen leaves on yards up to a half acre in size. It comes with a battery charger and 2.5 Ah battery that runs up to 19 minutes on “high” and recharges in just 30 minutes.

Right out of the box, we noticed that this model was lighter than many of the others in the group. The Greenworks blower was also one of the loudest in our test group (95.5 decibels at ear level), but it did a great job clearing grass clippings and collecting leaves into piles. It took a few minutes longer than the more powerful models to clear leaves from our 8,000-square-foot lawn, but it had plenty of runtime to get the job done. Also, the lightweight build made it less tiring to use than the bigger blowers.

If you are trying to match with equipment you already have or are shopping for an all-inclusive battery equipment brand, this blower could be a good option. It shares the same 80-volt battery platform with numerous Greenworks push mowers, self-propelled lawn mowers, string trimmers, and other lawn care equipment.

Get the Greenworks cordless leaf blower at Amazon or Greenworks.

As new and better cordless leaf blowers come out each year, we frequently test new models and update our recommendations. Through four years of testing, we have evaluated dozens of models. We typically test each of these blowers for a minimum of 2 hours, using them for routine yard cleanup tasks, and running them through an obstacle course that includes matted wet leaves, dry leaves, potting soil, sand, and water. During the test, we record battery charging times and runtimes where applicable and how long it takes to complete leaf, soil, sand, and water removal from a given area. We also note our observations with regard to the user experience: handling, noise, and overall operating comfort. At the end of testing, we score each blower on a rubric to determine the award category winners.

Before settling on any of our recommendations, it’s important to weigh your individual needs against the available options.

If you want a cordless leaf blower, you have two options: battery power or gas. The best option depends on your preferences, but it may also hinge on your usage patterns and blow-force requirements.

Battery-powered leaf blowers have come close to the capabilities of their gas-powered counterparts in recent years. But battery-powered models still cost a bit more than gas-powered leaf blowers with equivalent blowing force. That said, battery-powered blowers are quieter, require almost no maintenance, and eliminate trips to the gas station. The average working life of a lithium-ion battery is 300 to 500 charge cycles, or approximately 6 to 10 years, after which you’ll need to replace the battery or buy a new leaf blower altogether.

While battery-powered leaf blowers are the winners in terms of low noise and easy handling, power and runtime for the money are the top selling points for gas-powered leaf blowers. With higher usage, replacing lithium batteries at 6- to 10-year intervals could outrun the cost of fuel and gas engine maintenance over the same period. Although gas-powered leaf blowers require ongoing preventive maintenance, they can provide up to 20 years of dependable service.

A leaf blower is one of the handiest power tools for collecting leaves, clearing grass clippings, light snow removal, and various outdoor cleanup projects. Matching the machine’s air-handling ability to the size of the property will help you work efficiently without overspending on oversize equipment. This is where the cubic feet per minute, or CFM spec, comes into play.

For city and smaller suburban yards up to about a half acre, a blower with a rating of 400 to 550 CFM should be adequate. Compared to more powerful blowers, this may not sound like much, but it really is. These blowers could fill a balloon the size of a studio apartment in a minute or less. That’s plenty of blowing force to keep the yard, driveway, and sidewalks clean. These blowers also work better when you’re working in confined spaces, such as a courtyard, porch, or workshop.

Larger suburban and rural properties need a little more power to reduce work time. A blower that pushes 550 to 650 CFM is a good range for moderate work on areas up to 1 acre. Larger properties with large quantities of leaves will benefit from a 650 to 900 CFM leaf blower that can tackle heavy-duty work.

A blower’s air-moving ability, or blowing force, is determined by a combination of the volume of air coming out of the blow tube and how fast it is moving. The CFM air-volume rating relates more closely to the area the blower will cover, while mph air speed relates more to power. Faster air speed helps with tougher jobs like dispersing grass clumps, removing wet snow, and pushing wet and matted leaves.

Most cordless leaf blowers feature a variable-speed trigger so that you can use more or less blowing force as needed. Many battery-powered blowers are equipped with turbo, or power boost, buttons that can provide an extra boost of top-end power on demand. Cruise control is a feature that allows you to maintain steady air speed without constantly squeezing the trigger, which helps to reduce hand fatigue on large projects.

Other features to consider include the battery platform, blow-tube configuration, noise rating, and any comfort features included. These minor details add value and may make the deciding difference between two otherwise similar options.

Comfort features include the blower’s weight, balance, handle construction, control placement, noise level, and more. These aspects may have nothing to do with whether the blower will work, but they can strongly affect whether you’ll want to use it. If all of the other specifications are equal between two of your favorite options, comfort could be the deciding factor.

The shape of the blow tube, and any extensions or nozzles that come with the kit, can affect performance in subtle ways. A longer blow tube will make it easier to move leaves and debris from under automobiles, trailers, and low structures. Wider nozzles move more lightweight material, but narrow nozzles do a better job with heavier debris. Some leaf blowers even come with leaf vacuum conversion kits that can suck up and mulch dry leaves.

If you are shopping for a battery-powered leaf blower, be sure to consider the other tools from that brand that run on the same batteries. The best battery-powered brands offer a wide range of tools that all share the same batteries. Sharing batteries and chargers between tools can contribute to huge time, money, and space savings.

Now that you have read our reviews, you may have a few lingering questions. We’ve covered some of the most common queries below.

The most reliable leaf blowers come from several brands. For battery power, consider reputable brands like Ego, DeWalt, Milwaukee, Ryobi, and Greenworks. Stihl, Husqvarna, and Ryobi dominate gas-powered recommendations.

It depends on the size of the job. A good CFM (cubic feet per minute) rating for cordless leaf blowers ranges from as low as 400 for light-duty cleanup in small spaces to greater than 800 for heavy-duty tasks in larger areas.

A leaf blower can run continuously until its battery or fuel tank is depleted. Actual runtimes vary based on throttle setting, operating efficiency, and fuel capacity. Most battery blowers will run between 15 and 30 minutes per charge on full power, but they might last 90 minutes or longer on the lowest setting.

Yes, battery-powered leaf blowers are worth the money for those who value low-maintenance equipment and gas-free lawn care.

Mark Wolfe is a writer and product tester with a background in the green industry. He’s also an avid DIYer who lives in an older home. When he isn’t writing, he spends his time upgrading, repairing, and replacing anything and everything in his home, yard, and garden. He tests and writes reviews about hand tools, lawn care and home repair products, and outdoor-living goods.

#155. What Peonies Need in October – 6 Easy Tasks to Prepare for Winter and Ensure Fabulous Spring Blooms

The flowers may be long gone, but your peonies still have important work to do below ground. Fall is a key moment if you want the best flowers next year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I love peonies, but that isn’t something I announce very often among gardeners. It’s a little like saying “I love cheese” in France. Everyone loves cheese in France, and the vast majority of gardeners adore these large, plush flowers with their abundance of tissue-paper petals. That’s why a peony is called the queen of the flowers.

Are peonies drought-tolerant and the kind of plant that thrives on neglect? Not at all, but fans insist that their dramatic, over-the-top, lush beauty makes it all worthwhile. October is a key time for peony care – and I am here to give you the scoop.

Keep in mind that these glorious flowers come in three separate varieties: herbaceous, intersectional, and tree peonies. The steps you need to take in October will depend on which of the three types you have in your landscape.

Of the three types of peonies, herbaceous peonies are the most common in home gardens. Their stems are not woody; they grow in spring and die back each winter. Itoh peonies, also called intersectional peonies, are hybrids, offering bigger flowers, stronger stems, and a longer growing season than herbaceous peonies. However, they also die back in autumn.

Cutting back your herbaceous and Itoh peonies is an important chore for October, but don’t jump the gun. As long as the peony leaves are green, they still are feeding the peony roots. Don’t cut them back until your area experiences a hard freeze. You will know because the foliage will turn yellow or brown. Once that happens, cut them back to some 2 inches (5 cm) above the soil. I like to use Fiskars Bypass Pruning Shears, available from Amazon, for this task because they make clean cuts that are less likely to damage dormant buds.

Once the peonies have been trimmed back, it’s clean-up time. Pick up all the messy pieces and toss them in the trash. Don’t think of dumping the debris into the compost pile. Overwintering there can cause fungal or mold issues.

Unlike herbaceous varieties, tree peonies have woody branches that stay in the garden all year. Their flowers are larger than herbaceous peonies' blooms, and they flower earlier in the season.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The most critical rule when it comes to pruning tree peonies is: DO NOT EVER cut them back to the ground. Leave the woody stems and branches alone. Snipping off woody branches will reduce (or eliminate) next year's flower buds. October is not the time to do heavy pruning – wait for late winter.

On the other hand, you should trim off the mature seed pods in October. You’ll recognize them because they are leathery. Also clip off dead or dying brown leaves. While you clear these away, take the time to pick up other fallen leaves and plant debris from the base of the plant to prevent fungal issues.

If your tree peony struggled with fungal issues this year, thorough cleanup is your first line of defense. Then, in spring, consider applying a preventative copper fungicide, like Bonide Captain Jack's Copper Fungicide, as new growth emerges to help protect fresh foliage.

October is a great time to divide or transplant peonies if the plants are crowded or are currently growing in shade. If you move plants in the fall, they will have enough time to establish roots sufficiently to bear spring blooms.

Whether you are dividing or transplanting, the first step is to dig up the plant. A narrow perennial spade makes the job easier, especially when working around established plants. The Radius Garden Root Slayer Perennial Shovel, available from Home Depot, has a serrated blade that helps cut through tough soil and roots, making it particularly useful for dividing mature clumps. Work carefully around the peony to preserve as much of its root system as possible.

To divide peonies, dig up a clump of roots with healthy stems and leaves attached, then separate it from the main plant with a sharp knife or perennial spade. Each division should have at least three buds; they will grow into next year’s shoots. Plant each division about one inch (2.5 cm) deep.

All newly planted peonies need a deep, thorough watering right after planting. This includes both new bare-root plants and all transplanted peonies. After that, water them weekly, or twice a week during dry periods, unless it rains. The soil should be moist, not wet. If you're unsure when to water, a Yamron 4-in-1 Soil Moisture Meter, available on Amazon, can help you check moisture levels before you reach for the hose and avoid overwatering newly planted peonies.

So, when should you reduce watering? Do it gradually in autumn, as temperatures drop. Once the ground freezes, stop supplemental watering.

I like to think of mulch as a snuggy blanket for my plants, but it actually serves a bigger purpose. Mulch keeps the soil warmer, holds in moisture, and keeps down weeds. Autumn plant maintenance almost always includes mulch.

But when it comes to peonies, there are certain mulch rules that you have to keep in mind. First, established plants don’t need mulch. Only use mulch on new or newly transplanted peonies.

Second, don’t cover the buds (aka eyes). Instead of a snuggly blanket, apply a light, loose ring of mulch around each new or transplanted peony. This prevents frost-heaving during the first winter.

Third, pick your mulch type carefully. Don't use any mulch that can trap moisture since it can rot the crown. Instead, use a light layer of straw, shredded leaves, or evergreen boughs. If you don't have your own straw, EZ Straw Seeding Mulch, available from Home Depot, is a convenient option that provides insulation while still allowing air to circulate around the crown. Avoid compost, fresh manure, or sawdust.

Autumn is one of the best times of year to plant peonies. Cooler temperatures and still-warm soil give new plants plenty of time to establish roots before winter arrives, setting them up for strong growth the following spring. Whether you're planting a nursery-grown peony or a division from an established plant, getting it into the ground in October gives it the best chance to settle in before dormancy.

Choose a sunny spot with fertile, well-drained soil, and avoid planting the crown too deeply. The buds, or "eyes", should sit no more than 1–2 inches (2.5–5 cm) below the soil surface, as planting too deeply is one of the most common reasons peonies fail to bloom.

If you're planting into heavy clay or poor soil, mixing in a quality planting mix such as Miracle-Gro Garden Soil for Flowers, available from Walmart, can help improve drainage and give new peonies the best possible start.

Water thoroughly after planting, then apply a light ring of mulch around new plants to help protect the roots through their first winter, taking care not to cover the buds.

This dreamy pastel mix contains Bowl of Beauty, Sarah Bernhardt, Coral Charm, and Koningin Wilhelmina peonies.

Award-winning variety with strong stems and deep pink-red blooms that exude the most alluring fragrance.

This newly introduced Itoh peony has sophisticated oversized white flowers flushed with deep lavender centers.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

With the Felco 2e Electric Pruning Shears doing the squeezing for you, a long afternoon of pruning no longer ends in a sore hand. #158. Are Your Mums Dropping Buds Before They Flower? Try This Easy “Bottoms Up” Trick to Save Your Fall Blooms

Mums are viewed by many gardeners as the most reliable bloomer of the season, so what do you do if yours start shedding buds? This easy dunk can salvage your fall display

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every September, garden centers fill up with potted chrysanthemums (Chrysanthemum × morifolium), row upon row packed tight with promising flower buds. You might eagerly select two lush, rounded pots for the front porch steps, imagining weeks of rich fall color. But then, just a couple of days after bringing them home, you notice dozens of tight brown buds scattered on the porch floor, and the plant looks ready to collapse. And you’ll possibly conclude that you’ve bought a dud.

Usually, it wasn’t, though. In almost every case, that plant is healthy. The problem is lurking down in the pot, where nobody generally thinks to look. Mums (as they are affectionately known) are notoriously thirsty, fast-growing plants with dense root systems that devour water at an astonishing rate. Store-bought florist mums in plastic containers are frequently root-bound long before they reach retail shelves. Root balls can often lock up, depriving those thirsty buds of vital hydration.

The good news? You don't need expensive plant gimmicks or advanced skills to turn things around. All you need is a special soak – what I like to call the “bottoms up” soak, as it treats your thirsty flowers from the base of the plant. This special drink is all you need to pull your mums out of their slump before the rest of the buds are lost. It’s easy to carry out and the entire rescue takes less than 20 minutes, most of which can be spent with a warm cup of coffee while nature recharges your plant…

Commercial nurseries feed potted mums on intensive, high-nitrogen liquid fertilizers all summer to get those iconic domes of buds ready for fall. After months inside small plastic pots, fertilizer salts accumulate inside the potting mix. Sometimes this shows up as a white crust around the rim of the pot, but sometimes it doesn’t show at all.

As soil moisture evaporates, salt concentrations spike. The more concentrated those salts get, the harder it is for roots to pull in water. This can create an osmotic lock where the roots are blocked from absorbing moisture, even if the soil still feels damp to your touch. Once potted mums arrive on your sunny porch or patio, environmental stress compounds the problem. Bright fall sunlight and steady winds can dry a root-packed nursery pot to the core in under 12 hours.

When roots run dry, the plant makes a survival choice: it sheds its flower buds to preserve moisture for the stems. Growers may mistake bud drop for pest infestations or drafts, reaching for insecticides or overwatering from the top, which exacerbates root rot. Any buds that have turned crisp, dry, or dark brown are done, so gently pinch those off with your fingers or snip them with fine scissors or snips like team favorite Fiskars Micro-Tip Pruning Snips from Amazon. That way, “bad buds” don't wind up hosting gray mold (botrytis). Those plump, healthy, tight green buds, however, are just waiting to be saved…

Before soaking, perform the weight test. Lift the pot by the rim: if it feels heavy and water squishes up around your thumb, poor drainage or root rot is the issue, and soaking won't help. If the pot feels light as a feather, it's severely dehydrated. Be sure to strip off any decorative foil sleeves immediately! Foil wraps trap stagnant water against lower roots, inviting fungal disease. In dry nursery pots, peat-based potting soil shrinks away from the pot creating a gap down which top-poured water simply spills out of the drainage holes, leaving the dense central root core bone dry.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

To execute the "bottoms up" soak, fill a shallow tub, bucket or washbasin with 3-4 inches (8-10cm) of room-temperature water. Collected rainwater or distilled water is ideal, as it carries zero chlorine or mineral salts. A flexible tub such as the Tubtrug Original Flexible Tub from Amazon is ideal for bottom-soaking a big mum.

Lower the nursery pot into the water so the lower half sits submerged. Let capillary action draw water upwards directly into the compacted root core for 15-20 minutes. You'll know it's ready when the top surface of the soil turns dark, damp, and cool to the touch. Severely shrunken pots may need up to 30 minutes. Lift the pot out and allow excess water to drain freely. After this time, you are ready for a quick top-flush.

This is the crucial secondary step that is easy to skip – but please don’t. The natural impulse is to stop once the pot feels heavy again after its bath. While bottom-soaking saturates dry peat, water moving upward carries dissolved fertilizer salts toward the upper root zone rather than removing them. Leaving those concentrated salts in the soil will trigger another round of bud drop within a week. So the flush is crucial!

To complete your mum rescue, take the potted mum to an outdoor sink, gravel path, or garden bed where drainage can escape freely. Using room-temperature water, slowly pour a generous stream directly over the top of the potting soil until water streams out the drainage holes. Pause for a couple of minutes, then repeat the process. If you need a good watering can, a 2-gallon model like the Bloem Deluxe Mint Green Watering Can from The Home Depot holds plenty for both passes.

This top-flush washes away dissolved fertilizer salts and flushes out stagnant material from the roots. Never allow the pot to sit in its own drained runoff, as the roots will reabsorb those flushed salts. Once flushed, refrain from applying synthetic fertilizer for the rest of the bloom season. The plant already has more than enough stored energy to open its remaining buds. The combination of these steps is what helps to rehydrate stubborn peat soils, dissolve fertilizer crusts, and restore root flow.

Once your mum is rehydrated and flushed, a pot upgrade will help protect swelling buds for longer. While repotting in full bud may create slight stress, keeping it trapped in a cramped 6-8-inch (15-20cm) plastic nursery pot is likely to prompt further drying cycle crashes. The gentlest approach is potting on. Slide the root ball out of its plastic sleeve. Place it directly into a container 2-4 inches (5-10cm) wider, backfilling the gap with fresh potting soil. Self-watering planters with built-in drainage reservoirs work brilliantly. Tierra Verde Citadel Horizon Self-Watering Planters from Amazon have sleek, classic lines to show off bright mum colors.

Placement is your final secret weapon for long-lasting October blooms. While mums need sunlight to flower, placing them in scorching, full-day heat causes open blooms to fade rapidly. Aim for bright morning sunlight paired with some afternoon shade, such as a covered front porch or eastern-facing patio. Cooler microclimates slow down water loss and keep open flower heads crisp and vibrant for weeks longer.

If you are growing hardy garden mums intended for permanent beds, keep them well-watered in their new pots until flowers finish, then plant them into beds 4 weeks before ground freezes are anticipated. Use excellent Bloem 12-Inch Heavy Duty Terracotta Plant Caddies, available from Walmart, to move heavier mum containers into position. Their caster wheels make light work of moving heavy pots.

Once your mums have perked up, make sure you get the most out of their blooming season. Tending to your potted blooms with gentle tonics, tools, and root conditioners makes it possible to maintain vibrant porch displays into November. These curated essentials help you rescue, protect, and enjoy your flowers for longer.

Never guess when your mums need water again! This instant-read dual probe checks deep moisture levels right at the central root core while measuring ambient light conditions. It takes all the guesswork out of daily care, ensuring you hydrate your plants only when necessary to prevent both dehydration crashes and root rot.

This gentle, non-burning amendment is packed with enzymes and trace minerals to strengthen plant cell walls as weather changes. It helps stressed roots recover rapidly from dehydration, while encouraging unopened buds to swell and bloom reliably.

Rich in natural humus, beneficial microbes, and organic matter, mixing a few handfuls of this compost into your repotting mix dramatically improves moisture retention around root balls. It acts as a natural micro-sponge that holds onto water and prevents peat-based soils from shrinking or drying out in fall winds.

Seeing your mums drop tight buds is disheartening, but it doesn't mean your fall display is over! By giving dehydrated roots this 15-minute soak and flushing away accumulated nursery salts, you’ll give those remaining buds the hydration boost they need to open into a lovely long-lasting dome of fall color. So grab a bucket, give your thirsty mums a quick bath today, and enjoy a vibrant front porch all autumn long.

Need more ideas for getting the most from your plants, indoors and out, and looking for the best seasonal expert advice delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for the free Gardening Know How Newsletter!

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

If you’re familiar with the much-loved, much-lauded boutique empire Bird in Brooklyn, you know that the shops defined indie style in the borough for more than a decade (see the NY Times piece Saying Goodbye to Bird, “the shop that created the ‘Brooklyn Look’ of the aughts”).

Plot twist: In 2022, owner Jen Mankins closed her stores, moved to Sweden, and shifted her focus to interior design.

“I lived and worked in Brooklyn for more than two decades before my college boyfriend-turned-husband and I decided to move to Sweden with our twin toddler sons in 2022,” Jen says. “Our timing coincided with me landing my first professional interior design with Brooklyn-based clients I knew through Bird. Luckily, even though I was moving 4,000 miles away and embarking on a new profession, they didn’t blink an eye.”

In concert with Ingui Architecture, a NY firm known for its focus onm sustainable living, Jen designed the interiors of a six-story landmarked brownstone from 1895. Her inspiration? “Sweden has been hugely influential for me personally and continues to be a never-ending source of design inspiration. On my earliest visits to Stockholm with my husband, I was immediately drawn to the colors and patterns of Josef Frank designs championed by visionary retailer Estrid Erickson at Svenskt Tenn. I was charmed by the whimsical ceramics of Stig Lindberg and Lisa Larson. (Although I can’t deny that my first experience with Swedish design was via Ikea, the design emporium that has for over 80 years brought Swedish style to the masses.)”

Compact batteries are fine on a drill, but put one on a circular saw or grinder, and you’ll be swapping packs long before the job’s done. Fortunately, Home Depot has the DeWalt 20V XR Battery Starter Pack for $199 (was $399). That’s $200 off and ties for the lowest price we’ve seen on this kit.

The deal includes an 8Ah battery, a 4Ah battery, and a charger. We run the high-capacity 8Ah on the top-draw tools (circular saw, miter saw, grinder), where the extra capacity delivers longer runtime and steadier power under load. The 4Ah goes on the drill or impact driver, where less weight matters more than runtime.

If you already own DeWalt 20V MAX tools, this kit lets you run a two-battery rotation: one on the tool, one on the charger. Both packs also fit DeWalt’s Atomic tools, and the charger works with all DeWalt 12V and 20V MAX batteries, so it can replace an older, slower charger in your setup.

Both packs have a built-in fuel gauge, so you can check the charge before you climb a ladder or head to the far end of the site. This battery starter pack works with any DeWalt 20V MAX tool.
