#161. OmVed in North London: A Community-Focused Garden, But Make It Chic

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

OmVed Gardens in North London is rather chic. The brainchild of World Health Organization activists who wanted to create a space that provided food education with an emphasis on diverting food waste, they asked their friend Paul Gazerwitz, a Brooklynite by birth whose international portfolio is decidedly upscale, to help them develop a pocket of post-industrial land. The result is miraculously successful: OmVed is not only gorgeous, but it has soul. With views overlooking London, yet quiet and tucked away, it feels like a very nice bit of countryside, in microcosm. Let’s take a closer look.

Photography via OmVed Gardens unless otherwise noted.

The garden is in Highgate Village and easy to reach by bus. Hidden down an alleyway off Highgate High Street and perched on a hilltop, it has the fairytale look of a small village inside a forest clearing, with shingled wooden buildings of varying roof pitches, surrounded by gardens and paths that meander through the steep site.

Built in collaboration with Gazerwitz by Smerin Architects, the glorified huts (or “pavilions”) are for seed-saving, growing, cooking, and teaching; in addition, there’s a roof garden over the kitchen and an outdoor amphitheater. They are all connected, and once you have found OmVed, you will want to linger.

Entry to the garden requires a ticket to one of the frequent courses and dinners (at various price points) or via the free art show in summer. OmVed is a community interest company which feels like a well-oiled private enterprise, staffed by people who love their job.

Visitors come from far and wide, with a steady flow of loyal regulars from London. At the heart of the enterprise is human connection—and health that is both environmental and plant-based, communicated through food.

Activity in the kitchen never stops: There is always something to pickle or preserve, and discarded offcuts, such as strawberry tops or tomato cores, make their way into fruit leather or shrubs for drinks and dressings. At the end of the season, there are talks, demonstrations, and hands-on making; the upcoming Fermentation Celebration explores the “Four K’s”: kimchi, kombucha, kefir, and kraut. More of the harvest is preserved in an underground fridge—which is really a large hole in the ground like an old-fashioned root cellar, cooled by its subterranean position rather than external power. Lined with plywood, it’s as chic and efficient as the buildings above-ground.

The site has had many iterations: It was once a market garden for growing flowers for Highgate Cemetery (just down the hill); a drover’s yard, providing pasture for cattle on the way to market at Smithfield; and the worst kind of garden center, concreted over and no stranger to chemicals. From a developer’s point of view, it was an awkward site, which saved it from housing construction and allowed mature trees to thrive around the edges. A lower story of native trees and shrubs has been added slowly; cherry shows up in two ways, as a wild tree around the periphery and as an espaliered culinary tree by the kitchen garden.

Seed-saving is also a public-facing endeavor, with free seeds sent out to participants through the Seed Saving Network, of which this writer is one (I am currently growing and monitoring tomatoes, both orange and black, white cucumber, “giant” parsley, and stripey eggplant, all grown from the network’s seeds).

All of the materials at OmVed are top-notch, from wooden cobblestones by the kitchen, to a better class of cinderblock arranged as a holding wall by a sunny patio, for displaying rare edible plants and providing habitat. The aesthetic could be called industrial-rustic.

Up to 400 people can pass through the garden in a day, with concurrent events spilling out into different spaces, as well as quieter areas over the two acres. The genius is in the design. The steep site has lent itself to a contoured approach; the main path is based on a squiggly line that Paul made on a piece of paper during his first visit.

The lack of cars or parking adds to the garden’s feeling of enchantment. Replacing the former parking lot at the bottom of the site are two ponds that are replenished with rainwater as well as the overflow from several springs, which occur naturally here (a chemist on Highgate High Street used to sell bottled Highgate spring water).

#162. 5 Plants You Can Propagate So Easily With a Cutting in October, Even if You’re a Beginner Gardener

Snipping a stem and sticking it into potting mix is all you need do to create free plants from these garden favorites in fall.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Even in fall, your garden is full of potential and taking cuttings in October that will quickly root to become new plants is such a cost-effective way to bulk up next year's borders. It really couldn’t be easier, so even if you’re a beginner gardener or you’ve never tried this propagation method before, taking cuttings in fall should definitely be on your list of gardening jobs to do in October.

There’s a big advantage to rooting plant cuttings in fall because the current season’s growth is mature. Protected by a tougher exterior, the stems are far more resilient to drying out than softwood cuttings taken in summer. Lavender, rosemary, fuchsia, holly and boxwood all respond really well to fall propagation, so you can clone some of your garden favorites to get new plants for free.

Ready to have a go? Here’s exactly what to do.

All these plants can be propagated in October using semi-ripe cuttings, also called semi-hardwood cuttings. Don't be confused by this gardening jargon – it simply means that you’ll be using stems that are woody at the base but green and flexible at the top.

Choose a strong plant and then a healthy stem with leaves but no flowers. Look for recent growth that has firmed up but isn’t totally woody yet – a suitable stem will snap and make a clean break when bent.

Use bypass pruning shears such as these Fiskars SoftGrip Bypass Hand Pruners from Lowe’s and make sure the blades are razor sharp. Sharpening pruner blades takes moments with a cheap tool like this Sharpal Garden Tool Sharpener from Amazon and will make a huge difference to how well your cuttings root. Super-sharp blades will slice cleanly through the stem rather than crushing and bruising it, which is one of the main reasons cuttings fail. For the same reason, don’t use anvil pruners as their crushing action will bruise delicate stem tissue.

Make a cut just below a leaf node, where a leaf joins the stem. Each cutting should be about 4-6 inches (10-15 cm) long, and at this time of the year use the top of stems where growth hormones are concentrated. Remove the lower leaves, preserving a few at the top.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Fill a small pot with a sterile rooting medium that drains well – a soil-less mix such as this Propagation Planting Mix from Amazon is ideal. Poke a pencil into the mix to make a hole and pop 1-1½ inches of your cutting, cut end first, in. Dipping the cut end in a rooting hormone such as Garden Safe Take Root, available from Walmart, speeds success with some plants but this step isn’t always necessary. What is vital, however, is that at least one bare leaf node is submerged in the mix, but no leaves are beneath the surface.

Gently use your fingers to firm the soil around the cutting then water to settle the mix. Now pop a clear plastic bag – a resealable sandwich bag like these from Amazon work well as the zipper closure gives some rigidity – over the pot to make a mini-greenhouse. Use a rubber band around the pot to secure it in place if needs be. Stand this in a spot with bright, indirect light that’s away from cold drafts.

Because the cutting has leaves to support but no roots to supply moisture, you need to keep the rooting medium moist and provide some humidity. The plastic bag will trap moisture inside but mist the leaves every few days if needs be, or reduce moisture by wiping any very heavy condensation.

In a few weeks, you should spot fresh leaves beginning to unfold, which means your cutting has rooted. If there’s no sign of new growth after a month, try giving the stem a very gentle upwards tug – if there’s any resistance, there are roots. A successful cutting will also look firm and plump, while an unsuccessful one will be starting to shrivel by now.

As soon as you know the cutting has rooted, it can come out of its little nursery greenhouse. You'll need to acclimatise the baby plant slowly, so snip off the corners of the bag to let some fresh air in, then snip a little more off the following day and remove the bag entirely on the third day. You’ll now need to keep your young plant watered, and tend it over winter ready to plant out next spring.

Rosemary propagates readily from semi-hardwood cuttings. Choose healthy stems that are still flexible, not totally woody, and without any flowers. Make sure the rooting medium you use for the cutting drains very well as rosemary will not tolerate excess moisture. If your climate is mild, you may be able to keep it outdoors in a sheltered area with bright light. If not, keep inside by a window all winter.

Lavender is similar to rosemary in that it will readily propagate now. Taking lavender cuttings is such an easy way to propagate lavender, and family and friends will love a gift of this popular plant in spring. Avoid the woody stems and choose a flexible stem to cut. Use a rooting mix that drains very well and make sure it never gets too soggy. Overwinter lavender cuttings inside in colder climates.

Most fuchsias are hardy in zones 6 through 11, but leaving them outdoors in winter can be a little risky so taking cuttings and keeping them indoors for the winter gives you a back-up plan. Take a cutting from a healthy, non-flowering stem, and root it in a quality rooting mix.

Some evergreen plants can be propagated from cuttings right now and this an easy way to save money on spring landscaping. Look for semi-hardwood stems to cut that are mature but not totally hardened or woody.

Root your boxwood cuttings in a medium that drains well, and be patient. These cuttings will take a little time to develop adequate roots. For this reason, it’s a good idea to overwinter your new plants indoors rather than trying to get them in the ground outside before winter. It’s also a good idea to take more cuttings than you think you need, in case some fail to root.

Like boxwoods, holly can be rooted from semi-hardwood cuttings. Look for healthy stems, and take more cuttings than you want because, as with boxwoods, these cuttings take longer to root and may not all be successful. Keep your cuttings and potted new plants indoors in a spot with indirect light and good levels of humidity.

Propagating your favorite plants now is so rewarding, and a very cost-efficient way to boost next year’s garden. October cuttings require a little more time and patience than spring and summer cuttings, but they’re so easy as long as you have a little patience. If you are in doubt about cold-weather tolerance, keep cuttings indoors all winter and put your new plants outside only when the weather has warmed in spring.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

From wasp spiders to money spiders, your birth month spider might reveal more about your personality than you think...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

They say if you want to live and thrive, let the spider run alive (which can be hard to remember in the moment), and that feels even more true when the eight-legged critter in question is your birth month spider.

Birth flowers, birthstones, and zodiac signs have long provided us little excuses to find something that feels oddly specific to you. And we’re already familiar with, too, the idea of a birth month bird, birth month animal, and birth month bug , but why should they have all the fun?

If you're willing to look past the fact that spiders are considerably less cuddly than most birth month symbols, I think they make a surprisingly good match. There are thousands of spider species around the world, after all; some are tiny and easy to overlook, while others are spectacular creatures with intricate webs, extraordinary colors and some seriously impressive hunting skills. So you'd best believe there's one that matches you out there...

Keen to find out your birth month spider, then? Of course you are! I've matched each month with a spider based on personality traits commonly associated with people born at that time of year. Think of it as a little bit of nature, a little bit of personality quiz and a good excuse to appreciate the spiders living around us.

So, grab yourself a BugView 5X Magnifying Glass from Carson, and let's see which spider you've been given...

January is often associated with ambition, determination and a willingness to start something new. That makes the jumping spider – every bit as curious, clever and full of energy – a pretty good fit for you.

Jumping spiders are active hunters rather than relying on large webs to catch their meals. They have excellent vision for their size and can make surprisingly precise jumps when pursuing prey. If you're a January baby, you're apparently the type who likes to investigate, explore and figure things out for yourself.... and you probably don't like sitting around waiting for something to happen, either!

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Independent thinkers with a calm and thoughtful side, I'm giving February babies the crab spider. Widely considered to be masters of patience, these arachnids – rather than rushing around looking for prey – tend to sit quietly on flowers or foliage and wait for an insect to come within reach.

They can also be remarkably adaptable, with some species able to change their appearance to blend into their surroundings. In other words, you know when to make yourself noticed – and when it's smarter to sit back and wait.

March is a month of change, so it seems fitting that its spider is one that doesn't wait around for an opportunity. Wolf spiders are active hunters as, instead of relying on a web to capture prey, they move across the ground in search of it.

They're also surprisingly devoted mothers. Female wolf spiders carry their egg sacs with them, and once the spiderlings hatch, the tiny babies can climb onto their mother's back. So if you're a March baby, you're apparently independent and tough – but with a softer side that comes out for the people you care about.

Caring and dependable, April is often associated with optimism, renewal and a generous spirit, so the nursery web spider feels like a natural match.

No surprises, then, that this spider gets its name from the nursery web the female creates for her young. She carries her egg sac with her before eventually placing it somewhere safe and guarding the spiderlings once they hatch.

There's something rather endearing about that, right? Especially as it means you're the dependable one in your friendship group – the person people know they can turn to when they need someone.

May babies are often associated with energy, sociability and curiosity, which makes the green lynx spider a really fun match!

This striking birth month spider is an active predator that often waits among plants for prey. Its coloring helps it blend into vegetation, allowing it to get surprisingly close to insects before making its move.

You're confident, alert and quick-thinking, and probably not someone who misses much; just like your eight-legged pal, you notice what's going on around you, think quickly and aren't afraid to act when the moment is right. Win!

June is the month for the spider with one of nature's most impressive architectural skills, and orb-weaving spiders create those classic, wheel-shaped webs that seem almost impossibly precise. Their webs are functional, delicate and beautiful all at once.

Creative, then? Organized? A (whisper it!) perfectionist? All of this makes the garden orb-weaver a perfect match for June babies, who are often described as creative, detail-oriented and adaptable. You like things done properly – and preferably beautifully, too.

July babies are often associated with confidence, spontaneity and a love of adventure: enter, then, the fishing spider. These impressive spiders are associated with ponds, streams and other bodies of water, and some species can move across the surface of the water while hunting.

They're not afraid to venture somewhere most spiders wouldn't, basically. If this is your birth month spider, then, you're probably the person who hears “you probably shouldn't do that” and immediately becomes more interested in doing it.

August is not a month for blending into the background, so the golden silk orb-weaver is a suitably spectacular birth month spider. These spiders are known for their large webs, distinctive golden silk and striking appearance. Female golden silk orb-weavers can also be dramatically larger than males.

They're attention-grabbers, then – in the best possible way. If you're an August baby, you're more than confident enough to take centerstage when you want to, and comfortable being noticed when you do.

Choose Plants That Attract More Flying Insect:

Confident, dramatic and fiercely individual, September babies often get described as organized, intelligent and self-assured. They also get one of the most spectacular-looking critters on this list of birth month spiders, as it has bold black-and-yellow markings that make it almost impossible to mistake for anything else.

As if that weren't enough, its large web often includes a distinctive zigzag of silk. Subtle? Absolutely not, but if you're a September baby, you're apparently someone who knows who they are and isn't particularly interested in disappearing into the crowd.

October has to get something a little mysterious as its birth month spider, so who better to take that spot than the four-spotted orb-weaver is a striking spider, with four pale spots on its abdomen and a remarkable amount of variation in its coloring. In Britain, it's particularly associated with late summer and fall, making it an especially appropriate choice for October.

People born in October are often described as intuitive, perceptive and a little difficult to read, so this feels right; while you may not always be the loudest person in the room, but you're paying attention – and you probably notice considerably more than people realize.

November babies are resilient, intense and misunderstood, so obviously they get one of the spiders with the biggest reputations.

False widows have developed something of a sinister image, but like most spiders, they're simply predators trying to catch small prey and survive. That makes them a surprisingly good match for November, a month often associated with intensity, independence and resilience.

People may make assumptions about you before they really know you. Their loss, quite frankly.

You're optimistic, resourceful and lucky, so your birth month spider, and it comes with some irresistible symbolism in the money spider.

These tiny spiders are common in British gardens, and folklore has long associated them with good luck and prosperity. They're small and easy to overlook, but they're remarkably widespread and successful, and that seems fitting for December babies.

Basically, you don't necessarily need to be the biggest presence in the room to make an impression... and a little luck certainly doesn't hurt.

I'll admit that I didn't expect to love the idea of birth month spiders, but the more I looked at them, the more I liked the idea. Spiders are so often treated as creepy garden intruders, when they're actually fascinating little predators that play an important role in the ecosystem.

The next time you spot one in your garden, perhaps take a second look before reaching for the broom (or, my favourite, the glass and paper combo); that little arachnid might be doing some useful work among your plants. And, depending on your birth month, it might even have a little something in common with you, too.

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

#165. Kitchen of the Week: A Furniture Maker’s Cleverly Designed Multifunctional Space

From house tours and expert advice to favorite finds and DIYs.

Design-forward shops, hotels, and restaurants for your itinerary.

Renovating? Start here for expert advice, deep dives, and helpful tips.

Our catalog of more than 10,000 products featured on Remodelista.

Remodelista’s members-only directory of architects, designers, and landscape professionals.

There are small spaces, and then there are really small spaces. The apartment of Craig Ross and his partner, Jessie, falls into the latter category. At just under 400-square feet, their flat in Kentish Town, north London, on the first floor of a Victorian townhouse, has just three rooms—which means the kitchen has to also function as the dining and living areas.

Good thing Craig happens to be a furniture designer and maker who recently started fell, a multi-disciplinary design studio co-founded with architect Hilly Murrell (the two met while studying architecture at university). Craig and Jessie’s tiny home became fell’s laboratory, “an opportunity to explore ideas that had been developing in the previous years,” he says. “The main question was ‘could a kitchen be made without the use of sheet material?’—to which the answer was ultimately, yes.” Rather than resorting to using plastic and MDF (medium-density fiberboard) plywood boxes, Craig built a sustainable kitchen with solid beech cabinets and dovetail drawers.

As for the lack of space, Craig’s solution was to design the combination kitchen/dining/living area holistically, leaning on custom light wood built-ins and furniture pieces for cohesiveness. “We focus on the material first, designing and making within the constraints of each material,” he explains. “We’re all about minimising the number of processes and details to highlight the natural beauty, using good materials, and making pragmatic decisions to create a practical and functional end product.”

Craig and Jessie sold their flat not too long ago (see the listing here on The Modern House). We can’t wait to see what they do with their new space. In the meantime, let’s tour their first renovation project.

Photography courtesy of The Modern House.

Fall leaves can be a surprisingly thorny source of neighbor disputes. Find out what homeowners can legally expect from one another.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Autumn leaves have inspired poets and writers for centuries. Emily Brontë wrote, "Every leaf speaks bliss to me, fluttering from the autumn tree." In Virginia Woolf's novels, autumn leaves "fall like golden flakes." But the fiery beauty of falling foliage is somewhat diminished when your neighbor's leaves waft into your yard.

Gardeners may also view fall foliage as fiery and glorious. But when we rake up our oak leaves today then wake up to find the lawn full of the neighbor’s maple leaves, it’s harder to appreciate their beauty. Whether you accept the “leaves the leaves” philosophy or bag them up and dispose of them, nobody likes to have to deal with someone else’s dead foliage.

Are you wondering what your rights are when it comes to the neighbor’s leaves? You’re not alone. While the complete answer depends on the rules in your state, city, or neighborhood, I'm here to give you an overview, including tips about how to proceed. As a former attorney, I often deal with issues like this in my Gardening Lawyer series.

States make laws and cities enact regulations that can impact a property owner’s rights. This includes laws involving neighbors’ rights and responsibilities. Although state and local laws differ, the general rule is that each property owner is responsible for the leaves on their lawn, regardless of whose trees the leaves came from.

The reason for this general rule is fairly easy to understand. It’s all very well if you have oaks and your neighbor has maples. But the more usual case is that you each have both, and the policemen have better things to do than trying to figure out whose trees a lawful of leaves came from.

And look on the bright side, if you shred them (using a shredder like the WORX 13 Amp Electric Leaf Mulcher on Amazon), you will have lots of free leaf mulch for your garden.

Every rule has its exceptions. This includes the general rule that you have to deal with the fallen leaves on your landscape, regardless of whether they came from the neighbor’s yard. The rule applies if the wind blows the leaves over. The exception is when the neighbor blows those leaves over the property line or rakes them up and dumps them into your property.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

What to do if that’s the case? You should report it to your local code enforcement, home owners association (HOA), or local authorities.

Leaves drifting from the other side of the property line onto your lawn are annoying. But in your gutters, they are even more of a problem. Leaves blocking the gutters mean the water cannot run out.

But, like clearing leaves from a lawn, clearing the leaves from a gutter is the responsibility of the owner of the gutter. You cannot sue your neighbor to remove them in most circumstances. If the leaves-in-the-gutter issue causes other problems, like mold in the home, it becomes a nuisance. In that case, with proper evidence, you may be able to take the neighbor to court.

The number one issue that causes a neighbor’s leaves to land in your gutter is overhanging tree branches. The best course of action is to speak with your neighbor first to outline the issue. Ask if they could trim the overhanging tree branches themselves.

But what if they say no, or say yes but never get around to it? The good news is that you have the right to clip back those branches to the property line – from your own side of the fence. Don’t damage the tree and don’t go onto the neighbor’s land to make the cuts.

As described above, the general law is that your neighbor need not clear leaves from their trees that the wind blows onto your property. Leaves blowing in the breeze across the property line are an act of nature.

But what if it isn’t an act of nature? What does the law say if your neighbor blows the leaves back over the fence to your property? If the neighbor takes action to get those leaves on your property – using a leaf blower or raking up the leaves into a sack and dumping them over the fence – it is no longer considered an act of nature. It’s the same as dumping garbage on your land, and you can definitely get local authorities involved.

To prove that the neighbor deliberately shifts their leaves to your property, photographic evidence is essential. Photos are good; videos are better. Set up a motion-sensor camera in the backyard to get the evidence – HITELLARCAM is a well-rated budget choice.

In addition, start keeping a calendar. Put into the calendar when you talk to the neighbor, when your gutters or lawns fill up, when you empty the gutters or rake your lawn, when you cut back the branches.

If you are also claiming additional damage (like mold in the house), you’ll need expert testimony on the source. Call in a plumber to check for mold and write up an opinion linking the mold to the leaves in the gutters.

Going to court is neither fun nor cheap, and it almost always leaves bad feelings between neighbors. That’s why it pays to try to negotiate a solution with your neighbor.

The first thing to do in every situation is to let the neighbor know about the issue. Try to have a casual conversation about the issue – no threats, no attorneys, no rage. Walk out into the garden or invite them to climb up a ladder to peer into your gutters. Let them know that it’s becoming a problem for you, and you would like their help with it.

If discussions get stuck, suggest a mediator to work with you. If you have an HOA, they may be able to provide the mediator. If not, ask at City Hall.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. #168. 14 DIY Solutions for a Pest-Free Home

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Updated Oct 13, 2026 5:23 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Cohabitating with unwelcome critters is no one’s idea of fun. Armed with a few basic tools and a bit of knowledge, however, you can create a pest-free environment in no time. While professional pest-control services are certainly an option, they can be expensive and may involve the use of chemicals that can pose health risks to homeowners. Fortunately, these DIY methods can help you reclaim your home or garden from pesky invaders and restore your peace of mind.

Keep mosquitoes and biting flies from crashing your patio party with wine bottles. Fill a few empty glass bottles one- to two-thirds full with sand, small stones, or marbles. Then pour citronella-scented lamp oil in up to the neck of each bottle—this will give you several hours of burn time. Drill a hole through each cork and thread a piece of cotton rope through each hole, long enough to reach the sand or stones at the bottom with an inch exposed above the cork. As soon as the wick soaks up the oil, light and enjoy a bug-free backyard.

Ants are as big a nuisance inside the house as they are at a picnic. To keep them away from your food prep surfaces—and everywhere else, for that matter—deter them by washing countertops, floors, walls, and other surfaces with a mixture of equal parts apple cider vinegar and water.

RELATED: 15 Plants to Grow for a Pest-Proof Yard

It might seem like a shame to waste a good brewski, but beer will help rid your garden of slugs practically overnight. Take a wide-mouthed plastic or glass container, then bury it about two-thirds in the ground and fill it up about a quarter of the way with beer. The fermented yeast in the drink will attract slugs, causing them to fall in and drown. Empty the container every day or so, and refresh the beer until your slug problems are a thing of the past.

A mixture of 1/2 cup rubbing alcohol and 1 quart of liquid soap can make an effective pest-control spray to get rid of whiteflies, aphids, mealy bugs, scale insects, and thrips. Fill a spray bottle with the solution, shake it, and spritz directly on your plants. Let the mixture sit for 20 minutes, and then rinse the plant thoroughly to avoid damaging the leaves. Save this task until dusk; in direct sunlight, the solution can burn the leaves. Spray every 3 days for 2 weeks, until the bugs are gone.

RELATED: 20 Common Garden Pests and How to Get Rid of Them

Prevent biting flies, horseflies, and mosquitoes with natural repellents derived from plant-based ingredients. Natural pesticides are generally considered safe for human use and do not pose significant health risks, unlike chemical repellents. To make your own bug repellent, fill a spray bottle with 2 ounces of witch hazel, 2 ounces of distilled water, and 10-15 drops of essential oil (think citronella, lavender, and lemongrass). Mix well and spray on skin, taking care to protect your eyes.

If beetles are giving you trouble in the garden, whip up this recipe to protect your plants: Soak 2 cups of chopped tomato leaves in a pint of water overnight. Strain to remove the leaves, then add another pint of water and 1/4 teaspoon of liquid soap. Spray foliage and soil with this diluted mixture as needed. This solution also works against earworms and maggots.

RELATED: 15 Natural Pest-Control Strategies for Your Yard and Garden

Nematodes—tiny parasitic worms that live in the soil—as well as caterpillars and grasshoppers can wreak havoc on your vegetable garden. But molasses “tea” can be the natural solution for helping preserve your produce. To make it, dissolve 3 tablespoons of molasses in 4 cups of warm water in a spray bottle, and then shake well. Spray your plants and the ground around them every few days to keep pests away.

You can have your bananas and eat them, too, without fighting off fruit flies in your kitchen. Craft a simple homemade trap by pouring apple cider vinegar and a squirt of liquid dish soap in a cup or small dish. Cover the container with plastic wrap and poke a few small holes in the top so you can lure the flies in without their being able to slip back out.

Save your pet from endless itching with a little DIY repellent. Simmer 2 cups of water, a sliced lemon, and fresh lavender sprigs in a saucepan for 30 minutes. Strain out and discard the larger pieces, then add 2 tablespoons of alcohol-free witch hazel to the cooled concoction. Transfer it to a spray bottle so you can mist and rub the solution into Fido’s fur before he heads outdoors.

Save your friends and family from stings this season with a homemade wasp trap. Cut a recycled water bottle in half. Invert the top (the bottleneck) and slip it inside the bottom half like a funnel, and tape the pieces together. Then fill with a seasonally appropriate bait: In spring, wasps go for grease from cooked meat with water and a little dish soap, but in summer they’re more attracted to sugary fruit preserves with water and dish soap. The buzzing pests will fly in easily, but they won’t be able to fly back out through the funnel’s small hole.

RELATED: How To Get Rid of Bees (Without Harming Them)

Sticky traps can be wildly effective at snagging winged pests before they swoop in on your garden plants, so why not recreate their magic with the materials you have on hand? Mix 1 quart corn syrup with 1 quart water, bring the solution to a boil on the stovetop, then brush it on brightly colored paper to attract the offending insects. Place the sticky strip of paper in your garden on the end of a popsicle stick or clothespin, or hang it from a string, to trap flying invaders.

Vinegar is a common household ingredient that can be a powerful tool in getting rid of wasps. Combine 2 cups apple cider vinegar, 2 cups sugar, and 1 cup water in a spray bottle. Locate the wasp’s nest and, keeping a safe distance away, saturate it with the vinegar solution, focusing on the entry points and the nest itself. The vinegar’s strong odor and acidity will deter the wasps, eventually killing them. Note: Spray the nest during the evening, when wasps are less active, to avoid stings. Alternatively, you can pour the mixture into a DIY wasp trap and hang the trap near the wasp nest.

If you’re dealing with a cockroach infestation, try a DIY bait for removing them. Mix equal parts boric acid powder and powdered or granulated sugar. The sugar serves as an attractive bait, while the boric acid acts as an insecticide. Sprinkle the mixture in areas where cockroaches are frequently seen: think dark corners, under appliances, and along baseboards. The roaches will be attracted to the bait, consume it, and carry it back to their nests, where it will spread and kill other roaches.

Note: Borax can be toxic if ingested in large quantities, so don’t use this in accessible places if you have young children or small animals.

Diatomaceous earth can be an effective DIY bed bug treatment. Typically sold as a powder, it’s made from the fossilized remains of diatoms, a type of algae. Simply apply it to mattress seams, cracks and crevices, along baseboards, or under appliances to control bed bugs. Note: Be sure to use food-grade diatomaceous earth, as it is safe for humans and pets.

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned and Loved About Them

From crown molding and built-ins to creaky floors and drafty windows, old houses are full of charm and challenges. So we’re celebrating all the things that make old homes worth loving, living in, and fixing up. Learn about historic house styles; find practical advice for maintaining your old home; and discover quirky, forgotten features you simply won’t find in new builds.

All these smart techniques used by landscape designers to bring light and beauty to a dark garden can be achieved without spending a fortune.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The best landscape-designer tricks to make the most of a shady, north-facing garden will transform a dull, dark plot into an inviting outdoor space where you'll want to linger. Designing a garden with this aspect is all about bringing more light to the space as well as selecting the right shade-tolerant plants that will flourish in these conditions. A shady garden brings wonderful opportunities that simply aren't possible in a sunny south-facing garden, so rather than thinking of a north-facing plot as a problem, make it work to your advantage.

One of the main challenges will be the lack of direct sunlight, which can make your outdoor space feel dull and gloomy, as well as restricting the types of plants you can grow. Tall buildings or trees blocking available sunlight compounds the issue, especially as we head into the winter months when the sun is lower in the sky. But all these landscape designer tricks will overcome such issues to create a covetable garden that you won't want to swap for a sunnier plot.

Which will you use to brighten up your shady north-facing yard?

Opting for lighter-colored materials for paths, patios and other hardscaped areas will reflect light as well as brighten the space, making a shady or north-facing garden a much more pleasant place to be. Choose porcelain or limestone pavers, and pebbles or river stones in pale tones of soft gray, sand, buff or other light neutrals, to make the most of whatever sunlight your garden gets. This also visually expands the space, which is one of the most common methods landscape designers use to make a small garden feel bigger.

It needn't be an expensive job to swap out existing darker paving for a lighter option such as these limestone-look porcelain pavers from The Home Depot, as long as you don't change the dimensions of the paved area and choose tiles of the same size. Lifting old pavers carefully means you'll keep the substrate intact, and can sell the old pavers on Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist.

Shady garden design starts with a strong base of foliage-first plants, to which flowering varieties are added. Layered planting is a big trend with landscape designers right now and it can be used to create a relaxed, immersive feel that helps soften the edges of shady, north-facing gardens too. There are plenty of varieties of leafy plants that thrive in low sunlight levels, so you be very intentional in the shades of green you choose.

Ferns are one of the most valuable plant groups for north-facing gardens and work particularly well to add vibrancy when combined with Fatsia japonica and hosta. All these plants are available in varieties with zingy green leaves and lighter-colored foliage that catches the light and helps to brighten dark borders and corners. You can also use plants with variegated foliage to add colour and interest in shaded areas.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Choose this bushy and compact variety of fern to anchor your shady planting scheme. Growing to around 3ft tall, it's a perennial that reliably returns every year with fronds emerging green then turning a soft yellow.

Now's a great time to get cost-effective hosta bare roots into the ground, and this striking variety flourishes in full shade with leaves that open in a dreamy cream hue then develop eye-catching green veins.

This reliable Carex variety is a super choice for full shade and tolerates wet soil well in zones 5-8, with the white edges of its arching blades brightening up a gloomy border a treat. Grows 1-2 feet tall and wide.

Shade is often viewed as a disadvantage because it limits the choice of plants you can grow. But there are plenty of flowering plants that flourish in the shade, and by choosing varieties with luminous white blooms, the pale petals will lift any gloomy or shady space, dancing around the foil of zingy foliage you've created.

Flowering shrubs such as hydrangeas are one of the most consistently reliable shade-loving plants, offering masses of blooms right through summer and fall. There are plenty of pale-bloomed flowering varieties to choose from including garden favorite Hydrangea arborescens 'Annabelle', available from trees.com, that brings luxurious white pompom blooms to partial shade. In a more compact space, Hydrangea paniculata 'Little Lime', also available from trees.com, is a new dwarf form that also appreciates partial shade.

Landscape designers know the power of choosing several key plants and repeating them in groups of three, five or seven throughout the design to add continuity and flow. This is an easy planting solution for shady, north-facing gardens too, as you simply choose plants that will work in these conditions and multiply them to build up your collection.

But here's the clever bit. Choose three unfussy plants that flourish in partial shade to plant throughout as these will typically cope with both a little more sun and a touch more shade. Then in areas of deeper shade, add a couple of varieties that prefer full shade, and in sunnier spots, swap these out for two sun-loving plants. That way, the planting is cohesive, linking the shady and sunny areas rather than having a stark contrast between them.

Be intentional when choosing your three key plants so each takes on a different role in the design. In this garden, which ranges from partial shade to full sun, there are repeat plantings of clipped evergreen hebe shrubs for structure, tall perennial foxglove beardtongue for airy flowers, and low-growing Mexican fleabane for groundcover. All these plants prefer full sun but cope very well with partial shade.

North-facing gardens can be wonderfully immersive spaces, lush with green foliage and pale-petalled flowers. But landscape designers will always ensure there is also accent planting to create focal points that elevate the entire scheme.

It's an inescapable fact that plants that produce the most vibrant colors are typically those that prefer full sun. That's because a great deal of energy is needed to produce intense pigments, which plants generate through photosynthesis using sunlight. However, by carefully mapping how sun and shade moves through your garden over time, you can identify spots that get the most sunshine, and use these to add accent plants that landscape designers love but are easy to grow yourself.

To create a simple shadow map to identify where these prime spots are, do a very simple sketch of your plot from an upstairs window. Then every two hours throughout the day, mark on the patches of shade. By the end of the day, you'll quickly see where the deepest patches of shade are, and which areas are only cast into darkness for a couple of hours, where a showstopper plant such as this fabulous Japanese dogwood, which likes full sun to partial shade, will thrive.A useful tool to help you identify these prime accent-plant positions is a digital soil tester that also measures sunlight intensity such as this 4-in-1 moisture meter from Amazon.

One way to bring the illusion of light to a shady garden is a water feature that reflects the sky. This will help to stretch your space and bounce any available light around the garden to create bright spots in shady areas. Adding a few drops of black pond dye such as Aquascape, available from Wayfair, turns the water into a dark mirror that clearly reflects trees, sky, and surroundings. Add a micropond to a border and the water will reflect the overhanging leaf and flower shapes all around it, too.

Other reflective surfaces like garden mirrors can achieve the same effect and make a shady, north-facing garden appear lighter and brighter by reflecting sunlight across the space. Carefully positioned on a shaded wall, fence or shed, a garden mirror will add a bright note. They can also help make the garden feel much larger, in the same way mirrors are used in interior design.

Use mirrored balls like this Outdoor Gazing Ball from Wayfair to capture the reflections of plants, the sky and sunlight, too.

A well-designed garden lighting scheme is always a key element landscape designers add to the mix in a north-facing garden. Garden lights can be used to great effect in dark shade during the day to highlight planting, garden sculpture or architectural features.

In addition to brightening the space, lighting your garden will draw more attention to landscape design elements by enhancing shapely trees like Japanese maples and sculptural plants such as agave or yucca. If you're using solar lights like these stake spotlights from The Home Depot, you'll obviously need to position them in a spot that gets sun for part of the day to charge, but then they'll add a glow once light levels fall. Choosing warm-toned lights will add a far softer ambience than cooler bright white lights.

If you're on a budget and want to brighten a north-facing garden without a major overhaul, one of the most cost-effective solutions is to paint boundary fences or walls in a lighter tone. This will immediately transform the space, bringing a much brighter feel to a garden that's mostly shaded.

Try light neutrals and soft, muted pastels in shades like pale gray, buff, cream, and willow or sage green – one of the strongest fence-color trends in 2026. If you want to pick up on the green trend then Glidden Fundamentals Light Sage Satin Exterior Paint, available from Walmart is a lovely option. Alternatively for a neutral cream try Glidden Fundamentals Oatmeal Satin Exterior Paint, also available from Walmart. Opt for a satin finish rather than matt as this will bounce the light around rather than absorbing it.

To avoid a big stretch of painted boundary, soften the look with fence landscaping ideas.

One of the easiest ways to switch up the look in a north-facing garden is by planting up pots with shade-loving plants that love life in a container. Whether it's a small urban courtyard garden overlooked by apartment buildings or a patio close to the house that doesn't get much sun, there are plenty of attractive options to create an appealing combination in a planter.

Reliable container garden favorites including hydrangea, hosta, ferns and ornamental Carex, adding precious blooms and interesting foliage to bring life and light into dark corners of your yard. Containers in shady spots need less watering and deadheading, and flowers tend to last longer than those in scorching sunshine, so there really are advantages to having a north-facing plot!

Ever wanted to save harvested tomato seeds for future growing, only to find that they stick to paper towels? Here’s why a basket coffee filter is a brilliant (and cheap) workaround

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Many home growers still save tomato seeds (and seeds from other fall harvests) by smearing them across a damp paper towel. Yes, it feels quick and convenient in the moment. But that convenience vanishes in spring, when many prized seeds are frustratingly cemented to the towel. Some pull away with a papery crust torn onto their seed coats, while others refuse to budge no matter how carefully you scrape.

The result: fewer viable seeds to plant, and fewer mouth-watering crops to look forward to enjoying next summer. The thing is, that frustrating waste can easily be avoided. There is a simple, brilliant workaround that is equally affordable, remarkably easy, and far kinder to delicate seed coats. And the secret is likely sitting right next to your kitchen coffee machine.

Store-brand basket coffee filters are a game-changer for seed harvesting, especially in fall when tomatoes, peppers, squash, and juicy cucumbers are all finishing up in the same few weeks. Plain white coffee filters are cheap and readily available. More importantly, gelatinous seeds cannot bond to them the way they do to plush paper towels. Here’s how a simple pack of filters can set you up for a budget-friendly seed-starting season.

As anyone who grows tomatoes knows, the seeds are wrapped in a slippery gel called a mucilaginous sheath. This holds inhibitors that stop seeds from sprouting inside a warm, ripe tomato, and plain water won’t wash it away. Cucumbers have their own slippery coatings, while squash seeds are tangled in stringy pulp. Soft berries like blackberries and strawberries are messier still, with tiny seeds buried in sugary flesh.

So once you slice into your harvests, the clock is already ticking. If you’re looking for a knife, super-sharp Victorinox Swiss Classic 3.25-Inch Paring Knife, available from Amazon, comes with a range of colored handles (including fall-festive orange).

Once any of the slippery casings, pulp or berry stuff starts drying, it behaves like rubber cement, grabbing onto whatever it touches. This is why it feels instinctive to reach for a paper towel. Most paper towels are made by blowing hot air through wet pulp sheets at the mill, creating a fluffy, bulky texture full of microscopic air gaps and loose fibers.

When seed-starting this way, a wet seed sits on a paper towel, its damp coating wicks deep down into those paper gaps and sets hard. As moisture evaporates, the seed coat and paper fibers interlock permanently. Prying them apart risks damaging the outer seed coat or leaves paper fragments attached, which can trap excess moisture during planting and invite fungi.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Think about it: coffee filters are designed to survive a basket of heavy, wet grounds and a stream of near-boiling water without falling apart. Filter paper is dense and tightly woven using a wet-strength additive. Water passes through it rather than soaking in, allowing the sheet to dry rapidly in room air. Standard unbleached or white basket filters flatten out into a wide, shallow area that holds a generous spread of seeds.

If you need some fast at a bargain price, Great Value White Basket Coffee Filters (200 Count), available from Walmart, are just a couple of dollars. They can hold dozens of drying seeds without letting any stick or embed.

That tight, smooth paper surface is precisely what makes coffee filters the ultimate seed-drying tool. The gel coating of a seed has nowhere to sink into, so the wet seed gel dries on top of the paper rather than inside it. Once dry, most seeds pop free with a gentle flex of the filter or a light tap from your finger. A few stubborn seeds might hang on if they had pulp attached, but even those brush off without tearing.

Plain unbleached basket filters are best, as heavy cone filters are stiffer and less flexible, while textured or quilted paper towels should be avoided entirely. Paper plates, glass pie plates and old window screens might work too if those are on hand. Filters are just cheap, and they stack flat in storage between seasons.

The filter only handles the drying phase, so you need to clean your seeds first to ensure long-term viability. Wet seeds like tomatoes and cucumbers benefit from a short fermentation process to dissolve the gel and eliminate seed-borne pathogens. Squeeze seeds, juice, and gel into a small jar with a splash of water. Cover with a cloth and leave in a warm spot, around 72-80°F (22-27°C) for 2-3 days, stirring daily. A white film on top is normal. When ready, pour off the top liquid and floating dud seeds. Then rinse the plump, viable seeds at the bottom until the water runs clean.

Peppers, pole beans, and winter squash are simpler. Ripe pepper seeds can be scraped directly off the core onto a filter. Winter squash and melon seeds just need the stringy pulp picked off before a quick rinse. For tiny berry seeds or passionfruit, mashing gently through a fine mesh strainer separates the juice from the seeds.

If you need a good strainer, choose something with fine gaps. The OXO Good Grips 3-Inch Mini Strainer, available from Amazon, is a comfortable hand sieve for small batches of squash, cucumber, or berry seeds. Allow freshly rinsed seeds to drain briefly in your strainer (or a narrow colander) before transferring them to your filter, in order to ensure the excess pool water doesn't soak the paper.

Write your labels on the dry filter before adding damp seeds. Use a permanent marker or pencil along the outer rim to write the seed name, variety and harvest date. Dried tomato seeds look identical once dehydrated, making early labeling essential. Place the labeled filter on a wire cooling rack or ceramic dinner plate, so air can circulate underneath the paper. For a multi-tiered option, the Geesta Rose Gold 4-Tier Drying Rack from Amazon helps speed up drying times.

Spread seeds out using tweezers, a toothpick or fingertip so that none are touching, since crowded seeds dry slowly and can fuse together. Set your drying rack in a warm, dry room out of direct sunlight with good airflow. You can use the top of your fridge, which runs a little warm. However, avoid fast-heating shortcuts like food dehydrators, ovens, microwaves, or hair dryers. Any temperatures above 95°F (35°C) can kill the delicate living embryos inside your seeds.

Shake or stir your seeds on the filter once every day to ensure even air exposure on all sides. Most tomato and pepper seeds dry fully in 7-10 days, while squash and melon seeds take 10-14 days. To test for dryness, bend a seed: if it flexes softly, it needs more time; if it snaps crisp or feels rock-hard, your batch is ready for storage.

Once your seeds pass the snap-test, you can transfer them into storage containers. Paper seed envelopes, glassine packets, or tiny airtight glass jars or vials work well for seed storage. Just bear in mind that you need to add new labels. Store seed packets in a cool, dark, dry location: a closet shelf, a dry basement, or an airtight container in the refrigerator works best.

Avoid areas prone to humidity spikes or heat fluctuations, such as humid laundry rooms or sunny windowsills, as moisture and ambient heat are the main causes for degrading seed viability. If you’re looking for a seed tin to store multiple sets of seeds, we love the vintage-looking Haaray Seed Storage Organizer Box from Walmart. This charming tin comes with locks and a strap to keep your seeds safe, dry, organized and safe from pests.

Properly dried tomato, pepper, and squash seeds remain viable for 3-5 years, while brassicas and cucumber seeds can last up to 6 years. Always label your storage packets with the harvest year, so you know which batches to sow first come spring. When late winter or early spring arrives, your homegrown indoor seeds will slide out of their envelopes, ready to germinate into a rewarding new season of crops.

Saving your own seeds from fall harvests is one of the most satisfying, cost-effective ways to bulk up your future crops, without having to spend unnecessarily on seed packets. Just make sure you prepare your seeds with this method, and you’ll be safeguarding lots more seeds for next year’s plants. By swapping out sticky paper towels for simple coffee filters, you eliminate seed loss, protect delicate seed coats, and ensure a clean, easy release come spring. So, grab that box of filters, clear a quiet counter corner, and start saving your favorite heirloom varieties this weekend.

When landscape designer Emily Erlam and her family were searching for real estate in East Anglia—where she had grown up a few miles from the sea—they found an unusual home, in what might euphemistically be called “unused agricultural buildings.”

“We bought the old barn and piggery,” she recently told The Modern House, “down the road from my mum.”

After a major remodel (“we’ve kept the original flint wall of the piggery, and almost everything else is new,” she said), Erlam’s challenge was to create a garden that felt like an extension of the indoor living spaces. “As a family we live outside as much as we do inside; even in the winter the four of us will sit outside on the veranda and have a cup of tea,” she said. “And, being a landscape designer, I was focused on how to extend the internal footprint to outdoor living spaces by connecting the building with planted areas up close to the house.”

The solution? Two courtyards, entered through multiple doors in both buildings, planted with a rich mix of perennials, grasses, and evergreens for year-round color. Let’s look at how the indoor and outdoor living spaces connect:

#175. 7 Common Household Water Issues and How to Fix Them

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Updated Oct 13, 2026 11:59 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Clean, potable water is essential for everyday life: You need it to drink, cook, wash, and bathe all from the comfort of your home. When the water coming from your taps starts to smell weird, look odd, or taste funny, it can be distressing. The good news is that the causes of these problems are usually common ones, and the remedies well known and fairly easy to implement (especially for water quality issues that occur in specific geographical locations, as detailed by this EPA Consultants report).

While it may be frustrating to find out that your tap water might not be as clean and pure as you thought, there are solutions available to you. Troubleshooting is easy once you match your water’s problematic odors, appearance, or tastes with these corresponding solutions.

Solve multiple household water problems with one system. The Kind Water Systems E-3000 Whole House Water Filter and Salt-Free Conditioner treats every tap in the home: carbon block filtration reduces more than 155 contaminants, including chlorine, pesticides, and other chemicals, a sediment stage captures 95 percent of dirt and rust, and salt-free conditioning helps prevent scale buildup in pipes and appliances. Rated for 15 GPM with no loss in pressure, it fits homes with up to five bathrooms. Concerned about bacteria? The E-3000UV adds UV treatment that reduces 99.9 percent of bacteria and viruses.

Problem: When you notice white or chalky mineral deposits around your plumbing fixtures, this is a sign that your home has hard water. Hard water occurs when water has elevated mineral content, generally made up of high concentrations of calcium and magnesium. This can leave unsightly residue on your plumbing fixtures, create limescale buildup in your appliances that use water, and can make your hair and skin feel rough and dry.

Solution: There are a few ways to remove hard water staining, including using citric acid-based cleaners or vinegar to help dissolve any mineral deposits left on these surfaces. But to deal with the root of the problem Robert Schwachenwald, plumber and owner of Bizzy Bee Plumbing Inc., mentions that you can “treat high mineral content with a point-of-use filtration system to resolve taste concerns, but you should contact a plumber if the taste changes suddenly, indicating advancing corrosion or water quality shifts.” Alternatively, you can invest in a whole-home water softener to treat the water as soon as it enters the home.

Problem: If your water looks cloudy or rusty, it typically indicates a high amount of iron or manganese in the water. While this is not usually a direct health hazard, these contaminants can cause significant aesthetic problems, like rusty-orange or black staining. You will often see the stains on plumbing fixtures, sinks, tubs, and water-using appliances. And in some cases, it can even stain your clothing after using the washing machine.

Solution: The surest method for dealing with high iron or manganese in your household water is to invest in a water softener with an iron removal feature. Depending on the size of your home and how prevalent the issue, you can choose a point-of-use softener or a whole-home water softener as an effective solution for reducing iron levels. Another option is to install an oxidizing filter to help eliminate iron and prevent staining.

Problem: It’s never pleasant when your water has an odd scent or taste, such as a rotten egg odor. Schwachenwald explains that this is typically caused by “hydrogen sulfide gas from bacteria reacting with magnesium in water heaters.” It can occur outside of your water heater as well, though this is less likely for most homes. When hydrogen sulfide occurs in high enough concentrations, it causes the rotten egg stink, leaving an unpleasant odor on hair and clothing, while accelerating the corrosion of metal parts in appliances.

Solution: If the issue seems to occur in both the hot and cold water, then it’s best to install a whole-house activated carbon filter to remove the hydrogen sulfide from the water as it enters the home. You can also invest in a specific sulfur water treatment system designed specifically to remove these odors and improve the overall water quality. However, if the smell is only present in your hot water, Schwachenwald says that you can often fix this issue with “water heater flushing, but if it keeps happening, the element in the water heater may need to be replaced.”

Problem: The sight of brown water flowing out of your tap can be disconcerting, but this is often a minor issue caused by disturbed plumbing, such as when the water to the home is shut down for a short period of time. Similarly, a gritty texture in your sink usually indicates the presence of sediment, rust, or mineral buildup that has been dislodged. Schwachenwald mentions that it often “comes from aging pipes or water heater sediment. They should really be flushed every year to get rid of mineral buildup.”

Solution: Before you take any drastic measures, Schwachenwald suggests “running the cold water for a few minutes. If the brown color stops, it was caused by sediment disturbance, but if it keeps happening, it is time for a water heater flush or evaluation of your aged plumbing.” In extreme cases you may need to replace aging pipes in the home, but if you suspect the sediment is entering from outside your house, then installing a sediment filter with a low micron rating can effectively remove particles and improve water clarity.

Problem: A musty smell or fishy taste point to compounds that have been released into the water due to decayed vegetation. Generally, this type of issue is associated with different forms of algae. While it is not toxic, the scent and smell are unpleasant. For well water, these odors can indicate contamination from surface runoff or bacterial buildup within the well system.

Solution: These odors are not usually harmful, but it’s still recommended to have your water tested, especially if you use a well system. In the short term, you can run cold water for several minutes to flush out stagnant water and check if the smell disappears. If the home has a water filter, then this could be a sign that the filter is saturated and needs to be replaced. Musty odors that persist should be reported to your municipal water supplier.

For the cost of the kit, you’ll get comprehensive results from an EPA-certified lab covering 200 water-quality parameters. See our tested review.

Problem: One of the more serious situations you could encounter is a slimy, black or reddish-brown residue in your sinks, faucets, and water-using appliances. This residue is typically made up of bacteria colonies and bacterial waste. Seeing this type of residue in your drains is relatively harmless, but when it is coming from your clean water fixtures, it can indicate that the water is contaminated. Unfortunately, even well-operated, state-of-the-art treatment plants cannot always ensure that drinking water is entirely free of microbial pathogens.

Solution: The first step you should take if you suspect bacterial contamination is to have the water tested. This test will identify the type and concentration of the bacteria. In the short term, you should boil all water before using it and consider installing a whole-home water filter with a sub-micron rating. For long term bacterial contamination issues and preventative measures, consider installing an ultraviolet sterilization disinfection system or an automatic chlorinator that will continuously inject safe levels of chlorine into the water to eliminate bacterial growth.

Problem: When the pH of the water is low, the water is acidic. This acidic state can cause those blue-green stains on sinks, tubs, showers, and toilets. Acidic water isn’t generally a health hazard, but it does pose a risk to your plumbing infrastructure. Exposure to the water can lead to premature damage of the pipes, fixtures, and metal components of your water-using appliances.

Solution: Testing the water will confirm whether the water is acidic or not. Acidic water can be treated by installing an acid-neutralizing filter or putting in a soda ash feeder to raise the pH. “Over half of our service calls involve water quality or appearance concerns. Water is always interacting with pipes, valves and fixtures, so if it is persistent, worsening, or affecting multiple fixtures, call a plumber,” says Schwachenwald.

From the last glorious flowers to the first chilly nights, October brings a change in priorities for rose lovers. Here's where to focus your efforts.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

October is a transition time for roses in many growing zones. Your goal now should not be to promote more growth or flowering, but essentially to put them to bed for winter. You might still have some blooms right now, but the shorter days and cooler temperatures are signaling the plants to prepare for dormancy.

It’s not quite time yet for your roses to be dormant, but it is time to get ready. In October, you should be cleaning up, watering, doing a little light pruning, and avoiding triggering any new growth. Growing roses successfully depends on this end-of-season care, so take a little time to complete these important tasks while stopping others.

Some types of roses benefit from deadheading, which encourages reblooming. If you grow these varieties, which include floribundas and grandifloras, you’ve probably been picking off spent flowers all summer and into early fall. This prevents flowers from developing rose hips and, instead, puts energy into more blooms.

By October, you can stop this task. Let some rose hips develop to signal to the plant that it is slowing down and preparing to enter dormancy. Rose hips also offer good visual interest as the season winds down and help feed local wildlife.

Roses are notoriously prone to disease, so cleaning up around plants is an essential hygiene task. Removing and disposing of plant debris, whether it looks diseased or not, helps prevent the spread of pathogens, including bacteria and fungi, which can overwinter there.

Remove fallen leaves from around the bases of roses as well as any lower leaves that look diseased or are damaged. Don’t put these in the compost pile. Dispose of them with yard waste or garbage.

If your roses struggled with a disease like black spot or powdery mildew this year, thorough fall cleanup is your first line of defense. Then, next spring, consider applying a preventative rose fungicide before new foliage emerges to help protect fresh growth. I like BioAdvanced All-in-One Rose and Flower Care Granules, available on Amazon, because they double as a fertilizer.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As you clean up debris and remove any questionable leaves, you can also do some light fall rose pruning. Save the hard pruning for late winter or early spring. For now, it’s best to exercise restraint. Too much trimming triggers fresh growth that will only get damaged by winter conditions.

Focus on removing any dead, damaged, or diseased canes. It’s also a good idea to trim back the height a little on taller plants. This will protect them from winter winds that can damage canes or loosen roots in the soil. Remove about one-third of the height of tall canes. Climbing roses are exceptions to this. Rather than trimming them back, tie and train them against their supports.

When pruning roses, it's essential to use clean, sharp pruners to avoid damaging stems and spreading disease. In our testing, the best garden pruners were Felco F6 pruning shears, available on Amazon.

Along with stopping the chore of deadheading, you can also stop feeding your roses. Fertilizing now, especially with a high-nitrogen product, will trigger new, green growth. This new growth is wasted energy for a plant going dormant.

New growth is tender and highly susceptible to damage. Damaged green growth isn’t just wasted energy. It can also introduce pathogens and disease into otherwise healthy plants. Instead, wait until your roses begin actively growing again in spring before feeding. A balanced rose fertilizer, such as Espoma Organic Rose-tone, will provide a steady supply of nutrients to support healthy foliage and abundant blooms as the new season gets underway.

It’s a mistake to assume that cooler weather means plants don’t need any watering. While you may water less as temperatures drop, especially if your area is getting rain, roses benefit from water right up until the ground freezes. If it isn’t raining once or twice a week, you should be watering.

Water deeply at ground level to avoid splashing leaves. Water your roses whenever the top layer of soil feels dry. Potted roses may need watering more often. While you don’t want the soil constantly wet, adequate water will hydrate your plants and better prepare them for a healthy winter dormancy.

If you aren't sure how dry the soil is, use a moisture meter, like the Yamron 4-in-1 soil moisture meter, available on Amazon, which also checks for soil pH, light intensity, and temperature – all factors that can affect the performance of roses.

Depending on where you garden, October may or may not be the right time to apply winter protection for roses. Either way, it’s a good time to start planning and, if needed, implementing these protection measures. Older, hardier roses might not need much, but smaller plants, hybrid roses, potted plants, and roses in more exposed areas can benefit from protection.

Wait until a hard freeze before you use any significant protection. If you do it too early, you can interfere with the plants’ transition into dormancy. Protection options include applying mulch, like Miracle-Gro Organic All Natural Mulch from Home Depot, around the base, tying canes together, or using a rose collar around the plants. Rose collars, like these pop-up rose cones on Amazon, are especially useful for potted roses, which are more vulnerable to winter cold.

Effective October rose care is all about restraint. The focus is on doing less as the plants prepare for winter dormancy. This doesn’t mean doing nothing, of course. You’re winding down care, not stopping entirely. Clean up around roses, do any necessary trimming, keep watering as needed, and let the deadheading and fertilizing go. With these simple steps, your roses will enter dormancy healthy and ready to grow and bloom again next year.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.
