This pretty purple crocus produces the red threads behind the priciest spice on the shelf – and if you plant corms now, you can harvest in 6 weeks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Saffron is one of the tastiest, most expensive spices on the planet but if you have a sunny well-drained corner in your garden, it’s simple to grow your own. Grow saffron crocus and the purple petals are a beautiful fall addition to any yard, too.

Saffron comes from Crocus sativus, a fall-blooming crocus with lavender flowers that each hold three slender red stigmas. Those stigmas are the spice. When commercially grown, every single one is plucked by hand and around 150 flowers go into a single gram of dried threads — which pretty much explains the price on that tiny grocery-store jar.

Growing the plant at home is so easy, though, and you don’t need many of those stigmas to pack a powerful flavor punch. Grow saffron crocus and you can enjoy flowers the very first autumn in a sunny patch of ground, and the corms multiply for a bigger harvest every year after.

Crocus sativus grows from bulb-like corms and while August or September is the usual planting time, you can get away with planting in October as this is a tough plant, hardy in zones 4-8. Saffron crocus corms are available from Jackson & Perkins and should be planted as soon as they arrive. Corms left sitting in the bag too long can sprout and fizzle out before they ever touch soil.

In zones 5 through 8, saffron crocus overwinters outdoors without much fuss. Zone 4 works too, as long as the soil is very well drained. Good drainage is the key to growing these corms successfully in all zones, however, as they tend to rot in soil that stays soggy for long stretches. So, if you have heavy clay soil that hangs onto water, growing saffron crocus in a raised bed makes sense.

You can also grow crocus in pots around a foot (30cm) or so across, as long as they're set on the ground over winter, not up on a bench. Using a container also means you can choose a cozy, sheltered sunny corner in winter if you’re in a colder zone. If your soil drains well, though, the world is your oyster! A favorite method is to add saffron crocus to your lawn for drifts of pretty purple flowers in fall as you'll have stopped mowing the grass by the time they bloom.

Set corms roughly 4-6 inches (10-15cm) deep and 3-4 inches (8-10cm) apart, pointed end up, then water them in once. Rain usually handles it after that. Voles and squirrels will dig for the corms, though, so add galvanised steel mesh, particularly if you’re planting in pots or border soil. Everbilt Steel Hardware Cloth, carried by Home Depot, has a ¼-inch (6mm) mesh that bends easily into a container or a buried basket under and around a planting. Where deer visit often, netting keeps them off the grassy winter leaves.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Autumn crocus (Colchicum autumnale) and a few related fall bloomers often get sold as autumn crocus or even meadow saffron, and those plants are poisonous from top to bottom. Buying labelled corms from a trusted supplier beats squinting at flowers, but always check plant ID before you pick. Stamens give it away, with three on saffron crocus and six on a Colchicum. Only harvest from plants sold as Crocus sativus, and keep corms apart from other fall bulbs when storing, planting and growing, so they don't get mixed up.

Summer irrigation causes quieter trouble. Saffron goes dormant around June or July, and a planting sharing a drip line with thirsty tomatoes might remain wet enough to rot. Cutting the leaves early is another common slip. Leave them be until they yellow on their own as that foliage is still feeding next year's corms right up until dormancy. Fresh manure and heavy nitrogen are best avoided too. And don’t worry if the debut season is underwhelming – a good share of new corms may not flower until the second year.

Flowers open in October or November, not long after the first leaves poke up. Harvesting saffron is best done in the morning once dew has dried off, ideally right before the blooms open fully. Pull out the three red stigmas and leave the yellow stamens behind. Tweezers make this much easier.

Threads must be bone dry before they go in a jar for storage. Air-drying in a warm, dark corner of the house works, but slowly. A dehydrator speeds up the process, but be sure to use one with a fine mesh screen to stop the tiny threads dropping through the trays, such as the NESCO Snackmaster Pro Food Dehydrator, available from Walmart.

Store saffron in small, tight-sealing amber glass jars like these 2oz jars from Amazon. Tucked away from light, dried threads can hold their quality for a couple of years. The usual habit is to let a new saffron batch sit for about a month before cooking with it.

It’s important to say that if you’re pregnant, you shouldn’t ingest saffron as it can stimulate uterine contractions. This spice may also interact with medication – in particular blood pressure and diabetes medications – so consult your doctor before consuming. Only eat a moderate amount (no more than a few strands a day) as high doses can have severe side effects.

A little saffron goes a long way when cooking. Crumble a pinch into two or three tablespoons (30-45ml) of warm water and let it steep for 15-20 minutes and the golden liquid will carry flavor evenly into a pot of rice or seafood stew. Saffron steeped into a little warm water can also be whipped into mayonnaise that pairs well with seafood, or use it to add color as well as flavor to bakes.

Saffron crocus is one of the best plants to grow for herbal teas, too. To make a warming saffron tea, simply steep a few strands in a mug with honey to taste. This acts as a natural mood booster and can promote better digestion and sleep.

Saffron has also served as a textile dye for centuries. Its color comes from water-soluble pigments so a strong steep can tint silk or wool a warm yellow for a craft project, though the shade may fade with washing and sunlight.

Over one season, probably not. One flower yields only a few thousandths of a gram of dry spice, and a starter bed of three or four dozen corms might produce enough for a couple of dishes that first year. But the picture shifts in later years. Each established corm can form several offsets by spring, so a bed that gave a pinch in year one may produce noticeably more by year three, and while the corms are a one-time cost, the spice at the store never is.

To encourage a good supply, once blooms start thinning out from crowding, lift and divide the clump, using the crocus offsets to propagate new plants. What a homegrown supply really costs is labor, and a grower who has pulled stigmas with cold fingers on a November morning understands the price tag a little better! But of course the other benefit of growing your own saffron in your garden is that you get to enjoy these pretty purple flowers every fall, which is absolutely priceless.

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

Though it’s priced on the higher end, the Jolie’s high-quality build, modern design, and impressive performance make it worth the investment. If you’re looking for a shower head that combines powerful water pressure with eye-catching aesthetics, the Jolie is a clear winner.

Read our full review: Jolie Shower Head Review

Get the Jolie shower head on Amazon or Jolie Skin Co.

At around $25, we weren’t expecting the Ho2me handheld shower head to feel particularly luxurious, and it doesn’t. The plastic construction is noticeably less substantial compared to the pricier fixtures we tested. Still, after using it for a few weeks, we didn’t see any leaks, loose connections, or other problems. Installation was simple, and the bracket that holds the shower head in place remained sturdy throughout testing.

The three spray settings are fairly basic, but we appreciated having some choice. We especially liked the handheld design for tasks beyond showering. We used it several times to bathe our Australian Shepherd, and being able to remove the head from its holder and switch spray patterns made rinsing shampoo from her coat much easier.

Ho2me markets this model for low-pressure plumbing, though we didn’t notice a dramatic increase in pressure during testing. Our home’s existing water pressure is already strong, so that particular feature was difficult to evaluate. Our bigger complaint is the lack of finish choices. Chrome looks clean enough, but it stood out against the nickel fixtures in our test bathroom.

Those drawbacks aside, this is an easy shower head to recommend at this price. It’s inexpensive, versatile, easy to install, and worked without issue throughout 2 weeks of regular use.

There’s nothing particularly wrong with the Aqua Elegante shower head. It installed easily, worked reliably throughout our testing, and produced a perfectly comfortable stream of water. Its traditional appearance may also appeal to shoppers who don’t want a shower head that looks especially modern or conspicuous.

The problem is simply that there’s not much here to distinguish it from the many other inexpensive shower heads we tested. The body feels quite plasticky, and there are no alternate spray settings to experiment with. At roughly the same price, our SparkPod pick offers three spray modes and felt like a more interesting upgrade. The SparkPod has a more distinctive design, though, so shoppers who prefer a very conventional-looking fixture may actually favor the Aqua Elegante.

We did appreciate that Aqua Elegante offers four finish choices, which makes it easier to coordinate this shower head with existing bathroom hardware. And because it’s a fixed shower head with no handheld components or controls to operate, the lightweight plastic construction matters less during everyday use than it would on a model you’re constantly handling.

Ultimately, this is a straightforward shower head that does exactly what it’s supposed to do. We’d recommend it primarily to shoppers who value simplicity and a traditional design over extra spray modes or other features.

Get the Aqua Elegante shower head at Amazon or Aqua Elegante.

The Delta H2Okinetic was one of the first shower heads in this test where the jump in price came with a noticeable improvement in quality. It feels more refined than the cheaper models we tested, particularly when switching between its five spray settings. The selector rotates smoothly and clicks firmly into each position rather than feeling loose or imprecise.

We liked having several spray patterns to choose from, and the regular shower and massage-style settings all performed well. Delta’s H2Okinetic technology is designed to manipulate the movement and size of the water droplets to create the sensation of greater coverage without increasing water consumption. In practice, the different modes gave us much more flexibility than the single-spray models in the lineup.

We did run into one issue with the pause setting. Rather than cleanly reducing the flow, our test unit allowed a lot of water to leak from around the sides of the shower head while the supply remained on. That’s disappointing on an otherwise polished fixture, though it didn’t affect the other spray modes. We also rarely have a reason to use a pause setting on a fixed shower head, so it wasn’t a deal-breaker for us.

With solid construction, smooth controls, and five useful spray choices, this Delta feels like a worthwhile step up from the cheapest shower heads without entering premium-price territory.

We were immediately impressed by the Afina filtered shower head, which was one of the most stylish options we tested. It arrived in a sleek, well-designed box, and the shower head itself is quite large, making it a statement piece in the bathroom. Installation was a breeze thanks to the included wrench, detailed instructions, and a generous roll of plumber’s tape. Afina even threw in three filters to keep it going strong for months, plus a 50 percent discount coupon for a replacement filter, which is a thoughtful touch. Afina recommends replacing the filter every 90 days.

When it came to performance, the Afina delivered a noticeable boost in water pressure, even with our whole-house water filter already in place. There’s only one spray setting, and it’s pretty straightforward—don’t expect an ultra-pressurized massage setting like our top pick. Still, the spray was consistent and comfortable, making it a solid choice for everyday use.

Overall, the Afina combines good performance with plenty of thoughtful extras, from the spare filters to the handy tools and discounts. If you’re looking for a stylish filtered shower head with practical features and solid pressure, this one checks a lot of boxes.

Get the Afina filtered shower head on Amazon or Afina.

With its large 10-inch diameter, the Grohe Euphoria delivers a true rain shower experience, covering you in a relaxing cascade of water. However, in our testing, it seemed to actually reduce water pressure rather than improve it. So while it may be an appealing fixture if your home has ample pressure, it’s not best suited for those who want a more powerful spray.

To select our top shower heads, we started by researching more than 20 products from well-known and emerging brands, then put eight of the most promising models through hands-on testing. We focused on shower heads designed to provide strong water pressure while also considering price, build quality, appearance, spray options, filtration, and other useful features.

For each round of testing, we installed the shower heads in the same bathroom so we could make consistent comparisons. During testing, we evaluated how easy each model was to install, the strength and coverage of its spray, the usefulness and smoothness of any adjustable settings, and how sturdy the fixture felt during regular use. Handheld models were also removed from their brackets and used for targeted rinsing. We continued using the shower heads for up to a month to look for leaks, loose connections, and other durability concerns. Finally, we compared each model’s performance and features against its price to determine overall value.

Read on to learn about what factors to consider when picking the best shower head for a home with water pressure problems. Considerations involve the shower head’s materials, spray settings, and efficiency, as well as style or taste.

There are two main types of shower heads: fixed and handheld. Fixed shower heads attach directly to the shower supply line. They can support a wide variety of shower head shapes but have limited mobility. Handheld shower heads detach from a water supply line, adding versatility for rinsing hair, massaging sore muscle groups, or even bathing the family dog. Ahead, learn more about the two kinds of shower heads.

A fixed shower head mounts directly to the shower faucet that extends from the wall. These types have a threaded opening that screws onto the arm either by hand or with a plumber’s crescent wrench. A ball joint between the head and arm allows the user to aim the water to meet different desired angles or water-flow needs.

Most fixed shower heads have a knob or dial that makes it easy to switch between different spray patterns. Fixed models also come in various shapes, sizes, and finishes to meet a broad range of tastes.

Handheld shower heads use a long hose, with one end attaching to a fixed head with a long handle and the other end connecting to the shower arm that extends from the wall. The end that attaches to the shower arm typically has a clip fixture that holds the head in place. When resting in the clip, the handheld type functions much like a fixed shower head. Unlike a fixed one, however, the handheld type can be slipped out of the clip fixture when you want to use it for more targeted spraying.

Like fixed shower heads, handheld models have multiple spray settings and come in various designs and finishes. They are good options for parents needing to bathe young children or pets, for those with mobility issues, or for rinsing hair and washing up with a more precise stream.

Most shower heads are made of a combination of metal, brass, and plastic. The internal parts typically consist of brass, which is highly resistant to corrosion and won’t rust. In most cases, the outer housing consists of either plastic or metal.

While metal might seem like the more durable of the two, keep in mind that metal is more susceptible to water damage in the form of corrosion or rust than plastic is. That said, plastic is more likely to break if handled roughly. Metal finishes such as rubbed bronze and nickel are popular material options and hold up well in a wet environment.

Most shower heads feature neoprene nozzles, which are easier to clean and do a better job of resisting hard-water buildup than metal or plastic nozzles.

Shower heads come in various shapes and sizes, including standard, rain, and handheld.

To get around issues of low water pressure, manufacturers have come up with multiple ways to create pressure in the shower head. One of the most innovative designs involves aeration, which draws in air from the surrounding environment to add pressure inside the head. This results in greater water pressure, albeit with a flow pattern more akin to mist than a true water stream.

Other manufacturers use a series of plungers and channels inside the head that compress water flow to increase pressure. Some shower heads feature creative nozzle designs, using different spray patterns that feel intense even while using less water.

Like standard types, low-pressure shower heads come with a wide range of settings that let the user adjust the water output for relaxation, massage, or hair rinsing. Common settings include rainfall, high-pressure jet, and blast, as well as a gentle spray setting and a fire-hose-like drench option.

Basic models offer only one or two settings, though higher-end products and multi-head shower heads can include up to six different flow patterns. Manufacturers may equip their adjustable shower heads with spray patterns that increase the intensity of the water for low water pressure.

The maximum flow rate for shower heads in the United States is 2.5 gallons per minute (GPM) at a water pressure of 80 psi. However, the Environmental Protection Agency recommends that homes use products with a lower flow of 1.8 GPM. Some states, such as California, limit the maximum flow of shower heads to 1.8 GPM.

These lower-flow shower heads are the best option for those living in homes with low water pressure. Although this type of shower head uses less water, manufacturers use innovative designs that increase water pressure, making the user feel like more water is flowing. Shower heads that use less than 2 GPM have a WaterSense label from the EPA.

Often, older homes or those on well water have water pressure problems. These homes can have older pipes or hard water that is more likely to leave mineral and sediment deposits inside a shower head, inhibiting the water flow and reducing already low water pressure to little more than a trickle.

A good low-water-pressure shower head will have a replaceable or cleanable filter that removes these sediments before they can enter the head’s inner workings, ensuring a steady flow of water.

A separate filter canister between the shower head and arm goes a step further. These filters remove additional impurities, like chlorine and heavy metals, that can damage skin and hair.

The best shower heads for low water pressure are offered in different finish options to match the user’s decor. These finishes typically include brushed nickel, chrome-plated, silver, and stylized rubbed bronze and black finishes. Shapes also vary. Rainfall types, for example, have a wide diameter and can come in round form or a more modern square shape.

Rainfall heads can reach as much as 18 inches wide, making them a more conspicuous feature in the bathroom. Compact shower heads can be as small as 3 inches in diameter. These minimalist choices offer a more streamlined look with simple lines and understated designs.

Installing a shower head is one of the easiest bathroom upgrades one can undertake. DIYers typically can remove the old fixture and install a new one in about 15 minutes with just one or two simple tools. Installation typically involves unscrewing the old shower head from the supply line by hand or with a wrench and screwing on a new one. The required tools usually include a crescent wrench and plumber’s tape.

Rain shower heads that extend from the ceiling of the shower typically require custom plumbing that only a professional is qualified to handle.

For those still wondering about how low-pressure shower heads work, read on for answers to some of the most common questions.

There are a few reasons why the water coming from a shower head is closer to a trickle than a stream. In older homes, there could be a buildup of sediment in the pipes, hampering the flow of water. The head could also be clogged with residue from hard water, negatively impacting flow. Showering during peak-use periods in a city can also reduce pressure.

Yes. A high-pressure shower head increases water pressure by aerating the water or compressing it in the head before forcing it out of the jets.

A rain shower head has a significantly larger diameter—up to 1 foot or more—than a standard head. While standard shower heads mount so that they spray at an angle, rain shower heads mount above so that they spray straight down, simulating rainfall.

No. As all shower heads must comply with the 2.5 GPM restriction, rain types do not use more water than standard shower heads. Since rain shower heads are wider, they distribute the same amount of water across more nozzles, which reduces water pressure compared to standard shower heads.

Not necessarily. A well-designed large shower head can still deliver strong water pressure, especially if your home’s water pressure is adequate.

Yes, most shower heads fit standard plumbing, but it’s wise to check compatibility with your shower arm size and water pressure.

Yes, most shower heads are designed for DIY installation and come with clear instructions, often requiring no special tools. You usually just need to screw on the new shower head after applying a few rolls of plumber’s tape.

#181. White Snakeroot: A Pesky Weed—or a Welcome Low-Maintenance Fall Bloomer?

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

”What are those things? Weeds?”asked an interested observer when I was rooting around in a garden bed at Alice Austen House, the Staten Island museum and gallery where I garden twice a week. “No,” I said, “they’re not weeds. They’re white snakeroot.” The name didn’t help. There are also resident snakes in the garden. “They look like weeds,” he said. His untended garden is full of them. It is also full of autumn-active pollinators.

Fall-blooming white snakeroot is a brightening froth of white that lights up gardens and parks just when nights begin to lengthen and birds gather to leave their summer residences. So let’s keep the plant, instead of yanking it. While it self-seeds readily, it can be managed.

White snakeroot (Ageratina altissima) is very adaptable—highly tolerant of dry conditions, flowering in shade and in sun, and not minding damp roots, either. It seems to be designed for a world shaken by climate chaos. It will look after itself if you let it, and is the native gift that keeps on giving. The best time to manage new seedlings is in mid-spring when they are easy to spot and pull.

Altissima, the species name, refers to the stature of the plant, which can reach heights of five feet, although one-to-three is more usual. Blend masses of white snakeroot with asters and boneset for fall-blooming thickets of flowers.

#182. At Home on the West Coast of Sweden: A Plywood Retreat Filled with Cost-Conscious Design Ideas

From house tours and expert advice to favorite finds and DIYs.

Design-forward shops, hotels, and restaurants for your itinerary.

Renovating? Start here for expert advice, deep dives, and helpful tips.

Elisabeth and Dennis Dunker classify their apartment in Gothenburg, Sweden, as something of a compromise: it’s a rental so “a lot of it isn’t what we would have chosen,” says Elisabeth, who, nonetheless, turned it into a lovely place to hang your hat: see Making a Rental Your Own.

A designer, artist, and photographer, Elisabeth happens to be the originator of Fine Little Day, a Swedish creative studio that produces “objects with actual personality,” such as posters and patterned fabrics: not long ago we spotlighted Fine Little Day’s Combination Showroom and Shop. So when Elisabeth invited us to see the seaside escape she and Dennis recently built for themselves, we eagerly accepted. What would the two want if the choices were all theirs?

Surprisingly, the property they bought came with a derelict house and plans for its replacement—”the builder [Kustbyggarna] who also sold the land had hired Marieke DeGraeve, an architect friend, so he could offer a package solution. We loved the site and Marieke’s drawings right away,” explains Elisabeth. Of course, much personalizing and fine-tuning of the plans followed. Come see.

Photography by Elisabeth Dunker, courtesy of Fine Little Day (@finelittleday).

“The essence of the design lies in bringing these elements together,” DeGraeve continues. “The terrain made it possible to create an engaging split-level configuration resulting in a sequence of spaces that frame the forest and open toward the horizon.” Shown here is the back of the staggered structure, which opens to the kitchen. The house’s entrance upstairs leads to the living area and bedrooms.

Dennis, who is a physician, happens to also be passionate about design: he sketched the kitchen table and benches and their carpenter built them—and all of the cabinetry—on site. The fringed bench cover is a vintage handwoven röllakan runner from a second-hand shop. The red Rey stool is by Hay (and currently on sale at DWR). Ulla, their beloved companion, is a Boston Terrier.

The wooden cubes are a signature of Elisabeth and Dennis’s living quarters: these were made by their carpenter and are used throughout as tables and storage.

Note the homemade storage cubes. And also the free weights: in recent years, Elisabeth, who says she was never in the least bit athletic, has become a fitness powerhouse and inspirational leader: see her doing pull-ups on Instagram @elisabethdunkerr and stay tuned for her book on becoming fit in middle age. “Hormones broke me,” she writes. “Strength put me back together.”

Want all the flower power of zinnias in a perennial? Look this way...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Before we get into the wonderful world of floral dupes, I want it on record that I have nothing against zinnias. In fact, I love them. Honestly, give me a garden absolutely packed with those colorful blooms and I’m going to stop and admire it.

Zinnias have that wonderful ability to make a garden look instantly abundant, and I love how many colors and flower shapes there are to play with. And, when these beauties are at their peak, it’s hard to imagine a more cheerful summer flower.

There is just one small problem: they’re annuals, which means that, every year, I have to start all over again. Understandably, then, I’ve been looking for a perennial that gives me some of that same flower power. Something big, colorful and gloriously over-the-top... but something I can plant once and enjoy again the following year.

The best dupe, in my humble opinion, for a zinnia is a double coneflower (available at Amazon).

Now, if your mental picture of a coneflower is a simple pink daisy with a big brown cone in the middle, you may be in for a surprise; some of the newer double-flowered varieties are positively extravagant, with layers of petals creating rounded, almost pom-pom-like centers.

They’re not shy flowers; they are dramatic, and flouncing, and they have serious presence, which means that, if you plant a good-sized clump, you can get that same feeling of abundance that makes a bed of zinnias so irresistible.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Now, don't get me wrong; zinnias are brilliant for filling a garden with color, but their annual nature means there’s always a little bit of work involved in getting that display back each year. Coneflowers, on the other hand, are perennials. Once established in a suitable spot, they can return year after year, getting more impressive as the clump matures.

That makes them especially appealing if, like me, you love the look of a packed flower bed but don't necessarily want to rebuild it from scratch every spring. Even better, they aren't particularly precious plants. Once established, they can tolerate periods of dry weather, and it generally prefers a sunny position with well-drained soil, making it a useful choice for gardeners who want plenty of flowers without having to constantly fuss over them.

As if all that weren't enough, this zinnia dupe features stunning seedheads that can be left standing into fall and winter rather than immediately cutting everything back. They add structure to the garden when much of it has died back, and birds may make use of the seeds.

Zinnias are still fantastic, of course, and there are some things they do that perennial coneflowers simply can't replicate; they give you enormous flexibility with color, they're brilliant for cutting, and they can produce an almost ridiculous number of flowers in a single season.

If you want a perennial dupe, though, you can't go wrong with double coneflowers! They give me the same thing I love about zinnias (bold color, abundance and that slightly extravagant “look at me” quality) while promising to pop back each year to put on the same magnificent show.

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

Our top picks illustrate the range of features offered by electric fireplace inserts. We’ve awarded each of our favorite models an award, making it easier to find the best electric fireplace insert for every purpose.

The Masarflame 40-inch electric fireplace insert’s standout feature is its accurate rendering of an authentic log fire. Rather than a simple black interior, the sides have a brick pattern that adds visual depth. Lifelike resin logs enhance this with three different lighting effects and five flame heights, and a crackling sound completes the retro wood-burning effect.

This realistic-looking electric fireplace offers two heat settings, but it doesn’t have a programmable thermostat. However, it does feature a 9-hour timer and a safety cutout to prevent overheating. The Masarflame can be installed into a wall recess or cabinet, but it may look best in a false fireplace surround.

Get the Masarflame electric fireplace insert at Amazon.

The slender frame on the Touchstone Sideline Elite gives it a sleek, contemporary impression that we found instantly appealing, and its smart features only deepened that impression. While a remote is provided, this fireplace is also ready for Wi-Fi. The free smartphone app, which adds a range of additional functions, integrates with Alexa or Google Home.

Two power settings and a programmable thermostat can be set between 68 degrees Fahrenheit and 88 degrees Fahrenheit. The model contains an 8-hour timer. It comes in log, driftwood, and crystal bed effects in 10 color choices, plus flames that can be set to six colors and three speeds. The Touchstone Sideline has ETL safety certification and overheating protection

Get the Touchstone electric fireplace insert at Amazon or Lowe’s.

At 68 inches wide but just 18 inches tall, the R.W.Flame electric wall-mount fireplace insert makes quite an impression. A choice of 12 bed colors, 12 flame colors, and five flame speeds allows variety in visual impact and ambience.

The two power modes work in conjunction with a programmable thermostat to control room temperatures between 68 degrees Fahrenheit and 88 degrees Fahrenheit. A sleep mode provides heat but turns off all the effects. It has an 8-hour timer and ETL safety certification.

Despite being an electric fireplace insert with a built-in fan, this unit features an ultrathin body that measures just under 4 inches deep, making it the ideal wall-mounted fireplace for users who prioritize ease of installation. However, the wall must be structurally solid, as the R.W.Flame 68-inch fireplace weighs 67 pounds.

Get the R.W.Flame electric fireplace insert at Amazon or The Home Depot.

Many of us on the Bob Vila team are DIY fanatics, and we’ve completed remodels on various homes. As a result, we have extensive experience with electric fireplaces to draw on. With that as our starting point, we researched the most popular electric fireplace insert brands and a wide selection of retailers, including major names and specialist suppliers. After examining more than 60 appliances, we formed an in-depth view of the market, the products available, and the most recent developments in fireplace inserts, such as the potential for smart voice control.

Most electric fireplace inserts deliver similar heating performance. Many people are more concerned with the unit’s physical size and visual appeal, which are crucial to how it fits in the living space. Our top picks offer a wide range of different dimensions, and while appearance is a personal subject, we also sought to represent the many different styles available. Since cost plays a critical part in most buying decisions, we offered models to suit all budgets.

While the best freestanding electric fireplace is often just plug in and go, an electric fireplace insert typically requires at least minimal installation. Apart from that, along with their general appearance, they frequently share similar features. The following section explores the issues that buyers will want to think about when choosing the best recessed electric fireplace for a particular location.

Many types of fireplaces powered by electricity can be called “inserts”; however, the term usually describes those units that fit into a recess in the wall. These can either be pre-existing (replacing a gas fireplace or log fire) or new additions. A new installation can be installed at floor level or recessed into the wall above it. Several models have the flexibility to be used in either position.

Some electric fireplaces come as part of a complete surround and mantel package that’s fitted to the wall, mimicking a “real” fire. While electric fireplaces with mantels ​are sometimes called inserts, that’s not a very accurate description and can lead to confusion. The same can also be said of electric log sets that sit in the space formerly used by the grate of a log fire.

Regardless of their physical size, even the best indoor fireplace inserts seldom use more than 1,500W of electricity. More power than that and the unit could trip a standard breaker. Many models have two power settings to help save on costs.

In actual heat capacity, 1,500W of power is generally considered sufficient to maintain comfortable warmth in a room of up to 400 square feet. The high setting could be used for initial warmth, then lowered to maintain that temperature.

Heating capacity may also be listed in BTUs on some electric fireplaces. Technically, 1 BTU is the energy required to raise 1 pound of water by 1 degree Fahrenheit. At full power, most modern fireplace inserts emit about 4,000 to 5,000 BTUs. While useful for comparison, the figures don’t offer much practical help, and many manufacturers don’t even supply them.

Physical size is important when looking through the available electric fireplaces for two reasons: First, it helps determine the insert’s appearance in the intended location, and second, size affects the installation.

Generally, width is the main dimension used when describing an electric fireplace insert. The smallest unit currently on the market is just 22 inches wide, while the largest measures 100 inches. Height and depth should also appear in the details. The fireplace insert’s dimensions invariably differ from the dimensions of the recess required, so it’s important to have those measurements, too.

Visualizing the actual size from the dimensions can pose a challenge. To help judge the impact the fireplace insert will make, use low-tack tape to outline the fireplace on the intended wall.

Installing an electric fireplace insert is generally much easier than installing a gas fireplace insert or real fire alternatives. While it can be fitted as a replacement for either of these, an electric fireplace doesn’t need a chimney, flue, or venting.

Depending on the wall structure, electric fireplace inserts can be recessed at floor level or higher. If the existing walls are brick or concrete, experts may advise building out a false wall, which can also serve as a decorative element.

Most electric fireplace inserts need only to be plugged into a convenient wall outlet. Often, it’s possible to wire one into the recess or permanently hardwire it. Experienced DIYers may be able to perform the task, though it’s probably better to contact a qualified professional.

A programmable thermostat, which is a popular option, can help reduce heating costs. Once set to the desired level, the fireplace automatically adjusts its output to maintain it, so no energy is wasted. A shut-off timer is also frequently included.

Many manufacturers offer flame effects and colors to create a welcoming ambience without heat. Realistic log-crackling sounds also help enhance the atmosphere. Control is usually possible via a handheld remote, but the most advanced electric fireplace inserts also allow smart control via Wi-Fi and integration with home hubs that allow voice commands.

Safety is an important consideration. The best electric fireplace heater options have thermal overload protection that cuts the power if the device overheats. Cool-touch exteriors also are available.

When properly installed, with no exposed flames and no smoke or noxious fumes, electric fireplace inserts are among the safest home-heating devices. However, some potential for danger always exists. The following tips should help keep you, your family, and your property safe.

If you still have lingering questions about electric fireplace inserts, you’re not alone—there’s a lot to know regarding their safety features and functionalities.

No “standard” size exists. Widths can measure from 22 inches to 100 inches. Height also varies, and the depth required for installation can vary from 4 inches to 12 inches. Check sizes carefully when making your choice.

Yes, when properly installed, electric fireplaces are often considered the safest fireplace option. With no fumes or smoke, they are also kinder to those with respiratory difficulties and many allergy sufferers.

Electric fireplaces generate heat in a similar way to space heaters. They use a heating element that heats as electricity passes through it, and a fan then distributes the heat so that it radiates throughout the room. As for the flame effects, these are typically created by LED lights, though other interesting techniques are sometimes used, such as utilizing rotating mirrors (yes, really!). To control the unit, users can either use a remote or onboard control to adjust heat and lighting settings.

Electric fireplaces don’t generate enough heat to serve as a primary heat source; they’re more intended to be used as secondary sources. They also won’t work during power outages unless you have a backup power system. And if you forget to turn your electric fireplace off when you’re not using it, your electricity bill will suffer for it.

Not normally. Costs depend on the watts consumed by the fireplace and utility charges, but several independent tests show an average of around 15 to 18 cents per hour. If the unit is run for 6 hours a day, that’s roughly $30 per month.

Prices vary significantly depending on features, size, and quality, but generally speaking, most electric fireplaces cost somewhere from $100 to $500, with costlier, more sophisticated units ranging closer to $1,000.

Electricity consumption is measured in watts. Most electric fireplace inserts operate at around 1,500W maximum. That’s about the same as an electric space heater, though an electric fireplace insert is usually more efficient.

Installing an electric fireplace is very simple—especially compared to real fireplaces, which are not only costly to install but also complex. Electric fireplaces simply require plugging in to a proper electrical source (don’t use extension cords. Inserts must be measured properly to ensure they fit, and wall-mounts will require a little extra prep.

Placing a “fake” fireplace insert into an existing fireplace is typically possible as long as power can be supplied. The existing fireplace gap may need some modification. When in doubt, consult a professional.

#186. The Best Ratcheting Screwdrivers of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Published Oct 12, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Whether you’re working on a car, installing a doorknob, or driving a screw by hand into a piece of dense wood, the best ratcheting screwdriver can help. These handy tools can help you maintain contact with stubborn screws, nuts, and bolts when you need to apply a bit of extra torque.

These hand tools are all about convenience. They use interchangeable screw bits, many of which are stored onboard. Plus, their ratcheting mechanisms allow you to maintain contact with the fastener to quickly tighten or loosen—offering plenty of torque without resetting your grip between twists.

Choosing the best ratcheting screwdriver can be a bit tricky, so we decided to test some of the bestselling models to see if they lived up to their reputations. Some did, but others didn’t. Our top choice was the Wera Kraftform Kompakt 27 RA 2 SB Screwdriver, which is easy and comfortable for DIYers and professionals alike. Ahead, learn what to look for when shopping for one of the best ratcheting screwdrivers, and find out why the following tools earned a spot in our lineup.

Bottom line: The best ratcheting screwdrivers of 2026 offer a range of features for various needs, from ergonomic designs to comprehensive bit kits.

It’s time to find out how some of today’s most popular models fared in our tests. Rest assured, we didn’t go easy on them. We used them to remove stuck screws, insert new screws into different densities of wood, and to tighten and loosen hex and other fasteners. While each of the following ratcheting screwdrivers is designed for slightly different uses, each is a standout in its category.

If you’re looking for a heavy-duty ratcheting screwdriver capable of frequent use, consider the Wera Kraftform Kompakt RA Screwdriver. This ratcheting screwdriver has secure in-handle storage for your bits. It also has an ergonomically designed grip for comfortable use and plenty of torque.

The Wera comes with six bits, including two Phillips-head bits, two square drivers, and two slotted drivers. The shaft also doubles as a ¼-inch nut driver.

The Wera ratcheting screwdriver feels solid in the hand, and one of the first things we noticed was its nonslip, ergonomic grip that’s contoured to help the user get a firm grasp. The bit storage base slid out easily with just a light push of the button on the bottom, making it easy to select the bits. We inserted screws in pine, ash, and walnut boards, and the screwdriver held up to all densities.

This ratcheting screwdriver is well suited for general around-the-house and DIY use. The only downside—and it’s not a big one—is that the directional collar is a little wider than the grip where it attaches, and large hands can inadvertently change the direction without meaning to.What our tester says: “One of the nicest features of the Wera is its minimized ratcheting action, which meant we didn’t have to rotate the handle very far backward in order to engage the gear again. Another nice feature is the strong magnet in the head that locks the bit in place so it doesn’t fall out.”—Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

When it comes to really cranking down on a fastener, the Megapro ratcheting screwdriver has all the grip you could need. This ratcheting screwdriver’s shaft doubles as a ¼-inch nut driver, and it comes with 12 bits (six double-ended bits), including four Phillips bits, two square drive bits, two slotted bits, and four Torx bits.

The cartridge’s cap rotates freely at the end of the handle, so you can use one hand to apply downward force on the cap while the other twists the handle for maximum torque and control. Also, the thick handle is rubber-coated, providing plenty of gripping surface area. Switching from tightening to loosening, or locking the shaft in place is easy with the Megapro’s collar mechanism.

We found the Megapro well suited for use by those with large hands. Its handle features rubber inserts and is comfortable to grip, but it might be a little large for someone with smaller hands. The end cap slides out for easy bit retrieval, and the double-ended bits make it handy to find the right bit without needing to carry extra bits around. The directional collar is easy to switch, and the ratcheting action is smooth.

We used the Megapro to insert screws in pine, ash, and walnut boards, and then we tested it on removing stubborn screws. It stood up to strong twisting force, and the ratcheting action didn’t slip or break. We used quite a bit of torque. If we could ask for one thing to be different it would be a magnet in the head—when we turned the screwdriver downward, the bits often fell out.

Get the Megapro screwdriver at Amazon or Grainger.

If you’re looking for a quality ratcheting screwdriver with a few extra features, you should check out the Milwaukee Multi Bit Ratcheting Screwdriver. This screwdriver comes with six 3.5-inch driver bits, including three square drive bits, two Phillips bits, and two slotted bits. The longer bits are easy to manipulate, and they store on the handle in secure slots, so there’s very little risk of them falling out. The downside is that they were kind of difficult to get out without firmly pressing with our fingertips.

The screwdriver also features some handy extras. It has a wire stripper built into the handle as well as a wire loop bender. Also, the handle sans bit functions as a ¼-inch nut driver. As far as ratcheting goes, the Milwaukee has a collar to switch directions or lock the shaft in place. Although the bits do take up a bit of space on the handle, there is plenty of gripping area for applying lots of torque.

The Milwaukee is a solid little tool, and its ratcheting action is among the smoothest of the models we tested. This didn’t come as a surprise, since the Milwaukee brand is well known and has a great reputation for making quality tools. The head features a strong magnet that holds the bits in place, and the directional collar is well made and easy to switch.

We tested the Milwaukee’s ratcheting action on a variety of boards, and it didn’t bog down even when we used maximum force inserting screws into walnut wood.

We also tested the wire stripper, and it easily removed the insulated sheath from household electrical wires, making the Milwaukee a beneficial tool for DIY electricians as well as for assembling furniture and other projects.

Get the Milwaukee multi-bit screwdriver at Amazon.

The Makita Ratcheting Screwdriver and Bit Set is worth checking out if you’re looking for a ratcheting screwdriver that comes with a comprehensive set of bits and sockets. This 49-piece kit comes with a screwdriver, 11 Phillips bits, eight Torx bits, and four slotted bits. It also comes with seven sockets and several square and hex-drive bits. With this range of bits, most jobs around the house should be a cinch.

The screwdriver has a collar direction adjustment, as well as a lanyard hole for a wrist strap or hanging cord. However, it doesn’t have any onboard storage, so you should keep the case on hand for easy access to bits.

The Makita is a relatively compact tool—smaller than some of the other ratcheting screwdrivers we tested–but its ergonomic, rubber-nubbed handle made it easy to get a firm grasp, and the large selection of bits and sockets allowed us to use the tool to remove and insert screws as well as tighten and loosen nuts. It has a magnet in the head, but it’s not as strong as we would have liked. Still, it kept the bits from falling out. The Makita stood up to maximum driving force for inserting screws in dense wood, and it has a smooth ratcheting action.

While it doesn’t store bits onboard as some of the others do, the plastic storage box that holds the sockets and bits is relatively small, just 2.2 inches by 5.25 inches by 10.25 inches, so it fits neatly in a kitchen drawer or in the glove compartment of a vehicle. We’ve come to expect durability and functional design from Makita, and this little ratcheting screwdriver didn’t disappoint.

Get the Makita ratchet and bit set at Amazon or The Home Depot.

If you’ve ever tried to tighten or loosen screws in tight spots where a straight-handled screwdriver won’t fit, consider the MulWark Low Profile Mini Ratchet Screwdriver. It comes with 20 bits, featuring an assortment of Phillips-head bits, slotted bits, torx bits, and hex bits. It comes with a strong magnet in the head so bits don’t fall out. No onboard storage because this tool is just too small, but the bits fit in two plastic holders that can be easily stored together in a drawer.

Right off the bat, we’ll tell you that the MulWark isn’t suitable for tightening or loosening stuck screws in dense materials because it doesn’t come with a handle large enough to grip with a fist. But that’s not what it’s designed to do, anyway.

The MulWark is made to insert and remove fasteners where there’s very little room to maneuver. Although it was the smallest ratcheting screwdriver we tested, we were able to insert screws in different types of wood—even in walnut—without the ratcheting mechanism failing. But because the MulWark is intended for use with fingers, not a fist grip, our fingers wore out before the tool did. For those times when you need to insert fasteners behind a mounted flat screen or in another tight spot, the MulWark shines.

The WorkPro Ratcheting Screwdriver features a nonslip grip and solid feel, making it easy to get a firm grasp on the handle. The tool stores six 3.5-inch double-ended bits in its base, which gave us 12 different bits to choose from, including slotted, Phillips head, star, and Torx. The bits themselves are magnetic—rather than the head—but they remained firmly in the tool, even when we shook it upside down.

We tested the WorkPro by inserting screws in a variety of wood types, and it came through with flying colors—even when we used maximum force and dense walnut wood. We then tested the tool on a range of fasteners and found the bits are well made and appear to be hardened steel.

The directional collar switches smoothly from left to right. The longer bits gave the tool greater reach, and the head comes with a metal pull-back release that—along with the magnetic bits—keeps the bits firmly in place during use.

Get the WorkPro screwdriver set at Amazon.

Don’t expect frills or extras with the Williams T-Handle Ratcheting Screwdriver, because you won’t find any. What you will find is a solid screwdriver that comes with a long shaft and accepts standard ¼-inch bits. It comes with just one Phillips-head bit.

What the Williams T-handle lacks in extras it makes up for in durability. We were impressed by the hefty feel of the tool—the high-impact, molded-plastic handle is ergonomically designed to fit in the palm of the hand, which allowed us to exert pressure directly on the fasteners and helped prevent stripping out the screw heads.

We used the Williams screwdriver to insert screws in a variety of wood types, and its ratcheting action remained smooth and sure—even when we used force. The directional collar switches with ease, and the shaft head features a magnet that holds bits in place. The long, thin design of this screwdriver is well suited to reaching fasteners in tight spots while exerting pressure.

We really wanted to like these two Klein Tools ratcheting screwdrivers, but they failed to meet our high standards. While both came with nonslip grips and each had extra bits stored in its base, the shafts on both were loose, and the plastic directional collars stuck and were difficult to switch.

On the larger Klein Tools screwdriver, using strong force to insert a screw into a walnut board was more than it could take, and the ratcheting mechanism broke.

Another problem is that the bits are proprietary—they feature a snap-lock bearing on the side that holds them in place—so we could not use standard bits in either of the tools, which reduces their versatility. While these two are among the most affordable options, they just didn’t live up to the hype. We look forward to seeing new and improved versions coming from Klein Tools.

Each of the ratcheting screwdrivers we tested was pushed to its limits so we could get a good idea of how it would perform over time and in various situations. With each tool, we inserted screws into three types of wood—pine, ash, and walnut—to see whether the ratcheting action would stand up to the different densities.

We checked the directional collars of each tool to see if they switched directions easily and to make sure they didn’t slip while using the tool. We also inspected the overall solidness of the tool and checked whether onboard bit storage was easy to access.

While we considered whether the tool came with a variety of bits, we didn’t eliminate models that didn’t come with bits because the user can also pick those up later. We awarded points for the screwdrivers that accepted standard bits and subtracted points if they didn’t. Not all of the ratcheting screwdrivers we tested made the cut, but the ones that did are among the best options available today.

There are some things worth considering when shopping for the best ratcheting screwdriver beyond just the style of bit storage. Consider the length, the grip, and other built-in features you might find with certain models. Keep the following points in mind while shopping so you’re sure to get the best ratcheting screwdriver for your needs.

There are a handful of styles of ratcheting screwdrivers, so the results of our tests and this comprehensive guide let you know what’s out there before you start shopping. The main difference in style is how each screwdriver stores its interchangeable bits. There are benefits to each style, so it’s worth giving some consideration.

The most common style of ratcheting screwdriver stores its bits inside the grip. Often, there is a cap that threads on and off or pops out of the handle, providing access to the driver bits. Multiple bits clip to a removable ring, allowing you to choose the appropriate bit or store it away securely. Other models have bit-clips built into the cap.

The benefit of storing the bits in the handle is that it’s harder to lose them. As long as the cap stays shut, the bits are secure, even if they pop out of their clips. The downside is that switching between bits stored in the handle does create some downtime. Also, these bits are often smaller and harder to grip.

As opposed to storing your bits inside the handle, several models come with storage on the handle. These models have slots or holes for holding the bits right in the grip. They either clip into place or slide in from the bottom of the handle.

The benefit of these screwdrivers is that, many times, the bits are long. You can get a good grip on them when storing or swapping bits. The downside is that these screwdrivers are often heavier, and bits often fall or slide out of lower-end models when you aren’t looking.

Occasionally, you can get a ratcheting screwdriver in a comprehensive kit of driver bits and attachments. They come in their own boxes or cases with slots for storing driver bits, sockets, and nut drivers.

Some of the benefits of these screwdrivers are that they’re usually lighter and come with more bits. You can see all the bits at once, so you can grab one quickly, knowing easily if something’s missing. The downside is that you might have to keep a bulky case nearby if you’re frequently swapping bits.

When shopping for the best ratcheting screwdriver, you may need to choose between a kit and a single screwdriver.

The overwhelming benefit of purchasing a kit is that they’re usually fairly comprehensive. Phillips, slotted, square drive, and even Torx bits can be found in these kits. You can find nut drivers and socket attachments as well, which can be a big help on a variety of projects. The problem is that you can’t store all these bits in or on your handle, so be sure to keep the case nearby.

A single screwdriver is a far more streamlined tool than a ratcheting screwdriver kit. The bits all fit inside or on the handle, allowing you to keep everything with you. The issue is that you simply won’t get as many bits as you would with a kit. Also, when storing all of those bits on board, single ratcheting screwdrivers tend to be heavier.

Ratcheting screwdrivers aren’t new technology. One of the first popular models was the “Yankee,” manufactured by North Bros and first marketed in 1895. Not much has changed in the ratcheting function since then.

Most ratcheting screwdrivers use a gear-and-pawl system. Depending on the direction you set the screwdriver to, the pawl will engage with the gear, forcing the tip to rotate with the handle. When you twist the screwdriver in the other direction, the pawl skips over the gear’s teeth, rotating the grip independently of the tip.

While this mechanism is rather universal, engaging it and switching directions does vary a bit from screwdriver to screwdriver. Older models have switches in the shaft that allow you to toggle between clockwise, counterclockwise, and completely locked. More modern variations have collars that you twist to change directions.

The benefit of ratcheting screwdrivers is that you can get a firm grip on their handle and apply plenty of torque repetitively without adjusting your grip. Not all screwdrivers handle torque as well as others, so try to find a robust, durable model.

Not all screwdrivers will have their torque rating clearly displayed, but durable models can handle around 50 newton meters (nm) or about 36 foot-pounds of torque. Taking a screwdriver beyond its torque capacity will usually break the pawl or shave teeth off the ratcheting gear, making the screwdriver useless.

When looking for the best ratcheting screwdriver, notice they come in different lengths. Standard-length models are around 7 or 8 inches. Stubby models are under 3 or 4 inches. You can also find longer models with long shafts and handles over 9 inches long.

There are benefits to each. Stubby screwdrivers fit in tight places, and they’re easy to line up with the fastener. Longer screwdrivers provide plenty of grip, and they allow you to see the workpiece without blocking it with your hand or grip. Mid-length screwdrivers do a bit of both.

However, they have their downsides as well. Maintaining a solid grip with a stubby screwdriver can be challenging. Small variations in your grip can change the angle of the tip quite a bit, leading to stripped screws and scuffed knuckles. Conversely, longer screwdrivers are hard to line up with a fastener one-handed, but contact is easy to maintain.

Grip shapes and styles vary from screwdriver to screwdriver. Some brands have one handle design that they use on all of their products, and some tradespeople have come to prefer them. Other models use tapered grips, allowing for several hand or grip positions.

Primarily, the “right” grip comes down to personal preference and how the screwdriver fits in your hand. For the most torque, however, a thicker grip with plenty of surface area is best. For the best dexterity, you may want something thinner with a tapered design.

If you’d like a little more function out of your ratcheting screwdriver, there are several models available with additional capabilities. Some features are rather trade-specific. For instance, you can find screwdrivers with wire strippers, benders, and wire nut sockets for electricians. A few models come with small LED lights that help illuminate in low-light situations.

Beyond the added features, ratcheting screwdriver kits tend to be the most versatile. They include tons of bits and attachments for tackling a wide range of projects like renovations, automotive work, and routine home maintenance.

If you’re still a little twisted up about buying the best ratcheting screwdriver, the following section will help. It includes some of the most frequently asked questions and answers about ratcheting screwdrivers.

Ratcheting screwdrivers use a gear and a pawl to allow the shaft to rotate independently on the backstroke and engage the shaft on the forward twist. As the handle rotates backward, the pawl skips over the teeth, allowing the shaft to remain still. As the handle rotates forward, the pawl grabs the gear, engaging the shaft and rotating it with the handle.

Standard screwdriver shafts are permanently fixed to the handle, so every twist of the handle twists the tip. Ratcheting screwdrivers engage and disengage from the shaft, allowing you to twist the handle back and forth while only driving the fastener in one direction.

Most ratchet screwdrivers use ball detents or magnets to hold their bits in place. In either case, removing the bit simply requires pulling the bit straight out of the shaft.

After months of scouring the market and putting products through their paces, we’ve named the best of the best in new tools. There’s something for everyone, from veteran pros to average Joes.

For many, fall flowers usually mean mums or asters – but there are other blooms that are equally stunning, and you can plant all these fabulous flowering perennials this month

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Walk down any garden path this month, and you’ll likely meet the usual suspects. Tightly packed potted chrysanthemums and cheerful asters dominate porch steps and garden beds, and they represent the classic choice for fall color. Yet, for all their prolific hues, mums often act as short-lived annuals that tire quickly after the first hard freeze, leaving bare gaps right when late fall beds and borders need a lift.

Instead of settling for a quick fix, why not add something unexpectedly gorgeous that your neighbors can admire with fascination? These choice perennial plants provide fall color every year – and this month is both a great time to plant them and to enjoy their uplifting blooms. It might sound too good to be true, but these perennial treasures return year after year with breathtaking late-season brilliance.

Expanding your horizons reveals a wealth of underrated perennial stars, from delicate, dancing flower wands to clouds of nectar-rich blooms. By slipping these unsung hero perennials into your borders now, you aren't just saving late-season borders from fading away. You are actively investing in a richer, low-maintenance garden story that bursts into life every October.

The cooler air temperatures and still-warm soil are ideal for establishing these fall perennial plants before winter. While it may feel chilly in the air, the soil remains warm from months of summer sun, and is highly receptive to healthy plantings. This gentle ground warmth creates an excellent foundation for root development, allowing newly planted perennials to root deep without the threat of late summer heat.

Planting your flowering perennials in fall is all about timing. As long as your ground remains workable and you have 3-4 weeks before the first winter frost is anticipated in your area, the plant’s roots should settle in happily. Your growing or hardiness zone will determine how fast you move in October. In cooler northern regions (zones 3-6), you should aim to get plants into the ground early in the month, so root systems adapt before soil temperatures plummet. In the south (zones 7-10), growers have a longer runway, and warm soil conditions allow easy planting well into late fall.

Late-season soil is often depleted or compacted after busy summer growth. Take a moment to enrich your planting holes with rich organic matter to give young root systems a head start. Once your new perennials are tucked into place, apply a generous 2-3-inch (5-8 cm) blanket of shredded bark or leaf mulch. Organic favorite Back to the Roots Organic Premium Mulch, available from Amazon, will help maintain ground conditions and prevent winter frost heaving.

Finally, make sure you water your newly planted perennials regularly until the ground freezes. Deep, regular watering is the secret to winter survival for any late-season additions. That way, these unexpectedly lovely flowering perennials will add color and movement through late fall, and continue their fall shows year after year.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If you need a tall perennial to add texture, balance and beauty at the back of your fall borders, Joe Pye weed (Eutrochium purpureum) is a champion. Rising up to 6-8 feet (1.8-2.4m) tall on sturdy stems, this plant forms massive domed heads of dusty-rose or mauve flowers that glow in late afternoon sunlight. It’s also a lovely late-season refueling station for monarch butterflies and bees when other nectar sources are scarce. If you are looking for a stunning compact native that can add joy to small spaces, go for Little Joe Joe Pye Weed Plants from Plant Addicts.

Hardy in USDA zones 4-9, Joe Pye weed thrives in full sun to partial shade and craves soil that stays moist. It is naturally tailored for rain gardens, pond edges, or low-lying garden spots. Key varieties like Baby Joe offer compact choices for smaller yards without sacrificing bloom impact. Just keep soil consistently damp while the plant establishes. It looks amazing paired with golden ornamental grasses or towering black-eyed Susans.

Goldenrod (Solidago spp.) has suffered from bad publicity for decades, due to widespread confusion with ragweed. But despite fears, this native beauty will not trigger fall allergies, so don’t be afraid of its joyful blooms. Capable of flowering all the way to November, goldenrod produces feather-like sprays of honey-gold flowers that bring electric light to fading borders. Choose Green Promise Farms Fireworks Goldenrod Plants, available from Walmart, for an award-winning bargain that will establish quickly to service this season's late-visiting pollinators. Its heavy, sticky pollen is carried by beneficial insects rather than the wind.

Extremely hardy in zones 2-8, goldenrod is virtually indestructible once established. It handles full sun, average-to-poor soil, and drought conditions with ease. Modern cultivars stay neatly behaved: look for Fireworks for golden explosions, or Golden Fleece for low, edging groundcover growth. Just avoid overly rich, nitrogen-heavy soils, which can cause the stems to become floppy. Combine its brilliant yellow plumes with deep purple aster varieties or dark blue salvias for classic contrast.

Plumbago (aka blue leadwood) is the ultimate groundcover for fall drama. Blue leadwood (Ceratostigma plumbaginoides) is a gorgeous double hitter for color, with vivacious red or bronze fall foliage as well as lush sapphire flowers. Growing just 8-12 inches (20-30cm) tall, this spreading dwarf shrub carpet produces intense, gentian-blue flowers from late August into November. To bring jewel-like color to gloomy parts of your yard, buy Blue Plumbago Plants from Nature Hills for luminescent blooms in the shade.

Hardy in zones 5-9, plumbago excels in full sun to partial shade, though morning sun with light afternoon shade yields the richest foliage tones. Excellent drainage is essential, as these plants don’t like waterlogged winter soil. Plumbago is especially pretty along garden edges, rockeries, and retaining walls. Don't worry if it emerges late: it often saves its best energy for a dazzling late-fall showing. Pair it with yellow-flowering bulbs or emerging colchicum for a sensational low-growing display.

For one of the most magical names in this roundup, meet whirling butterflies, more commonly known as gaura. Bringing an airy, magical texture to October borders, Gaura is a joy to grow in late fall. Rising on wand-like stems 2-4 feet (60-120 cm) high, its delicate pink and white blooms dance in breezes until the first frost. It creates an ethereal display that breathes continuous movement into quiet beds. Buy Gaudi Rose Gaura Starter Plants from Amazon for lush sprays of hot pink blooms.

Hardy in zones 5-9, gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri) loves full sun and lean, sharply draining soil. Thanks to a long, deep taproot, it has exceptional heat and drought tolerance once settled. Key varieties like Siskiyou Pink bloom for months on end. Just avoid heavy clay soils that retain winter water, and avoid hard spring pruning until new growth shows. Interplant this beauty with ornamental grasses like Pennisetum or dark-leaved heuchera for effortless elegance.

When a lot of other flowering stalwarts are finally fading in shade gardens, the toad lily (Tricyrtis hirta) adds breathtaking elegance. From September to November, its arching stems bear intricate, star-shaped, orchid-like flowers, heavily speckled in shades of amethyst, magenta, and creamy white. Growing 2-3 feet (60-90 cm) tall, these exotic flowers reward close inspection, making them a must-have for pathway edges and courtyard borders. You can buy Emerald Goddess Garden Store Toad Lily Live Plants from Amazon if you hurry for unique color in the gloom.

Hardy in zones 4-8, toad lilies require partial to full shade and rich, organic soil that remains consistently moist but drains well. Standout varieties include Miyazaki for cascading speckled blooms or Empress for larger individual flowers. Top-dress with rich leaf mold or compost each year, to mimic their native habitat. Most shady flowers bloom in spring, so this is a memorable perennial for fall color in shade gardens. Plant them along edges, where their delicate blooms won’t be missed.

Hesperantha (formerly Schizostylis) is unmissable, yet often gets overlooked in fall flower roundups. This vivacious South African native pushes up gladiolus-like spikes of bowl-shaped flowers in saturated shades of scarlet, crimson, and salmon pink. Blooming through October and November, it brings an astonishing flush of tropical color right when frost threatens. For satisfying salmon pink blooms ready for late season planting, choose Sunrise Hesperantha Starter Plants from Amazon.

Hardy in zones 7-9 (and easily overwintered in zone 6 with mulch), Hesperantha coccinea reaches 18-24 inches (45–60 cm) tall and multiplies into lush clumps. It just demands full sun and rich soil during the growing season. Popular varieties like hot red Major or Mrs. Hegarty'(satin pink) make outstanding, long-lasting cut flowers. Pair this sassy late season bloomer with silver foliage like stachys or blue-toned ornamental grasses for dramatic color pop.

Some of you may already be familiar with the delights of this elegant beauty, especially if you have shady spaces that need a bit of sparkle. Japanese anemones (Anemone × hybrida) bring effortless grace to late-season borders. Held on slender 3-4-foot (90-120 cm) stems above lush grape-like foliage, their single or double flowers sway gently from August through November. The gold central stamens provide a stunning focal point to these ethereal flowers. For the ultimate dancing bright white blooms, buy Whirlwind Japanese Anemone Plants from Plant Addicts.

Hardy in zones 4-8, they flourish in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-draining soil. Cultivars like crisp white Honorine Jobert (pictured) or dark pink September Charm are famous for long bloom windows. Be patient after planting: they grow modestly in their first year, but spread happily once settled. Mulch well in winter to protect young crowns, and try grouping with toad lilies, autumn ferns, and hellebores for a multi-season shade border.

From house tours and expert advice to favorite finds and DIYs.

Design-forward shops, hotels, and restaurants for your itinerary.

Architect Saba Ghorbanalinejad is particularly good at undoing a floor plan. In the projects of hers we’ve featured previously, the most consequential changes have often been reconfiguration: rooms are rearranged around central hubs, passages become places in their own right, and compact interiors begin to feel remarkably generous. Her latest project is closer to home. In fact, it is home.

In 2025, Saba acquired a 47-square-meter apartment in an Art Deco building overlooking the Parc des Buttes-Chaumont. Its conventional cellular layout largely ignored the view, so she consolidated the living spaces along the park-facing side and moved the bedroom to the quieter courtyard. The bathroom was treated less as a room than a series of functions woven into the plan, with full-height pocket doors allowing the apartment to shift between openness and privacy.

The apartment also gave Saba the opportunity to explore the materials she had long imagined for herself: warm okoumé, stainless steel, black lacquer, and deep-blue mosaic. The resulting look is rigorous but not austere, its more emphatic elements balanced by pale walls, tactile surfaces, and the trees beyond.

This is the first home Saba has designed for herself, and its success lies in how naturally it accommodates the day. “I particularly love the morning ritual of using the bespoke vanity and bathroom, getting ready for the day, and of course looking out towards the park,” she says. “Those everyday moments are what make the apartment feel most successful to me.”

#192. Gisele Bündchen’s Garden Is a Beautiful Escape From Modern Life – Steal Her Ideas for a Mindful Retreat
