Gisele Bündchen's lush, calming garden isn't as out of reach as it looks. Three experts share tips that can help you replicate the look.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What I wouldn't give to be like Gisele Bündchen, meditating in a tropical garden full of climbing bougainvillea, towering palms, and lush greenery. Her expression was so peaceful that I went out to my patio and felt (gently) judged for my single pot of basil.

The supermodel has created a space where you can actually slow down, breathe, and hopefully take in the sweet fragrance of your flowers. Fortunately for me, and you readers, these meditation garden ideas are entirely replicable, and I talked to some experts who gave me some tips. Now I'm sharing that information with you, like I’m Yoda to your Luke Skywalker.

The first mistake most people make when creating a "relaxing" garden is designing for the photograph rather than the experience. Dhriti, founder of mindful décor brand Root & Still, puts it well: "A mindful garden is one you feel before you analyze it. It isn't so much a style as an intention. A wellness-focused garden is designed around how you want to feel in it – calmer, slower, a little more present – rather than how it might look in a photograph."

That reframe of going from “How can I make this look nice on Instagram?” thinking to, "What do I actually want to feel out here?" is key.

A post shared by Gisele Bündchen (@gisele)

The path to a more restful garden usually involves taking things away, not adding them. Dhriti tells me, "A space full of competing features rarely feels restful, however lovely each element is on its own. I always encourage people to give the eye somewhere to rest: a single quiet focal point, softer planting, a sense of enclosure."

At nearly two feet tall, the Kante slender weathered concrete planter, available on Amazon, has the kind of quiet presence Dhriti describes. Plant lavender or rosemary in it beside a doorway or seating area, and it will look like it's always been there.

Thery Jean Christophe, founder of Musa Art Gallery, agrees: "One common mistake is designing a 'relaxing' garden that becomes too difficult to maintain. If the space creates constant work, it stops feeling peaceful. Low-maintenance planting, comfortable seating, shade, and a few repeated materials usually matter more than having a perfect layout." In other words, resist the urge to fill every corner because the space between things is actually doing a lot of the work.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The plants recommended by all three experts have one thing in common: they look considered even when left somewhat untended. Lavender, rosemary, jasmine, ornamental grasses, and ferns are the names that come up consistently.

Cameron Figgins, owner and president of Absolute Maintenance & Consulting, notes, "Plants with slow, consistent movements and low amounts of debris tend to promote a greater sense of calm. The right variety of plant should require little to no correction and remain healthy during its life cycle."

Structural, forgiving planting is important. Evergreens, grasses that catch the breeze, and fragrant herbs along a path are the backbone of Gisele's garden aesthetic. These are the kind of plants that do their job year-round but never expect much in return.

Plant Hidcote lavender (available from Plant Addicts) along a path or around seating, and you'll have the fragrant, low-maintenance anchor plant all three experts recommend. It smells incredible and gently tells your nervous system to take a breath.

In a garden, the visual element is obvious, but people often miss everything else our senses can offer. Dhriti points out that "...sound and movement matter too. The gentle trickle of a tabletop water feature, leaves shifting in the breeze, the scent of herbs – these are the things that quietly tell your nervous system it's safe to slow down. A mindful garden engages all the senses gently, never all at once."

A small water feature is probably the single highest-impact addition you can make to a garden that currently has none. The sound of moving water masks city noise, anchors the space, and does more for the atmosphere than many planting decisions. Pure Garden Store's weatherproof four-tier fountain delivers that gentle trickle Dhriti describes, and it works just as well on a balcony as it does in a full garden.

A post shared by Gisele Bündchen (@gisele)

If a Mediterranean garden with climbing bougainvillea feels like a stretch (and it really can for many people), Dhriti wants you to know that a balcony or courtyard is actually easier to work with: "A compact space already has a natural sense of enclosure, which is exactly what we try to create in larger gardens. You don't need more; you need the right one or two things, given room to breathe."

Jean Christophe echoes this: "Even a balcony can support this idea with planters, herbs, warm lighting, and one quiet corner to sit. Mindful design is less about size and more about atmosphere."

#193. How to Know If Your Home Is Actually Losing Heat (and Where)

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

Published Oct 11, 2026 10:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

If you live in an older home and haven’t updated the insulation, there’s a good chance that new insulation could make your house more comfortable and energy efficient. While drafty windows are to blame when you have to keep raising the thermostat during cold weather, heat loss is also often a result of unknown gaps, unsealed attics, and poorly insulated wall cavities, sending your heating bills soaring.

Don’t rely on guesswork to identify hidden cold spots in your home. Instead, use the following five tests and diagnostic tools recommended by experts so you can determine exactly where your home is losing heat and take targeted steps to ensure both comfort and financial savings this winter.

One of the cheapest and simplest methods to locate any heat loss is to conduct a visual inspection, says James Medina, HVACR instructor at Universal Technical Institute. “Simply check around doors and windows for any openings where the air and heat would be able to escape,” he advises. Wooden frames are particularly susceptible since they can decay and become soft or spongy.

Next, look for deteriorated weatherstripping, cracked caulking, gaps around pipes and/or wiring, and any insulation problems the home may have. Finally, look for gaps or holes around electrical outlets, light fixtures, and ceiling fans.

Another option is a touch test to feel for drafts. On a cold winter day, run your heating system and walk around the exterior of your home, feeling for any heat that may be escaping through door or window frames. “You can also do this on the interior of the home; as the heat escapes, it will feel cold to the touch,” explains Medina. Also, pay attention to temperature shifts around recessed lights, electrical outlets and receptacles, and baseboards.

When you hold a lit candle or an incense stick near the edges of closed windows and doors, you can quickly spot heat loss. “Walk around the interior of the residence that borders an unconditioned space, such as the outside or the garage, and watch for places the smoke pulls toward cracks or penetrations, as this would be an indication that air is leaving the conditioned space and carrying heat out with it,” explains Medina.

For this one, step outside and observe the roof on your home and your neighbors’ homes. “Check whether you have less frost or light snow on your roof compared to your neighbors,” says Kevin Bohnet, HVAC program director at Fortis College. “If your attic is not insulated well, heat will penetrate through and warm the inside of the attic, causing the frost or light snow to melt, which is a definite sign of losing heat.”

The most technological approach is to invest in a thermal camera. This vital diagnostic tool can quickly pinpoint heat loss by scanning walls, floors, ceilings, windows, and doors throughout the home. It works because most objects give off infrared energy, which is known as a heat signature.

The thermal camera detects and measures ‌infrared energy and converts the data into an electronic image, which displays the measured surface temperature of the object. It’s best to conduct this test on a cold day and turn the heat up inside the house so there is a big thermal contrast between the indoors and outdoors, says Medina.

Capable of measuring temperatures between -4 to +1022 degrees Fahrenheit, this thermal camera was deemed “best overall” by our testing team.

It is common for homes to experience some heat loss. “What you can do is try to mitigate this as much as possible by making sure your home is properly insulated and sealed,” says Medina. Most heat exfiltration problems can be resolved by sealing cracks and gaps with something as simple as caulking and insulation, he notes. “One of the best and most inexpensive ways to prevent heat from escaping your home is to have your attic insulated with the proper R-value, which is basically the rate at which your insulation allows heat to get in or out.”

If all else fails, contact a reputable energy auditing company to conduct a full inspection to identify issues and the best remedies to address them. You may end up needing to replace some doors or windows, especially if you have decaying wooden frames.

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned and Loved About Them

From crown molding and built-ins to creaky floors and drafty windows, old houses are full of charm and challenges. So we’re celebrating all the things that make old homes worth loving, living in, and fixing up. Learn about historic house styles; find practical advice for maintaining your old home; and discover quirky, forgotten features you simply won’t find in new builds.

Am I jealous? Obviously – but it’s an easy enough fix: I just need to plant one flower, stat...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I hate to admit it, but I’m getting a little jealous of my neighbors’ gardens... and it’s all down to one flower that looks like it’s been having an absolute blast as we veer headfirst into the ‘ber months.

All summer long, I’ve watched them fill up with the usual stars of the season – roses, hydrangeas, lavender, dahlias, and all those other perennial flowers that make a garden look incredible when everything is growing at full speed. My own garden has done its best to keep up, but... well, then fall arrived, and something rather unexpected happened.

Some of those gardens actually started looking better, and as far as I can tell, it’s all down to one flower (a late-season hero, no less) that everyone but me seems to have planted in abundance.

Yes, it seems as if Japanese anemones are the 'it' flower of the season, as I’ve started noticing them everywhere in my neighborhood. One garden has them spilling over a low wall, another has a whole mass of them towards the back of the border, and another seems to have an almost ridiculous number of flowers swaying above everything else.

Honestly, every time I walk past, I have pretty much the same thought: I really need some of those, whether it's a traditional Honorine Jobert Japanese Anemone, a bright and bold Fantasy™ Red Riding Hood Japanese Anemone, or a sweet and cold-hardy Fall in Love® Sweetly Japanese Anemone.

Part of the appeal of this one flower, I think, is the timing of it all; by the time Japanese anemones are putting on their best display, a lot of the flowers that made the garden feel so abundant in June and July are starting to fade. These, however, seem completely unfazed by the fact that summer is disappearing.

Depending on the variety and growing conditions, they can flower from late summer well into fall, with many continuing into October (depending on your USDA planting zone). So just when the garden might otherwise start looking a little tired, you suddenly have these tall stems covered in fresh flowers.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

And when you see them growing in a group, they can make a surprisingly big impact, especially as they can begin flowering in late summer and continue through fall, depending on the cultivar and conditions.

If you want to add one flower to your garden that will do its bit for pollinators, the Japanese anemone is a good shout; their open blooms can provide food for bees and other visiting insects, and their late flowering period is particularly useful because there are generally fewer flowers available in the garden as the season progresses.

Honestly, if I’m going to give something valuable garden space, I like the idea that it can earn its keep in more than one way. And a plant that gives me a beautiful display in September and October while also offering something to visiting bees, butterflies, and other critters? That ticks a lot of boxes for me!

Still, it's worth thinking about whether your garden is suited to this flower before you rush to buy one of your own; Japanese anemones generally prefer a sunny or partially shaded position and reasonably fertile soil that doesn’t dry out completely. They can also (fair warning) spread, particularly when they’re happy, and established plants can eventually stage something of a takeover.

Now, that can be a very good thing if you have the space and want that abundant effect (part of the reason I keep noticing them in my neighbors’ gardens is that they don’t look like one lonely plant that has been carefully tucked into a gap), but it’s worth thinking about before planting one right next to a delicate little perennial that you’re particularly fond of.

For a long time, I thought of the gardening year as having a fairly obvious hierarchy; spring was exciting because everything was waking up. Summer was the main event, when the garden was overflowing with flowers and everything seemed to be growing at once. Then fall arrived and the whole thing gradually started winding down.

Now, when I walk past my neighbors’ gardens in September or October and see that everyone has one flower covered in blooms, I see a garden having one last really good moment before winter arrives... and yes, I’m jealous. So you'd best believe that I’m going to stop admiring everyone else’s Japanese anemones and finally plant some of my own. I bet I spend all of next fall wondering why I waited so long.

Temperatures may have dropped, but the ground holds heat for weeks – so get those quiet beds working for you while you have time, with these vital soil repairs

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For many of us, the backyard can get abandoned in the weeks after summer – partly down to deteriorating weather, and partly not wanting to be reminded that some of our favorite lovely flowers are starting to fade and disappear. Key crops have been lifted and enjoyed, and there’s a general sense of things winding down, so the hose gets coiled, and the ground is left to sort itself out until March.

But your soil can still be working for you if you take action now. The earth in your yard will not be this warm again until May, and the window closes quietly – so why not make the most of it while you can? Improving soil in fall takes less effort than the same job come spring. Anything you put into the ground now lands while biology can still act on it, rather than sitting on frozen ground waiting for a thaw. These key tasks are all due before the first hard frost, and a couple carry real deadlines.

Getting your soil ready for next season doesn't mean you need to embark on a back-breaking overhaul. Think of it as your backyard’s peaceful recovery hour, with small and easy actions now that can pay off tenfold come spring. By taking just one afternoon session to tuck your beds in properly now, you are laying the groundwork for nutrient boosts, vibrant early blooms, and bountiful harvests when the sunshine returns…

Whether your garden spent the summer baking under intense drought, handling relentless downpours, or simply feeding hungry crops, late-season soil is often left exhausted, compacted, and depleted. Left bare over winter, heavy rains might leach away remaining minerals, while severe freeze-thaw cycles can strip away topsoil structure. Acting now, while the ground is still warm, helps beneficial soil microbes and earthworms to process new goodness before spring planting begins.

Keep your local hardiness zone in mind as you plan your fall workflow. In northern regions (USDA zones 3-6), it’s critical to move swiftly before the hard freezes lock up the ground. However, southern growers (zones 7-10) have a longer runway with which to make these soil boosts, and the warmer soils will allow cover crops to establish well into late fall.

To prime your tired beds ahead of these soil repairs, give the ground a drench with a diluted seaweed formula like Neptune’s Harvest Hydrolyzed Fish & Seaweed Fertilizer, available from Amazon. Seaweed is an excellent tonic for weary autumn soil, strengthening microbial life ahead of dormancy. And if your soil needs a quick physical boost, top-dress with a sprinkling of Espoma Natural Mushroom Blend Fertilizer, available from Walmart, which works wonders for exhausted autumn beds.

Essentially, any garden bed that is headed into winter needs a little timely TLC and then it wants leaving alone. Everything here is really one instruction repeated 7 ways: keep something living or something rotting on the surface from now until spring. The beds you have to work on next year will be dark and loose, with worms right up under the surface, if you dress and prepare the ground now with the following steps…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Cover crops run on a hard clock, making this one of the most urgent fall tasks. Legumes need 6-8 weeks of active growth ahead of a killing frost, while hardy grains will manage with 4-6 weeks. Crimson clover (Trifolium incarnatum) works closely with soil bacteria to fix atmospheric nitrogen directly into the ground. In colder zones, it winter-kills into a manageable mat that easily pulls apart by hand come April. Cereal rye (Secale cereale) is another option if time gets away from you a bit. It germinates in cool soil and continues growing at temperatures that shut down other plants. You can buy Crimson Clover Seeds from Eden Brothers for just a few dollars.

Rake the bed smooth and level, scatter seed at twice the standard drilled rate to guarantee dense growth. Then rake again to bury the seeds a quarter to a half-inch (0.6-1.3 cm) deep. A handheld spreader like the Chapin 8706G Spreader from The Home Depot gives more even coverage than scattering by hand, eliminating patchy gaps where weeds might move in. Water thoroughly, and keep the ground damp if the week stays dry. Germination is the only part of the process that needs babysitting. Once established, the living roots safeguard your soil all winter long.

Fall is officially the quiet season at soil labs. Turnaround time for September samples is fast, whereas April submissions can sit in long backlogs. Take a little time now to get a soil test. Pull some core samples from 6 inches (15 cm) down in several spots around your bed. Mix them in a clean bucket to get a representative average, and send it off. You will receive a detailed report about soil pH, phosphorus, potassium, and organic matter levels. Why guess at what your soil is short of and waste money buying the wrong feed next year, when you can get reliable answers now?

Timing matters most if your lab test indicates a need for adding lime. Limestone is slow-acting and requires around 4-6 months to break down and adjust soil pH. So applying it in fall gives the amendment the entire dormant season to react with the soil. Untilled garden application rates stay around 5 pounds per 100 square feet (2.3 kg per 9 sqm). If you do need to add some lime, Down to Earth Organic Agricultural Lime, available on Amazon, delivers natural calcium that buffers soil gently. Remember that lime can interfere with phosphorus availability, so give it about a month on its own before adding other fall amendments.

When applying compost in fall, just remember that it goes on top, not down in. Spreading half an inch (1.3 cm) over an established bed is a perfect maintenance dose, while a 2-3-inch (5–8cm) layer suits any ground that’s in rough shape after a demanding summer crop. Nightcrawlers and earthworms then do the heavy lifting through fall, dragging rich organic material down before the cold sends them deep.

Do not expect a massive surge of nitrogen during the first year. Finished compost releases very little nitrogen the season after application, operating primarily as a soil structure amendment. What it does deliver is a boost in water-holding capacity and a thriving population boom for beneficial subterranean microbes and fungi. This really pays off in mid-July, when beds retain moisture days longer during heatwaves than untreated ground. To supercharge humic development under your compost layer, dust beds with some Sta-Green Earthworm Castings, available from Lowe’s. This introduces beneficial microbes and enzymes to work quietly all winter long.

Nitrogen washes easily out of bare soil over winter, but phosphorus and potassium do not. Amendments carrying either element can be safely laid out in fall, resting until spring roots wake up to find them. Traditional bone meal is the premier phosphorus source, breaking down very slowly on a timeline of months. You can get Epoma Organic Bone Meal from Walmart for a reduced price. Kelp meal supplies potassium alongside a spread of micronutrients, delivered at concentrations too gentle to burn roots.

However, consult your soil test results before applying either one. Bone meal rapidly loses availability as soil pH rises past 7, and it offers zero benefit to soil that is already loaded with phosphorus. Excess soil phosphorus can be harmful, too. Plants supplied with too much stop investing in mutually beneficial mycorrhizal fungal partnerships (and that relationship does far more for long-term plant health than any bag of bone meal). Where needed, some Down to Earth Organic Kelp Meal from Amazon nourishes underground soil life steadily. Gently scratch any amendments into the top inch (2.5 cm) of soil and cover with mulch.

Exposing bare soil to winter weather exacts a heavy toll for every month it remains uncovered. Rain drives fine soil particles down, crusting and sealing the surface so air and water cannot penetrate. Repeated freeze-thaw cycles heave shallow perennial roots clean out of the ground, while any soil left bare until January quickly fills with winter annual weeds. So add some protective mulch. Light straw and shredded leaves can go on thick at 4-6 inches (10-15 cm), whereas dense wood chips perform best at 2-4 inches (5-10 cm).

Timing is important, though. Wait for the ground to cool before applying thick mulch layers. Laid too early in warm soil, it may trigger late, tender plant growth that won’t harden off in time. Your goal is holding cold soil cold, preventing temperature fluctuations that can snap fine feeder roots. Always pull mulch back 2-3 inches (5-8 cm) from the stems and crowns of perennial plants. Field voles love nesting in warm mulch, where they chew on bark and stems all winter long. One of the team’s favorite organic mulches is Back to the Roots Organic Mulch, available from Amazon, which holds its integrity well in rough weather and looks lovely.

One rich soil treat is readily available in fall: fallen leaves. Just be sure to shred your leaves before you use them. Whole leaves mat together into a slick, water-repellent sheet that sheds rain off the top of your beds. Running over leaf piles with a lawn mower solves the problem. A dedicated electric leaf mulcher such as the Grasstigon Electric Leaf Mulcher, available from Amazon, also makes quick work of large yards. Leaf mold is a great way to rebuild soil structure. Heavy clay soils, in particular, respond with a looseness that is nearly impossible to achieve through other routes.

Beneficial fungi are the main drivers of leaf mold breakdown, whereas bacteria dominate traditional hot compost piles. This difference explains why leaf mold piles stay cool and break down slowly over a year or two, rather than heating up quickly. Construct your leaf pile roughly 3 feet (90 cm) wide and tall, keeping it damp so fungal networks can colonize the leaves. If you are gathering fallen leaves, use sturdy Joyhalo 72-Gallon Leaf Bags, available from Amazon keep your collected organic mulches dry, contained, and ready to spread.

Every single pass with a power tiller inadvertently resets the hard work your soil has already accomplished. Fungal networks that took a whole season to build get instantly shredded. Furthermore, buried weed seeds are brought up to the light where they can germinate. The crumbly, sponge-like soil structure that holds water and allows air to circulate is being built slowly by roots, fungi, and earthworms. It won’t survive being churned by metal blades.

Compaction still needs addressing before winter – just without the rotary blades. A heavy-duty tool like the Ergonomic U-Tools Broadfork, available from Walmart sinks its tines nearly a foot (30 cm) deep and levers the soil open without turning it over, so the right layers stay where they belong over winter. If clearing spent crops, cut plants off at the soil line and leave the roots. As those roots rot over winter, they create perfect drainage channels and pathways for spring moisture, with zero extra effort.

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#199. The Best Driveway Alarms of 2026, Tested

Gifts That Promise to Get Used 🎁 30 Gifts of the Year

By Tony Carrick, Additional research provided by Emily Blackwood

Published Oct 11, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

A driveway alarm can offer a level of protection for your home when security cameras aren’t in the budget. Not only can they keep you informed of your family’s comings and goings, but an alarm can also alert you when there is an unwanted guest. These devices consist of a motion-activated sensor installed outside your home and a receiver inside your house. When vehicles or people trigger the sensor, the receiver lights up and plays a sound. Since driveway alarms can have a range of up to half a mile, they’re an ideal choice for those with larger properties and longer driveways.

We tested five of the top driveway alarms to determine which ones offer the best home security. After a week of testing, we found the HTZSafe Driveway Alarm to be the best of the bunch, largely thanks to its attractive design, reliable detection, and many sound options.

Bottom line: Driveway alarms are an affordable, effective way to enhance home security, with options to suit various needs and properties.

A clever design, a bevy of sound options, and impressive detection and transmission ranges make the HTZSafe one of the best affordable ways to add security to your property. It consists of a receiver designed in the likeness of an owl, along with a transmitter that also has an owl shape. When the alarm goes off, the owl’s eyes light up. There’s also an audio alert with 35 different sound options on the receiver, ranging from classical music to an owl call. Some of the sound options include voices naming specific locations, such as the backyard, garage, or front door. A single receiver is capable of supporting up to 32 sensors. The HZTSafe also allows you to assign different sounds to different sensors, which made it easy to tell which area was detecting motion.

This long-distance driveway alarm has three sensitivity settings. During testing, this helped us reduce the number of false alarms due to animals or passing traffic. It also has one of the longest ranges of any driveway security alarm we tested, working reliably up to about a quarter mile away with houses and hills as obstacles.

What our tester says: “The HZTSafe driveway alarm is accurate, has a long range, and offers some of the more entertaining designs and sound options of any driveway alarm.”—Tony Carrick, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the HTZSafe driveway alarm at Amazon.

After extensive testing, we also highly recommend the following driveway alarms.

This reliable driveway alarm has a long range and sends alerts directly to your phone.

Long range makes this alarm ideal for homes with longer driveways.

This driveway alarm, which also doubles as an alarm clock, offers excellent range and can support up to eight sensors.

This driveway alarm has a simple easy to set up design with a broad range of sound options.

We tested driveway alarms by setting them up in our driveways, then letting them do what they’re designed to do through a week of testing. During this period, we evaluated each alarm based on several factors. We considered how easy it was to set up each alarm, then assessed how accurately they detected vehicles and people and how frequently they produced false alarms. Since none of us have ¼-mile long driveways, we tested range by taking the sensors in some cases up to a half a mile from the receiver.  While we only tested the driveway alarms for a week, we did put them through a durability test by repeatedly spraying them with water.

As we tested each model, we assigned ratings from 1 to 5 across five categories: setup, detection performance, alert performance, signal strength, and value. We then aggregated all of the ratings to produce an overall score.

It’s time to dive into the various features and capabilities offered by alarm systems. From weatherproof designs that will survive a storm to solar-powered devices that never need replacement batteries, there are a few factors to consider when looking for a driveway alarm system.

There are three common types of driveway alarms. All of them can increase your home security and provide more protection for your family, and each type has specific benefits.

Passive infrared (PIR) driveway alarms have infrared light beams that sense nearby movement using heat. Because they detect objects that radiate warmer temperatures, these alarms will sense not only car engines but also animals and people.

When this alarm detects a change in heat patterns, it transmits a signal to the receiver, alerting you of the change. PIR alarms are generally inexpensive and easy to install, as they usually come as a single unit for outdoor mounting.

Unlike PIR alarms, active infrared alarms (AIR alarms) consist of two parts: the transmitter and the receiver. The transmitter shoots a beam of infrared light that the receiver picks up. When an object crosses the beam’s path, the receiver is alerted to the interruption, and an alarm is sent out.

Usually, users place one part on each side of their driveway to detect movement. The downside to AIR alarms is that the area under watch is very small and specific. Someone could easily walk around the driveway and avoid being detected.

The third type of driveway alarm is the magnetic probe. This model is built out of an encased PVC pipe with a metal detector hidden inside. The pipe is buried a few inches partially underground next to your driveway and is triggered whenever a vehicle crosses its path. That alert is then transmitted to an indoor receiver.

Because the detector only senses metal, there is less risk of false alarms. Both PIR and AIR alarms can falsely detect rustling leaves or a friendly neighbor as an intruder. While it can’t detect everything, magnetic probe alarms are reliable in letting you know if there’s a vehicle in your driveway.

The transmission range of a driveway alarm refers to the maximum distance you can place the sensor from the receiver while still getting a signal. Typically, people place the receiving device inside their home, so it helps to choose a product that can function properly while indoors.

Before you start shopping, decide exactly where you’ll mount your receiver and install the sensors so you can decide how much distance you need. Most sensors have a range of at least 500 to 1,000 feet. A range of up to 50 feet is considered very short.

Today’s models can be powered by three sources: batteries, solar energy, and your home’s electricity.

The biggest complaint with motion sensor driveway alarm systems is that they can trigger false alarms. As previously stated, solar-powered devices can be set off by changing weather conditions, while heat-sensing PIR devices can be triggered by children or animals running by.

Because of this risk, some brands are manufacturing their alarms with sensitivity settings that let you adjust the sensor range to reduce false alarms in a specific area. These settings can usually be changed by moving a dial on the unit.

This new technology has made driveway alarms more effective than ever before, and it’s a great feature if you have numerous high-traffic areas around your home.

Since driveway alarm sensors live outdoors, weatherproofing is key for a driveway alarm. Most driveway alarms have an IP44 or IP65 weather rating, which means they can withstand rain, snow, and UV rays from the sun.

A driveway alarm isn’t much use if it continually cries wolf whenever the wind blows or a squirrel happens by. Proper installation is key to reducing the number of false alarms. Installing the alarm at the right height to avoid picking up small animals and pets, setting it the right distance from the road to prevent it from picking up traffic, and adjusting the sensitivity are all key to avoiding false alarms:

While no one wants to believe their home is vulnerable to unwanted guests, a high-quality driveway motion alarm can help eliminate vulnerabilities and provide real security. There are benefits to any kind of home security, and driveway alarms stand out because they are affordable, simple to use, and easy to install. If you’re just beginning to create a home security system, driveway alarms are a great place to start.

Here are some of the advantages of owning a driveway alarm:

Now that you’ve seen what is offered by some of the best driveway alarm systems, you might have a few more questions about alarm selection. Below are answers to some of the most common questions about driveway alarms to help you choose the highest-quality option for your home’s security system.

A driveway alarm can alert you to who’s approaching your home, which can provide a level of security.

Driveway alarms use a sensor and a receiver to detect motion and alert the recipient of that motion.

Yes, PIR and AIR alarms can detect people. Magnetic probe alarms can only detect metal.

Yes. If you have a PIR or AIR alarm, it can be triggered by a pet. Some devices come with a sensitivity setting to reduce the possibility of pets triggering the sensor.

It depends on your driveway, but generally, you want to install the system far enough away from the road so it isn’t triggered by traffic.

Yes, for most people, driveway alarms are worth it. You can typically find driveway alarms for less than $30, making them an affordable alternative to a home security camera. Most models are expandable, so you can add multiple sensors to one receiver, helping to secure various areas around the home.

The volume of the alarm really depends on where the base is located in your home. If the base is in a central location, such as a living area or kitchen, then chances are the alarm doesn’t need to be particularly loud to let you know when something or someone triggers a sensor. If you have a larger home, you may need to crank up the volume to broadcast those alerts to all parts of the home.

Yes, there are smart driveway alarms, such as the YoLink Lora Smart Outdoor driveway alarm, which send push alerts, emails, or text messages to your phone when the sensor is triggered.

#200. A ‘Permanent Camping Trip’: The Landscape at Phillip Johnson’s Glass House

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

Modernist architect Philip Johnson, perhaps best known for his urban work like New York CIty’s former AT&T building and the classic Four Seasons restaurant, used to refer to himself as a landscape artist.

Architecture and landscaping, Johnson once said, are “one art.” At his own home, the Glass House in New Canaan, Connecticut, where he lived for almost 60 years until his death in 2005, he deliberately made the walls between the two virtually invisible.

“This was their house in landscape,” says architectural historian Hilary Lewis, who walked the property with Johnson countless times and collaborated with him on his memoirs. “He used to call it a permanent camping trip. He would get cross with me because I didn’t know my trees.”

Johnson and his partner, David Whitney, were passionate about the trees and wanted light to penetrate to the bottom of the forest floor. Working with arborists, they carefully removed branches and trees from the forest of mostly second-growth oaks, maples, and elms to create alleys of light and to make it look like a more mature woods.

The original Glass House was built in 1949, but over the years Johnson and Whitney added both land and buildings to the estate. Now open to the public for tours, the Glass House property covers about 49 acres and one can visit a series of 14 structures. “The buildings,” says Lewis, “punctuate the landscape. They were designed to be an interesting location to pull your eye towards or walk towards.”

We got permission to photograph the secluded 49-acre property at dawn. Join us for a tour:

From itchy skin to sneezing fits, some popular indoor plants can cause surprising allergic reactions. Luckily, there are a few simple precautions that can help.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Closed windows and the season’s first furnace run can quickly change the air inside your home. Dust gets stirred up, humidity drops, and outdoor plants come back indoors – bringing dust, damp potting mix, and other potential allergens with them.

During summer, houseplants barely register as an allergy issue. Many plants sit on porches or patios, while open windows help keep indoor air moving. By late September, those windows are closed and the pots are back inside. For some people, that shift can turn indoor plant allergies that went unnoticed for months into a stuffy nose that won't quit.

Good houseplant care covers the basics, but fall calls for a few extra precautions. Dusty leaves and soggy potting mix cause most flare-ups, but a handful of common species also carry allergens in their sap or pollen, which deserve a closer look this time of year.

Once the furnace runs for the first time, it can stir dust, dust-mite particles, and whatever settled in the vents over the summer into the air. Swap the filter before that first cold night. The faint burnt smell on day one is usually dust burning off the heater. Closed windows can make the problem worse because less outdoor air comes in to dilute it.

The other half of the trouble starts at the watering can. Houseplants grow more slowly indoors as the days shorten, yet many still get watered on a summer schedule. Potting mix that never dries out can develop mold on its surface. Bagged mixes may carry molds such as Aspergillus fumigatus from the start, although one study of plant-filled homes found very little of it in the air unless plants or soil were disturbed. Wet soil is a watering problem first and an allergy problem second.

Houseplant allergies are fairly uncommon overall, but they can still be troublesome for sensitive people. Each plant below has documented cases associated with it, and all five are common enough to find in living rooms, bedrooms, and home offices. That does not mean you need to remove them automatically – the risk depends on the plant, how it is handled, and your own sensitivity.

Weeping fig (Ficus benjamina) is probably the best-known allergenic houseplant, and the trouble starts with its milky sap. The allergens don’t always stay put, either. They can turn up in the dust on the leaves and on the floor around the pot, so a plant that nobody has touched recently can still be a source of exposure.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Some of its proteins can cross-react with natural rubber latex, so anyone with a latex allergy should wear latex-free gloves when pruning it. Amazon sells Supmedic disposable latex-free gloves in a range of sizes.

Yucca (Yucca gigantea) is grown for its foliage, so people rarely suspect it. But skin-prick testing has still turned up yucca sensitization in people with allergic rhinitis, and plant keepers who handle it for work have broken out in hives. Its long, stiff leaves hold dust along their whole length. Wiping each one down with a damp cloth now and then keeps it from piling up.

Peace lilies (Spathiphyllum wallisii) can rebloom indoors, and the pale, powdery spike inside each white hood is where the pollen comes from. Documented allergy cases have involved both that pollen and the leaves. The simple move is to snip spent blooms early and keep flowering pots out of the bedroom.

Mums start coming indoors as table decor around now. Their allergens, including sesquiterpene lactones, sit on the flowers and in the fine hairs on the leaves, where they can become airborne. Rashes tend to start on the fingertips of whoever pinches off the buds. Anyone who already reacts to chamomile or feverfew may react to mums as well – they're all in the same plant family.

If you’re sensitive, wear gloves when handling mums, wash your hands afterward, and keep the plants away from your face and main living areas.

English ivy turns up among the more frequent houseplant sensitizers in skin testing of people with allergic rhinitis. It also contains falcarinol, a compound that can irritate skin or set off an allergic rash. Reactions usually follow pruning or pulling runners by hand. Ivy that summered outside should get a thorough rinse and a close look before it comes back in.

Dust is the easy win. Wipe broad leaves with a damp cloth, like these Amazon Basics microfiber cleaning cloths. Dry dusters just move spider mites and insect eggs from plant to plant. Smaller plants can go under the sink faucet in the morning so the leaves dry by evening. For the bedroom, a Levoit Core 300 HEPA air purifier can pull fine dust and pollen out of the air. It won't do anything for dust on the leaves, though.

Let the top of the potting mix dry between waterings, and pour off whatever collects in the saucer. A white, cottony film on the soil means it's staying too wet. Scrape that layer off outdoors and top the pot with fresh houseplant potting soil. Allergists generally advise keeping indoor humidity on the low side – dust mites and mold both thrive in damp air – so skip the humidifier near slow-drying containers.

Nobody has to give up a favorite plant over a few sneezes. If the stuffy nose sticks around into October, an allergist can test for specific houseplants, and a weeping fig that tests positive can move to a friend's sunroom.

If you’re prone to houseplant-related allergies, choose foliage plants with smooth leaves, little or no indoor flowering, and low watering needs. These three plants won't guarantee no reaction, but they avoid several common trouble spots.

The parlor palm is a good choice for living rooms because it is foliage-led, does not have milky sap, and is generally considered pet-safe. Choose a young plant that is unlikely to flower indoors.

Also known as baby rubber plant, Peperomia obtusifolia is not a rubber tree and does not produce the latex-like sap associated with ficus plants. Its thick, smooth leaves and low watering needs make it a good low-allergen option.

Cast iron plant (Aspidistra elatior) has large, smooth leaves, which won't trap dust as much as fuzzy foliage. It rarely flowers indoors and tolerates low light and infrequent watering.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#202. Expert Advice: A Landscape Designer Shares Her Best Money-Saving Tips

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

No doubt new landscaping can be a costly home project, especially if it involves high-end materials and large specimen plants. I know this firsthand as a landscape designer who has to supply cost estimates to clients; I often find myself explaining (sympathetically) that plant prices have dramatically increased, that certain materials are more expensive than others, and that labor costs can slowly add up—especially if the yard sits on a steep hill.

The bottom line is that landscaping costs can fluctuate depending on the size of your yard, where you live, the materials you choose, and the amenities you want. But that said, your new garden doesn’t have to completely rock (and sink) your financial boat. What you need to do is approach your project honestly, smartly, and thoughtfully.

Here are some ways to save some money when designing your new garden:

This is, perhaps, the most important thing you can do to save money. Start by making your wish list (start big because you can always whittle it down), browse gardening books and magazines for design ideas, visit local nurseries and landscape supply stores to get an idea of what materials cost (and then remember that your landscape designer will probably mark that up). If you’re on a strict budget, be mindful and focus on what you actually need (a flat space for a grill) and not what you want (a built-in outdoor kitchen).

If I had to list the top things to splurge on, I would say: quality hardscaping like retaining walls, patios, and walkways as these are the bones of your garden and will look good all year. Also on my list: nutrient-dense planting soil or compost to get your plants off to a healthy start (never skip on proper soil prep) and an irrigation system with a smart controller to automatically supply the right amount of water to your plants. Where to save? Consider buying plants in smaller sizes (think 4-inch instead of one gallon, and 5 gallon not 15 gallon) and buying fewer plants at first and adding more slowly as your budget allows.

Asses what materials you might already have and what can be repurposed. Also scour yard sales and local neighborhood online sites and see if someone is offloading bricks, pots, or patio furniture. You may have to change your design a bit based on what you discover, but adopting this mindset can really help your bottom line.

If you’re trying to fill a bunch of pots or amend large areas, don’t even think about reaching for bagged soil. Get a truckload delivered, and if you have extra you can always store it and save it for the next time you need it. Also, if you can be patient, wait for sales at nurseries to buy some of your plants like annuals, herbs, and veggies for your beds and ground covers to fill in bare spaces.

By including a veggie/herb garden into your design, you will save money on store-bought produce and be able to harvest what you need. (How many wilted, half-used heads of cilantro or lettuce do you have in your fridge?) Be realistic, though, about how much time you have to tend to and harvest your crops; otherwise that is a money- and food-waster. Try also incorporating plants that do a job, like lemon balm to repel mosquitoes, rosemary to keep away munching invaders like deer, or flowers that provide seeds you can save to grow more plants. Last, consider adding perennials and bulbs good for cutting and making homemade bouquets.

A garden that is relatively easy to take care of either by you or a crew will save on maintenance costs. Plan for trees, hedges, and shrubs that don’t need routine shearing to look tidy; avoid fussy annuals and perennials that need constant deadheading; and abandon the large lawn idea that will need tons of water and fertilizer to look green. A water-conscious garden that incorporates natives, succulents, and drought-tolerant plants will also translate into a money saver.

You may be tempted to DIY it all in the interest of saving money, but before you assign yourself the role of head contractor or lead horticulturist, write yourself a reality check and acknowledge that you’ll likely have to let the professionals do at least some part of the project. You can certainly do a portion of the work yourself, but if done improperly it could actually cost you more in the long run. One thing to remember is that it’s okay to call in favors if your aunt is an architect or your brother works in a nursery. I believe in the it-takes-a-village philosophy. Ask for help. And remember that people usually love a homemade pie as a thank-you.

End rot is a common challenge for winter squash in fall but once you've identified the cause, it's simple to rescue the remaining crop.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Winter squash is so easy to grow but dark or soft patches around the fruit’s base is a common challenge in October, indicating end rot. Rotting bases are such a disappointment in fall, just as you’re looking forward to a harvest of butternut, acorn, honeynut and other winter squashes like spaghetti and delicata squash.

Don’t fear the worst, though. End rot on winter squash in October is easily fixed, so great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Act fast and you don’t have to lose your entire harvest. Identify and fix the issue, sand you'll save the rest of your homegrown gourds from a similar fate.

If you’re growing winter squash this season, it’s useful to know the signs to look out for, and what they indicate, even if you haven't noticed any dark patches on fruit bases, so you can take swift action at the very first whisper of a rotting bottom. Come on in to Garden ER and let’s diagnose and treat those ugly patches on the bases of your winter squash.

A winter squash rotting from the base up is easily spotted. A discolored patch on the bottom of the gourd appears: it may look darker, bruised or as if it’s been soaked in water. The spot will gradually grow larger and turn black or brown, and often becomes flat or slightly sunken. Press it and it’ll feel a little softer or spongier than the rest of the squash’s firm skin.

If the rotting base has been developing for a while, the patch may have collapsed into a hole, become moldy or emit a foul smell.

A healthy squash will have a base that's firm, with the spot where the blossom once grew having developed into a dry, pale, roughly circular patch.

While you can’t help the affected squash’s rotting bottom, it’s vital to diagnose what caused it so you can save the rest of your harvest. While plants grown at ground level are vulnerable, end rot is also a common issue when growing winter squash vertically up a trellis.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Blossom end rot is the most common reason, caused by a lack of calcium in the fruit which leads to weak cell walls. The problem isn’t typically a lack of calcium in the soil, but the plant's ability to take up and use the calcium. And the underlying cause of this is typically acidic soil, drought or inconsistent watering.

If blossom end rot is the problem, the rotting patch at the base of the fruit will look even and will have a brown, leathery, sunken appearance. Because calcium is used to build cell walls as the gourd grows from its base, deformed fruit formation is another clue that you’re dealing with blossom end rot.

Contact with wet ground is the next most likely cause of end rot on your squashes. With more rain and cooler temperatures, it’s common at this time of year for the soil to remain moist. Contact softens the rinds where fruits are resting on permanently damp ground, giving pathogens like soil-borne fungi and bacteria a chance to start rotting the fruit.

Distinguishing between wet ground and blossom end rot being the cause is simple. Look at where the rot occurs: if wet ground is the cause, the fruit will likely look healthy except for the portion in contact with the soil; blossom end rot causes more even rotting, though it’s likely to be worse at the base.

Pests are the least likely source of rot in squash ends in October, but it's a possibility. If pests start gnawing on the end of a fruit, the open wound can quickly become infected and start to rot. Signs of pest damage such as bites and holes will be clear, and these wounds are very likely to start rotting if they’re in contact with wet ground.

Squash already affected with rotting bases cannot be saved, and rot can spread and contribute to worsening conditions for the rest of the plant. Cut fruit from the plant with a sharp pair of hand pruners, as soon as you spot the first signs of a rotting bottom.

If you’ve caught the problem early and the problem is wet ground or pest damage, the squash is still safe to eat – just cut away the affected part with a safety margin of a good inch of healthy flesh. Inspect the flesh and if it’s firm, hard, smells sweet and has its usual color, it’s safe to cook.

If blossom end rot is the cause, dispose of the squash even if the patch is still tiny. Because the calcium deficiency affects the fruit’s growth, the flesh is likely to be less sweet.

Regardless of cause, throw out any fruit that has a lot of rot, is very soft or leaking, or has a bad smell.

As acidic soil is a common cause of blossom end rot, check pH levels. A comprehensive soil meter such as this from Amazon tests pH along with moisture levels, temperature, sunlight intensity and soil fertility so is a really handy helper when you’re growing vegetables. If you simply want a fast answer to whether your soil is acidic or not, test strips such as Rapitest Soil Test Kit, also from Amazon, is a quick and cheap method. Testing your soil is a smart move, however you choose to do it, as it'll alert you to any deficiencies that may be affecting others crops too.

Your local extension office can provide guidance on how to lower the acidity of your soil if results reveal a low pH level.

Good watering practices lowers the risk that remaining fruit will develop blossom end rot. Aim to keep soil consistently moist rather than letting it dry out completely and then soaking it. Water at the soil line low to the ground near the stem, keeping leaves and fruits dry as excess moisture on squashes can contribute to rot, especially in cooler fall temperatures.

A soaker hose such as this Kink-Free Flat Soaker Hose from Walmart is a simple solution, or you’ll find some great deals on drip irrigation starter kits now summer’s over, like this Garden Irrigation System, also from Walmart.

Elevating developing fruits off the ground is a great way to prevent rot, keeping them off damp soil. It can be as simple as placing individual fruits on top of rocks or wood planks, or lay straw under the lot. A wheat cover straw such as CleanStraw mulch, available from Walmart, is ideal. Don’t worry about a few seeds being left among the threshed straw – wheat seedlings are shallow-rooted and very easy to pull up.

Move young fruits carefully so you don’t damage the stems.

Good airflow around plants will also reduce localized moisture and the risk of rotting. Adding a layer of straw over the soil will do the job of improving airflow as well as lifting fruit off the soil, but general care will help, too. Squash plants tend to get very dense with vegetation as they grow so regularly remove any yellow, damaged or mildewed leaves, being careful not to prune healthy leaves too aggressively as plants need these to make energy.

You can also boost airflow by removing debris under and around the plants, especially around the fruits. A small hand rake like Fiskars Xact Hand Rake, available from Lowe's, makes the job easier.

Keep a closer eye on your squashes once October arrives, and harvest them as soon as they’re ready. The longer they sit outside, the more likely they are to rot. Signs they’re ripe and ready include a full, mature color, a hard rind that resists your fingernail, and a dried or hardened stem.

The hard rind of winter squashes mean they store well, so even if you have a glut, harvest what you can, as soon as you can.

In colder growing zones, early cold snaps, shorter daylight hours, and damp fall weather in October can slow down root activity, making it harder for plants to transport calcium efficiently to developing fruit, making this a likely cause behind blossom end rot.

In warmer zones, late-season heat and drier soil accelerates plant growth and transpiration, which can cause severe moisture fluctuations, making inconsistent watering a likely trigger for blossom end rot.

Every week, the Garden ER series brings you simple solutions to this season's most pressing problems, for happy and healthy plants without any hassle.

A lost leaf or two doesn’t spell disaster for a Christmas cactus in October but you can't afford to ignore this distress signal.

Chafer grubs have devastated drought-stressed lawns this year but are easily treated if catch this crucial fall window.

Work out what your peace lily needs to recover if spathes develop brown patches or look dry and crispy around the edges.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

#205. Garden Visit: A Mill Valley Artist’s Obsession with Dahlias

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

An explosion of dramatic dahlias makes it nearly impossible to miss the house and garden of mixed media artist and teacher Bibby Gignilliat—particularly because it’s in the middle of a quiet street in Mill Valley, California. In 2013, Bibby purchased the property and began working on the garden almost immediately. “The previous owners were avid gardeners, particularly of roses, but there were several aspects of the garden that didn’t feel like me, including two old sheds, a decomposed granite pathway and a rather unappealing hedge across the front,” she says. Bibby hired a garden designer and together they created its first iteration. Since then, the garden has continued to evolve in stages, without a formal plan—which, not surprisingly, is the part she loves most.

During the isolating COVID period, Bibby decided her garden should function as an outdoor living room. She extended the deck and created three separate gathering areas so that she could essentially have a “progressive dinner party” through the garden. “I loved the idea that instead of sitting in one place all evening, guests could move through the garden as the evening progressed.” Professionally trained as a chef, Bibby also ran a cooking and events business for 20 years before becoming a full-time artist, so food, creativity, and entertaining have always been central to her life.

The original garden had just one hot pink dahlia, and Bibby was instantly drawn to its incredible colors and forms. This year, she planted a staggering 100 dahlia bulbs in the front and another 25 in the backyard, concentrating them around the sunny areas and the fire pit. She routinely brings them inside for arrangements, gives them as hostess gifts, and brings bunches to her artist’s studio in Sausalito for her Open Studios.

Like Bibby’s unstructured, free-flowing garden, her artwork is layered and textural. “I build up surfaces and then dig, sand, and excavate back into them to reveal what is underneath,” she shares. Working intuitively, Bibby embraces bold colors and unexpected moments along the way. “There is a freedom and flow to my work that I think is also very present in my garden.” Bibby definitely didn’t want a perfectly manicured garden. She adds, “I am much more drawn to the feeling of an English garden: organic, abundant, a little wild and allowed to do its own thing.”

Gardening over the years has taught Bibby a lot about letting go and not trying to control every detail. As every seasoned gardener knows, you may have a plan for your garden, but sometimes the garden has its own. “I actually love that lesson because it is very similar to making art. I can begin a painting thinking I know where it is going, but at some point I have to listen to what the painting is telling me rather than forcing my original idea. Some of my favorite moments in both painting and gardening come from things I never planned.”

Photography by Kier Holmes, unless otherwise noted.

Before you mow a neighbor's lawn as a favor, it's worth knowing the etiquette – and when a kind gesture could be interpreted as trespassing.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It’s right out of a Norman Rockwell painting: the kind man mowing the elderly neighbor’s lawn as a surprise. But don’t try this at home. Times have changed, America has changed, and American laws (and lawns) have changed, too. What might once have been viewed as a courtesy gesture could be called trespass today.

When it comes to lawn mowing tips, here’s an important one: don’t mow any lawn but your own without permission. In many cases these days, the person entering a neighbor’s property to mow does so because they don’t like the unkempt look, rather than being courteous. But even if your motive is kind, don’t take the step without asking.

Any time you enter another person’s property without their express permission – with or without a lawn mower – you may violate their property rights and be charged with trespassing. As a former attorney, I explore common issues like this in my Gardening Lawyer series, which looks at the legal issues that can catch gardeners by surprise.

America has changed over the past decades in many different ways. One big change is the growth of urban and suburban areas. The number of people living in cities or in nearby suburban areas has increased, so more people are living closer together. That makes property boundaries more of an issue. Many residences have little squares of land as backyards.

This may help explain why trespassing laws in this country have become increasingly strict over the past 50 years. But this shift has also been driven by new technology, like GPS. Fifty years ago, if you crossed an unfenced field, you could excuse yourself by saying you were just following local custom.

Today, modern smartphones and GPS apps can map property boundaries instantly. That means a trespasser cannot claim ignorance, and you may be arrested for trespassing for entering the same unfenced field today. And you may be arrested for entering your neighbor’s backyard to mow their lawn uninvited.

We all know it’s true: Americans sue more now than they did years ago. Anyone who owns property may be liable for any injuries that occur on that property, whether the person injured was invited or not. This is called premises liability.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Private landowners want to avoid the massive legal risks they face under premises liability. To protect themselves, landowners are much less likely to allow people to enter their property uninvited.

The risks are real. If you enter your neighbor’s property to mow their grass, anything might happen. You may put your foot in a gopher hole and trip and break your leg. You may get bitten by a protection dog or a wild animal like a snake. You may be hit by a tree branch falling to the ground. Your neighbor does not want a premises liability suit.

Finally, mowing the neighbor’s lawn without permission can lead them to sue you for property damage. Obviously, if your lawn mower takes out a special shrub or leaves holes in the soil, you've damaged your neighbor's property.

But even if there is no accident like this, your neighbor may be unhappy with you. First, you may think of the lawn as overgrown, while they may be in the process of growing a prairie lawn instead of turfgrass. And they may have developed their own routines, like letting grass grow taller to foster a natural ecosystem or aid wildlife. In these cases, your uninvited “favor” may feel disrespectful or invasive to your neighbor.

If you really want to help a neighbor who is elderly or incapacitated, all you have to do is ask them if they would like you to help. If they need help, they will be happy to agree to your proposal. If they prefer keeping their lawn as it is, or if they would prefer you not come for privacy reasons, they can say no.

If you were thinking of mowing the neighbor’s lawn because it is overgrown and makes the neighborhood look sloppy, you can also ask for permission. If they refuse, you might complain to the neighborhood association or the city.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#207. What’s Causing Your Fall Allergies? It’s Not What You Think

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

Did you just sneeze? You did? Bless you. Late summer and fall allergies kick in when wind-pollinated plants shed their fine powder. While ragweed is well known as a main cause of seasonal allergies in North America, some identification issues persist. Especially this one: What is yellow and showy, often in bloom against a backdrop of early fall grasses and reddening foliage? That would be goldenrod. Because it blazes so brightly it still tends to be blamed for the seized-up sinuses caused by inconspicuous, allergy-inducing ragweed. Goldenrod is not to blame. Nor is ragweed the only culprit.

Here’s a quick review of ragweed versus goldenrod, with a side of mugwort.

Goldenrod is the common name for species of Solidago, which number over 100. Most are native to North America. They are valued for the beauty of their vivid flowers and for supporting the pollinators that visit them in droves when they begin to bloom in late summer and into autumn.

Goldenrod does not cause allergies because its pollen grains are too bulky to be tossed around by a breeze and inhaled by us. Its vivid little flowers evolved to be seen and are designed to lure pollinators. Bees, wasps, hornets and hover flies, beetles and butterflies all find pollen-rich goldenrod flowers irresistible, and that is the point. The pollen is heavy and sticky and clings to the insects’ legs and bodies and is carried by them to the next flower, and, poof: Pollination happens.

(And this is true of all conspicuous—bright, beautiful, obvious—flowers. They are pollinated by creatures. Not by wind.)

Unlike goldenrod, ragweed (Ambrosia spp.) is a wind-pollinated plant. It produces clouds of fine pollen that irritates humans as the season shifts to autumn. But because goldenrod amplifies its presence at the time that ragweed blooms, its fireworks of yellow flowers often get the blame.

While goldenrod is showy and bright, ragweed flowers are aesthetically unexciting. Their tall green male flower spikes look more like seedheads than blooms. They call no attention to themselves and need no pollinating visitors. All they need is some moving air.

The pollen in male ragweed flowers is released by a whisper of wind. It is fine enough to travel hundreds of miles. (The female flowers are on the same plant, below the male flower spikes, hidden in clusters in the leaf axil, where the petiole joins the stem.)

If it’s any comfort to the seasonally afflicted, ragweed can be eaten. Curious? Visit Ragweed: Allergen or Appetizer.

And then there is mugwort (Artemisia vulgaris). Unlike native ragweed and goldenrod, it is an introduced and invasive species that grows prolifically in some regions, like the Northeast. Mugwort’s tiny, demure flowers mean one thing: They are wind-pollinated. Any pollen designed to travel by air is very, very fine (think tree pollens, in spring). Mugwort is also an irritant when ragweed is causing headaches, and is sometimes more prolific than ragweed. (Read more about mugwort in Invasivore: Mugwort the Weed vs Mugwort the Herb.)

N.B.: This post was first published September 2023.
