Dreaming of a fall garden full of bright blooms? Look this way...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most gardeners will tell you that, come October, the summer blooms are fading, the leaves are starting to change, and the garden can feel like it’s getting ready for winter. Still, there are plenty of flowers putting on a show... and they’re doing something even more important than brightening up our yards.

Fall-blooming flowers are undeniably beautiful, but they can also provide a valuable source of food for bees, butterflies and other pollinators at a time when fewer flowers are available. For me, that's brilliant news, as I’ve always thought of my garden as more than just a place to grow pretty plants; it’s also a tiny patch of habitat, and choosing flowers that provide nectar and pollen can make that patch a little more useful to the wildlife passing through.

As recent headlines have made all too clear, pollinators face a range of pressures, from habitat loss and pesticide use to climate and weather changes, resulting in some bee species being declared endangered. And, while none of us can solve those problems from our backyard, a few well-chosen plants can turn an ordinary flower bed into a much busier place.

Fall is a particularly good time to think about helping the (humming)birds and the bees, and all it takes is a few late-season flowers that keep on going for as long as the weather allows.

So, if you’re looking for flowers that can keep your garden colorful into October (while giving pollinators a reason to stop by), these are seven I’d put at the top of the list. Bloom times will vary depending on the variety and where you live, but all are worth considering for a fall-friendly garden.

Japanese anemones are one of my favorite ways to add a little elegance to a fall garden, as their delicate-looking pink or white flowers can continue blooming well into October.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

They’re especially useful to pollinators because their open flowers make it relatively easy for bees and other insects to reach the pollen and nectar, and I particularly like them planted toward the back of a border, where their tall stems can rise above shorter perennials.

Look for Japanese anemone cultivars suited to your USDA growing zone, as flowering time can vary with climate (although, personally, I love this September Charm Japanese Anemone from Nature Hills). Give them a spot with good light and reasonably well-drained soil, and they can become a reliable part of the late-season garden.

If I had to choose one group of flowers to represent the late-season pollinator garden, asters would be near the top of my list. Their daisy-like flowers can bring a splash of purple, pink, blue or white to your garden come October, when many other plants are fading.

These little beauties are especially valuable in fall because bees and butterflies are still looking for food, while the number of flowering plants available to them is beginning to shrink. And, unsurprisingly, native asters are particularly worthwhile if supporting local wildlife is one of your gardening goals.

Of course, there are many different aster varieties and cultivars available, so check the expected bloom time and mature size before planting. In the right spot, they can provide a spectacular late-season display (especially if you pick something like the vibrant Grape Crush New England Aster from Nature Hills).

Goldenrod (which just so happens to be the birth month native flower for November babies everywhere, if you're wondering!) is one of those plants I think deserves a much better reputation. Its clouds of yellow flowers are practically synonymous with fall, and they can be absolutely covered in visiting insects when they’re in bloom.

Despite its reputation, goldenrod isn't the main culprit behind fall hay fever — ragweed is much more commonly responsible for those airborne allergies. Goldenrod, meanwhile, is an important source of nectar and pollen for a wide variety of insects.

Native goldenrod species are especially valuable for wildlife. If you have the space for one, it can turn an otherwise quiet corner of the garden into a buzzing little feeding station in late summer and fall (not to mention some eye-popping majesty if you go for something like Fireworks Goldenrod).

Zinnias are one of my favorite choices when I want maximum color with relatively little fuss, as they come in an almost ridiculous range of colors and flower shapes. Better still, with regular deadheading, many varieties will continue producing flowers well into fall.

They’re also a favorite with butterflies. On a warm October day, it’s not unusual to see butterflies moving from one zinnia flower to the next, while bees make use of the blooms too. Plant something like Burpee's Zesty Mix Zinnia Seeds & Plants in a sunny spot, keep picking or deadheading the flowers, and they can help keep the garden colorful until frost puts an end to the show.

Autumn-blooming sedums are another plant I wouldn’t want to be without. Their dense clusters of tiny flowers open just when the garden is beginning to lose some of its summer color, and the blooms can attract plenty of bees and butterflies.

One of the things I like most about sedum is how easy it is to work into a garden; honestly, it’s generally drought tolerant once established, and the upright varieties add structure as well as late-season color.

Look for autumn-flowering types such as 'Autumn Joy' (available at Nature Hills) and similar cultivars. Their flower heads can start out pale and gradually deepen in color, giving the plant a long season of interest even before winter arrives. Plus, who doesn't love that extra-terrestrial vibe of theirs for added texture and fun, eh?

Black-eyed Susans bring a cheerful burst of yellow to the late-summer and fall garden, which has made them somewhat synonymous with October. Their daisy-like flowers, centered around a dark brown cone, are instantly recognizable and work beautifully in informal borders and pollinator gardens.

Depending on the species and cultivar, they can bloom from summer into fall, making them useful for extending the flowering season. Bees and butterflies are among the visitors they can attract, while their seed heads can provide food for birds later in the year.

For the longest possible display, remove spent flowers regularly. If you leave some seed heads standing, though, you can trade a little tidiness for additional wildlife value later in the season. And, if you plump for something like Prairie Glow Black-Eyed Susan from Nature Hills, you get bicolored blooms that make people stop and take notice.

Mexican bush sage is a particularly good choice for gardeners in warmer parts of the U.S, as its velvety foliage and spikes of purple-and-white flowers can provide a spectacular late-season display, with flowering often continuing into October.

The tubular flowers are attractive to bees, butterflies and other nectar-seeking insects, and the plant can be especially useful when other flowers are beginning to disappear. That being said, it's worth noting that Mexican bush sage isn't hardy everywhere in the country. In colder climates, it's often grown as an annual or overwintered indoors, while gardeners in warmer zones can enjoy it as a perennial.

If your climate allows it,, it's a beautiful way to keep the fall garden buzzing. And it's easily done, too, as you can buy Mexican Sage Salvia Live Plants from Walmart.

And just like that, you have some serious MVP plants for a pollinator-friendly garden in October. Time to get planting, then...

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

Don’t get too dazzled by this season’s fabulous show of dahlia flowers because you need to start preparing tubers for winter to enjoy even bigger blooms next year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early October is peak flowering time for most dahlias, and the right care now will influence not just how many more blooms you enjoy into fall, but the health of their tubers you’ll soon be digging up to store over winter. Dahlias thrive during this season’s warm days and cool nights, and will reward you with spectacular and abundant blooms. But if you want to enjoy the same dazzling show next year, you need to strike a balance between pushing for more flowers and prepping those tubers for storage. So, if you're wondering what dahlias need in October, balanced care is critical.

Fall dahlia care also depends heavily on your growing region and climate but for most gardeners, early October should bring a focus on cleaning up plants, preventing new green growth, supporting tall stems, and monitoring and managing pests and diseases. Get it right and you’ll get plenty more blooms as well as plump tubers full of energy that’ll overwinter well, ready for a repeat performance next year.

Ready? Let’s dive into what to do with dahlias in October.

Part of the fall balance for dahlias is irrigation levels. While plants are still putting out impressive blooms, they’ll be using plenty of water, but their tubers are also preparing to toughen up for winter – and too much moisture means those roots get soft and won't store well. Add rainfall into the mix and there’s even more to consider, especially if you're growing dahlias in containers.

The best guideline is to water your dahlias if it doesn’t rain, once the soil has dried out. But then water deeply. A rain gauge such as this pretty precipitation gauge stake from Amazon is a really simple but effective way to keep an eye on how much rainfall your plants are getting, so you can water accordingly. Irrigate at soil level, never over the plants, and try to avoid getting foliage and stems too wet.

As October proceeds, gradually cut back on how much water you provide so the tubers start to toughen their skins.

As long as you keep removing spent blooms, you’ll direct the plant’s energy into growing more blooms rather than seed production. To deadhead dahlias, cut the faded flower stem back to the next branching point. Of course, you don’t need to wait for the petals to fade before cutting, as now you can be enjoying cut flowers as your reward for all your hard work. Snipping freshly opened blooms will also encourage plants to continue producing more.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

With some dahlia varieties, the spent flowers look very similar to new buds. If you're not sure which is which, give it a gentle squeeze: fresh about-to-open buds will feel firm to the touch while spent blooms will feel a little mushy.

Of course, if you plant to collect seeds, leave some of the flowers in place.

All these heavy blooms can start to weigh down the stems, especially if you're growing dinnerplate dahlias, and it’s common to see plants splay at this time of the year. If you don’t already have them in place, add stakes to help top-heavy stems stay upright. Not only do vertical stems look better, broken stems can create wounds that are vulnerable to disease.

Bamboo canes will do the job just fine, but make sure you buy poles that are long enough, like these reusable 5' support stakes from Walmart, as you’ll need to push a quarter of the length into the ground. Tie individual stems into the stakes using soft twist ties such as these from Amazon that won’t cut into the plant material, or simply fashion a cradle around the whole plant with canes and twine.

If you do have supports in place, check them and make adjustments as needed, especially after heavy rain or windy weather.

As part of regular maintenance, you should be looking out for signs of pest infestations or diseases taking root in your dahlias. Do this throughout the growing season, but especially now, as you want your plants to stay healthy as they build up energy and tough, healthy tubers for winter storage.

Some of the typical pests you’re looking for in October include spider mites and aphids, both of which feed on dahlias. Pests are less of a concern this time of year as growth is wrapping up anyway, but it’s still worth removing them with a spray of water or use an organic neem oil spray such as Bonide Captain Jack’s Neem Oil, available from Lowe’s, to keep your plants looking tidy for the rest of the season.

Increasing rain and lower temperatures in fall can increase the prevalence of powdery mildew and leaf spot. While there’s no need to worry, if you spot a white dust-like coating to leaves, it’s best to remove them to reduce the amount of infected plant matter in your garden beds. A collapsible waste bag like Fiskars 10-Gallon Yard Waste Bag, available from Amazon, makes it easy to transport them straight to the trash, as you don’t want these fungal spores in your compost bin.

Feeding dahlias as we head deeper into fall pushes the plant to make new growth rather than harden off its tubers ready for storage. Particularly, avoid the temptation to use up any high-nitrogen fertilizer which promotes leafy growth. If you're gardening in a warmer zone and still feeding to promote flowering, make sure the fertilizer is designed specifically for that job. Look for a low- or zero-nitrogen feed such as TPS Flower Fertilizer, available from Amazon, that’s rated 0-10-10 or 5-10-10 – the first number indicates nitrogen levels, so this must be lower than the second two numbers that indicate potassium and phosphorus.

Aim to stop fertilizing completely 4-6 weeks before your first expected frost date, to give your plant time to mature its tubers.

In zones 7 and below, you’ll need to dig up and store your dahlia tubers over the winter. Depending on the zone you garden in, your first frost could hit in October, so make sure you’ve got everything ready. Coco coir such as this from Walmart in a cardboard box makes for cheap and effective storage.

Always wait until the first good frost has killed the stems above the ground, as this triggers the plant to send a rush of sugars and starches down into the tubers. Not only does this mean lots of energy stored for next year, it tells the plant to enter dormancy and mature the tubers, when they’ll store better.

It’s best to leave tubers in the ground to rest for 1-2 weeks after this frost to allow this process, unless you suspect the soil will freeze, when tubers will die, or rainfall is heavy and incessant, when roots may start to rot.

If you live in the warmer climates of zones 8-11, you can safely leave dahlia tubers in the ground as long as you have well-draining soil. If you have a frost, wait a week or two to allow the energy transfer into the tubers then cut stems down to around 3-4 inches and pile a 5-inch layer of mulch such as Back to the Roots Organic Mulch, available from The Home Depot, over the soil to act as a cozy duvet.

In frost-free zones, cut stems by mid-December at the latest to ensure plants rest, and there’s no need to mulch.

As you look ahead, adjust your plans to the weather as temperatures and rainfall can vary widely in fall. Keep enjoying those spectacular October blooms but remember you need to start caring for the tubers, too, if you want next summer's display to be equally stunning.

October is a great month to buy dahlia tubers as you'll be able to find more unusual varieties and dahlia types that are usually snapped up months before the first hint of spring. Most specialist dahlia retailers open for pre-orders in October then send tubers out in spring, though it's fine to physically buy tubers now as you can safely store them for spring planting.Take a look at Dutch Grown's impressive dahlia collection of over 150 cultivars for inspiration, and here are just a few varieties new for 2027 to give you a taste of the incredible flower shapes and color combos now available.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

#211. How to Choose the Best Greenhouse – Expert Guide on Buying the Right One for Your Yard

Whether you want to extend your growing season or create a dedicated garden space, the right greenhouse will set you up for years of happy plants. This expert guide helps you find a trusted model

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As a home grower with several decades of hard-earned wins and lessons learned behind me, I know that the right greenhouse can fundamentally transform what you can achieve as a gardener. It can add weeks (if not months) to sowing and growing timelines and harvesting opportunities, and let you regulate your plant’s environment in critical ways. The right greenhouse lets you safeguard tender perennials through freezing winters, nurture delicate seedlings from seed, and cultivate heat-loving crops that would otherwise struggle in your local climate. It also offers a unique sanctuary, a weather-proof haven, and a wonderful space in which to play.

However, choosing the right greenhouse is a structural decision, not an impulse purchase. There are so many tempting greenhouse ideas that look amazing in photos – but how do you know which is really right for you? Unlike buying a terracotta pot or a garden bench, adding a greenhouse to your yard means you are in charge of a functioning, climate-controlled ecosystem. A model that thrives in a sheltered suburban yard might buckle under Midwestern prairie winds or turn into a furnace in a hot Southern summer. Falling in love with a particular shape or design without considering location, insulation, ventilation, or foundation stability is one of the quickest routes to buyer’s remorse.

To make an investment that brings joy for decades, you need to balance your personal growing ambitions with the realities of your space, budget, and local weather. Whether you are seeking a compact pop-up shelter to start tomato seedlings, a durable polycarbonate kit for family food production, or an elegant glasshouse that serves as a centerpiece for your backyard, this masterclass guide breaks down every critical factor to help you choose with complete confidence.

This buying guide aims to take the sting out of many of those key questions you'll definitely be having, before you reach for your wallet – providing you with a useful foundation for your growing space, based on an honest assessment of the following fundamentals:

Where you put your greenhouse is often key to deciding on the right model. Selecting the ideal site requires balancing sunlight, shelter, and everyday convenience, based on your regional climate and your USDA growing zone. A common error is placing a greenhouse in a forgotten corner of the yard, where it quickly becomes an out-of-sight chore to maintain.

Northern gardeners need maximum exposure to natural light, positioning the ridge along an east-west axis to capture low winter sun and trap precious early spring solar radiation, while sheltering the frame from prevailing north winds. Southern and humid-zone growers face the opposite challenge. Professional horticulture expert Bethany Lakatos points out the need to balance full winter light with protection from intense afternoon summer heat.

"If you have a space with a deciduous tree that can shade your greenhouse on summer afternoons, this will also allow maximum sunlight when the tree is dormant,” says Bethany, who works at Trees.com. “However, before moving ahead with your plans, assess the tree for health: if you see any weak limbs, large wounds, or if the tree is a weak-wooded type, contact an arborist first.” As Bethany notes, in Southern climates, hurricane season and severe thunderstorms can lead to downed limbs and trees that may damage structures below their canopy.

Equally critical across all regions is siting your structure near existing household water and electrical supplies. Running hoses across long distances or relying on distant outlets creates unnecessary friction during busy spring seed-starting routines. "I placed my greenhouse close enough to my house so I can run an extension cord out there if needed," explains Trisha Nieder, master gardener and regenerative farmer at Nieder Farms. "Outside of electricity, you’re definitely going to need water, so having a greenhouse set up next to your home where you can easily connect a hose to an outdoor faucet makes things far easier when it’s time to water."

When estimating size, most first-time buyers underestimate the floor space required. Remember, a greenhouse is not merely storage for potted plants; it is a working environment that must accommodate staging benches, soil bags, watering cans, and comfortable human movement. An 8x10-foot footprint may sound spacious on paper, but once you deduct a central walkway and staging benches on either side, space fills up rapidly.

The ground is the final location decision. Groundwork options range from simple, free-draining gravel beds over weed membrane to timber mudsills, concrete pads, or raised brick knee-walls. Skimping on ground prep or building over uneven surfaces introduces major thermal and structural vulnerabilities. "Our biggest rookie mistake was trying to build our first greenhouse with a wooden floor made of pallets because the ground was so uneven," reveal Staci and Jeremy Hill, homesteading experts and co-authors of The Preserver’s Garden, available from Amazon. "This put air between the ground and greenhouse, which made it a lot colder inside."

How much greenhouse space do you need? “The bottom line is that your goals and reasoning for having a greenhouse will determine both the size and layout," says Staci and Jeremy Hill. Thinking about your primary growing needs will help you to determine the right dimensions (which in turn helps with picking a model).

Glancing online can give you a mass of riches in terms of greenhouse shapes and sizes, but most fall into one of the following categories:

Choosing the right structural frame and glazing panel dictates how well your greenhouse will retain heat, survive winter storms, and resist daily wear. For structural framing, home growers can typically choose between rot-resistant cedar wood, heavy-duty galvanized steel, or lightweight powder-coated aluminum. While timber offers natural insulation and a rustic aesthetic, aluminum remains the top choice for modern kits due to its zero-maintenance, rust-proof longevity.

"When selecting frame materials, long-term durability and resistance to moisture should be your top priorities," emphasizes Shane Pliska, biophilia authority and President of Planterra Conservatory in Michigan. "Powder-coated aluminum frames offer an exceptional balance of structural strength and weather resistance without requiring seasonal sealants or rust treatments, making them ideal for high-humidity growing environments."

As you evaluate different glazing materials, make sure you balance aesthetic clarity against thermal efficiency, impact safety, and light diffusion:

While clear glass looks beautiful in a landscape, diffused light through twin-wall polycarbonate often creates a superior growing climate inside the structure by scattering sunlight into lower leaf canopies. "Many growers love the traditional look of glass, but twin-wall polycarbonate is far more forgiving and practical for everyday home gardening," advises Anna Ohler, plant expert and co-founder of Bright Lane Gardens in northern Michigan. "It diffuses direct sunlight, so your plants don't scorch on hot afternoons, it retains heat better during cold spring nights, and it won't shatter if a stray branch or storm debris hits it."

To protect your investment and maintain a balanced climate during peak summer heat, managing direct UV exposure is critical. To extend panel life and prevent midday heat scorch, it’s a good idea to pair your build with a pre-grommeted shade cloth, such as the Agfabric 50% Sunblock Shade Cloth, available from Amazon, which provides instant, affordable cooling in midsummer without blocking the essential light your crops need.

Managing internal temperatures and air movement is what keeps a greenhouse from becoming a stifling oven in July or an icebox in January. The most reliable cooling method relies on passive thermodynamics rather than costly electricity. Cold air entering low side openings forces rising hot air out through high ridge vents. "Natural ventilation is essential," explains Shane Pliska. "Roof vents and side vents work together: hot air escapes through the roof and draws fresh air in through the sides. This is the stack effect, a principle used to ventilate buildings for centuries."

To make the most of this, structure your vent placements based on the length of your building frame. "As a rule, use one roof and side ventilator per every 6.5 feet (2m) of greenhouse length," advises Bethany Lakatos. "Louver windows can also be used for extra ventilation and are a good option for the South, as they can let in drafts in colder climates." To prevent heat spikes when you aren't home, pair roof panels with a heat-activated arm, such as the Bibistore Temperature Sensitive Automatic Greenhouse Vent Opener, from Amazon. This uses heat-expanding cylinders to lift windows as interior air warms above 60°F without needing electricity.

At the other extreme, controlling cold snaps requires understanding how fast closed glass structures radiate warmth once the sun goes down. "I think people can underestimate how quickly a greenhouse can overheat, or drop in temperature at night," warns Anna Ohler. "For really cold weather, I like to create another layer of protection directly over the plants. Frost cloth or row cover over low hoops essentially creates a little greenhouse inside the greenhouse." Three good heat-retention strategies for winter include:

For growers in severe northern zones needing heavy freeze protection, pairing internal row covers with a portable forced-air electric heater, such as the Airchoice 1500W Electric Greenhouse Heater, available from Walmart, provides thermostat-controlled circulation that keeps air moving and prevents frost pockets from damaging tender foliage.

Transforming an empty greenhouse frame into an efficient growing space requires thoughtful zoning for staging benches, seed-starting stations, and utility access. Setting up slatted aluminum shelving makes the most of vertical space, while allowing soil spills and water to drain freely. To build a durable workspace that maximizes growing area while keeping walkways clear, go for modular steel shelving, such as the CuisinSmart 4-Tier Greenhouse Shelving Staging from Walmart, which can support heavy potted plants as well as propagation flats.

Before running permanent plumbing lines or installing misting bars, focus on flooring drainage and electrical safety to prevent standing water hazards. "The biggest thing with electricity is remembering that a greenhouse is basically a giant wet environment," says Anna’s husband and business partner, Nick Ohler. "Anything electrical needs to be designed for that environment, including GFCI protection, outdoor/wet-location rated outlets and covers, and properly protected wiring. For water, think about drainage before you think about irrigation." Factor in these interior setup and care rules:

Automating daily watering ensures that crops receive steady hydration even during busy workdays or weekend trips. To easily manage drip irrigation cycles without manual effort, pair an exterior hose bib with an automated water controller, like the Rain Bird Digital Hose End Timer, available from Walmart. This has programmable watering intervals and an automatic rain-delay button to prevent water waste.

Monitoring internal temperature swings and managing supplemental heat sources also encourage a stress-free growing environment. "We like to use portable electric radiator-style space heaters plugged into a cheap thermostat for heating," say Staci and Jeremy Hill. "Coupled with inexpensive Bluetooth and Wi-Fi wireless thermometers and high/low alarms to keep an eye on temperatures, this saves us lots of extra trips."

Choosing the right greenhouse comes down to balancing your growing ambition against local weather realities. While budget pop-ups offer an accessible entry point, permanent structures require engineered wind ratings, heavy-gauge frames, and long-term foundation planning. "Budget greenhouse kits are budget for a reason. The lower cost definitely comes with caveats," explains Trisha Nieder. "That said, if you’re on a budget and want a greenhouse, you can absolutely make these work. They are an affordable way to see how often you’ll use it and what kind of features you'd like to have." The following highlights some key suitable brands based on goals and budget:

Ohuhu, Outsunny, Sanerto, Quictent, Eagle Peak, ShelterLogic

Palram Canopia, Veikous, Outsunny Cedar, Eartheasy, Vegepod

Planta Greenhouses, Climapod, Yoderbilt, Riga, Hobby Gardener

Backyard Discovery, HOWE, Palram Oasis, Hartley Botanic, BC Greenhouses, Janssens

Ideal for temporary spring propagation, balcony growers, and testing your green thumb without a major financial investment.

The undisputed king of urban and small-space starters, boasting over 7,000 verified positive reviews on Amazon. Its powder-coated steel frame and heavy-duty, grid-reinforced PE cover trap warmth while shielding delicate fall seedlings from light frosts. It features heavy-duty metal shelf clips that prevent seedling tray slippage and a zippered roll-up door for quick morning ventilation. A major favorite for beginner growers and space-conscious gardeners. 58"L x 30"W x 77"H | Reinforced PE Cover | 1 Person, 20-min tool-free assembly.

An incredible bridge model for gardeners stepping up from flexible plastic tarps to a rigid frame. Built with UV-resistant twin-wall polycarbonate and a rust-proof aluminum frame, it scatters harsh mid-day sunlight to prevent leaf scorch. Includes built-in rain gutters for rainwater harvesting and an adjustable roof vent to regulate humidity. Holds up far better to light snowfall than PVC pop-ups. Praised for great insulation at an approachable price. 6' x 4' x 6.5' | 4mm Polycarbonate | 2 People, 3–5 hours assembly.

A massive favorite across online homesteading forums for providing huge square footage on a modest budget. The galvanized steel arch frame supports a tear-resistant green PE mesh cover with roll-up side windows for cross-ventilation. When anchored down with spiral earth stakes or perimeter sandbags, it easily protects large vegetable beds against seasonal winds. A favorite for winter crop protection and high capacity, and a monster for square footage. 13' x 10' x 6.5' | Reinforced PE Mesh | 1–2 People, 2 hours assembly.

Rigid aluminum frames and insulating twin-wall polycarbonate designed for year-round growing, severe weather, and frost protection.

Excellent for backyard kits. Some online reviews caution that assembly requires patience, but many owners praise its long-term durability once locked together. It combines 100% UV-protected twin-wall roof panels with crystal-clear side walls, withstands 56 mph winds and holds up well against storms. Includes plant hangers and a magnetic door catch, plus a roof vent. 6' x 8' x 7' | 4mm Twin-Wall Polycarbonate | 2 People, 5-6 hours assembly.

A top-seller for growers who need ample interior clearance without breaking $500. Its thick twin-wall panels provide excellent heat retention during cold fall nights, while the spacious 8x10 floor plan comfortably accommodates 2 parallel tiers of potting benches alongside overwintering citrus trees. Features smooth-sliding doors and integrated rain gutters. Reviewers love its roomy interior. 8' x 10' x 7.3' | 4mm Twin-Wall & Aluminum | 2 People, 6-8 hours assembly.

Crafted from 100% solid fir wood, this model trades cold industrial aluminum for a traditional aesthetic that blends beautifully into borders. Solid wood offers superior thermal insulation over metal frames, and the 6mm thick polycarbonate panels lock in heat better than thinner starter kits in cold snaps. Reviewers love the frame and the aesthetics. 6.6' x 8' x 6.5' | 6mm Polycarbonate & Fir Wood | 2 People, 5-7 hours assembly.

Engineered lifetime structures featuring architectural timber, heavy-gauge aluminum, and smart utility integrations, treasured by serious growers.

For growers seeking timber warmth paired with modern utility, this is a standout premium kit crafted from 100% rot-resistant FSC cedar. What truly sets it apart is its PowerPort electrical pass-through and exterior hose hookups, allowing you to run interior grow lights, heating pads, and automated misting systems without trailing extension cords across your lawn. Includes temperature-activated automatic roof vent openers. Praised for an authentic look with features that serious hobby gardeners love. 6' x 9' x 7.8' | 6mm Twin-Wall & 100% Cedar | 2 People, 8-10 hours assembly.

Designed as a hybrid growing sanctuary and elegant garden sunroom, the hexagonal Oasis features heavy-gauge aluminum framing and high-impact clear side panels offering a 360-degree panoramic view. Overhead twin-wall roof panels diffuse harsh sunlight, while side louver vents and wide double doors maintain optimal airflow on warm afternoons. A major star on Amazon and Home Depot for combining structural elegance with functional growing space. 8' x 8' x 8.7' | Clear Side + Twin-Wall Roof | 2 People, 8-10 hours assembly.

Delivering the classic English Country Estate aesthetic beloved of the Beckhams, this massive pavilion creates an architectural centerpiece. Its towering 9.5-foot apex peak provides massive head clearance for tall potted fruit trees. Constructed with heavy-duty graphite aluminum truss bracing, multiple roof vents, and swing double doors, it easily divides into dedicated propagation zones and an outdoor seating lounge. Highly rated by Amazon buyers for its breathtaking visual impact and massive interior clearance. 16' x 12' x 9.5' | High-Impact Polycarbonate | 2-3 People, 12-14 hours assembly.

Remember, buying your greenhouse kit is only the first step in creating a long-lasting backyard growing space that will justify your investment. To that end, it’s vital to prevent post-purchase headaches by addressing some real-world logistical “gotchas” before you spend any cash. To avoid costly surprises during assembly, you can calculate the true total cost upfront using this simple budget formula:

True Total Cost = Kit Price + Freight Shipping + Foundation Site Prep + Climate Accessories + Local Permit Fees

Beyond the sticker price, improper ground anchoring is a massive hidden gotcha for new owners because, as Staci and Jeremy Hill caution, an unanchored greenhouse frame acts like a giant kite in severe winds. While lightweight DIY kits promise fast weekend setups, navigating hundreds of structural fasteners and frame alignments can quickly get overwhelming. Be honest about your DIY confidence early and budget for a local landscape contractor if site grading or heavy foundation work is needed.

Also, before you commit to your greenhouse, make sure you have ticked off the following key logistical and structural considerations:

"Restrictions on building a greenhouse will boggle the mind of the average home gardener," cautions Gardening Know How’s gardening expert and legal authority Teo Spengler. "Generally, if you are putting in a concrete slab foundation for your greenhouse, or even permanent footers, you may need to go through the building permit process. This is also the case if you attach your plumbing or electrical system."

Once those legal permits and site preparations are secured, make sure you do anchor your structure against high winds. Gravity alone will not protect lightweight aluminum frames or polycarbonate panels from severe spring shear winds. "Secure it with some kind of inground framing," recommends Trisha Nieder. "Four 2x2x6 cedar posts placed on each of the four corners, set 2 feet (60 cm) into the ground with 2x4s screwed into the bottom, will keep the greenhouse level and secure against winds."

For larger glass or heavy-duty aluminum builds, deeper footings are essential to prevent structural shifting during seasonal freeze-thaw cycles. "Our latest greenhouses are anchored on 4x4s buried in the ground below the frost line and set in concrete," says Staci Hill. "We attach wall materials directly to those corner posts, alleviating the wind issue entirely."

It’s a lot, absolutely. But it’s good to know this stuff before you buy. While municipal codes and storm anchoring might feel intimidating, there are services out there to help you. And taking time to secure your greenhouse foundations ensures decades of stress-free growing. Once your permits and base frame are locked in place, you are ready for the most exciting step: selecting what to grow! Happy greenhouse shopping…

For most residential properties, small unheated modular kits under 100-120 square feet (9.3 to 11.1 m²) are classified as temporary accessory structures and do not require formal building permits. However, tying into municipal water lines or hardwiring electrical sub-panels usually triggers local zoning reviews. "Building permits for residential greenhouses depend on structure size, permanent footings, and utility hookups," says Teo Spengler. "Unattached, temporary kits rarely require permits, but pouring a concrete slab or running electrical conduit typically requires local approval."

In the northern hemisphere, orienting your greenhouse long side facing south (an east-west axis) maximizes low-angled winter sunlight for year-round growing. If nearby mature trees, garages, or house walls block southern exposure, a north-south orientation provides uniform light distribution in peak summer months. "Positioning the long side toward the south maximizes low-angled winter sunlight," explains Shane Pliska. "This keeps internal temperatures higher during the coldest months of the year without extra heating costs."

You can, provided you cultivate frost-tolerant cold-hardy crops like spinach, kale, winter lettuce, and radishes rather than warm-season crops. Unheated glazing acts as a windbreaker and provides a passive thermal buffer, raising internal temperatures by 5-10°F (3-6°C warmer than outside), protecting crops against killing frosts. "An unheated greenhouse won't keep tomatoes alive in January, but pairing your structure with internal frost cloth over low hoops lets you harvest hardy greens all winter long," says Anna Ohler.

Lightweight aluminum frames can easily catch wind like a kite during 40+ mph spring storms if merely rested on topsoil. Base frames must be bolted down to concrete slabs, secured to heavy 4x4 pressure-treated timber sleepers, or pinned into deep earth auger anchors. "Never rely on gravity alone," warn Staci and Jeremy Hill. "Securing your base frame to pressure-treated wooden posts buried below the frost line or using heavy auger earth anchors is essential for surviving spring storms."

Excess internal moisture breeds devastating fungal pathogens. "Powder-coated frames and twin-wall panels keep heat in, but stagnant air breeds botrytis and powdery mildew," explains Bethany Lakatos. Combat high humidity by running lower wall louvers alongside automatic roof vents, and applying drip irrigation to root zones rather than spraying foliage. "Watering early in the morning also keeps canopy humidity balanced," says Bethany.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Squirrels can empty a feeder fast, but a few seeds don't appeal to them. Swap in the right ones, and more of the food ends up with the birds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fill a feeder in the morning, and by afternoon a squirrel may be hanging upside down from it, cheeks stuffed. Here's the good news, though. There are some types of bird seed that squirrels don't enjoy – but they still bring in plenty of songbirds.

Good bird feeding isn't only about what goes in the feeder, though. Pair the right seed with smart bird feeder ideas, and you'll make life much harder for determined squirrels. Where the feeder hangs, how it's built, and what spills beneath it all affect how often squirrels show up. Fall makes this especially timely, as squirrels spend the season gathering and stashing food, and a full feeder is an easy stop on their rounds.

The three seeds I've covered here all get left alone more often than sunflower does, but that's no promise – a hungry enough squirrel will taste just about anything once. Pair the new seed with a better spot for the feeder, and the birds get more of each fill.

So why do squirrels keep coming back? Eastern gray squirrels (Sciurus carolinensis) like a lot of what birds like. Sunflower seeds are a favorite, and corn and peanuts may tempt them even more. That's bad news for anyone buying bargain bags, since cheap mixes often lean on sunflower and corn.

Squirrels are also gifted athletes. From a roof, branch, or fence, a squirrel can cover about 10 feet (3 m) in one leap, and from the ground it can spring roughly 5 feet (1.5 m) straight up. That's why squirrel-proof feeders and baffles can make such a difference. Any feeder within reach of those launch points is fair game, no matter what seed it holds.

Safflower looks like a small white sunflower seed with a thick shell. Squirrels usually pass it by, and so do house sparrows and starlings, for the most part. In some areas, squirrels have picked up a taste for it anyway. Pick up a bag of Wagner's Safflower Seed Wild Bird Food on Amazon.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Despite the old “thistle” label, nyjer has nothing to do with North American thistles. It comes from an African plant. Those tiny black seeds rank among the seeds squirrels don’t like much. Use a feeder with very small ports and serve it by itself, not in a mix, or a lot of it ends up wasted. Kaytee sells quality nyjer seed at a reasonable price.

White proso millet is the pale little seed that fills out most budget blends. Squirrels will eat it, but with corn or peanuts on offer, they usually go for those first. That's why a mix that leans hard on millet tends to lose their attention sooner. If you buy it on its own, pick white, like this Morning Bird White Proso Millet. Birds will choose it over red.

Cardinals go for safflower more than most. Grosbeaks, chickadees, titmice, nuthatches, and mourning doves eat it, too. There is a catch, though: plenty of birds still prefer sunflower, and a feeder switched straight to safflower may get quieter. Mix a little safflower into the current seed and raise the share over time for an easier switch.

Nyjer is finch food. Goldfinches crowd it, both American and lesser, and house finches, pine siskins, and redpolls show up as well.

Millet works from the ground up. Juncos and native sparrows are the regulars, with towhees and mourning doves close behind, and cardinals will pick at it, too.

Each seed does best in its own feeder. Safflower goes in a hopper, tube, or platform feeder without any trouble. For nyjer, you’ll want tiny ports or fine mesh, like this Kingsyard feeder from Amazon.

Millet belongs low, on the ground or a low tray that drains well, where juncos and native sparrows forage. A 10-pound (4.5 kg) bag of plain white millet makes a fine start. Go easy on the amount. Seed still lying around at dusk means you overdid it, and squirrels will happily clean it up.

Distance comes first. Give a pole-mounted feeder at least 10 feet (3 m) of open air between it and the nearest tree, fence, roof, or deck. Height matters as well – about 5 feet (1.5m) up keeps it out of a ground jump. If you’re buying a pole, a heavy-duty 76-inch adjustable shepherd’s hook from Home Depot sits on a seven-prong base that stays put in soft soil.

Then add a baffle. On a pole, it goes below the feeder so squirrels can’t climb past it – for a feeder hanging near trees, a dome-style baffle goes above instead. This Koralakiri 19-Inch Squirrel Baffle from Walmart will do the job nicely.

The feeder itself can do some of the work. Weight-activated models close their seed ports when anything heavier than a songbird climbs on. With the Brome Squirrel Buster Classic from Amazon, a squirrel’s own weight pulls the shroud down. Hang it with roughly 18 inches (46 cm) of open space all around.

Caged designs take a different approach. The iron cage around this Veehoo caged tube feeder keeps squirrels at arm’s length from its four feeding ports. A seed tray under a tube feeder catches spills before they reach the ground. Keep spare seed sealed, too – a lidded metal or plastic container works well to keep pests out.

Leave sticky and greasy tricks alone. Sticky coatings meant for squirrels can just as easily trap a chickadee. Grease is no better. Smear petroleum jelly or cooking oil on a pole, and it mats fur and feathers alike – a bird with matted feathers loses the insulation it needs on cold nights.

Hot-pepper seed is the other common shortcut. Birds don’t feel the heat of capsaicin, but squirrels do. It burns their mouths and causes real discomfort, which is a fair reason to leave it on the shelf. Skip salty or sugary kitchen scraps, too. Both can hurt small birds.

Squirrels won’t vanish from the yard, and that’s fine – they’re fun to watch when they aren’t eating the cardinals’ dinner. Give them a seed they don’t love and a feeder they can’t reach, and more of each bag ends up where it belongs.

#215. What Your Christmas Cactus Needs in October – Get These 5 Things Right for Fabulous Holiday Blooms

Those festive flowers won’t appear all on their own. Give your plant the seasonal cues it needs now to help it form those all-important buds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Christmas cactus is an extremely popular holiday plant that seems to bloom forever, offering some of the most exotic-looking flowers in the plant kingdom. It takes second place only to the Christmas tree in terms of plants associated with the holidays. And it’s a tropical cactus that doesn’t have needles that get all over the carpet!

When it’s not playing a starring role in Santa season, this beautiful plant can keep on looking lush and lovely in spring, summer, and fall with proper Christmas cactus care. However, while it's an easy houseplant to grow, getting it to produce another spectacular holiday flower display takes a little more planning than simply keeping it alive.

October is when that preparation begins, but the change in seasons can also trigger stress, which is what causes a Christmas cactus to drop leaves if it's not being cared for well. The shorter days and cooler nights also help trigger bud formation, and a few simple care tasks can make all the difference to the quality of this year's display. Here are five essential autumn care steps for Schlumbergera × buckleyi (also sold as Schlumbergera bridgesii) to encourage healthy growth and plenty of buds for December. You can also use this advice on the other main type of holiday cactus, the Thanksgiving cactus (Schlumbergera truncata).

Holiday prep for your Christmas cactus starts in October. This is the single most important step if you want to enjoy the same fabulous display of blooms you had the previous year. The key is striking the right balance between daylight and complete darkness.

Starting in October, control the amount of daylight your plant receives. To trigger bud formation, a Christmas cactus needs around 12 hours of uninterrupted darkness every night. It won't mind whether that darkness comes from being placed in a spare room or closet, as long as no light reaches it.

You can also simply cover it with an opaque box or a black fabric grow bag, such as these 5-gallon black grow bags from Amazon, which are large enough to fit over most mature Christmas cacti while still allowing plenty of airflow.

After its nightly blackout, return the plant to a spot with bright, indirect light for the remaining 12 hours of the day. This routine will trick a Christmas cactus into flowering right on time for the holidays.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

This cactus may look like a beautiful holiday decoration, but don't forget – it's a real plant. If you only want to enjoy it for one season, that's your choice. But if you want your Christmas cactus to bloom year after year, you need to provide the right conditions before it flowers.

In the wild, Christmas cacti spend the early months of winter in cooler conditions, and this drop in temperature helps stimulate bud formation. That means now isn't the time to display your plant in front of a crackling fire. Instead, keep it in a room where temperatures stay between 50–55°F (10–13°C). Don't let it get too warm, but don't let it get too cold either.

Do you hear the term "cactus" and think of the Sonoran Desert? Yes, some cacti are native to arid climates and require infrequent watering, but others, like the Christmas cactus, call the tropical rainforest home.

Even so, autumn should be a relatively dry period in the life of a Christmas cactus. In the wild, this is a season with little rainfall, so don't flood the plant now. Stop the weekly watering routine and make sure the pot isn't sitting in a saucer of water.

Instead, check the soil every week to see if it has dried out. Push your finger into the soil up to the first knuckle, and only water if it feels dry at that depth. If you'd rather take the guesswork out of watering, an inexpensive XLUX Soil Moisture Meter from Amazon is a worthwhile investment. It gives an instant reading of moisture levels below the surface, helping you avoid the overwatering that can prevent Christmas cacti from setting buds.

Okay, we get it. There are a lot of directions to follow if you want your Christmas cactus to burst into bloom for the holidays. But many of them involve not doing things: no lights at night, no warm room, less water, and... no fertilizer.

Stop fertilizing your Christmas cactus completely in October and November. Fertilizer encourages leafy growth, and that's not what you want at this stage. Instead, the plant needs to direct its energy into setting flower buds for the holiday season.

Once flowering has finished and your plant resumes active growth in spring, you can start feeding again with a balanced houseplant fertilizer, such as this TPS Nutrients Christmas Cactus Fertilizer. Regular feeding through spring and summer will help support healthy stems and set your Christmas cactus up for another spectacular display next winter.

After a few weeks, start checking your Christmas cactus every day for developing buds. A good time to do this is each morning when you move it from its dark location back into bright, indirect light. The buds will first appear as tiny, brightly colored points at the tips of the flattened stems.

As soon as you spot the first buds, your care routine changes. The nightly 12-hour blackout has done its job and is no longer needed. Move the plant to a bright, warm spot, where the buds can continue to develop into the spectacular flowers that make Christmas cacti such a holiday favorite.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#216. At Home with Landscape Designer William Dangar: Downsizing a House to Expand the Garden

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

Though he’s a landscape designer known for designing gardens to complement large houses, Australia-based William Dangar often gets to work with only a little land. Time and again, he says, “the structure takes up all the space and the landscaping becomes mere icing around the edges.”

When Dangar and his family built their own home near Sydney’s Bondi Beach, he got the chance to rectify the situation. They bought an unsalvageable California-style bungalow on a lot “shaped like a pizza slice,” tore it down, and started anew with a double-height house with a smaller footprint (to leave more land for the garden).

Dangar commissioned friend and architect Michelle Osazaczky to design the house in partnership with interior architect Romaine Alwill. It was to be simple and modern, inspired by photos of “modest little huts on the sides of glaciers in Greenland” taken by photographer Murray Fredericks, and imagery Dangar found of black barns in Queenstown, New Zealand.

For the generous backyard, Dangar was influenced by Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx, “who was the master of mass plantings,” he says. “It is hard when you are your own client, but in the end I thought it best to challenge myself,” with a graphic scheme of new plant mixes such as “weeping mulberries, bamboos that originate from northern Asia, and Japanese blood grass which turns red in summer,” he says. “It’s my contemporary take on a Japanese native garden.”

Photography by Prue Ruscoe, courtesy of William Dangar.

The sliding doors open the northwest face of the house to the garden, “to allow for a genuine merging of inside and out.”

#217. Get Thee to a Nursery! 14 of the Best Independent Nurseries, According to Garden Pros

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

Once someone gets the gardening bug, they often become pickier about where they shop for plants (those big box stores just won’t do!). Soon, the gardener has a wish list of harder-to-find plants they’d like to source for their garden, and eventually, they’re making special trips to visit nurseries. It’s a familiar tale because the truth is that plants make a garden. Many specialty and independent nurseries thrive on word of mouth. So, we asked some of our favorite garden professionals where they shop for their gardens. Here’s where garden pros buy their plants:

Caleb Davis, the founder of ecological landscape design firm Songscape Gardens in Bar Harbor, Maine, shops for locally-appropriate plants through New England-based nurseries, among them Bunker Farm Plants. Songscape collaborated with Helen O’Donnell, the grower behind Bunker Farm’s plant operation, on a Mount Desert Island project last year. “We got to use a bunch of Helen’s amazing plants,” says Davis. “A gardener and designer, Helen grows a very fun mix of reliable garden performers, unusual annuals, and tender perennials (she spent time with Fergus at Great Dixter in her early days). She also grows native plants, sometimes using local ecotype seed collected by botanist friends. She grows mostly from seed using organic practices.”

Loree Bohl, the author of Fearless Gardening and the blog Danger Garden has a penchant for all kinds of spiky and exotic plants that thrive in the Pacific Northwest. “You can visit Bird Rock Tropicals in-person, if you make an appointment (which I was lucky enough to do once!),” says Bohl, who notes that the rest of the time their website is where she goes to daydream about warmer climates and drool over bromeliads, tillandsia, and orchids. “I typically place at least one order each winter when I need a little pick me up and Bird Rock Tropicals’ plants never fail to put a smile on my face,” she says.

“You don’t have to be a member—or even pay admission to the garden—to shop at the nursery at the Rhododendron Species Botanical Garden, but trust me, visit the garden, too,” says Bohl. “The nursery sells plants that are propagated on site from the garden’s vast collections, and while there is a great selection of Rhododendrons, that’s definitely not all there is. You’ll also find rare ferns, groundcovers, shrubs with fabulous foliage, and on occasion even agaves.” Bohl notes that members enjoy early access to the spring and fall online catalogues, so plants with limited quantities can sell out before ordering opens to the public.

Cecelia Bedford, founder of Wattle Design Studio, a small Nashville-based design studio specializing in ecological landscapes and integrated hardscapes, likes to source locally grown materials for her projects. “This retail nursery is a fantastic source of native plants for gardeners in the South,” says Bedford. “Joy, the owner has an outstanding wealth of knowledge of the ecological benefits of native plants.” In addition to regional plants, Wonder sells plants that produce food and have medicinal properties; there’s also an excellent garden gift shop.

Fi Campbell, the founder of Fi Campbell Design, primarily works and gardens in Southern California using a palette of heavy on California natives. Tucked away, close to the Rose Bowl, this nursery is a hidden gem with a vast selection of California native plants as well as Mediterranean varieties and fruit trees. “Ramon and his family have operated this nursery for decades and it’s one of my go-to’s,” says Campbell. “Their product is impeccable.”

With two locations in Los Angeles (one in Silver Lake and one in Glassell Park), Plant Material Nursery is “the standout brick-and-mortar nursery on LA’s east side,” says Campbell. Plant Material specializes in California natives and drought-tolerant plants, and they sell  garden tools and curiosities. She notes, “They also host fun events and pop-ups and just do good for the community.”

This is an appointment-only, backyard native plant nursery based in Sierra Madre (they also host occasional pop-up sales). “Hardy Californians has become a leading voice for swapping thirsty lawns for California native gardens,” says Campbell. “When you want to find that unicorn plant, Hardy Californians just might have it.”

Jeff Lorenz, founder of Refugia Design in Gladwyne, Pennsylvania, and Rebecca Dragonetti, one of the firm’s designers, seek out hyper-local plants for their projects. Lorenz appreciates this small garden center for its emphasis on native and pollinator-friendly plants. “The owner creates these really nice design spaces with plants,” says Lorenz. “When people walk in, she’s educating them.”

This nature preserve has a nursery offering more than 200+ native plants (96 percent are straight species). “The super knowledgeable staff, who are mostly volunteers, make this nursery and preserve worth a visit,” says Dragonetti, who along with the rest of the Refugia team toured the propagation facility last year.

Austin-based landscape architect Cameron Campbell’s firm knows the right plants for Texas’s aesthetics and ecology.  “Barton Springs Nursery has a wonderful selection of native and adaptive plant species laid out in a beautiful garden setting,” says Campbell. “Their staff is wonderful and I like how they have grouped their plants based on sun/shade and planting types: vines, grasses, evergreens, perennials, etc.” He notes they also propagate and grow hard-to-find native species such as Melica mutica, Sabal Brazoria, and Leersia.

This well-stocked wholesale nursery is open to the public during their “DIY hours” on Thursdays, Fridays, and Saturdays.  “Sometimes I like to go there and walk around to get inspired to see what they are selling, as the inventory is always changing,” says Campbell.

Benjamin Vogt, the owner of Prairie Up, which offers garden design, online classes, workshops, and guidebooks, is known for his native, prairie-inspired design. While Midwest Natives only holds plant sales in spring and fall, Voght says this nursery is worth seeking out for its huge selection of diverse species that are 100 percent native to the local ecoregion (they are said to have the largest selection in Nebraska). He says, “Nathan, the owner, produces smaller, younger plants, which are more economical and settle in faster than gallons.” He notes that the spring and fall sale times coincide with the best time for plant health and establishment in the local climate.

In addition to writing a newsletter and producing a podcast, professor and plantsman Dr. Jared Barnes documents his own garden in Nacogdoches, Texas on his Meristem website. “They have incredible plants at very reasonable prices,” says Barnes. “I love to shop their perennial selection as they have an incredible selection of different cultivars.” He says he will load up a duffle bag and bring it back to Texas and has heard of other people driving hours to fill up a truck. (Taylor, the creator behind the account Tiny Green Thumbs also told us she loves this nursery!)

If none of these nurseries are local to you, Barnes has a suggestion for a mail-order only nursery: Digging Dog Nursery. “I find they have a lot of herbaceous options that you can’t find anywhere else,” says Barnes. “I’ve gotten a number of asters, sunflowers, and other fall flowering plants from them.”

So, dear readers: Get thee to a nursery! Autumn is a great time to go plant shopping. Many perennials benefit from fall planting: The earth is still warm, but the days are cooler, so it’s a low-stress time for plants to put down roots. Plus, you can often nab discounts later in the season.

#218. The Best Flower Seeds to Sow in the Fall for a Spring Bloom

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

Of course, the descriptor “best” is very subjective, but after countless years of trying/failing—and trying/failing some more—I think I’ve earned the right to come up with a list of “best” seeds to sow in the fall. Why fall? The short answer is that many seeds need a period of cold and moisture to properly germinate. Your seeds will lie dormant through winter and germinate in the spring. Not to mention, autumn’s blissfully cooler temperatures and increase in rainfall can reduce stress on seedlings and improve water absorption. Another bonus of sowing in the fall is that this method is a cost-effective way to plant, as a seed packet is much more affordable than nursery-grown plants.

Pro planting tip: As everyone’s climate differs, before you choose seeds to sow, always look up your USDA plant hardiness zone and learn the average minimum winter temperature of your area, as well as the first and last frost dates. Then research your chosen seeds’ requirements and make sure they are compatible. When ready, prepare the soil by removing weeds and amending it with compost. After planting per the packet’s specifications, water seeds gently. If rain isn’t a frequent occurrence, continue keeping the area moist until seedlings sprout and become established in the spring.

Please keep reading to learn my highly opinionated list of favorite seeds to sow in fall:

N.B.: Featured photograph above of Iceland poppies by Katherine Porter via Flickr.

As a proud California native, I suppose that I’m partial to these iconic flowers as they are the state flower, lure a plethora of pollinators, are drought tolerant, and brighten up any garden. I have success when I direct-sow the seeds into a sunny, well-draining spot by lightly scattering the tiny seeds on the soil surface. I have also used a can of these seeds that come with a dispersal additive to help separate the seeds upon scattering. If you want to sow a lot of California poppies, a large can, or bag, is the way to go. Look for these poppies in the classic orange hue but also in creamy white, peach, pink and yellow. Once I get a good year of healthy California poppies, I seem to get a repeat the next year without any effort.

I love this plant for its unique flower and even more unique seed heads that look fantastic added to dried flower arrangements. In mild climates, direct-sow the minuscule black seeds onto well-drained soil in a sunny or mostly sunny spot, and then keep the soil consistently moist. Love-in-a-mist seeds require light to germinate, so be careful not to cover them up when planting. Bonus: these seeds readily re-seed in my garden every year.

Another easy-to-grow favorite. I adore how nasturtiums effortlessly scramble about the garden and pump out colorful flowers and lily pad-like leaves. These hardy annuals prefer a sunny spot, tolerate poor soil, and grow well in containers or trailing from raised beds. Some gardeners recommend soaking and scarifying these hard seeds for better germination, but I’ve never done that and have had total success. I encourage my nasturtium family to come back year after year by re-scattering the seeds upon pruning them back.

Every year I grow some hollyhocks from seeds saved from last year or acquired from generous friends and family. Not to be blasé, but I generally just throw theses flat seeds about at the end of fall, all willy nilly. But I suppose the “proper” way is to sow them a week before last frost at just ¼ inch deep and about 2 feet apart. I find that hollyhocks thrive in a sunny to partly sunny spot. Too much shade and they bloom way less and lean too much. Also know that most hollyhocks are biennials, meaning the first year the plant just puts out leaves and then flowers the next year.

Differing from California poppies due to native origin, use, and flower type, Iceland poppies thrive in cool temperatures, appreciate regular water, and their papery translucent flowers are great for adding to arrangements. You can get a head start on your cutting garden by planting these seeds about four to six weeks before your average first fall frost, or in early to mid-fall in milder climates. Plant the tiny seeds in a sunny spot in well-draining soil and remember not to cover the seeds as they need light to germinate. Theses poppies can be slow to germinate, so be patient. I especially like the Champagne Bubbles mix.

By now I’m sure you know how critical milkweed is to the survival of the monarch butterfly as it is the only plant the caterpillars will eat. Help our winged friends and put these seeds on your late fall planting list. After the first frost, scatter seeds directly on the soil surface in a sunny, well-drained location, and then press them lightly into the soil. If the ground gets dry, lightly water the seeds. Just be sure to choose a milkweed that’s native to your area. Why? Planting non-native types of milkweed risks the health of the butterfly.

N.B.: This post was first published September 2025.

#219. Partridge Pea 101: A Native Annual for Late-Season Flowers

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

As late summer steps into the shorter days of fall, a native annual whose generous yellow flowers festoon its upright and feathered stems begins to show off. Touch those fine-cut, pinnately compound leaves and they fold up, sensitively. This is partridge pea, sensitive plant, sleeping plant—a legume that resembles a delicate shrub but whose lifespan is a growing season. Its seeds will ensure that it stays around the following year, and the next. That self-seeding habit makes partridge pea a helpful stabilizer of sunny slopes and a filler for wide-open spaces. Its flowers attract butterflies and other pollinators, and those seeds, maturing in fall, feed birds.

Here are some of the benefits (and caveats) of growing partridge pea.

Like other plants in Fabaceae family, leguminous partridge pea fixes atmospheric nitrogen in the soil via beneficial bacteria that occur on the plants’ roots. This can improve poor soil over time (and it can also lead to the dominance of the species that hosts the bacteria—worth bearing in mind), and it is an especially rewarding plant for urban gardeners facing the drought, pollution, and compaction challenges of so-called hellstrips: sidewalk, roadside, and highway margins.

I first met partridge pea at the edge of a wildflower meadow in the northern part of Central Park, one early September. Its wiry, vertical stems made me mistake it for a shrub, and I was surprised to learn that it had grown from seed, and would do so again the following year. Later, during fall migration, the same population was besieged by seed-eating birds. It was enchanting.

#220. Travel Diary: The Trip that Made Me Want to Move to Hudson, NY

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

By the end of my second trip to Hudson, NY, I had already bought a property, planted my dream garden, opened a small neighborhood bar, and settled into a simpler life upstate—in my head, that is.

My first visit to Hudson was last November, two days after a massive windstorm had swept through the Hudson Valley and taken nearly every fall leaf with it. I loved the town anyway, but I knew I needed a redo. This summer, my husband and I finally made our return, trading bare trees and frigid walks for hydrangeas, afternoon swims, thunderstorms, and more antique shopping than our luggage could reasonably accommodate.

We drove up from New York City and made our first detour before we even reached Hudson, stopping in Millerton, where I promptly bought a gorgeous vintage rug from a shop on the main street. By the time we reached our destination, I had fully mapped out our future life Upstate. Below, my highly opinionated guide to Hudson.

Our home base for three nights was The Amelia, a charming B&B and historic old home just off Warren Street that quickly became part of our daily routine. After spending the mornings walking around town, eating, shopping, and then eating some more, we’d retreat to the backyard pool for the afternoon, surrounded by towering hydrangeas and grasses.

One day, we struck up a poolside conversation with a woman who writes for The New York Times. Naturally, we ran into her again later that evening while drinking martinis at what had, within roughly 24 hours, become our favorite bar in Hudson. More on that in a few.

After a long, winding drive up from New York, we wanted exactly three things on our first night: a burger, a cold martini, and somewhere we didn’t need a reservation. Hudson Diner delivered on all three.

I was not prepared for the sheer size of my bagel at Circles. It was enormous, delicious, and just what we needed before setting off for another full day of walking Warren Street and convincing ourselves that, yes, maybe we could get that chair back to Seattle somehow.

About a 10-minute or so drive outside Hudson in Ghent, Bartlett House was one of the places I knew I wanted to revisit from my first trip. The café and bakery are housed in a gorgeous historic building. We sat outside on the front porch overlooking the garden below, coffee in hand.

For one of our dinners, we decided to splurge a little and booked a table in the conservatory at The Maker Hotel, in their newer (refreshed) restaurant, Serre. Dinner was excellent, including one of the best roast chickens I’ve had, and our server was hilarious. But the real show arrived toward the end of the meal, when a thunderstorm rolled over Hudson. Within seconds, the entire restaurant went quiet. All you could hear were the clinks of forks and knives against plates while rain pounded against the glass ceiling overhead.

A family friend who grew up in Albany told my husband and I that we had to stop in at least once while we were in Hudson.

Two of those visits were in the same night where we closed down the bar with our new favorite bartender (Lionel), whose phone number we somehow left with, alongside a handful of local regulars we’d met. The drinks were great, but what stuck with me most was the hospitality. Red Dot is one of those increasingly rare establishments where you walk in knowing no one and somehow leave feeling like you’ve been coming there for years. It’s something I wish more restaurants and bars, frankly anywhere, could recreate.

We never actually made it past the bar, which gives me an excuse to return to try the restaurant. Next time we’ll be having dinner in the back garden.

We were so excited about all the shopping to be had in Hudson that we purposely packed light to leave room in our luggage for our return trip.

Our final haul included the aforementioned vintage rug from Millerton, a canvas painting from The Modern Exchange, a metal basket from The Antique Warehouse, and an assortment of small tchotchkes collected from shops along Warren Street. And, of course, we stopped at FINCH, which manages to combine an exceptionally good home and furniture assortment with men’s clothing and accessories.

The best discovery required no purchase at all: spotting our very own Gardenista book on display, looking quite at home and in good company.

By the end of three nights, Hudson had officially carved out a special place in my heart. I can very easily imagine my husband and I living there one day, whether part-time or full-time, with a garden, an old house that probably needs far more work than I’m anticipating, and, apparently, a small bar where everyone knows each other.

Besides, moving there may ultimately be the more practical choice. How else am I supposed to buy all the furniture that won’t fit in my checked bag back to Seattle?
